en: The Lotus Sutra, Scroll One.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Yuezhi in the Western Jin Dynasty.
Chapter One: The Portentous Light. Chapter One: The Portentous Light.
Thus have I heard:

At one time the Buddha was staying at Vulture Peak Mountain near the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus, numbering one thousand two hundred. All were free from attachment; their taints were exhausted, and they were no longer subject to the dust of desire. Having attained mastery, they had realized their own benefit; birth and death were ended, and all fetters were severed. Having by themselves attained the ultimate liberation, they were delivered through wisdom and their minds were emancipated. Their names were as follows:

The wise ones who know the ultimate limit: the venerable Mahākāśyapa, Uruvilvākāśyapa, Nadīkāśyapa, Gayākāśyapa, Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Kātyāyana, Aniruddha, Kapphiṇa, Gavāmpati, Revata, Pilindavatsa, Bakula, Kuṭhika, Nanda, Subāhu, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, Subhūti, Ānanda, and Rāhula;

and eighty thousand bodhisattvas, all of whom are non-retrogressive, firmly established in the unsurpassed, true, and correct path, having attained the dhāraṇīs and great eloquence, constantly praising the non-retrogressive wheel of Dharma and making offerings without ceasing.
Hundreds of thousands of Buddhas have planted the roots of myriad virtues for him throughout immeasurable eons; he is praised and extolled by all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.

His body constantly practices loving-kindness and enters the wisdom of the Tathāgata. With skillful means, he universally attains the Great Knowledge (Mahājñāna) and the Perfection of Wisdom (Prajñāpāramitā).
Having heard extensively over countless kalpas, his fame reaches the ten directions as he rescues and protects [sentient beings].
Measuring hundreds of thousands of sentient beings, they roam through the three realms like the brilliance of the sun;

they understand all phenomena to be like illusions, transformations, mirages, shadows, and echoes—utterly non-existent and abiding nowhere. Though they perceive beginnings and ends, there is no coming or going;
having seen that forms and appearances are fundamentally without shape or feature, they manifest all manner of births forever [in this way].
Without arising or ceasing, they guide and benefit the masses without clinging to the three realms;

through discerning the wisdom of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, they give rise to the three gates of liberation and attain the three types of supernormal knowledge. Free from notions of past, future, or present, they transform and enlighten the common people, causing them to realize that all things are fundamentally non-existent.
Their names were:

Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta, Bodhisattva Nityodyukta, Bodhisattva Anikṣiptadhura, Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi, Bodhisattva Mudrāhasta, Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja, Bodhisattva Suvīra, Bodhisattva Ratnacandra, Bodhisattva Candraprabha, Bodhisattva Pūrṇacandra, Bodhisattva Mahātara, Bodhisattva Aparimitābhibhū, Bodhisattva Lokātikrānta, Bodhisattva Vimuktibandhana, Bodhisattva Ratnakārin, Bodhisattva Varadatta, Bodhisattva Vīradatta, Bodhisattva Varuṇadeva, Bodhisattva Indradeva, Bodhisattva Mahānāyaka, Bodhisattva Sumati, and Bodhisattva Maitreya. Such great beings as these were the eighty thousand leaders.

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, arrived together with twenty thousand devaputras; the Sun Deva, together with countless retinues; the Moon Deva, who illuminated everywhere with the radiance of jewels, together with the Jewel-Radiance Deva and the Resplendent Radiance Deva; the Four Great Kings, together with ten thousand devaputras; the Great Brahmā Ābhāsvara, together with thirty thousand devaputras; the Brahmā Sahāmpati, together with thirty-two thousand devaputras; the Great Brahmā Śubhakṛtsna, together with countless devaputras; and the Brahmā named Ābhāsvara, together with a vast multitude. They approached the place where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves, and withdrew to sit at one side.
There were eight dragon kings, together with their retinues of countless thousands of dragons;
and four kinnara kings—Kinnara King Venerating the Dharma, Kinnara King Great Dharma, Kinnara King Benevolent and Harmonious, and Kinnara King Upholding the Dharma;
as well as gandharvas, each accompanied by their attendants, came to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves, and then withdrew to stand to one side.

The four devaputras of the Pure Body—Mṛdumṛdu, Svarasvara, Madhurasvara, and Manojñasvara—all came together to where the Buddha was; having approached and prostrated themselves before him, they withdrew to sit at one side.

The four asura kings—Vemacitra Asura, Śatapuṣpa Asura, Sunirmita Asura, and Garuḍa Asura—together with countless hundreds of thousands of asura subjects, came to where the Buddha was. Having approached and prostrated themselves, they withdrew to sit at one side.
The four Garuḍa kings—Mahākāya-rāja, Mahāsampūrṇa-rāja, Ṛddhilabdha-rāja, and Acala-rāja—all came to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves, and then withdrew to stand to one side.
King Ajātaśatru of Magadha, together with his ten sons and his retinue, came to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself, and withdrew to sit at one side.
Among the devas, nāgas, spirits, and worldly people, there were none who did not take refuge, pay homage, and attend him as he sat.

At that time, the World-Honored One, surrounded by a retinue of the fourfold assembly, preached a sutra, expounding upon the vast and great verses of the Bodhisattvas and the pure and adorned deeds of all Buddhas.
Having spoken this sutra, he ascended the natural lion-throne and sat cross-legged, entering into meditative absorption with a concentrated mind called "Establishing Immeasurable Verses."

In accordance with what was appropriate, he could not perceive their physical forms nor grasp their minds; yet wherever they sat or stood, auspicious omens appeared: the heavens rained *manojñā* flowers, *mahāmanojñā* flowers, *mṛdusvarā* flowers, and *mahāmṛdusvarā* flowers, which were scattered upon the World-Honored One and the fourfold assembly gathered there, while the entire Buddha-land shook in six ways.

At that time, the great assembly—monks, nuns, laymen, laywomen, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans—as well as kings, sovereigns, and powerful universal monarchs (cakravartins), each with their retinues, all with single-minded devotion gazed upon the World-Honored One; their minds were all struck with amazement at this unprecedented marvel.

At that time, the Buddha emitted from his face and mouth a boundless radiance that universally illuminated eighteen thousand Buddha-lands in the eastern direction. This great light shone throughout all those Buddha-realms without exception, reaching down into the Avīci Great Hell and extending upward to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. As it circulated through the six realms of existence across these worlds, the people therein were all made manifest; the Buddhas currently residing in those lands and the assemblies of beings in this land were all seen from afar.
It was likewise for those in those lands who beheld this here. They heard everywhere the sutras and dharmas preached by the Buddhas of the ten directions.

The monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen who practice in solitude and have attained the fruits of virtue all manifest themselves; furthermore, the Bodhisattvas whose minds are tranquil and liberated, as well as those renunciants seeking the practice of karmic retribution, all likewise appear.
Moreover, the precious stupas erected for the various sages who have entered parinirvāṇa in the worlds of the Buddhas manifest spontaneously.
Thereupon, Maitreya Bodhisattva thought to himself:

"Now the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, having entered into samādhi, manifests great miraculous transformations and subdues many beings; this is something unprecedented that I behold. Throughout the heavens and the world, the temples and shrines of the Buddhas have become vast and manifest; what cause will arise for such an auspicious omen as this?"
"From antiquity until now, I have never seen such a thing.
If I wish to inquire about its destination, who is capable of dispatching it and explaining this meaning?
He then changed his mind and said:

"Now, the Great Being Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta has accomplished all that was to be done and has attained mastery over all things; he has made offerings to countless Buddhas of the past and has personally beheld Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas. We wish to inquire about such a miraculous response as this."

At that time, the fourfold assembly—bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—as well as the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas, were filled with hesitation and experienced what they had never before encountered. Beholding this Great Sage’s boundless majesty, radiance, and miraculous transformations, each of them resolved to question the World-Honored One in order to unravel the net of their doubts.
The Great Being Maitreya, perceiving the thoughts of the assembled multitude, addressed Pūrṇa, saying: "Virtuous one, please explain:

by what causes and conditions has this auspicious omen appeared? Why does the Great Sage, through his supernormal power, emit such great radiance that it illuminates eighteen thousand lands in the eastern direction, causing the worlds of all Buddhas to manifest spontaneously, and why can we hear from afar all the sūtras and dharmas being preached there?"
Thereupon, Maitreya addressed Pūrṇamukha in verse, saying: "Mañjuśrī!
For what reason now do you guide and benefit the multitudes by emitting and spreading forth this radiance?"
A most great and brilliant radiance issues from the gateway of his face; its divine transformations shine everywhere, making the ten directions suddenly bright.
Like falling blossoms, there are the *manojñā* flowers and the *mahāmanojñā* flowers, the *mṛdusvara* flowers, and many other varieties;
their colors are exquisite and wondrous, and they possess the fragrant scent of sandalwood.
Delighting the hearts of the multitudes, it is majestic, pure, and sublime, pervading everywhere.
Today, the fourfold assembly rejoices and leaps for joy;
throughout this buddha-field and the worlds of the ten directions, the earth quakes in six ways, such that nothing remains unshaken.
That radiance then illuminated eighteen thousand lands in the eastern direction;
its brilliance pervaded everywhere throughout the realms of all Buddhas, which were the color of purple-polished gold,
resplendent and dazzling, with their flames reaching one another without interruption.
The people of the kingdoms and cities all rely upon [this teaching] for their benefit; yet from the highest realms down to the Avīci Hell,
the multitudes undergo birth because of ignorance, perishing and falling away as they return to these various destinies.
The various realms of existence, now appearing in their majestic purity— those who are wise, those who are unworthy,
and those of intermediate character— I dwell here and behold them all from afar.
Furthermore, I behold the various Buddhas, who let out the lion’s roar,
expounding the sutras and elucidating the Dharma gates, thereby eliminating the countless defilements of sentient beings.
Chanting the holy teachings, he utters a gentle voice; its resonance is profound and wondrous, causing people to leap with joy.
He expounds parables and the retributions of a hundred million eons, analyzing and unfolding them in detail.
Regarding this Buddha-dharma,
those who lack skillful means treat old age, sickness, and death; such as these are they who speak of the nirvana of quiescent extinction.
The multitude dwells in peace and joy; having accumulated merit, they behold the Honored Sage.
Furthermore, they attain the stage of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, causing all to enter this path of practice and perceive the Buddha’s extraordinary excellence.
Among all the scriptures and texts, there are those who aspire to seek the unsurpassed wisdom.
Throughout all worlds, they manifest in various forms; these diverse classes of beings sing praises of the Buddha’s virtues.
O virtuous Prabhūtaratna!
Standing here, I now see and hear all of you, as well as the countless billions of others who dwell and travel about in this place; I behold them all.
Furthermore, I see Buddha-lands beyond calculation, where bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of rivers,
numbering in the hundreds of thousands of millions, do not diminish;
they establish their resolve with diligence and give rise to the aspiration for the Way.
Some relinquish all their wealth and enterprises to practice giving:
bright moons and pearls, musāragalva and agate, male and female slaves, vehicles, couches, beds, and stools—
whatever rare and precious things there may be, including rings, pendants, and necklaces.
Thus, having attained full perfection, he bestows it all as gifts and encourages others to assist in the supreme,
honored Way of the Buddha.
Abiding in the state praised by the Perfectly Awakened One, he dwells within the Great Vehicle and wanders through the three realms.
Yet remaining without dependence, such a person will swiftly attain and fulfill this vow.
Or by means of various vehicles, they bestow them as gifts; with flowers, music, balustrades, and adornments;
with flutes, drums, and wind instruments; and with the delights of melodic rhythms.
According to what is appropriate for the four matters, he bestows gifts and offers them respectfully;
through this giving, his mind feels no stinginess.
Anticipating impermanence, he gives away his hands and feet to others, his will free from self-indulgence or attachment.
All were used for giving in charity, desiring thereby to seek after this honored Way of the Buddha.
Furthermore, there were those who sacrificed their bodies, providing all that they possessed—heads, eyes, limbs, and members—without any lingering attachment;
the reason for such giving was to achieve the Way of the Buddha.
I vow to attain the noble wisdom of the Tathāgata.
Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta!
I behold the king, together with his retinue, standing as he goes out on a stroll.
The ladies of the inner palace, the consorts, the court ladies, and the noblewomen, together with their attendants, all paid homage to the Buddha’s body.
Then, before the Dharma King, they inquired about the scriptures; thereupon, they cast off their secular garments.
Having shaved off their hair and beards, they donned the *kāṣāya* robes as their standard practice.
I beheld numerous bodhisattvas and bhikṣu companions dwelling among mountain crags,
living in solitude and seclusion, thoroughly understanding and expounding upon emptiness and non-existence.
There are those who receive the sutras, reciting and praising them.
Belonging to the ranks of the Bodhisattvas, they are the peers of heroes;
entering and exiting mountain valleys, they concentrate their minds in contemplation, scrutinizing all characteristics and explaining them with discernment.
Manifesting the vehicle of all Buddhas, he casts off and abandons craving and desire so that none remain.
Constantly cultivating and refining himself, he aspires to and reveres right practice;
establishing his sons in stability, he does not depart from secluded dwelling, and thus he attains the five supernormal powers.
Noble beings of lofty character, whose resolve is fixed upon the state of equality,
turn toward the Teachers with palms joined in reverence; their hearts overflowing with joy,
they extol the virtues of the Buddha with thousands of verses, praising the King among Men.
With a joyful and harmonious resolve, clearly understanding and discerning the practice of renunciation, he consulted and received the scriptures from the Honored One Among Two-Legged Beings.
Having heard them repeatedly, he immediately took them up for study; establishing himself among the sons of the Buddha, he first cultivated himself.
I again saw from afar the descendants of the Buddhas preaching the Dharma for countless billions of people;
manifesting karmic retributions beyond calculation in the millions, they harbored joy in their hearts,
took refuge in the True Dharma, and exhorted others toward transformation and enlightenment.
Countless bodhisattvas, having subdued the hosts of Māras and commanded their retinues of officials,
strike this Dharma drum with a thunderous resonance— the sacred teaching of the Sugata.
I have further observed that among all devas, humans, and spirits, those who are honored and revered,
and those sons of the Buddha who dwell in peace, do not rely on the marvelous or the elegant; rather, they become all the more tranquil,
practicing meditative seclusion without depending on or clinging to anything, just like lions.
He transforms and delivers the multitude, causing them to resolve upon the Way.
As the beings dwell there, holding offerings in their hands and harboring hearts of joy, they all proceed together.
Furthermore, O sons of the Buddha, established in diligence, having cast off the dust of desire,
they always attain mastery; setting their resolve upon walking meditation, they roam among the trees,
vowing to practice with earnestness and seeking the Buddha-way from its very root.
Always practicing purity, with precepts secure and at peace, they do not fear birth and death;
maintaining their resolve therein, they fulfill all practices, and by means of these precepts,
they awaken those who are unawakened.
Toward those who are arrogant, one should remain humble, modest, and compliant;
even if they treat one with contempt, revile, or strike and lash them, one seeking the Buddha-way should remain silent and not retaliate.
Furthermore, I have observed that the assembly of Bodhisattvas has completely abandoned all frivolous play and music;
together with their various powers and kinsmen,
their minds are firm and as level as space.
With a mind free from agitation, establish a single-pointed concentration;
extinguish the hindrances and cultivate meditative reflection for hundreds of thousands of millions of years, setting one’s intent upon giving to seek the supreme path of the Buddha.
Having eradicated greed and envy, he dwells in tranquility without fear;
whatever food, drink, and requisites are required, as well as medicines for the countless people who are ill, [he provides].
Furthermore, he bestowed upon them garments and ornaments; having practiced dāna, he relieved those who were naked, without hoarding anything for himself.
Together with his retinue, he beheld the Most Victorious One standing in transformation above him, making offerings of hundreds of thousands of millions.
Various crafted precious gems and sandalwood incense, many couches and seats, and treasuries of bright pearls—
all these are present before one's eyes; they are offered up for his peaceful dwelling,
with a value of hundreds of thousands of millions.
The gardens and groves that are beheld, with their leaves, flowers, and fruits, are complete, fresh, and pure, bringing delight to the human heart.
Furthermore, these are offered as gifts to the Superior Persons, the True Sages, and the various Śrāvakas;
such are the categories of benefits derived from wisdom, diverse and manifold in kind.
Joyfully relieving the destitute, he deeply rejoices within himself;
establishing himself in the practice of the Way, he dedicates these gifts, vowing to seek supreme enlightenment.
In the profound and silent Dharma, he examined all karmic retributions; among the many billions of beings,
he inspired the common people, causing them to repent their transgressions and renounce their vast treasures,
so that they might set their will upon the Buddha-way.
Having extinguished these three things, they are as tranquil and equal as space;
the sons who dwell in peace have no attachments whatsoever, and through such wisdom, they seek the supreme path of the Buddha.
With a pervasive and gentle voice, I again behold all the Buddhas who have entered parinirvāṇa,
dwelling in peace and transforming beings;
as well as all the great bodhisattvas currently present, who together revere and honor the most supreme śarīra.
I have visited Buddha temples numbering in the hundreds of millions and billions; their total is beyond all calculation, like the sands of the Ganges.
Throughout these myriad lands, I have constantly seen them revered and honored; all that is manifested through transformation is most supreme because of him.
The seven treasures appeared spontaneously, pure and manifest; they were complete in their dimensions, measuring two hundred and fifty thousand [yojanas].
Each was several thousand [yojanas] in breadth, length, and circumference, each being two thousand li;
their canopies were exquisite, marvelous, and purely adorned.
Wherever these various fragrances and precious jewels exist spontaneously, where all fruits are aromatic and musical performances are harmonious and elegant;
where ghosts, spirits, and rākṣasas reverently honor the Honored One among Men;
and where the sons of the Buddha dwell in peace—whatever they produce and move others to do, they employ as offerings for the śarīra relics such as these.
Now this Buddha temple is brilliantly radiant and exquisitely beautiful; fragrant flowers are spread everywhere like the *pārijāta* tree.
Beholding it all from afar, its splendor and variegated hues cause the hair on one's body to stand on end.
The retinue hastens forth, desiring to see the Most Victorious One who radiates light.
Supreme among men, he manifests a great brilliance; how wondrous is his sagely wisdom!
Free from defilement and untainted, he is thus able to reveal such vast splendor.
He reveals buddha-fields numbering in the many thousands;
seeing this auspicious response, we have attained what we have never known before.
Such manifestations as these, these great transformations—O Mañjuśrī, we pray that you fully explain their meaning.
I now feel deep admiration, as do all the sons of the Buddha; among the fourfold assembly, our hearts are filled with joy.
We thirstily look up to you, O Benevolent One, and behold you observing us.
For what reason do you today abide in peace, emitting such great radiance from your mouth?
Dissipating all doubts and inspiring joyful exultation:
for what reason does the Buddha manifest such boundless, great radiance?
Such transformations as these must surely be moved by some profound resonance.
O son of those who dwell in peace, pray speak at this time.
This subtle and wondrous Dharma, accomplished by the Great Sage, was expounded by the True Being at the site of enlightenment.
O Hero of the World, Guide, please explain for us the direction from which these bodhisattvas have come.
They wish to behold the Buddha-lands— those countless thousands of realms inhabited by various classes of sentient beings,
adorned with many jewels and purified, where the Buddhas manifest themselves.
O you of immeasurable and clear vision!
May all those who are newly learning be free from hesitation; may all the sons of the Most Victorious One together pose their questions.
He brings joy to all the people, the devas, and the rākṣasas; the fourfold assembly all look up to him with reverence.
Now, Samantabhadra, please explain this in detail.
Thereupon, Viśeṣacintin addressed Maitreya and the assembly of great bodhisattvas, as well as the sons and daughters of noble family:

"I have reflected in my mind that now the Tathāgata shall expound the Great Dharma and proclaim the infinite scriptures; he shall scatter the rain of the Great Dharma, beat the drum of the Great Dharma, blow the conch of the Great Dharma, and preach the immeasurable teachings."

Furthermore, as I recalled from the past, when I beheld such auspicious signs before the various Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, the light emitted by those Tathāgatas was also just like this; through such discernment, I knew that they were preaching the Great Dharma.
All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas manifest these responses in order to cause sentient beings to hear the infinite scriptures. Why is this so?

The World-Honored One, wishing to cause all sentient beings to wash away worldly defilements and to hear and don the Dharma of the Buddha, manifested great transformations, radiant light, and divine manifestations.

Furthermore, I recall that in the past, incalculable, inconceivable, and immeasurable eons ago, there was a Tathāgata named Candrasūryapradīpa, an Arhat, a Samyaksaṃbuddha, one perfected in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed leader, a charioteer of men and gods, a teacher of devas and humans, a Buddha, a World-Honored One. He expounded the sūtras, which were excellent in their beginning, excellent in their middle, and excellent in their end; they were subtle and complete in their analysis of meaning, ultimately pure, and cultivated as the holy life. For the sake of those following the Śrāvaka vehicle, he proclaimed the Noble Truths, thereby enabling the multitudes to cross over birth, old age, death, sorrow, affliction, and all manner of suffering, entering the proximity of Nirvāṇa.
"For the sake of the assembly of great bodhisattvas, he proclaimed and analyzed the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā) of unsurpassed, true, and correct enlightenment.
Furthermore, son of good family, after the parinirvāṇa of that Tathāgata Candrasūryapradīpa, there was another Buddha who was also named Candrasūryapradīpa."
After his parinirvāṇa, there was another Buddha, also named Candrasūryapradīpa.
After his parinirvāṇa, there was yet another Buddha, also named Candrasūryapradīpa.
These eighty Tathāgatas of such a kind were all of one name, Sūryacandrapradīpa, and descended from the same lineage.
There were twenty thousand Tathāgatas of this sort, whose Buddha-words could not be surpassed.

Among those twenty thousand Tathāgatas, the one who first appeared was named Candrasūryapradīpa; the last to appear was likewise named Candrasūryapradīpa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. That Buddha’s preaching of the sūtra was excellent in its beginning, excellent in its middle, and excellent in its end; he analyzed its meaning with subtlety and perfection, and purely cultivated the holy life. For the sake of the śrāvakas, he expounded the Four Noble Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, so as to bring about the extinction of birth, old age, sickness, death, grief, lamentation, and all such afflictions, leading them ultimately to the state of non-action (asaṃskṛta).
He preached the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā) for the sake of the bodhisattvas, enabling them to attain the unsurpassed, true, and correct path and reach all-encompassing wisdom.
Before the Tathāgata Candrasūryapradīpa had left the household life, he had eight sons:

the first was named Chih-yu (Aspiration), the second Shan-i (Good Intention), the third Chia-chuan (Encouragement), the fourth Pao-chih (Jewel Aspiration), the fifth Chih-i (Upholding Intention), the sixth Chu-man (Removal of Arrogance), the seventh Hsiang-i (Resonant Intention), and the eighth Fa-i (Dharma Intention). These eight princes were the sons of the Tathāgata, possessing vast and universal supernormal powers (ṛddhi).

At that time, each of the sons individually presided over the four quarters of the world. Their lands were fertile and prosperous, governed by the True Dharma (Saddharma) without any oppression or injustice. Upon seeing the World-Honored One renounce his kingdom to cultivate the Way and attain Supreme Perfect Enlightenment, and having just heard that he had become a Buddha, they all immediately left secular life, disregarding their high positions. They went to the place where the World-Honored One was and all became śramaṇas. They all resolved upon the unsurpassed, true, and correct Way (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi), and all became Dharma-preachers. Constantly practicing the pure conduct (brahmacarya), they planted many roots of virtue under countless hundreds of thousands of Buddhas.
He spoke again, saying: "Ajita!
At that time, the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa exhorted the bodhisattvas to protect all Buddha-dharmas, and for the sake of the assembled multitude, he expounded the great verses of the Vaipulya Sūtra."

At that time, the World-Honored One remained silent upon his seat; through the meditative absorption of the Samādhi of Immeasurable Verses, he no longer appeared, being without body and without mind, entirely ungraspable, and with no mental state established.

As soon as the World-Honored One had entered samādhi, the heavens rained down *māndārava* flowers, *mahāmāndārava* flowers, *manojña-śabda* flowers, and *mahāmano-jña-śabda* flowers, scattering them over the Buddha and the fourfold assembly gathered there. At that moment, the earth shook in six ways. The people of the land each took heavenly flowers and scattered them over the Buddha, while the fourfold disciples, devas, humans, and worldlings were struck with amazement and filled with doubt and wonder.

Not long after that Buddha’s samādhi, through the power of his majestic spiritual merit, a ray of light issued from his face. This light shone universally throughout eighteen thousand Buddha-lands in the eastern direction, pervading them all without exception. All the activities and formations within those Buddha-lands appeared spontaneously, just as the Buddha-lands appear today.
At that time, the World-Honored One was together with twenty billion bodhisattvas, preaching the Dharma within the great assembly.

When the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas beheld a great radiance illuminating the world, there was among those Buddhas of the world a bodhisattva named Vimalaraśmi (Transcendent Light), who had eighteen attendants. Among them was one bodhisattva who alone was weary and indolent, named Yaśas (Renown). The Buddha entered samādhi and, arising from that samādhi, preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*—the work of the Vaipulya—to the bodhisattva Vimalaraśmi. He expounded all the practices of the bodhisattvas and the teachings of the Buddha, sitting in one place for a full sixty kalpas to preach this sutra; the assembly likewise remained so, their bodies unmoving and their minds free from causal conditions.
Furthermore, for sixty intermediate kalpas, that World-Honored One preached the Dharma for the various assemblies; those who listened felt not the slightest weariness, nor was their mind disturbed.

During those sixty kalpas, the Sun-Moon-Lamp Radiance Tathāgata expounded the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the Vaipulya Sūtra of the True Dharma, for the sake of the bodhisattvas, and then declared: "I shall now enter parinirvāṇa."
He addressed the devas and humans, the hosts of Brahmās and Māras, śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, asuras, spirits, and bhikṣus, saying:
"Observe this moment: at midnight, the Tathāgata shall enter parinirvāṇa in the realm of no-remainder."
He conferred upon that Bodhisattva the prediction of the Śīrasaṃcaya and addressed the bhikṣus:

"After my parinirvāṇa, the bodhisattva Śīrasaṃcaya shall attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path and realize supreme perfect enlightenment, and his title shall be Vimalagātra Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha."
After the Buddha had bestowed this prediction, he entered parinirvāṇa at midnight.

The eight disciples of that World-Honored One all turned to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Transcendent Light (Atikara) and followed his instructions; they all resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, true, and correct path, beheld countless billions of Buddhas over many eons, made offerings to and served them, and all attained perfect enlightenment, the last of whom was named Dharmakārya.

Among the eighteen people, there was one bodhisattva who, being unrestrained in seeking gain, zealously pursued offerings; he honored himself, was greedy and defiled, and suffered greatly from the three ailments. Amidst the analysis of the meanings of the phrases, he suddenly forgot them; thus, he attained seclusion and no longer felt anxious about his duties.

At that time, the son of good family attained the samādhi named Renown; by virtue of these roots of merit, he sought and made vows before incalculable billions of buddhas, aspiring to behold and serve all the holy sages.
Pūrṇamati said to Ajita:
“If you wish to know who that bhikṣu Dharma-master named Atikiraṇa was at that time, it was I myself.
As for the bodhisattva mahāsattva named Yaśaskāma, who was then indolent, he was none other than you, Ajita.”

Therefore, you should know this: having observed this auspicious omen manifested by the World-Honored One—the emission of his radiance—I have discerned that today the Great Sage shall preach for us the Vaipulya scripture, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Viśeṣacintin, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"I recall from the distant past, through inconceivable and countless kalpas."
The most supreme benefactor, whose wisdom is unsurpassed, was named Candrasūryapradīpa.
He preached the Dharma with infinite holy realization, transforming and enlightening immeasurable billions of sentient beings.
Exhorting and inspiring countless bodhisattvas— hundreds of thousands of millions, beyond conception—
all of whom were but young children, upon seeing the Buddha, the Guide, followed their honored teacher.
They all became śramaṇas, casting aside all craving and desire for everything they possessed.
The Guide and Benefactor of the world expounded the Dharma for them;
the sūtra he preached was titled "The Immeasurable Verses," renowned as supreme, its meaning being as follows:
Having converted the common people, numbering in the hundreds of millions,
the Most Honored One, the Tathāgata, sat upon his Dharma-seat in the full lotus posture.
Immediately, there was a miraculous response as he entered into samādhi.
Named "The Immeasurable Verses," he further manifests flashes of lightning and the sound of great thunder.
The devas and spirits dwelling in the void single-mindedly pay homage and revere the Honored One among Men.
Immediately, all the Buddha-lands were moved; from between his eyebrows, a wondrous radiance was manifested.
He emitted this light, which was immeasurable and limitless, such that countless beings marveled at this unprecedented occurrence.
His radiance shines everywhere throughout the Buddha-lands of the east, extending for eighteen thousand billion worlds.
Always acting in accordance with the proper time, he makes manifold distinctions and reveals to sentient beings the fundamental origins of their beginning and end.
The light is like lapis lazuli, And like rock crystal;
By the radiance of the Guide’s divine majesty, Various kinds of Magnificent, extraordinary, elegant, and beautiful forms appear.
The devas and humans, along with the ghosts, spirits, nāgas, and gandharvas,
were filled with rare wonder and joy.
For those who are single-mindedly diligent, who serve [the Buddha] and dwell in peace, all those worlds appear spontaneously before them.
Each one is autonomous, upright and exquisite, with a complexion like purple-polished gold;
as if within lapis lazuli there were many jewels, they remain amidst the assembly,
raining down the teachings of the Dharma.
Those śrāvakas are beyond measure and calculation; their praises are immeasurable, for they dwell securely as disciples.
In every world of each and every Teacher, there is again a radiant brilliance, all of which is most majestic.
Constantly practicing diligence, with precepts unviolated, possessing the power of forbearance like a bright moon-jewel;
dwelling in seclusion within mountain forests and vast wildernesses, [practicing] all forms of meditative concentration.
Without giving rise to causal conditions, even if there is harm inflicted, they do not harbor anger or resentment.
The assembly of Bodhisattvas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, dwell securely in radiance;
moved by such [realization], they contemplate impermanence and do not fall into negligence.
Patient in endurance and delighting in dhyāna, they do not abandon single-mindedness.
All appear before them, yet they subdue their own wills; yearning for the honored Way of the Buddha, they establish themselves in discerning abiding.
Their minds are tranquil, each according to their respective conditions.
He brings many to transformation and enlightenment across countless Buddha-realms;
the World-Honored One extensively expounds the Dharma, and his responsive manifestations are such as these.
Furthermore, beholding the Great Sage, who is like a master mariner, the radiance he emits eclipses the brilliance of the sun and moon.
All sentient beings, established in joy, each ask one another:
"What miraculous transformation is this?"
Honored by gods and humans, he arose from samādhi; not long after, the Guide sat down.
Named Suprabha, he served as a Dharma teacher.
The Buddha, the Eye of the World, expounded the teaching for him, purifying all realms of existence and bringing me alone peace and joy.
Reveal the various great elements and analyze them for me.
Regarding this sutra-dharma, out of compassion for sentient beings, I shall provide instruction through it and establish encouragement and assistance.
The assembly of bodhisattvas, hearing the Buddha’s instruction, joyfully uttered words of praise.
At that time, the World-Honored One preached the Dharma of the Great Sūtra;
his exposition was complete and full for sixty intermediate kalpas, while he remained seated cross-legged upon a single couch.
The Teachers who transformed the world preached the extraordinary teaching;
those Buddhas and others have all already entered parinirvāṇa.
As for that Dharma-master, the benevolent one Suraprabha, he expounds the most excellent teachings and lectures upon the sūtras.
Countless people are all filled with joy; we pray only that the Great Sage will analyze and explain it.
Throughout the heavens above and the world below, preach the sūtra and its natural meaning, revealing this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* to the multitudes.
I address all you bhikṣus: the time has come for me;
at midnight, I shall enter parinirvāṇa. Cultivate heedfulness and make firm your minds.
I have already explained the teachings of all the sutras;
it is difficult to encounter them even in countless billions of nayutas of kalpas,
so one should always make offerings to them.
Countless sons of the Buddha, beset by the afflictions of grief and suffering, were also deeply distressed.
Then, hearing the verses manifested by the World-Honored One, they contemplated the unconditioned and gathered to practice his verbal teachings.
Having encountered the Honored One among Men, all who see him are comforted; he gathers countless people, beyond thought or recollection.
Monks, do not fear: I shall enter parinirvāṇa; after I have departed, I shall no longer appear.
Free from all outflows, there is nothing he cannot enter;
he shall ultimately attain the most honored path of the Buddha, which is designated by the name "The Body Free from Defilement."
Then, at that very moment, in the middle of the night, he entered parinirvāṇa,
extinguishing all his radiant splendor.
His Buddha-relics were widely distributed, and stupas and temples were erected for immeasurable billions of years.
And the bhikṣuṇīs, all of whom aspire with resolve to seek the supreme, honored path of the Buddha—
beyond measure or limit, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges— they constantly practice with diligence and respectfully abide by the teaching.
The Great Being Transcendent Light, upholding the sūtras,
expounded the honored Dharma during a single sitting for the full duration of eighty intermediate kalpas.
At that time, there were eighteen attendants whom he taught and delivered,
all of whom attained peace and security.
With sincere hearts they made offerings to the Great Holy Ones and always reverently upheld their teachings.
By means of the Dharma of gentleness and compliance, they shall each attain Buddhahood throughout all worlds.
Having attained supreme mastery and upholding the immeasurable, each shall receive their prediction of enlightenment and reach perfect awakening.
The World-Honored One Dīpaṃkara was the last to attain Buddhahood; the Great Sage, like the sun and moon, transformed and enlightened the assembly of sages.
Those converted by the Guide numbered hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis;
they abide securely in what has been established, possessing great majestic transformations.
The Dharma Master Chao Guang was none other than my own self.
Seeking material gain, relatives, and friends, his aspirations and desires were directed solely toward fame and reputation.
Wandering about and coming and going, he visits various clans; having abandoned what he has studied, he does not recite or read it.
At that time, he refuses to explain it in detail; for this reason, that person’s name is borne in vain.
Regarding the teachings of the Buddha-Dharma, if one desires to bring forth praise, that person,
by virtue of the roots of merit they have cultivated while the World-Honored One was dwelling in the world,
will encounter and behold billions of Buddhas, even though there may be some flaws remaining.
The universally pervasive Great Sage, devotedly practicing correct conduct, has attained the supreme patience of accord;
furthermore, beholding the World-Honored One, he is able to practice herein.
In the final age, you shall attain the unsurpassed, noble, and true path of the Buddha;
becoming a supreme World-Honored One, you shall be named Maitreya.
He transforms and edifies countless billions of sentient beings, attaining valorous prowess and freedom wherever he may be.
Abiding peacefully in nirvana, he acts with benevolence and compliance toward their teachings; in that world and time, his likeness was such as this.
At that time, my body was that of a Dharma teacher; for this reason, I exercise such compassion.
Having observed such beings in past lives, you who dwell in benevolence should understand that transformations occur in this manner.
This is the first examination: such are these auspicious responses.
At that time, the World-Honored One, possessed of immeasurable clear vision, the King among the Śākyas, manifested the foremost truth;
now he wishes to proclaim the scripture of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
The path and practice I heard during my past lives have today been transformed and brought to full completion.
The Honored Guides employ skillful means;
the Great Lion of the Śākyas has established and inspired them, preaching the Dharma and the natural teaching.
All those who harbor the aspiration for the Way join their palms in reverent devotion.
Now, as I distinguish and analyze, I shall rain down the Dharma-rain;
with the gentle teaching of the Dharma, I shall universally moisten and satisfy all who tread the path of the aspiration for the Way.
There are devas who have entered the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), yet their minds harbor doubt and they remain hesitant.
If there are bodhisattvas seeking this resolve for the Way, they should now eliminate all notions of self (*ātman*).
2. Chapter on Skillful Means. In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the second chapter, "Skillful Means," the World-Honored One arose from samādhi and addressed the venerable Śāriputra:
"The Buddha-way is exceedingly profound; the wisdom entered by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is difficult to understand, difficult to comprehend, and beyond the reach of knowledge."

Although the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas have for billions of years from the beginning served and taken refuge [in the Buddha], and throughout incalculable kalpas have established the foundations of merit, reverently following the Buddha-dharma with diligent toil and practicing with vigor, they are still unable to fully comprehend the transformation of the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa).

Furthermore, Śāriputra! The Tathāgata observes the conditions from which beings arise; through skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), he guides them according to their circumstances. He manifests wisdom in a supple and harmonious manner, providing distinct explanations for each, and disperses the meaning of the Dharma to deliver all living beings. By the power of great wisdom and fearlessness, with single-minded concentration, liberation, and meditative absorption (*samādhi-samāpatti*) that are immeasurable, the sūtras he speaks are beyond reach; yet the Honored Tathāgata has here provided but a brief summary.

What the Great Sage has taught is unprecedented, sublime, and immeasurable. The Tathāgata fully understands the origins of all phenomena—whence they come—and that all phenomena are of their own nature (*svabhāva*). He discerns the characteristics, appearances, and fundamental roots of phenomena, knowing that phenomena are naturally so.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to explain the meaning once more, spoke again in verse:
"The Hero of the World is immeasurable; Among all the devas, humans, and every class of sentient beings, Who could possibly know the Teacher?"
The liberation door free from defilement is serene and fearless;
like the physical form of all Buddhas, there is none who can equal it.
Having followed hundreds of millions of Buddhas in the past, one has cultivated practice based upon those causes.
Entering into the profound and wondrous meaning, that which is manifested is beyond reach.
Having studied the practices of the Buddha-way for incalculable eons,
the fruit is the arrival at the site of enlightenment, just like the practice of loving-kindness and compassion.
May I obtain this wisdom, like that of the Buddhas of the ten directions,
with all marks fully perfected and all secondary characteristics likewise;
may my body be invisible and beyond all verbal expression.
Observing all classes of beings, there is none in the world equal to them.
When the sutras and Dharma are being preached, those who are able to discern and understand them are solely the bodhisattvas,
who always practice with faith and joy in their hearts.
Even if all Buddhas and their assemblies of disciples,
having completed what was to be done and abiding according to the teaching, were to entirely eliminate all illness and govern their own minds,
they could not reach that manifold wisdom.
The realm of the Buddha is entirely filled with the seven treasures;
these are offered to the Most Honored and Divine One who dwells therein.
Those who wish to understand this wisdom can never fully comprehend it.
All those who are wise and sagacious fill it completely;
likewise, all my present assembly of śrāvakas is fully endowed in this same way.
At that time, the entire assembly gathered together and contemplated this; yet, even calculating their abiding wisdom, none were able to know it.
The Buddha’s wisdom is thus immeasurable; those who wish to know its limit can never reach it.
Awakened through all conditions, free from all outflows, his faculties are fully realized and his mind is completely concentrated.
Even if the ten directions were entirely filled with people—
like a field of sugarcane, or bamboo, or reeds— all gathered together and contemplating at once, [they could not surpass him].
If one wishes to examine and know the Buddha and the Dharma he has taught for liberation,
even by calculating and contemplating for billions of nayutas of kalpas, one would never be able to know it, nor its benefits and meaning.
Those who have newly begun their studies and resolved their minds, the various Bodhisattvas and others—
should they make offerings to countless billions of Buddhas, expound the Dharma, and analyze its meanings,
and further cause these [teachings] to fill the ten directions, their number being like...
Rice, hemp, and forests throughout all worlds flourish and are not diminished;
they all gather together and contemplate what the World-Honored One has clarified:
the source of all dharmas, which is inconceivable, throughout countless billions of kalpas.
Like the sands of the Ganges, they are immeasurable; with a mind free from change and transcendent wisdom, those who wish to know them do not fall within their sphere of experience.
Countless bodhisattvas, all of whom are non-retrogressive,
throughout boundless kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, with single-minded diligence, have all together contemplated this;
yet even such as these are not capable of it.
The holy wisdom of all Buddhas is unattainable; having exhausted all outflows, it is beyond the reach of mental conception.
Only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is able to understand and know, discerning the worlds of the Buddhas throughout the ten directions.
Only the Buddha is fully endowed with it; he understands and knows that [reality], the most excellent guide and benefactor who has thoroughly and completely realized it.
He has been expounding this unsurpassed meaning for a vast duration of time.
Today the Buddha has declared to the assembly of śrāvakas:
"The vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, according to the positions they established, have been left behind and passed away;
those who have entered nirvāṇa have each attained deliverance through the transformation they were able to bring about."
Through skillful means and expedient methods, he still expounds the Dharma to transform the world;
always walking alone, he delivers many beings by manifesting this true Dharma of the sutras.

At that time, within the great assembly, all the śrāvakas and arhats whose outflows were exhausted and who had realized the limit of existence—the twelve hundred followers and those still in training, including bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās of the Śrāvaka vehicle—each gave rise to this thought:

"For what reason does the World-Honored One so earnestly praise skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) and proclaim the profound and subtle scriptural teachings of the Tathāgata, which lead to the wisdom of supreme perfect enlightenment that is unattainable, and which neither śrāvakas nor pratyekabuddhas can know?"

Now that the World-Honored One has expounded this teaching, there is no attainment of Nirvana within these Buddha-dharmas; although he has preached this sutra, we do not understand the direction toward which its meaning tends.

The worthy Śāriputra, seeing that the fourfold assembly harbored doubts in their hearts and wishing to pose a question to resolve their web of uncertainty, hoping thereby to be graced by the Buddha’s teaching, stepped forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Indeed, World-Honored One!”

Today, for what reason does the Tathāgata alone proclaim these skillful means, having attained supreme perfect enlightenment through this profound and wondrous Dharma, with a virtue and majesty so sublime as to be beyond measure?
Then Śāriputra spoke in verse:
“The Great Honored One, who delights in wisdom, Has long proclaimed such teachings as these:
The powers, the gates of liberation, and meditative concentrations— Those he has upheld are beyond measure.”
Praising the Buddha’s place of enlightenment, none dared to pose a question;
they could only sigh in admiration of the True Dharma, unable to initiate a discourse on its subtle mysteries.
Manifesting the Dharma of the Great Sage, he himself extolled his own conduct.
Wisdom is boundless, yet you wish to discern the profound Dharma.
Now we, the humble ones, harbor doubts; you speak of the exhaustion of all outflows, and those who seek the unconditioned have all heard the Buddha’s praise.
Those who seek the state of a pratyekabuddha— monks and nuns,
devas, nāgas, and spirits, gandharvas, mahoragas,
and all other such beings— each harbor doubts in their hearts.
I ask the Honored One among Two-Legged Beings, O Virtuous One, please explain this:
All the śrāvakas dwell securely within what they have been taught;
the Great Sage sees them and praises them, yet I alone have attained the infinite.
My humble mind lingers in hesitation, unable to reach a definitive resolution regarding the ultimate attainment of Nirvana.
Now that I have heard this teaching once more, I pray only that you will explain and analyze it, proclaiming it with a voice like the roar of thunder.
The teaching now being proclaimed is like the roar of a lion;
the most excellent sons of the Buddha all join their palms in homage.
Now is the time for those who wish to hear it—please explain it in detail for us.
The hosts of devas and nāgas, spirits, and gandharvas—numbering hundreds of thousands like the sands of the Ganges—all together proclaimed: "We shall make offerings to the World-Honored One."
All desired to pose questions regarding the honored Way of the Buddha.
The wheel-turning sage kings, with one accord, numbering in the hundreds of thousands of myriads, all paid homage with reverence;
standing with palms joined, they asked: "By what cause is your virtue so magnificent?"
"All practices are fully perfected.
At that time, the World-Honored One said to Śāriputra:
"Cease, cease! There is no need to inquire further into this matter."
"Why is this? Because when the devas and people of the world hear this teaching, they will all be struck with terror.
At that time, Śāriputra again addressed him, saying:
“I only pray that the Great Sage will take pity and explain this meaning. Why is this?

Within this assembly, there are countless hundreds of thousands of billions of beings—those that crawl, breathe, fly, and wriggle—who have previously seen past Buddhas, known how to plant various roots of merit, and who, upon hearing what the Buddha speaks, shall all believe with joy, receive and uphold it, and practice it accordingly.”
Then Śāriputra spoke in verse:
“May the King of Men, out of compassion, speak at his own ease.
The multitude, numbering in the billions, abide in reverent composure, respectfully trusting in the meaning of wisdom.”
"Those of such a kind will surely all rejoice.

At that time, the World-Honored One praised Śāriputra in this manner up to three times, saying: "Do not repeat it; the devas and people of the world will all harbor arrogance and self-indulgence, and the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs will fall into great hardship."
The World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra in verse:
"Cease, cease! Why do you ask this? This wisdom is subtle and profound, beyond the understanding of the multitude."
"Suppose I were to speak on matters that are easy to understand; yet those who are foolish and obscured by darkness harbor arrogance and self-indulgence.
The worthy Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying: "I pray only that the Great Sage will compassionately speak at this time.

There are countless multitudes who, in past lives, have received the Buddha's teaching; for this reason, they now long to hear the Sage’s voice. Those who hear it will believe and find great peace and security, and we hope they will not harbor doubt or arrogance."
Then Śāriputra spoke in verse:
“I am the eldest son of our Buddha; I now respectfully offer this exhortation. I pray that the Honored One among Two-Legged Beings will compassionately explain it for me.”
All should believe with joy in what the Holy Honored One has proclaimed; they shall ultimately attain fundamental virtue and resolve the net of all doubts.
These [beings], with palms joined, standing respectfully and solemnly to one side, will surely revere and delight [in it].
Regarding this Dharma and its meaning,
we and our like— twelve hundred people, as well as the rest of the assembly— seek the sublime path of the Buddha.
"If they should see or hear [this], and abide securely in the verbal teachings, they will immediately rejoice and give rise to the Great Resolve.
At that time, the World-Honored One, seeing that Śāriputra had exhorted and assisted him three times, addressed him, saying:
"Since you have now made your earnest request as many as three times, how could I not speak?"
Listen attentively, listen attentively!
Reflect upon this well;
I shall now explain it for you.

As soon as the World-Honored One had uttered these words, five thousand bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās, harboring extreme arrogance in their hearts, immediately rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew from the assembly.
Why is this? Because pride lacks skillful means;

one imagines having attained what has not been attained, and claims to have accomplished what has not been accomplished, gathering up and concealing one's robes, bedding, and requisites before departing.
The World-Honored One remained silent and did not restrain him.
Furthermore, Śāriputra,
those in the assembly were startled and some departed in secret, having become detached from the vast meaning and the flavor of the sound.
Furthermore, Śāriputra,
it would be well indeed if these people of extreme pride were to retreat.
Why then would the Tathāgata preach this Dharma?

Just as the *ariṣṭa* flower is seen only from time to time, the Buddha praises this Dharma as rare and difficult to encounter after a long interval. You all should believe the profound sutras spoken by the Tathāgata with sincerity and truth; their meaning is most subtle and their words are never false. Through various sounds, he manifests diverse chapters and verses, each distinct and beyond what people can conceive; though they were never previously thought of, the Tathāgata knows them all.

Why is this so? It is because that which the Perfectly Awakened One brings forth in the world praises but one thing; all great manifestations arise from a single source. He appears in the world to respond to the hopes and expectations of sentient beings; he appears in the world to encourage and assist such types of people; he appears in the world because the common folk hope for and seek the Buddha-wisdom; he appears in the world because the masses hope for the Tathāgata’s precious resolution; he appears in the world to awaken the thoughts of all living beings through Tathāgata-wisdom; and he appears in the world to instruct the populace in the Eightfold Path, causing them to eliminate their hopes and expectations.

Therefore, you should know that all that arises from the Perfectly Awakened One is for a single purpose: to accomplish the great task through infinite wisdom, which is like the single wisdom of emptiness; and to appear in the world through unobstructed compassion. Just as it is with the conduct of the Buddha, so too is the benefit and purpose of his transformation of beings.
He then preached the Dharma for them, instructing the bodhisattvas to manifest the wisdom of ultimate truth, discerning it through the sublime illumination of the Buddha.
He further caused them to progress solely toward the Great Vehicle of Awakening; there are no two vehicles, much less three!
The Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, of the worlds in the ten directions—those of the past, future, and present—are likewise thus.

Through various skillful means and diverse teachings, they each use different voices to transform and enlighten all beings, preaching the Dharma so that all may give rise to the Mahāyāna: the Buddha’s Vehicle of Perfect Enlightenment and the Vehicle of Universal Wisdom.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
These sentient beings have all made offerings to the Buddhas of the past and have also heard the Dharma; according to their original practices, they have attained the realization of its meaning."

I see that the fundamental practices of sentient beings differ; the Buddha observes the various inclinations of their minds and, through skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), establishes retributions and expounds the principles of the Dharma. All these are for the sake of the equality of perfect enlightenment and the Mahāyāna. When one reaches the ultimate wisdom and the Way and Virtue (*mārga-guṇa*), they are uniform and singular, without duality. Throughout the worlds of the ten directions, all are equal and without distinction; how, then, could there be three vehicles?
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
Suppose the Tathāgata were to speak of the defilements of sentient beings for an entire eon without reaching their end.
Now, I have appeared in this world of five turbidities:"
First is worldly affliction; second is violence; third is false views; fourth is a short lifespan; and fifth is the defilement of the kalpa.

Because those belonging to these factions have shallow roots of virtue, are stingy, greedy, and full of impurities, [the Buddha] employs skillful means to manifest the teachings of the Three Vehicles to exhort and transform the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

If he were to preach the Buddha Vehicle, they would ultimately not listen, accept, enter, or understand it; do not say that the Tathāgata’s Dharma contains the paths of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, for such paths are profound, distant, and fraught with many difficulties.

If a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī, having already attained arhatship and realized their own fulfillment, refuses to accept the teaching of the unsurpassed, true, and correct path, they will certainly be slandering the Buddha-vehicle!

Although he possesses this intention, it is through the Buddha’s impartial instruction that those who are extremely arrogant finally come to know it when the time for his parinirvāṇa arrives. Why is this so?

Furthermore, those bhikṣus who have attained arhatship have no further aspirations and their outflows (*āsrava*) are exhausted; yet, when they hear this sutra, they do not believe or rejoice in it. At the time of their parinirvāṇa, the Tathāgata appears before these śrāvakas in person and says:

"The Great Sage does not pass into extinction by such means as these; he causes you to receive, uphold, and expound the Vaipulya verses and sutras. Only after you have had your doubts resolved by other Buddhas—Worthy Ones, Truly and Fully Enlightened Ones—will you then come to have deep faith that the Tathāgata’s words are truthful and correct: there is only the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), and there is no second."
The World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“Monks and bhikṣuṇīs, harboring extreme arrogance and self-indulgence,
And five thousand faithful laymen and women lacked faith.”
Not seeing one's own flaws and impurities, one fails to observe the precepts with integrity;
thus encountering many situations of ruin and peril, one gives rise to foolish and deluded thoughts,
acting instead to pursue a mixture of things, utterly lacking skillful means.
The Buddhas’ most supreme dhyāna, By which one hears the Dharma;
Making offerings to Pure Wisdom, The assembly remains in solemn stillness;
All receive the grace of the teaching, Attaining resolve and establishing the essential vision.
Śāriputra, listen to this: the Buddha is the supreme among men;
having realized all dharmas through true awakening, he has preached various teachings.
Through hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of skillful means, he acts in accordance with the mental conduct of sentient beings.
And he preached the Dharma for them:
that matters of sin and merit differ in many ways, and according to one's past lives, each receives their respective retribution.
These sentient beings each have different minds; their karmic actions are manifold, entangled and bound.
Due to the various views arising from causes and conditions, there are hundreds of thousands of millions of such defilements across all categories.
The Tathāgata, the Great Sage, has preached this sūtra; what he says is most sincere and shall never be false or deceptive.
