The Buddha said to Śāriputra:

“In a future age, after immeasurable, incalculable, and innumerable kalpas, you shall make offerings to hundreds of thousands of millions of buddhas and receive their teachings of the true Dharma. By reverently practicing this Vaipulya sūtra and perfecting all practices, you shall attain the Way of the Buddha, known as Padmaprabha Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām; the world shall be named Vimalā.”

It was equal in its happiness and majestically radiant; all conditioned phenomena were pure, and that which was established therein was secure. Grain was abundant and cheap, and the population was flourishing. Men and women were numerous, fully provided for, and complete in every respect. Lapis lazuli and gold formed long ropes that stretched continuously along the sides of all roads. Beside every path stood trees made of the seven treasures, with eightfold intersections of streets, where the branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits of the rows of trees were ever lush.

The Perfectly Awakened One Padmaprabha shall likewise continue to preach the Dharma of the Three Vehicles; that Buddha will preach the Dharma for the duration of one kalpa, expounding sutras that manifest extraordinary vows.
The eon is named Mahāratnavyūha. Why is it called Mahāratnavyūha?
It is because the assembly of bodhisattvas in that Buddha-land is infinite, inconceivable, and immeasurable; only a Tathāgata is able to know their number.

In that buddha-field, the bodhisattva mahāsattvas act as jewels of awakened intent, like lotuses; there are none who are newly trained, yet all have long planted the roots of virtue. They purely cultivate the brahma-faring without limit of time, drawing near to the Tathāgata and constantly responding to the Buddha’s wisdom. Endowed with great supernormal powers, they set their will upon the essentials of the Dharma, possessing courageous and steadfast resolve.

The assembly of bodhisattvas will be complete and without deficiency; therefore, that eon shall be named Great Jewel Adornment. The Buddha Padmaprabha’s lifespan shall be twelve intermediate eons, not counting his time as a youth; the people of that land shall have a lifespan of eight eons.

After twelve kalpas have passed since the Tathāgata Padmaprabha’s departure, there shall be a bodhisattva named Dṛḍhapūrṇa who will receive his prediction of enlightenment. The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"This Great Being Dṛḍhapūrṇa, after my parinirvāṇa, shall attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path, and be known as the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Padmottara."

After the Parinirvāṇa of the Buddha Padmaprabha, the True Dharma and the Semblance Dharma shall remain for twenty intermediate kalpas; that buddha-field will be equal to the lands of the previous buddhas, without any difference.
The Tathāgata Padmavikrāmin also lived for twenty-two intermediate kalpas before entering parinirvāṇa.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, his True Dharma and Semblance Dharma remained for twenty-two intermediate kalpas.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“You, Śāriputra, in a future age, shall attain Buddhahood and manifest the dignity of a Tathāgata;
your name shall be Padmaprabha, the Universal and Impartial Eye.”
The Teacher transforms and enlightens hundreds of thousands of millions of beings.
Through the power of cultivation over billions of Buddhas, he establishes many things;
wherever he exhorts and transforms others, he attains the Ten Powers and shall soon achieve perfection.
The supreme Buddha-way is inconceivable;
throughout incalculable kalpas, that kalpa shall be named Great Jewel Adornment.
The world is named Free from All Defilements.
It is spread everywhere with deep blue lapis lazuli as its ground, adorned with continuous cords of purple-golden sandalwood.
Various kinds of trees are all composed of the seven treasures.
The flowers and fruits of those trees are all made of pure gold.
Their intentions are firm and resolute; their deeds, words, and conduct are sagely, wise, and brilliant.
Having skillfully studied the Buddha-way for hundreds of thousands of millions of nayutas, these beings have now appeared.
Regarding this most supreme teaching of the Dharma:
while still a youth, he had no worldly desires or attachments;
renouncing love and lust, he immediately left the household life and attained the realization of the most honored path of the Buddha.
This most supreme Honored One shall attain mastery; his lifespan shall be twelve intermediate kalpas.
His Dharma teaching shall be established for the duration of eight kalpas.
The limit of his lifespan is such that it shall consist of twenty-two intermediate kalpas, fully completed, following the parinirvāṇa of the Great Sage Buddha.
At that time, the Dharma shall endure for a certain number of years, out of compassion for those in the heavens and the people of the world.
After the Buddha’s True Dharma has been extinguished, the Semblance Dharma shall remain for twenty-two intermediate kalpas.
That Great Sage of Supreme Clarity has disseminated his relics; gods and female spirits alike make offerings to this Most Victorious One.
The virtues of that World-Honored One shall likewise be thus.
Furthermore, you should rejoice: the land of this Benevolent One is adorned in such a manner;
the Honored One among Two-Legged Beings is naturally peerless.

At that time, the fourfold assembly—monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—as well as devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas, having heard the Buddha, the World-Honored One, bestow the prediction upon Śāriputra that he shall attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path, were filled with joy and exultation. Overcome with delight, they could not contain themselves; each removed their own upper robe and spread it over the Buddha.

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, Brahmā Sahāmpati, and countless billions of other sons of the gods each took garments to offer to the World-Honored One. They scattered celestial flowers, *manojña* flowers, and *mahāmanojña* flowers upon the Buddha. The celestial robes and garments all remained suspended in the void, arrayed in rows. Celestial music played spontaneously, and a great celestial roar resounded like thunder. A rain of celestial flowers fell everywhere, and all together raised their voices in praise, saying:

"The Dharma we have heard today is unprecedented since antiquity. That which was first turned at the Deer Park in Vārāṇasī was hardly worth mentioning; now the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has once again proclaimed the unsurpassed Wheel of Dharma."
Then the sons of the gods praised him in verse:
"Without peer in the world, you now turn the wheel of Dharma;
For the sake of men and women, you preach upon that from which the aggregates and the decays arise."
He was the foremost in eloquently explaining the twelvefold chain of dependent origination;
yet now that the Teacher has expounded it, few are able to believe and rejoice in it.
Having heard countless teachings directly from the Great Sage, the Hero of the World, [they still find it difficult to understand].
From the past until now, I have never heard such a scripture as this spoken by the Great Teacher.
I now offer my encouragement and assistance,
so that the valiant Śāriputra may receive his prediction of enlightenment.
To praise the original aspiration and the number of Buddhas he has honored,
may I likewise attain it and become a Buddha, the most supreme in the world.
Having performed various kinds of pure conduct many times over, [I shall achieve this].
"I pay homage to the Buddhas of the past, and vow to attain the noble goal of the Buddha-way.
Thereupon, Śāriputra addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I am now free from fetters and my doubts have been eliminated; in the presence of the present Buddha, I have received the prediction that I shall attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path."
He spoke again, saying:
"Great Sage!
As for these twelve hundred who have attained mastery, did they not formerly dwell on the stage of training?"
Will the Buddha-dharma endure in this way in the future?

These bhikṣus will abide in the gates of practice and honor the Dharma and Vinaya; they will cross over old age, sickness, and death, and extol nirvāṇa. These bhikṣus, numbering in the many thousands, will make offerings to the World-Honored One, study all that is to be learned, dread the self, fear the three periods of time, and reject all views and manifold heterodoxies.
While practicing and abiding in parinirvāṇa, I already harbored this thought that I would reach the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
Yet, I had never before heard of such a Dharma as this, and my mind was constantly filled with hesitation.
How excellent!
World-Honored One!
We pray that you will explain the essential meaning so that this bhikṣu’s net of doubt may be entirely removed.
Now the minds of the fourfold assembly are all filled with despondency; please cause them to become serene and free from all remaining resentment.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"Did I not speak this Dharma just now?

Through various kinds of skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), I have manifested it according to their causes and conditions. All that has been analyzed and expounded by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is for the sake of the unsurpassed, perfect, and true Way. You should know that all whom I have praised are indeed bodhisattvas."
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
Now I shall provide a further illustration to explain this meaning; those with clear wisdom should understand this parable.

Suppose there were a great elder in a commandery, a kingdom, a district, or a town, who was advanced in years and found it difficult to sit or rise, yet possessed boundless wealth and pleasure and immeasurable treasures.

There was a great house, vast and spacious on all sides with high and wide walls; the dwelling was ancient and dilapidated, and within it were hundreds of thousands of people, with only a single gate and a guardian.
The hall was leaning and collapsing, its beams and pillars were rotten, and since the eaves and windows were numerous, firewood and straw had accumulated there.
At that time, a great fire broke out, starting from one side and burning the entire residence.
The elder had sons, perhaps ten or twenty.

Desiring to bring his sons out, he found that the sons were negligent, indulging in play, merriment, and food and drink. Suddenly seeing a fire break out, they each fled in haste; they were panicked and bewildered, not knowing how to escape.
The father thought to himself:
"Now that this disaster of fire has occurred and the house is ablaze, by what skillful means can I rescue my sons?

At that time, the father, knowing the specific preferences of each son, immediately prepared elephants, horses, chariots, and various means for sightseeing; he opened the gates and doors to lead them outside, provided the most exquisite music performed by musicians, and entertained them with laughter and play to save them from the calamity of the fire, intending to bestow many vehicles upon them.

"I have prepared and stationed outside the gate elephant chariots, horse chariots, goat chariots, and carriage chariots; run out quickly to escape this fire disaster, and do as you wish according to your own desires."

Hearing what their father had commanded and bestowed—the elephants, horses, carriages, musical instruments, and other such things—each of the sons applied themselves with diligence and devised extensive plans, covering themselves with dust and dousing themselves with water, until they were able to run out.
Seeing that his sons had emerged safely, the elder sat exposed to the open air on all four sides; their hearts leaped with joy and they were no longer afraid. Each addressed him, saying:
"We pray that our father grant us the various kinds of entertainments and vehicles—such as elephants, horses, and chariots—as he previously promised."

"Furthermore, Śāriputra! That great elder bestowed upon all his sons equal gifts of great carriages made of the seven treasures. These carriages were adorned with canopies of interlaced pearls, exceedingly high and wide, decorated with various rare and precious ornaments never seen before, and embellished with pure fragrant flowers and necklaces. They were spread with silken rugs, woolen carpets, and embroidered mats; their coverings were bright white, flashing like lightning; and their crowns, turbans, shoes, and sandals were such as the world rarely possesses. Each youth held one, and they were all identical in kind and color, being exactly the same for each son."
Why is this? These young children are all my own sons; I cherish and respect them with equal love, without partiality. For this reason, I bestow upon them equally the Great Vehicle.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!

I am likewise the father of sentient beings; I store away a treasury full to overflowing with no vacancy. With such a form and appearance, I teach, transform, and encourage them, enabling them to be shown the Mahāyāna."
The sons then obtained this Mahāyāna, regarding it as a rare treasure never before encountered, and they traveled about riding upon it.
What do you think?
Would it be false for the elder to bestow such precious treasures and Mahāyāna vehicles upon his sons?
Śāriputra said to the Buddha,
“No, World-Honored One!
[He would] abide securely.”
"No, World-Honored One!
That person is most sincere."

Why is this? That great elder rescued his children and did not wish for them to encounter the harm of this fire; he granted them whatever they desired, and once they had safely emerged, he gave each of them a Mahāyāna vehicle. For this reason, the elder did not act in falsehood.

Having thoroughly understood the inclinations and aspirations of his sons, he used skillful means to enable them to escape calamity and misfortune; how much more so when he possesses immeasurable treasuries of jewels, which he bestows upon his sons as the Great Vehicle of equal nature, without fail.
The Buddha said:
"Excellent, Śāriputra!"
It is exactly as you have said.

The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha transcends the ten directions and illuminates all darkness; he liberates beings from sorrow and fear, uprooting them by severing their very roots and sprouts, so that the branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits of the Tathāgata’s wisdom may manifest.

The Dharma King, through his supernormal powers, acts as the father of the world; with skillful means and expedient devices, he sustains all beings with compassionate resolve. His practice of the path of great compassion is inexhaustible, and out of pity for the three realms ablaze with raging fires, he manifests in the world because sentient beings do not understand. He rescues and delivers living beings from the afflictions of birth, old age, sickness, death, and the various disagreeable bonds of attachment; he tears asunder their clinging, liberates them from lust, anger, and ignorance, and guides them toward the three vehicles, gradually exhorting and showing them the unsurpassed, right, and true path.

Living at ease in this world, one observes that among the various beings, there is deluded attachment to wealth and possessions, cherished with insatiable greed; because of these sensual desires, they bring about immeasurable suffering. Now, in the present, they pursue their cravings with frantic haste, yet later, when deprived of protection, they fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals—where they are scorched, roasted, and boiled, suffering from hunger, thirst, and heavy burdens, with pain beyond description.
Even if one is born in the heavens or among humans, one encounters the inevitable, suffers from the separation from loved ones, and endures immeasurable grief and affliction.

For a time, one leaves suffering behind, indulging in song, dance, and laughter, unaware of fear; having no sense of caution or difficulty, one fails to realize the truth for oneself, refuses to contemplate or calculate the beginning and end of things, seeks no refuge, and yet is seen again being consumed by flames.

Regarding the afflictions and sufferings of sentient beings within the three realms, I shall bestow and establish upon them the boundless great peace and the inconceivable, hundreds of thousands of correct wisdoms of the Buddhas.

For those who are excessive, dissolute, deluded, or attached to sensual pleasures, the Tathāgata establishes the spiritual power (*ṛddhi*) of the wisdom of the Path; through skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), he manifests the Buddha-wisdom, causing them to hear of the Buddha’s powers (*bala*) and fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*).

Sentient beings find it difficult to awaken and are unwilling to seek and accept [the truth]; bound by causes and conditions, they have not yet escaped birth, old age, sickness, death, and the afflictions of grief; they have never yet attained deliverance from being scorched and roasted within the three realms, nor do they understand where their ultimate refuge lies.
What is meant by "understanding the Buddha’s wisdom"?

It is like a wealthy elder who stations strong, valiant, and powerful men to rescue his children from the calamity of fire; he employs skillful means to entice them until they have safely emerged outside, and only then does he bestow upon them exquisite and extraordinary chariots adorned with various jewels.

Thus it is, Śāriputra! The Tathāgata, the Perfectly Awakened One, establishes all virtues through the powers and fearlessnesses; he cultivates courageous wisdom through skillful means and expedients. Beholding the triple world as a house ablaze with fire, and desiring to rescue sentient beings from their various perils, he manifests the paths of the śrāvaka, the pratyekabuddha, and the bodhisattva. By means of these three vehicles, he instructs, transforms, and urges them on so that they may abandon craving and desire. He teaches all living beings to extinguish the fires of the triple world—the bonds of lust, anger, and delusion—and the dharmas of form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch. These five desires of the three bases burn people; by not relying upon the triple world, one attains the three vehicles. Diligently applying oneself to the three vehicles transcends the triple world; advancing in the three vehicles is the instruction of all Buddhas.

The common people gathered in numbers beyond measure; the World-Honored One manifested playful conduct for their entertainment, cultivating these faculties, powers, factors of awakening, meditative concentrations, liberations, samādhis, and right attainments, so that in future lives they might achieve the great joy of the Dharma, dwelling in peace, happiness, and freedom from all hindrances.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!

There are sentient beings who have not yet awakened; when a Tathāgata appears in the world, those who possess faith and joy, who delight in the Buddha’s Dharma teachings and practice them with diligence, and who finally seek to attain parinirvāṇa at the end of their time—these are called the śrāvaka vehicle."
To seek arhatship in accordance with the truth and emerge from the triple world is like a wealthy elder who,
to rescue his children from danger, promises them goat-drawn carts.

Furthermore, if there is a person who, lacking the teacher’s Dharma, follows their own inclinations to seek the state of ultimate stillness, desiring solitary nirvana while awakening to all causes and conditions, and practices with diligence within the Tathāgata’s Dharma— this is called the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle.
He emerges from the burning house and promises horse-drawn chariots.

Suppose there is a person who seeks the wisdom of universal penetration, the path-wisdom of all Buddhas, the sovereign holy wisdom that arises spontaneously from the mind, and the teacherless wisdom that brings great compassion and provides great peace and security to gods and humans; who desires to benefit the people of the heavens and the world, to bring liberation to the masses through the Dharma of the Tathāgata, and who, practicing with diligent effort, seeks the Great Sage’s universal vision, power, and fearlessness—this is called the Way of the Tathāgata, the vehicle traversed by Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas.
It is like the elder who entices his children to escape the calamity of the fire by promising them elephant-drawn chariots to drive them out of the burning house.

Seeing that his sons had been safely delivered from the peril and were free from fear, and observing that the treasures within his house were immeasurable, the father bestowed upon all his sons equally the great and wondrous Great Vehicles made of the seven precious gems.

The Tathāgata’s perfect enlightenment is likewise so: beholding countless multitudes numbering in the hundreds of thousands of myriads, he causes them to cross over the three calamities, the diligent sufferings, and the terrors; according to their aspirations, he opens the gate of birth and death, and finally enables them to escape from difficult perils and fears, leading them to extinction and peace.
“Furthermore, Śāriputra!

At that time, from the house of beginningless birth and death, the Tathāgata—by means of his innumerable wisdoms, powers, and fearlessnesses—beheld all those suffering in calamity and took pity upon them as if they were his own children. He universally exhorted and urged them to return to the Buddha Vehicle, not allowing them to enter parinirvāṇa according to their own individual inclinations; rather, the Tathāgata enticed them all with the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa and brought them to parinirvāṇa thereby.”

If sentient beings attain liberation from the three realms through the wisdom of the Tathāgata, the gates of liberation, meditative concentration, and the noble gates of deliverance, he will comfort and gladden them, bestowing the meaning of the Dharma and granting them the singular appearance of the Great Way of the Buddha.

Just as that elder had originally promised his sons three kinds of vehicles, yet upon seeing them escape danger, he bestowed upon each of them equally one kind of Great Vehicle; being true and not false, each attained exultation without any resentment.
The Tathāgata is likewise: having originally manifested the three vehicles, he subsequently transforms all beings so that they enter the Great Vehicle;
this is not false. Why is this?

You should know that the Tathāgata possesses an infinite number of treasuries and storehouses; having attained mastery, he manifests for all sentient beings the great Dharma-transformation, the various supernormal powers, compassion, and wisdom. You should understand it thus, and you should comprehend this meaning.
"The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, through his skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) and the sound of the practice of wisdom, teaches only the One Vehicle, namely, the Buddha Vehicle.
The World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Just as there was once an elder who possessed a great house, Which had become exceedingly dilapidated and decayed."
Rotten, decaying, and on the verge of collapse.
There is a great hall and residence that is about to fall into ruin; its beams, pillars, rafters, and ridgepoles have all been shattered and broken.
There were many porticos and gateways, as well as various windows; there were also storehouses with wooden frames plastered with mud.
The high and steep walls had their partitions collapsed, and the thatched roofs, having stood for a long time, were worn away and falling apart.
At that time, there were many people, a multitude of five hundred, all dwelling together in those houses.
There were immeasurable accumulations of grass and wood; whatever was required was stored there in infinite quantities.
All the gates were closed at that time.
There were various pavilions and lotus flowers, with billions of kinds of incense emitting a fragrant aroma.
Various kinds of birds, surrounded by their kin; various kinds of vipers and snakes, bats and stinging insects, fleeing and hiding.
There are many kinds of monkeys, wildcats, and mice, each with its own distinct name.
Alas, the chirping and squawking!
In this latrine of excrement and urine, filth overflows; swarms of insects and thorny brambles fill its interior.
All together they gnaw upon the corpses of the dead; who, having seen or heard this, would not be struck with terror?
Countless dogs crouch and lie in their dens, each surrounding [the corpse], all pulling and tugging at it together.
Suppose that when these beings are hungry, they all compete for food; emaciated, weak, and frail,
they fight one another and bite each other, their cries resounding loudly, and their dwelling becomes terrifying,
transformed into such a state.
There were various spirits and ghosts, their minds harboring malice and harm; flies, fleas, and bedbugs were also exceedingly numerous.
Centipedes of every kind, along with various *piśāca* demons, swarmed on all four sides, giving birth and nursing their young.
Each taking their portion of the food— whether it be a goat, a ram, or a sheep—
cannot flee back to its own place.
Even if various spirits and deities come to protect them, they cannot deliver them or prevent them from being harmed.
Those various ghosts and spirits also feed upon sentient beings; though they may attain full satisfaction, their minds continue to harbor evil.
As the categories of beings differ and their lineages are distinct, when there are those who die, they are all buried in burial mounds.
The Kumbhāṇḍas and Gandharvas, whose minds are set upon violence and corruption, stretch out their two arms and come and go in their pacing;
there is no incantation or spell by which they may be warded off.
At that time, the dogs seized his two feet, threw him down so that he lay on his back,
and began to strike him.
Grasping his two legs and twisting them around his neck, they sat there acting wantonly, their minds dissolute and unrestrained.
Its form was tall and large, its physical strength and vigor abundant; it was arrogant and self-willed.
Having been hungry for ten days, it went about seeking food and drink, and seeing hay and mugwort from afar, it ran toward them.
There are needle-mouthed insects and iron-beaked birds dwelling amidst the mounds and graves, beholding the corpses of the dead.
Malevolent ghosts, fierce and treacherous, let their hair hang loose and shriek; various *pishācas* swarm about, greedy and arrogant.
The windows and doors are bright and clear; looking out and surveying the four directions, one sees here that nothing can be found to endure.
Various malevolent spirits and ghouls, as well as hosts of hungry ghosts, vultures, eagles, crows, and owls, all go about seeking food.
Of such a kind was this great park and villa,
with crumbling walls and dilapidated rooms and gates, shattered and broken apart,
guarded by a single man alone.
That person is inside, staying and dwelling there.
At that time, a fire breaks out, immediately burning down the house; it spreads on all four sides, and everything is consumed by flames.
Countless thousands of people, struck with terror and weeping aloud, cried out: "Now the fire rages, consuming our children!
Furthermore, that venerable one raised his voice in lamentation as the pillars of the hall collapsed and the walls and screens were shattered to pieces.
The various hungry ghosts raised their voices in joyful cries; hundreds of vultures and eagles flew about, seeking to avoid the fire.
Countless *kūṭāgāras* shook with terror at the rafters and beams, while hundreds of thousands of malevolent spirits fled in frantic haste.
Countless multitudes of living beings are scorched by fire; like withered reeds reduced to ashes, those who are feeble and decayed are struck down by the calamity of fire.
Each was filled with anguish as they were seen being burned; scorched and charred to a pulp, their boiling blood flowed away.
At that time, within this house, a multitude of fierce beings—every single one of these malevolent spirits—all devoured them together.
Foul smoke billows and swirls, while fragrant scents are praised; all beings rush toward it, circling in tangled confusion.
Centipedes and millipedes emerge alongside maggots and grubs; malevolent spirits roam with bold ease, causing much gnashing of teeth.
With fire blazing upon their heads, they wander about in play, all devouring those who are being burned by the flames.
Within their dwellings, there is such frantic terror; hundreds and thousands of people are consumed and scattered in ruin.
At that time, the master of the house, the powerful elder, seeing things thus, hurriedly attended to his duties.
Hearing of this calamity and taking pity on his sons, he prepared music and established precious vehicles to entice them out.
There are those who are deluded and ignorant, unable to understand; amidst their jesting, they indulge in negligence and self-indulgence.
The elder listens and observes, then enters the hall; the foolish man remains unaware, having no thought of liberation.
Now my sons are shrouded in darkness and obstruction;
all are blind and deaf, lacking both eyes and ears. For the sake of play and pleasure, they bind themselves;
such a lineage and progeny are exceedingly difficult to encounter.
Ordinary people of all classes and various ranks, Encountering this great calamity of fire, Each suffers in pain and distress.
Ghosts, spirits, snakes, and vipers Harbor venom within their hearts.
Countless malevolent spirits leaped for joy;
wolves, foxes, and dogs, beyond all reckoning, were likewise hungry and thirsty, seeking food and drink.
"My children are numerous, and all have perished here; even if there were no fire, it would not be a place of joy.
With such intense suffering caused by doubt and manifold fetters, how much more so when one sees it blazing all around?"
The sons, greedy for play, took delight in one another;
they never contemplated the instructions spoken by their father, nor did they think within their own minds to quickly devise a plan.
At that time, the elder reflected within himself:
"I have brought this son into the world and nurtured him with great toil and hardship; will he not be consumed and scorched by fire?"
"How may I rescue my sons and deliver my grandchildren?
he thought to himself, and immediately devised a skillful stratagem:
"Now, while my children are indulging in music and performance, disaster has arrived; this is no time for play and pleasure."
How painful it is to be so ignorant and deluded as not to perceive such bitter suffering! These children are flawed and base; they do not recognize this peril.
Now my heart is filled with dread, yet you take pleasure in dissipation and indulgence. You must follow with diligent effort to escape and be saved from this great wall.
I have prepared the musical instruments and the various implements for play that you hold dear;
their melodies and rhythms have been harmonized, and they shall all be performed together at once.
Hearing of the reward, the sons were greedily delighted by the sound of music;
each with great speed and exerting all their strength, they drove away everything and rushed out from the house of calamity, escaping from suffering and distress.
Gathering the sons together in one place, they were peaceful, secure, and joyful.
No longer is there any fear;
my heart is broad and serene, and my mind has attained freedom.
Having extensively prepared various requisites and the lion throne, today my very self has realized the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Those various sufferings and afflictions have already been forever exhausted and removed.
Having cultivated the power of diligence, one realizes that those who were lost in the house of calamity and indulged themselves at will have previously experienced,
without limit, sleep and slumber while the flames blazed fiercely.
When people encounter such calamities, they are shrouded by the dark veil, and their minds find no liberation.
Today, all have attained deliverance; they have reached spontaneity, the very wish of their hearts.
The father saw his sons, their hearts set on peace and security.
At that time, the sons went to the elder and said, "O Father,
we pray that you grant each of us the various kinds of vehicles as previously promised."
My home has caught fire, yet I am lost in darkness and do not awaken.
The Great Man issues his instructions, which all must respectfully receive; he shall bestow upon his sons the three kinds of vehicles.
Now is precisely the time—may he deign to grant them to us.
By imperial decree, the attendant was commanded to open the treasury, wherein were found purple-polished celestial gold,
bright moon-jewels, and other exquisite, rare treasures seldom seen in the world.
The grand and elegant chariot is most honored and difficult to equal; it is adorned with solemn ornamentation and surrounded by railings.
Pearl necklaces and jeweled pendants, along with banners, streamers, and silken fabrics, provide a magnificent spectacle. Canopies of interlaced gold and silver cover its top.
Resplendent and firmly established were the various precious flowers;
surrounding on all four sides, they hung down everywhere.
Layered upon the chariot were countless celestial silks and white garments, spread out as seats.
With soft cushions and countless silken hangings, arranged as seats within the carriage;
its adornments were beyond calculation, the value of the carriage reaching billions, with wondrous and rare treasures numbering in the trillions.
The elephants are tall and massive, their forms majestic and docile; harnessed to precious chariots, they serve as great vehicles.
Each of these has been bestowed upon the assembly of true sages; all of you are my children.
Everything was distributed equally.
At that time, the sons were filled with joy and leaped for gladness; each in their respective places, they celebrated and took delight together.
I tell you, Śāriputra, such is the Great Sage: for the sake of all living beings, he acts as a protector and savior for their parents.
All the multitudes of beings are my children, yet they are entangled and bound by the desires of the three realms.
Exertion, suffering, affliction, and distress—these are fully present in their hundreds and thousands;
this is what is called being universally ablaze without exception: birth, old age, sickness, death, and the pain of lamentation.
The Buddha, for the sake of the three realms, delivers all without exception;
whether dwelling in seclusion or sitting beneath forest trees, he always acts in accordance with the proper time to protect the three spheres.
Seeing them all being scorched and roasted— none of whom are strangers to me—
I awaken the common people so that they may find refuge for themselves. For this purpose, I manifest myself there.
All common people, ignorant and refusing instruction, sit bound by their own attachments to desire and craving.
Through skillful means and expedient methods,
[the Buddha] provides the great panacea, distinguishing the three vehicles to reveal them to sentient beings.
Having heard that the three realms are filled with immeasurable defilements, he accordingly exhorts and urges them to depart.
Those bodhisattvas who come to rely upon the Buddha attain the six supernormal powers and the three types of penetration,
thereby perfecting the great wisdom of the sages.
Some shall attain success as followers of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, reaching the stage of non-retrogression and attaining the path of the Honored Buddha.
The sons present here, through the Buddha’s sovereign power, shall, by means of this parable, be free from all resentment.
By this cause one draws near to the vehicle of the Buddha-way; receiving all of this, one attains the state of supreme excellence.
Having subdued and cast off all worldly forms, one possesses the wisdom of all perfectly awakened ones.
Extraordinary are their virtues and the Way;
with faculties, powers, and doors of liberation, their single-mindedness is thus.
Their samādhis and concentrations number in the billions; these sons of the Buddhas are always honored and revered.
This is what is called the Honored and Sublime Mahāyāna.
With the resolve to subdue Māra, he was constantly dedicated at night;
admiring it without weariness, for a period of one year, as if it were the span of many kalpas, he brought sentient beings across to liberation.
Countless thousands of myriads;
that which is likened to the precious vehicle is precisely this, by means of which one travels to the Buddha’s site of enlightenment.
Countless sons of the Buddha take this as their delight; those who hear it shall dwell securely as disciples.
I tell you, Śāriputra, you should know this: when reckoned, there is but a single vehicle, and not two.
Knowing those who are supreme among men, he universally practices skillful means; gradually inducing them forward, from the minute to the great.
When their virtue has suffused the three realms and they desire to depart from them, only then does he manifest [the truth].
The Great Path of the Bodhisattvas:
the Buddha’s grace moistens all universally; it is like a fertile field where, according to what is sown, each receives its own kind.
What is sown by the planter does not increase or decrease because of the soil; the Buddha is likewise, universally equal to all.
He constantly reveals the Great Way, yet it is those who receive it that experience increase or decrease;
thus, the Buddha is the father of all people.
I constantly observe the suffering and affliction of the multitudes, who for countless billions of kalpas have been seen being burned and boiled.
Within the three realms, amidst fearsome calamities, the Buddha acts as their guide and leader, enabling them to attain nirvana.
O worthy ones, you have attained the unconditioned; today you have come to know it. Having cast off birth and death, you are liberated from the afflictions of toil and suffering.
For those bodhisattvas who dwell in this state, their resolute sincerity is illustrated by such an analogy.
On the day after the Buddha’s [attainment of enlightenment], the great guides, employing skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*),
should provide encouragement and assistance; just as the various bodhisattvas regard the defilements of craving and desire as things to be loathed and abhorred,
so too do they see those whose minds are obscured and obstructed as being defiled.
Therefore, the Guide speaks of diligent effort and suffering, manifesting the Four Noble Truths;
these should be discerned.
Because they are deeply attached to the darkness of sensory objects and are unwilling to abandon them, for their sake—
Yet he shows them the path;
following what they have practiced leads to various sufferings, but when craving is severed, one is forever free from attachment.
Regarding these three categories, there is no difference at all; one thus attains liberation.
If one cultivates the Eightfold Path, one shall then achieve transcendence.
I say to Śāriputra: What is it that constitutes deliverance?
To receive nothing at all is itself liberation.
That [liberation] is not something produced; it is the complete liberation of all.
Without anything to be extinguished or delivered, one beholds the Teacher.
For what reason does the Buddha speak of liberation?
It is by having nothing to be attained that one realizes the Way of the Buddha.
One shall become like me, a holy Dharma King, appearing in the world for the sake of peace and security.
I tell you, Śāriputra, this is my Dharma-seal;
it is the Buddha’s final, subtle, and excellent teaching, out of compassion for the devas and the world.
Wherever they travel, they shall always be able to practice alone.
If there are those who encourage and assist them in preaching this scripture, or who rejoice on their behalf,
they should hear this wondrous Dharma and uphold it, making offerings to them all.
The Buddhas of the past, Upheld this Dharma And reached the stage of non-retrogression.
If there should be someone Who believes in and delights in this sutra, They have already seen the Teachers of the past;
They too have fully followed and obeyed All the Honored Ones among the Sages.
Furthermore, those who have attained the hearing of such scriptural models as these shall all have seen my physical form.
Constantly observing and looking with diligence, they shall now behold the Bodhisattva; those who believe in this scripture—
Virtue is likewise so:
all gaze upon it; those bodhisattvas who have faith in this sutra are also just like this.
Those who are unwilling to have firm faith, even if this sutra is preached to them;
those śrāvakas who have attained supernatural powers— it is beyond their reach— and even the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas cannot comprehend it.
Now, all those śrāvakas who belong to me, such as the person of Śāriputra, possess firm faith.
You, sirs, likewise believe in the Great Dharma-scripture; you have fully realized it in the present and do not cling to causes and conditions.
If one should not accept this sutra scroll, then one would be slandering the Buddha,
the God among Gods.
Those who are shrouded in darkness, always harboring desire and lust, have never understood the nature of dharmas that are unarisen.
Furthermore, they slander the Buddha’s skillful means and all that exists in the world, which the Buddha constantly illuminates like the sun.
Upon hearing the Buddha’s teaching and his exposition of these transgressions and blessings,
their minds find no joy and their countenances change.
Whether now in my presence or after my parinirvāṇa, if there should be those who slander such scriptures as these, do not allow bhikṣus to transcribe this sūtra;
the Buddha has explained the causes for such offenses, and all should listen to their meaning with universal attention.
Having failed to lose this human body, one falls into the Avīci Hell;
dwelling therein for a full kalpa,
and for countless aeons beyond that limit, even when the retribution for the sin has ended, one remains constantly in ignorant darkness.
Within the hells, one shall fall; among birds, beasts, and livestock, one becomes a dog, a fox, or a wild beast, its form withered and emaciated.
When entering a person’s house, one may even be harmed.
Should there be those who harbor hatred for the Buddha’s scriptures, their complexions will turn abnormal, becoming as dark and murky as ink.
On account of their transgressions, their countenances are as dark as lacquer; their bodies are emaciated and lack any luster.
They are treated with contempt and loathing by all classes of beings, who strike them with tiles and stones, while they wail and shed tears.
Such people are constantly subjected to beatings, floggings, and lashings; famished, parched, and utterly exhausted, their bodies become emaciated and withered.
Camels, donkeys, and mules are perpetually burdened with heavy loads and receive whips and sticks;
their hearts burn with distress as they seek fodder and grass.
Slandering this sutra of the Buddha brings such retribution as this:
though one may obtain human form, the body will be afflicted with carbuncles and leprosy; its appearance will be hideous and deformed, and the flesh and skin will be ulcerated and putrid.
If a practitioner is treated with contempt by children in towns, villages, or settlements— mocked, toyed with, struck, or trampled—
that foolish and ignorant person, when their life eventually ends,
shall fall into birth among the borderlands and barbarians, becoming a blood-drinking creature of the wriggling and crawling kind.
Or they may become deaf or mute, lacking self-mastery.
Because of the transgressions committed against this sutra, they will constantly suffer many ailments;
sores and worms shall arise upon their bodies, and countless lives shall swarm to devour their frames, while their minds are perpetually clouded with sorrow.
Illness does not leave one behind.
That man is without wisdom and lacks clarity; wherever he goes, he is stingy and greedy, his nature always voracious and gluttonous.
Born blind and sightless, he is cast aside by all people.
People sit in disbelief;
their evil vapors externally infect others, and ghosts and spirits become weary and malevolent, meticulously provoking and harassing them.
Among the common people of the world, there is no one who will listen to these words.
If one does not delight in this stage of the Path, wherever they may be destitute, they shall always be impoverished.
They will never obtain fine clothing to wear; though their wealth and resources be abundant, they will not dare to eat or drink.
Even if one seeks the requisites for peace and security,
whatever may be obtained will soon be lost again.
Such is the retribution for the arousal of unwholesome conduct.
Even if one were to summon a physician who compiles various prescriptions and medicines,
who is skilled in expedient means and treats them accordingly, yet there are those whose ailments are not cured, but rather increase in severity,
remaining constantly afflicted by disease and finding no relief.
When one engages in other worldly affairs, one encounters turmoil;
through the karma of strife and contention, one further suffers humiliation and is subjected to flogging.
Those who violate the precepts constantly meet with such evils.
If there are those who slander the sin of this sutra, they shall never behold the World-Hero, the Teacher and Guide.
Under the Buddha’s Dharma-teachings, such as the violent *pūtana* ghosts and the *asura* deities, they shall constantly suffer calamity;
their ears will be deaf and blocked, and they shall remain ignorant, dull-witted, and benighted.
They shall not hear this sutra;
even if they exist, those who slander this scripture shall never see it again in future ages.
For the fruit of this sin, the calamity shall last for countless billions,
calculated in hundreds of thousands and many *koṭis* of kalpas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
one shall always be mute and unable to speak.
Those who destroy [the precepts] regard hell as a place for recreation, and the realms of suffering and evil destinies as their dwelling;
for the transgressions they have committed, they bring about calamities such as these.
Many people suffer from ailments; they hasten their own muteness and infirmity. If one remains in the world, one shall incur such faults.
When life is about to end, one raises the voice of a merchant’s son, yet one's body constantly encounters [suffering].
Subject to manifold sufferings,
numbering in the hundreds of thousands of millions, with a hundred thousand ailments, his countenance is perpetually dark, and he is disliked by all people.
Constantly emitting foul odors, they perceive a self; their complexions are dark and sallow, and harboring the poison of anger, their malevolence and harm increase ever more.
Their lustful desires are fierce and unrestrained; whatever they encounter, whether pleasing or offensive, they react like beasts.
Śāriputra, I tell you: today the World-Honored One, possessing all-knowledge, has proclaimed the transgressions of such a person.
If there should be those who slander this Buddha-sūtra, the limit of their calamities cannot be fully calculated.
Having seen this meaning, you should contemplate it; for this reason, I now speak thus for the sake of Śāriputra.
Not for those who are foolish or ignorant, nor for those who do not understand the Way, is this teaching of the Semblance Dharma intended to be analyzed and expounded.
Those who hold their resolve firmly and constantly cultivate mindfulness and discernment— if they are encouraged and inspired— [should practice].
Honoring and revering the Buddha-way, you shall then hear and receive this unprecedented Dharma.
By beholding hundreds of thousands of millions of Buddhas, you will plant immeasurable and boundless merits that fulfill all wishes.
That person’s disposition shall be as fierce as moonlight; only then will they listen to and receive such scriptures.

Their resolve shall always harbor compassion, and throughout the day and night, they shall radiate a sense of sorrow, casting away their physical bodies and having no regard for their own lives; only then will they listen to and receive them.
Regarding this sutra scroll, their minds shall be single-minded; they shall not harbor foolish vows, but shall constantly dwell in the wilderness or reside in secluded caves.
Only those who are thus benevolent and virtuous shall listen to and receive it.
Form close bonds with virtuous friends and always rely upon one another; abandon and stay far away from all evil associates.
Only by doing so can you hope to behold such sons of the Buddha, who are able to encounter teachings such as these.
Like a precious luminous gem, one should resolve to study and receive the various Vaipulya sutras;
one should view them in this way. As a noble son of the Buddha, one should always single-mindedly apply oneself to even a single fascicle of such a sutra.
Always with compassion, he turns toward all sentient beings; ever intent on reverence, he upholds the teachings of the Abiding One.
For this reason, I now proclaim this Dharma of the sutra for his sake.
Those who, amidst the great assembly, recite this sutra,
will have minds that are always in accord with reality and attain non-attachment; through the citation of countless billions of eons of parables,
they shall thus belong to this class and behold this scripture.
Furthermore, today the Buddha expounds upon the factors of the path; wherever he goes, he strides with leaping joy.
If a bhikṣu desires to seek the excellent teaching, upon seeing this sutra, he should receive it with joyful reverence.
With a mind always focused and diligent, taking no pleasure in other activities, one should uphold even a single verse with an unwavering resolve;
only then can one hear and receive such a vast and sublime model.
If there should be anyone who aspires to and seeks this sutra, they should revere it as if it were the body of the Tathāgata.
If a person desires to study this Dharma with earnest intent, should they obtain it, they should receive it by bowing their head in prostration.
That person should not, in their thoughts, seek out other sutras, nor ever contemplate the various secular texts of the world.
Practicing the Buddha-way with their resolve fixed upon the faculties and powers, they should completely abandon all else and lecture exclusively on this sutra.

I tell you, Śāriputra: even if a Buddha were to spend an entire eon providing billions of parables and explaining them in detail, should there be those who aspire to the supreme path of the Buddha, they should proclaim and disseminate this sutra.
The Lotus Sutra, Scroll Second;
The Lotus Sutra, Scroll Third.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Yuezhi Kingdom during the Western Jin Dynasty.

Chapter Four: Devotion and Joy At that time, the venerable Subhūti, Kātyāyana, Mahākāśyapa, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, and others, having heard the exposition of the Great Dharma, attained what they had never experienced before—something they had never heard in the past.

Seeing the World-Honored One bestow upon Śāriputra the prediction of his future attainment of the unsurpassed, right, and true path, they were filled with wonder and leaped for joy. Rising from their seats, they approached the Buddha, bared their right shoulders, and after performing prostrations, joined their palms and gazed reverently at the Honored One’s countenance. Within themselves, they reflected with hearts full of serene joy; their limbs and joints felt harmonious and pleasant as sorrow and joy converged within them. They addressed the World-Honored One, saying: [End of Chapter]

"Only the Great Sage possesses such supernormal penetration. We are decrepit, advanced in years, and among the elders we are all worn out and frail. Having taken refuge in the World-Honored One, we hope to attain nirvana; our resolve is set upon the unsurpassed, true, and correct Way, yet our advancing strength is meager and we are incapable of much. We shall listen attentively to what the Tathāgata expounds. As the assembled multitude sits down in order, we dare not be weary or fatigued, nor do we feel any weariness or distaste."

Previously, when the Tathāgata taught the Dharma for our sake, we attained emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*). Regarding everything from the Buddha’s scriptures to the lands of the buddha-fields, we have performed no contrived action among all phenomena (*sarvadharma*); this is that which the bodhisattvas delight in, and it is that which the Tathāgata exhorts and transforms in great measure.

I loathed the three realms and was driven about by them; constantly reflecting within myself, I thought I had attained nirvāṇa. Now that I have reached this state of exhaustion, you have instructed me in the extraordinary meaning: that one finds joy in equanimity, whereby I have conceived the great resolve for the unsurpassed, right, and true path.

Now that the Great Sage has bestowed upon us śrāvakas the prediction of our future attainment of perfect enlightenment, our minds were struck with amazement at such an unprecedented occurrence; we have gained a great benefit and each shall serve him, having now been granted the opportunity to hear such a sūtra as this.

Having constantly heard this Dharma from past Buddhas, my initial encounter with it was like obtaining a wondrous treasure through my great merit; it fulfills the aspirations of countless sublime intentions. Presently, within the realm of form, I am without fear; rare and exquisite music resounds spontaneously, great lamps are lit to illuminate ever more widely, and groves of sandalwood exude a dense and fragrant aroma.
"Yes indeed, World-Honored One! How could I possibly be capable of explaining it? He replied, "You may."
At that time, the śrāvakas addressed the Buddha together, saying:

“In the past, there was a man who left his father and wandered abroad, staying in another land for twenty or thirty years. He traveled everywhere in search of food, clothing, and shelter, yet he remained constantly impoverished and destitute, possessing no means of livelihood.”

The father traveled to another city and acquired countless gold, silver, and precious jewels—crystal, lapis lazuli, musaragalva, agate, coral, and amber. His treasuries were filled to overflowing, and his attendants, servants, elephants, horses, and carriages were beyond calculation. Surrounded by an infinite number of kinsmen and abounding in the seven treasures, he engaged in the management of wealth, farming, and trade.
Seeking food during his time of distress, the son traveled throughout the kingdoms, cities, towns, camps, and villages.

He arrived at the residence of a wealthy elder just as the autumn season began; entering the city, he went through the storerooms. Having been parted from the son for a long time, the elder suddenly yearned to see him, yet he did not know where he was.
He thought to himself:

"This man possesses immeasurable wealth and provides for those far and near. I consider that I am now old, decrepit, and approaching death; should my estate be scattered and dissipated upon my passing, I wish to see my son so that he may enjoy his possessions as he pleases. If this is achieved, I shall attain a state of non-action and no longer have cause for grief."

By chance, the son arrived at the elder’s house and saw from afar before the gate a great assembly of brahmins and gentlemen gathered together, surrounded by their retinues. A lion throne was fashioned from gold and silver inlaid together, and a great jeweled canopy was made of interlaced pearls and necklaces. His father sat upon it, distributing instructions and teachings; flowers of liberation were strewn across the ground, and hundreds of thousands of millions of pieces of gold served as food and drink.

When the son beheld the elder’s countenance and majestic bearing, he was struck with fear and could find no peace; thinking him to be a sovereign or a great lord, he hesitated in his advance and did not dare to go forward, but fled in haste.
The father saw his son from afar and felt great joy in his heart; he dispatched an attendant to pursue and call him back.
Terrified, the son fell prostrate on the ground and said to the pursuer, "I have committed no offense against you; why do you seize me?"
The attendant took him and they went together to the elder’s residence.
The elder said to him:

"Do not be afraid, do not be terrified. I have diligently expanded your business and filled your treasuries for your sake. It has been a long time since we parted, and I have often thought of seeing you; my age is advanced and my strength is failing, yet our father-son bond is deep."
As he was about to enter the house, he did not speak with the assembly. Why was this?

The father knew that the impoverished son’s aspirations were base and inferior, and that he did not recognize his father as one who possessed merit; yet after a long time, the son’s mind was awakened, he recognized his father through their harmonious appearance, and he beheld the rare treasures.
The elder said,
"This is my son. I have told you this by way of a stratagem."
"Now, for the time being, let me indulge you in whatever you wish to receive.

The impoverished son marveled at this, having never experienced such a thing before; he rose from his seat and went to the poor quarters to seek clothing and food. The father, knowing his son's circumstances, used skillful means to speak with him:
"Go now by yourself, accompanied by a small group."
The son came to this place and presented the seal once more, saying, "I have come to this residence to oversee its decoration.

The father handed over the elephants and horses and ordered him to train them roughly; when anyone questioned him, he answered in the same manner. He was to train the chariots and horses, strictly prepare the precious objects, and bestow them as he pleased; the father sought for the impoverished son whatever he might require for relief, providing it all in full accordance with these instructions.
At that time, the son was in the stable training horses and chariots and repairing precious treasures; he further instructed those within the household, both young and old.

From his window, the father saw from afar the excellence of what his son was doing. He removed the garments he was wearing, bathed his body, and with his right hand washed him. He adorned his body with precious necklaces, fragrant flowers, and robes, making it radiant and entirely pure, and then addressed him, saying:
"From whence have you originally arisen and established yourself?"
To whom do you belong?
You have abandoned me to go elsewhere, enduring toil, hunger, and cold.
I am already advanced in years; I tell you this out of affection—marry at once, enjoy yourselves with food and drink, and ensure the prosperity of our lineage.
"The karma I have created is beyond calculation; do you know that I am fully endowed with all manner of treasures? You sought me for many years, yet you were attached to evil friends.

Now that you have finally returned, you should rid yourself of your flaws and impurities. I possess wondrous treasures, such as the *yāma-prabhāsa* pearl and various rare and exquisite jewels, all of which I bestow upon you. My male and female servants, attendants, and laborers—both great and small—are at your disposal to fulfill your every desire; I entrust them all to you."
"I love and cherish you, just as a king favors his crown prince.
The venerable śrāvakas together addressed the Buddha, saying:

"At that time, the impoverished son had wandered and drifted for twenty or thirty years before reaching the elder’s house, where he was finally able to meet with him; he then recalled all that he had experienced during his travels and excursions from the past, and remembered it all in his heart."
At that time, the great elder was lying ill upon his bed and, knowing that his life was coming to an end, summoned his son and addressed him, saying:

"I am now weak and exhausted; you should follow my grand example. As for the household estate and the precious treasury, receive them all in their entirety. Use them to provide relief to the poor and destitute, bestowing them according to your own inclination. You shall immediately fulfill my instructions with joy beyond measure, and your conduct shall be one of utmost sincerity, never failing your original vow."

The father, knowing his son’s resolve and observing his prudent conduct, felt even greater joy and celebration at having first been poor and now become wealthy. He honored his kinsmen and paid obeisance to the elders, then spoke before the assembly of the king, the sovereign, and the ministers:
"Listen clearly, each of you: this is my son, born of me, whose name is so-and-so. Having abandoned me, he wandered abroad for twenty or thirty years; only now have we met again."
"In this case, you are my son and I am your father; all the wealth and treasures belong to my son.
When the son heard the voice of the proclamation to the great assembly, his heart was filled with even greater joy, and he thought to himself:
"By what past merit have I been granted command over the family treasury?"
The śrāvakas and others again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"The great wealthy elder is like the Tathāgata; the various students are called the sons of the Buddha. He exerts himself to rescue us from the diligent suffering of the triple world, just as the wealthy elder returns to take hold of his son and deliver him across from birth and death."

Thereupon, the World-Honored One, possessing a jewel-like assembly of countless holy ones who had removed the veils of the five aggregates through the five supernormal powers, constantly cultivated diligence within that teaching and was intent upon extinction (nirvāṇa), regarding it as the wondrous seal.

With earnest devotion and longing, they never cease their pursuit; desiring to attain the state of non-action, they remain silent within their minds. Having thoroughly contemplated what they have gained as immeasurable, they follow the practice of the Dharma under the Tathāgata, cultivating meditative concentration with constant faith and joy.

It means that observing ourselves to be indolent, inferior, and lacking the discernment or aspiration [to seek it], this treasury of the Tathāgata’s precious Dharma—now, through the skillful means of the World-Honored One, who observes the primordial limit (*pūrvakoṭi*) and the storehouse of the treasure of wisdom—he has cleared away our hunger and bestowed upon us the Great and Sublime Seal.
"Indeed, Great Sage, now that you have reached old age, this Mahākāśyapa has received the seal of the Tathāgata at dawn; he shall soon attain the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

Furthermore, World-Honored One, you have manifested for us the meaning of the wisdom of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas. We, your followers, shall perform [this teaching] and preach the Dharma for the assembly, so as to manifest the holy brilliance and great virtue of the Tathāgata, causing all to thoroughly enter into the meaning of the timely [teachings]."

Why is this? The Hero of the World, possessed of great penetration and skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), knows that my aspirations do not yet comprehend the profound Dharma; therefore, he manifests as a *śrāvaka*. Fearing the phenomena of the triple world (*tridhātu*) and birth, old age, and death, as well as the matters of form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch, he seeks only his own deliverance and does not save all beings. Devoid of great compassion, wisdom, and skillful means, he understands the minds of others through meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and samādhi, yet he does not perceive the fundamental capacities of the roots of all sentient beings.
It is like a destitute man seeking clothing and food, while his father waits for him, desiring to bring him peace and happiness, yet the son fails to perceive it.
The Buddha, through skillful means, manifests himself according to the occasion, yet we do not awaken to it.
Now I know for myself that I am a true son of the Buddha, an unsurpassed grandson whom the Buddha cherishes, and upon whom he bestows great wisdom. Why is this?

Although I am a son of the Buddha who is lowly, base, and timid, if the Tathāgata perceives my heart’s faith and delight in the Bodhisattva vehicle, only then will he preach the Great Dharma of the Vaipulya sūtras.

"Furthermore, the World-Honored One acts for two purposes: to manifest the Dharma of ambrosia for the sake of all bodhisattvas, and to further exhort those of inferior capacity and small aspirations to enter into the profound and subtle meaning."
It is like a son who has been separated from his father for a long time; while traveling, he sees him from afar but does not recognize him, and calling out in fear, he is startled.
Only later, as the father gradually displays his dignified bearing and proper conduct, does the son realize it is his father.

The Buddha is also like this: we do not understand how these Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, though born from the Dharma as sons of the Tathāgata, seek only their own extinction and do not set their minds upon the site of enlightenment to sit beneath the tree, subdue the hosts of Māra, and deliver all beings.

"We considered ourselves to have already attained liberation; for this reason, what we have seen and heard today has not brought us fulfillment. We have not truly left the household life, nor have we become śramaṇas."

Now that the Honored Tathāgata has manifested all supernormal powers and wisdom, we have obtained the precious jewels of the Great Sage; the Buddha is our father and we are his sons—since father and son share the same essence, how could there be any distinction?

It is just as when a householder, at the time of his death, issues a proclamation before a great assembly of kings, brahmins, householders, and gentlemen, saying: "All the treasures and precious jewels currently held in my storehouses are now bestowed upon this son. Upon hearing this, the son rejoices, experiencing something he has never known before.

As for those who speak of sensory opposition (*sapratigha*), such people do not believe.
If there were a skilled physician who examined the fundamental illness of a person, why would they be sightless?
It is because of the seeds sown by fundamental transgressions, which produce the blindness of ignorance and the grave illness of a tumor upon the body of the luminous essence.
What are called the grave illnesses?
Wind, cold, heat, and chronic disorders—these are the four illnesses.
Then, he thought to himself:
"The illness of this person cannot be cured by any ordinary medicine.
On the Snowy Mountains there is a medicine capable of curing four ailments:
the first is called Manifest, the second Excellent, the third Luminous, and the fourth Peaceful; these are the four names of this medicine."

At that time, the skilled physician, out of compassion for the sick man, devised a skillful means and immediately entered the Snowy Mountains. There he gathered four kinds of medicinal herbs, which he chewed, ground, and compounded together to treat the man's blindness; his eyes were then restored to clear vision.

Furthermore, by applying acupuncture and the techniques of regulation, supplementation, and depletion, this person’s vision will become completely clear both internally and externally; they will behold the light of the sun and moon, the five colors, and the ten directions, and only then will they gain conviction.
He immediately reproached himself, saying:
"In my blindness and ignorance, I had seen and heard nothing, yet I considered myself enlightened.
Now that my eyes can see, I realize for the first time the extreme depth of my original folly and obscuration."
"Now, looking at those far and near, high and low, there is none who can be compared to me.

At that time, there was a seer dwelling in seclusion who possessed the five supernatural powers; he could see through and hear clearly, his body could fly, and his mind could know the thoughts of others. He knew for himself the beginning and end of his own cycle of birth and death, and spoke thus:
"Do not be arrogant and consider yourself enlightened. You remain within your house, shut away and not venturing out, ignorant of external affairs."
When a person reflects on another’s good or evil deeds, they cannot yet perceive them;
the sound of speech ten or fifteen li away, or even the sound of a drum twenty li away, one still cannot hear;
and as for being within one or two li, even without taking a single step, one cannot reach it.
If you cannot even recognize what you recalled while in the womb before birth,
how can you claim to have such penetration that nothing remains unseen?
Now, as I examine your body, that which is dark within becomes bright, and that which is bright within becomes dark.
The man asked: "By what method or artifice can one attain such holy penetration?
I pray that you will deign to grant me wise instruction."
The seer replied, "You must enter the deep mountains to dwell in solitude and seclusion; only by eliminating all sensual desires will you achieve success.
He then followed this instruction, abandoning his home to live as a hermit in the crags. With single-minded devotion and free from any longing for pleasure, he attained supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*).

Thereupon he attained self-awakening and examined what he had previously perceived; he realized that it was insufficient even to be called by a name. Now that he has attained the five supernormal powers (pañcābhijñā) without any obstruction, he finally understands for himself that his former perceptions were shrouded in darkness.
The Buddha said:

"In this way, you should understand this parable: when a person within the five realms of birth and death is shrouded by the veils of the aggregates (*skandha*) and does not realize their fundamental non-existence, this is called delusion."

From ignorance arise volitional formations; from volitional formations arises consciousness; from consciousness arises name-and-form; from name-and-form arise the six sense bases; from the six sense bases arises contact; from contact arises feeling; from feeling arises craving; from craving arises clinging; from clinging arises becoming; from becoming arises birth; and from birth arise old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair. Because these evils thus accumulate, it is called "blind darkness."
For this reason, the World-Honored One takes pity on those people who ascend and descend within the three realms, revolving without end and unable to extricate themselves.

Observing the fundamental nature of the minds of sentient beings, he perceives that illnesses vary in severity, defilements vary in thickness, understandings vary in difficulty, and insights vary in depth; thus, he reveals the Three Vehicles. Some give rise to the bodhicitta and reach the stage of non-retrogression; others attain Buddhahood directly through the path of non-arising, like those with eyes who become immortal seers.
The skilled physician is the Tathāgata.
One who does not give rise to the great resolve is one born blind.
Greed, lust, hatred, ignorance, and the sixty-two views are the four diseases.
Emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness are the gates leading toward Nirvāṇa; these are called the four medicines.

When the administration of medicine brings about the healing of the disease, there is no longer delusion, and ignorance, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, sensation, craving, clinging, existence, birth, and the suffering of old age, sickness, death, grief, lamentation, and affliction are all completely eliminated.

Their aspiration is neither directed toward doing good nor toward evil; they are like those born blind who have regained their two eyes. This refers to the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, whose birth and death have been severed and who have crossed beyond the three realms, having scrutinized and mastered the five destinies. They consider themselves to have attained thorough understanding, such that nothing can be used to illustrate it.

As he was about to enter parinirvāṇa, the Buddha stood before him and instructed him with the essential Dharma, causing him to resolve upon the mind of a bodhisattva: "Do not abide in saṃsāra, nor dwell in nirvāṇa; understand that the three realms are empty. All things in the ten directions are like transformations and illusions, like dreams, mirages, and echoes in deep mountains—they are entirely non-existent and free from longing. There is nothing to grasp and nothing to abandon; there is neither darkness nor light. Only then does one deeply perceive, reaching everywhere yet seeing nothing seen, perceiving and knowing all the various beings and their nascent conditions."
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Just as the radiance of the sun shines, illuminating the entire world,
its brilliance neither increases nor decreases, nor does it discriminate between the beautiful and the ugly."
The Tathāgata is just like this: his wisdom is equal to and surpasses that of the sun and moon;
he universally transforms beings throughout the ten directions, yet there is neither increase nor decrease.
It is as if a potter were to mold clay to fashion earthenware vessels.
Some are filled with ambrosial honey, others receive ghee and oil for food;
though the clay is fundamentally of one kind, the vessels are each distinct.
What they receive is likewise different, and names are established based on what is contained within.
Human beings are likewise fundamentally thus: there are no three realms or five paths;
they follow their actions and are reborn accordingly, transmigrating without self-awareness.
Those who understand emptiness are called Bodhisattvas; those who abide in the middle are Pratyekabuddhas.
Relying on emptiness without understanding wisdom is what is called being a śrāvaka.
Like a person born blind who does not see the light of the sun and moon,
the five colors, or the ten directions, and thus claims that these do not exist in the world.
The skilled physician probes the root cause and perceives the four diseases and the veils of darkness;
out of compassion and pity for them, he enters the mountains to seek medicine.
The medicine he gathers is wondrous and marvelous, renowned as Excellent, Bright, and Peaceful.
Chewing and pounding the ingredients together, he prepared a remedy for those born blind;
by adjusting his treatments and applying acupuncture, their illnesses were cured and their eyes regained sight.
Seeing the sun, the moon, and the five colors, they finally realized how fundamentally ignorant they had been.
People do not understand that there is no fundamental basis, And thus they sit fallen upon the path of birth and death.
Bound by the twelve links of dependent origination, They do not comprehend the disease of beginning and end.
The World-Honored One appeared in the world To observe the source of the three realms.
According to their illnesses, one follows their fundamental dispositions and transforms each accordingly.
One who realizes emptiness is a bodhisattva; one whose mind is inferior becomes a pratyekabuddha.
Because they fear and loathe the suffering of birth and death, they fall to the level of a śrāvaka.
He considers himself of such lofty virtue that none can surpass him;
his insight is so thoroughly refined that he has no anxieties, defects, or obstructions.
He is like one who possesses the five supernormal powers, known by the name of a *ṛṣi*.
He took pity on him and said: "Your Majesty, you still possess obscurations and hindrances, such that you cannot fathom what is vast and profound. To the ignorant, you appear wise;
yet because you do not see what lies within yourself, though you seem wise, you are in fact ignorant."
At a distance of several tens of li there is a sound, yet the ear cannot hear it;
if someone intends to cause harm, one does not know what they are thinking.
When wishing to go several li outside, one cannot reach the destination without taking steps.
When one has grown to adulthood, one no longer remembers the events within the womb.
Only when the five faculties have penetrated both internally and externally does one become a Siddhārtha;
why then do you tolerate such arrogance, claiming yourself to be without equal?
Those who wish to attain the five supernormal powers should dwell in seclusion, contemplating with focused mindfulness on the Way; thus can one come to understand this.
Thereupon, following the instruction he had received, he left his home and entered the deep mountains.
With a single mind free from defiled thoughts, one may immediately become an immortal.
If one attains the stage of a śrāvaka or achieves the vehicle of a pratyekabuddha,
considering oneself to be fully endowed with wisdom and equal to the Buddha in nirvāṇa—
As he was about to enter parinirvāṇa, the Buddha stood before him and manifested for him the Dharma of the Bodhisattvas:
the three types of perfect knowledge free from obstruction,
the perfection of wisdom, and the advancement of skillful means.
Having transcended emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, the Bodhisattva is born from this.
Through the four immeasurable minds and the four debts of gratitude, they transform and enlighten the masses;
they understand that all things are like illusions, like phantoms, dreams, mirages, and reflections.
In the deep mountains, the sound of the *bābā* palm echoes; in the three realms, nothing exists.
There is neither grasping nor abandoning, neither delusion nor clarity, neither birth-and-death nor nirvāṇa—all are entirely equal to empty space.
Without seeing and without not-seeing, one beholds the fundamental source of all things.
At that moment of vision, one does not construct views of the three realms;
all things are universally equal, and those delivered are beyond measure.

6. Chapter on Bestowing Predictions upon the Śrāvakas. From the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, Chapter Six: "Bestowing Predictions upon the Śrāvakas. Now, as the World-Honored One was speaking these verses, he addressed the entire assembly of bhikṣus:

“I declare to you all: this śrāvaka bhikṣu Mahākāśyapa has already made offerings to three hundred billion buddhas, and shall likewise make offerings to as many as previously mentioned. Having served, honored, and followed these Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, he has received the True Dharma and upheld its practice. When this number is completed, he shall become a Buddha. His world shall be named Pratyudgata-āloka (Returning Light), and his kalpa shall be named Mahā-vipula (Vast and Great). He shall be known as the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-sampanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān, named Mahā-prabhāsa (Great Radiance). His lifespan shall be twelve intermediate kalpas.”
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma shall remain for twenty kalpas, and its Semblance Dharma shall likewise remain for twenty kalpas.

That buddha-field will be exceedingly pure, free from pebbles, thorns, brambles, impurities, or defects; it will be devoid of mountains, hills, or mountain torrents.
