It will be universally and greatly blissful, with ground of deep-blue lapis lazuli and trees made of various jewels. Golden cords will connect the rows of trees, which intersect at eight points. These jewel-trees will always bear flowers and fruit, all of them flourishing and luxuriant.
In that land, there are incalculable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of bodhisattvas, and the śrāvakas are likewise immeasurable in their hundreds of thousands of millions of billions.
In that land, there are no demonic activities nor any of their retinues; all the hosts of Māras protect the Buddha-dharma, constantly practicing with diligence without any transgression or failure.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to explain the meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"With my Buddha-eye, I behold this bhikṣu; Kāśyapa dwells here and shall become a Buddha."
Making offerings to all Buddhas, the most honored among saints, fully and completely fulfilling three thousand billion Buddhas;
one shall then transcend and cross over the three grades of practice and shall attain the Way of the Buddha.
By drawing near to the gift of Dharma and making offerings to the Buddhas, the Honored Ones of gods and men,
one shall gather these merits and attain the unsurpassed Great Way.
In the future age, he shall be the most honored among those peerless, becoming a Great Sage on the Path, an Infinite Immortal.
His Buddha-land shall be the most excellent and foremost, pure and free from defilement, radiant in various ways;
according to one's desires, it shall always be accessible through a sincere heart.
Of the color of purple-polished gold, adorned with rare jewels;
furthermore, with rare jewels forming trees, there are various pathways, strictly laid out as eight-fold intersections.
Gods and humans release fragrances, which naturally flow as sweet scents. At that time, the land—
All such flowers as these, of the color of purple-polished gold, emit light and sound as their natural law;
they are universally and eternally subtle and wondrous, such that there is none who does not behold them.
The assembly of bodhisattvas, numbering in the billions, their minds disciplined and settled,
have attained great supernormal powers; incalculable,
numbering in the hundreds of thousands of koṭis, they are free from all outflows.
Upholding [the Dharma] with resolute will;
even if one possessed divine vision and sought to calculate the limits of kalpas, the number of disciples could not be reckoned.
The True Dharma shall remain for twenty intermediate kalpas, and the Semblance Dharma shall likewise endure for twenty intermediate kalpas.
Such shall be the virtue of the Buddha Mahāprabha.

Thereupon, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the Venerable Subhūti, and the Venerable Mahākātyāyana, with one mind, stood to one side with heads bowed in reverence; gazing upon his radiant countenance with unblinking eyes, they prostrated at his feet with trembling awe and, at that moment, each spoke these verses in praise, exclaiming:
“The Great Hero, free from attachment, The King of Śākyas, the peerless man, Out of compassion for us, Proclaims the Buddha’s voice in praise.”
Now that you know us, you have compassionately bestowed upon us our respective prophecies;
we have been sprinkled with the nectar of immortality and bathed in the resolution of the World-Honored One’s blessings.
It is like a man in a time of famine who has obtained a fine meal.
Emaciated and crying out in search, someone handed us food from their own hands.
We were all filled with joy; though we were originally of inferior capacity, we had left the multitude behind at the wrong time, and in our exhaustion, we could not find resolution.
Even if he were to attain equal enlightenment, the Great Sage would not bestow it by prostration;
yet now, while dwelling among the ranks of the world, he no longer partakes of food or drink.
The World-Honored One saw and exhorted him, and he heard the voice of the Most Honorable One.
Only by being granted a prediction of enlightenment can you attain great peace.
O Greatly Compassionate One, please dispel our doubts; out of pity, have mercy on us who are so many.
With a mind that consoles the poor and destitute, lead us, your children, with the nectar of the Dharma.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One, perceiving the thoughts and intentions in the minds of the elders, again addressed the assembly of bhikṣus:

“Bhikṣus, you should know that this senior Great Śrāvaka, Subhūti, shall serve and make offerings to eight thousand three hundred billion nayutas of Buddhas. Under those Buddhas, he will constantly cultivate the holy life (brahmacarya), accumulating merit until it reaches ultimate fulfillment. When his final lifetime arrives, he shall attain Buddhahood, known by the titles Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, and Bhagavat. His world shall be named Ratnasaṃbhava, and the kalpa shall be called Ratnaruta.”

Throughout the entire circumference of all Buddha-lands, there were various jewel trees naturally adorned, free from sand, gravel, stones, mountains, hills, streams, or ravines. The sounds from those trees were mournful yet harmonious, gentle and elegant; the wealth and livelihoods of the multitudes were beyond counting, and the dwellings where people resided consisted of various types of halls and pavilions, with multi-storied towers and latticed balconies.
There is an infinite multitude of śrāvakas, such that no one could calculate their number; they all possess the knowledge of past lives.
The bodhisattvas in that land are likewise beyond reckoning—billions, trillions, hundreds of thousands.

That Buddha’s lifespan shall be twelve intermediate kalpas; after his parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma shall remain for twenty intermediate kalpas, and the Semblance Dharma shall likewise endure for twenty intermediate kalpas. Then, seated in the void, he will preach the sutras and the Dharma for all people, transforming and enlightening countless hundreds of thousands of bodhisattvas.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Now I announce to all, the assembly of bhikṣus: listen all clearly to what the Buddha proclaims."
Venerable Subhūti, this disciple of mine shall, in a future age, attain the state of a Buddha.
This is true and not false; he shall be fully endowed with thirty thousand *nayuta-koti* [of qualities].
He shall, within the world, follow and cultivate the path of practice, always setting his mind upon seeking this.
The essential path of the Buddha:
his countenance is exceptionally wondrous, endowed with the thirty-two marks; his majestic radiance is lofty and sublime, his form like purple-polished gold.
Abiding in the world in purity, he is filled with great compassion.
The lands are blissful, appearing wherever they may be; countless people behold them and leap for joy with satisfaction.
They shall all travel forth to visit the World-Honored Ones, delivering and liberating hundreds of thousands of millions of beings.
Incalculable and yet constantly expounded at length, the non-retrogressive wheel within the most supreme teaching—
those whose faculties are keen and sharp shall all be reverent and compliant.
In that Buddha-land, the matters concerning the śrāvakas are immeasurable;
were one to wish to calculate them with limits, no one could reach their ultimate end.
Having attained great supernormal power (*ṛddhi*), liberated from the gates of obstruction, and dwelling in peace and security,
the power of their supernormal faculties is inconceivable.
The Buddhas, the Honored Ones of the Path, and the devas and humans, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
should always join their palms in reverence and take refuge in the Holy Honored One.
The True Dharma shall remain for twelve intermediate kalpas;
the Semblance Dharma shall likewise endure for twenty intermediate kalpas; and for twenty intermediate kalpas, the World Hero, the Guide—such are the kalpa-counts.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the assembly of bhikṣus:
"The bhikṣu who wishes to know the essential distinction of firm grasping and equanimity is my śrāvaka Mahākātyāyana."

In the future, you shall serve and make offerings to eight thousand billion Buddhas. After each Buddha has passed into parinirvāṇa, you shall erect for them stūpas and temples four thousand li in height, and two thousand li in both length and breadth; all shall be composed of the seven treasures—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, musaragalva, agate, coral, and green jade—and adorned with incense, flowers, blended perfumes, powdered incenses, silken banners, streamers, and pennants.

After passing beyond this number, you shall again make offerings to twenty billion buddhas; thereafter, in a future age, you shall attain buddhahood, with the name *Pratyāgatāmaragauravarṇa Tathāgata*, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavat.

The land is adorned and pure, impartial and free from depravity; its fame is manifest, and its ground is made of lapis lazuli. It is embellished with various kinds of trees and many jewels, with cords of purple-golden sandalwood strung together. The trees are lush with abundant flowers and fruits, and their blossoms spread everywhere.
In that buddha-field there are no hells, hungry ghosts, or animals; it is instead filled and teeming with many devas and humans.
Furthermore, it is adorned by incalculable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of śrāvakas and incalculable hundreds of thousands of bodhisattvas.

That Buddha’s lifespan shall be ten small kalpas; after his parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma shall remain for twenty intermediate kalpas, and the Semblance Dharma shall likewise remain for twenty intermediate kalpas.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"O assembly of bhikṣus, listen all to my instruction.
The Buddha’s voice shall be beautiful and gentle; The Venerable Kātyāyana shall become a disciple of the Buddha."
When making offerings to the Buddhas, those various Teachers, one should serve, revere, and comply with them with immeasurable respect and diligence;
the countless people of the world cannot calculate [the merit thereof].
If, after his parinirvāṇa, one should erect temples and monasteries,
and offer him flowers and incense,
then in a future age one shall attain Buddhahood; one’s buddha-field will be pure, free from all blemish or defilement.
He shall preach and inspire, fully guiding and instructing billions of sentient beings and all the people of the world.
Adorning the world with his radiance that illuminates the ten directions, he shall attain Buddhahood,
surpassing many analogies.
His name is Purple-Golden Color; his virtue is majestic and sublime. He brings ultimate fulfillment to the masses—billions, hundreds of thousands, and myriads.
Countless bodhisattvas and śrāvakas fill his buddha-field, immeasurable and beyond calculation.
"Constantly practice diligence regarding the teachings of the Buddha-Dharma; sever all obstacles and extinguish the afflictions of beginningless and endless existence.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One again addressed the assembly of the fourfold community, saying:

"Now the Buddha, the Great Sage, proclaims to you all: This is my śrāvaka, the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, who shall provide full offerings and service to eight thousand Buddhas, following and obeying all the immeasurable World-Honored Ones."

When the various Buddhas pass into extinction, one should erect stupas and temples, fashioned from the seven treasures—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, musaragalva, agate, coral, and pearl—fourteen thousand *li* in height and twenty thousand *li* in length and breadth. With various exquisite objects made of many kinds of jewels, one should make offerings to these stupas and temples, as well as providing incense, flowers, blended perfumes, powdered incenses, silken banners, flowered canopies, pennants, and the delights of music.
After this number has passed, you shall again revere and honor two hundred trillion buddhas, making offerings to them and following their teachings with obedience.

In your final lifetime, you shall attain buddhahood, named Huanyijin Huan Jinhua Candanakhya Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavat. Your land shall be named Iṣṭā, and the eon shall be called Sukhaparipūrṇa.

That Buddha-world is joyful, peaceful, pure, and pristine; its ground is composed of deep blue lapis lazuli, and its trees—with their flowers and fruits—are formed from the seven treasures. It is universally adorned with pearls and various blossoms, and is uniformly majestic and complete with all manner of jewels.
There will be hundreds of thousands of millions of great sages and saints sitting in silent meditation, known as the "Immeasurable.
All these bodhisattvas shall extensively expound the Dharma of the sutras.

That Buddha’s lifespan shall be twenty intermediate kalpas; after his parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma (Saddharma) shall remain for forty intermediate kalpas, including the period of the Semblance Dharma (Pratirūpaka-dharma).
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“Mahāmaudgalyāyana, this disciple of mine, having cast aside benevolent conduct,
yet still attains mastery.”
For two hundred trillion kalpas, one should provide offerings to all these Buddhas;
universally practicing the pure conduct (brahmacarya) toward all Buddhas, one should set one’s aspiration upon this path of the Buddhas.
One should serve all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, attending to them with complete devotion.
One should widely and universally uphold the teachings of the Guides for many hundreds of millions of kalpas,
through hundreds of thousands of such reckonings, serving and following them with earnest diligence.
Not transgressing the Great Command, those who dwell in peace and so forth,
using the seven kinds of precious jewels, erected stupas and temples, performing supreme deeds for the sake of all the Most Victorious Ones.
Using sandalwood incense to form its pillars and beams, and offering various fragrances and music as worship;
when these tasks were completed, his speech was elegant and brilliant, such that he was revered by all people and moved many with compassion.
Because he acted in this manner, he shall attain Buddhahood.
His name shall be Suvarṇacandana.
That Buddha’s lifespan shall last for twenty intermediate kalpas; such shall be his abiding and his conduct and virtue.
When he shall become a bodhisattva, he will expound the sutras and the Dharma; throughout these kalpas, he will analyze their refined meanings.
His most excellent śrāvakas shall be innumerable thousands, numbering in the hundreds of millions, like the sands of the Ganges.
Possessing the six supernormal powers and the threefold penetration, they have attained great spiritual mastery; while abiding in this world, they have achieved wondrous transcendence.
Countless bodhisattvas are all non-retrogressive, diligent and courageous, possessing resolve and wisdom.
Practicing as is appropriate, following these teachings of the Buddha, they shall be beyond measure, numbering in the thousands.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, his disciples will study much; the True Dharma shall remain and spread throughout the ten directions.
The True Dharma and the Semblance Dharma shall endure for forty intermediate kalpas; when the True Dharma has completely vanished, the Semblance Dharma will then appear.
These śrāvakas of the Buddha, having attained great supernormal powers, were all exhorted by the Buddha to establish themselves in the Great Honored Way.
Relying upon the Great Sage, not deviating from the True Dharma, in a future age, one shall attain the sovereignty of Buddhahood.
*Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, Scroll Three;
*Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, Scroll Four.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Yuezhi Nation during the Western Jin Dynasty. Chapter Seven: The Past.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"In the distant past, in an incalculable and immeasurable number of kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, World-Honored One. His world was called Mahāvyūha, and the kalpa was named Varṇāvabhāsa."

The sutras preached by that Buddha are beyond measure and limit. For example, suppose there were a man who took all the land within this trichiliocosm and crushed this entire buddha-field until it was like fine dust; then, taking a single grain of dust, he would pass through as many worlds in the eastern direction as there are grains of dust in a thousand buddha-fields, and there he would set down one grain of dust.

Proceeding in this manner, take another mote of dust and, having crossed as many Buddha-fields to the east as there are motes of dust in the aforementioned number, place that mote there. Continue until all the motes of dust within the trichiliocosm have been exhausted, leaving none remaining, and thus fill the eastern direction entirely. Proceed in this same manner through immeasurable Buddha-lands.
"What do you think?
Is it possible to measure or limit the boundaries of the realms of all Buddhas?
The bhikṣu replied:
"No, World-Honored One! No."
"Abide in peace! The Buddha said to the bhikṣu:

"The number of such buddha-fields is vast and remote; it is as if someone were to take up dust grains one by one and place them in those various buddha-fields until they reached a certain limit. Even the dust of all those buddha-lands would be immeasurable. For hundreds of thousands of koṭis, nayutas, and kalpas, if one wished to know the length of time since that Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, it would be inconceivable, immeasurable, and unfathomable. The manifestation of the power of the Way of Great Universal Wisdom, and the number of kalpas during which the Dharma remains after his parinirvāṇa, are likewise so."
The World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"I recall the past, Countless billions of kalpas ago, When there was a Tathāgata,
the Honored One among two-legged beings, Named Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, Of infinite compassion and benevolence."
At that time, the World-Honored One, before the multitude, took this buddha-world as an analogy:
he completely shattered it, reducing it all to dust.
Suppose there were a person who, taking up a single atom at a time, passed through a thousand Buddha-fields before placing that one atom down;
proceeding in this manner through all the lands of the Honored Sages.
That person coats the dust, causing it to cover everything completely;
in such vast numbers, it is made to pervade everywhere, throughout the various limits of worlds that are beyond counting.
All that exists within the lands of the Great Sage— every single atom,
beyond measure— is entirely shattered until nothing remains.
The Great Sage, the Most Honored One, has passed away and come forth in this manner; that Buddha remains in peace, having already completed his parinirvāṇa.
Such are the kalpas, immeasurable billions in number; were one to attempt to calculate their limits, no one could conceive of them.
Since his parinirvāṇa, many kalpas have passed; that Guide of that time has been gone for so long.
Yet the assembly of disciples, as well as the bodhisattva practices and the wisdom of the Tathāgata, remain as majestic and sublime as this.
O bhikṣus, you who wish to know the Buddha’s wisdom: it is holy and luminous, universally pervasive, and equal without distinction.
The Buddha has fully awakened to it; throughout incalculable kalpas, he has not reckoned it as subtle or profound, for it is the meaning of the outflow-free (anāsrava).

The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus: “That Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū had a lifespan of forty-four billion hundred thousand kalpas. By means of the unsurpassed, right, and true path, he first ascended to the site of enlightenment and sat beneath a tree for one kalpa in silence; yet through a second kalpa he did not attain perfect awakening, continuing thus for up to ten kalpas. Without rising from his seat and without moving his body, his frame neither leaned nor tilted, and he harbored no self-conceptions. Being entirely free of discursive thought regarding all dharmas, he finally sat beneath the Bodhi tree, subdued the hosts of Māra’s officials, and was about to achieve perfect awakening.”
The sons of the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven manifested great lion thrones forty *li* on each side, upon which the Buddha sat.

Once the World-Honored One was seated, the Brahmā-sons rained down celestial flowers over a circumference of four thousand *li*, and a natural wind arose that blew and scattered the various flowers over the Buddha.
The Buddha remained beneath the tree for a full ten intermediate kalpas; celestial flowers fell profusely, continuing without ceasing throughout the entire kalpa.

Furthermore, the Four Heavenly Kings and the various devaputras performed manifold musical performances with sounds like the roll of thunder, constantly making offerings of flowers, incense, and music to the Great Sage, never once flagging or wearying.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"At that time, from when the World-Honored One, Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, attained unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment as the Most Perfectly Awakened One until his parinirvāṇa, [the king] made offerings without ceasing for ten kalpas."

When that Buddha was still at home and had not yet renounced his kingdom, while he was a crown prince, he had sixteen sons who were handsome and exceptionally beautiful, possessed wisdom beyond compare, and were foremost in appearance, refined, gentle, and harmonious.

At that time, each of the princes of the sixteen kingdoms possessed various kinds of musical instruments; the pleasure of their dwellings and excursions was beyond description, manifesting in manifold ways, and the lutes, harps, and performances were likewise immeasurable.

When he saw the Buddha, the World-Honored One, having attained supreme perfect enlightenment, there spontaneously arose a great sound of the Dharma. Immediately, he abandoned his kingdom, relinquished the rank of a wheel-turning monarch, his myriad subjects, music, and all pleasures of desire; surrounded by his retinue and accompanied by hundreds of thousands of noble and holy kings of great renown, as well as an incalculable multitude of billions of living beings gathered as attendants, he proceeded to the site of the Way where the World-Honored One resided, desiring to prostrate himself and reverently receive the Buddha’s teaching.
The entire assembly followed in unison, grave and reverent; they bowed their heads at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times, and withdrew to stand to one side. They then spoke in verse:
“Greatly Penetrating One of Universal Wisdom, Supremely Honored and Unsurpassed, You have accumulated impartial merit for immeasurable billions of eons.
With this most sublime meaning, you take pity upon all beings.”
His vows were fully realized among these noble sages.
For ten intermediate kalpas, he remained single-mindedly focused, seated in one place;
his body was pure and unwavering, burning away all sufferings and afflictions.
Like a tree uprooted, he neither advances nor retreats;
He neither leans nor slants, and there is no increase or decrease.
Responding in silence, he is ultimately tranquil and settled, Free from all outflows (*āsrava*).
Now auspicious and always attaining great peace, because they are free from attachment and conceptualization, they have attained the honored path of Buddhahood.
We, seeing them, increase in wisdom and fearlessness; through such examples, our virtue and righteousness are long increased.
Disregarding body and life, they sever all suffering and affliction; accumulating patience, they do not crave ease or pleasure.
Discerning the wisdom of the Path, they do not dwell in distress or pain;
dwelling in seclusion, they arouse diligent effort.
Through the long night, they increase their offenses in the evil realms;
thus they lose their human form and fall into the miserable destinies, becoming objects of slander and defamation by all the world.
Now that I have come to behold the Sage Father of the world, whose Way is supreme and free from all outflows;
in this world, he provides protection and refuge, as do the Great Sages and Guides of the past.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

“These kings and their crown princes—the princes and their brothers being still young in years—uttered sighs of praise and extolled the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū. Having finished proclaiming this refined eulogy, they entreated the World-Honored One, wishing for him to preach the Dharma with analytical exposition, so as to bring peace and stability to many, to show compassion to many, to benefit sentient beings, and to settle all devas and humans.”
Furthermore, he praised him with this verse, saying:
“I only pray that the Great Sage will expound the scriptures, transforming and enlightening all beings and inspiring the common people.”
The multitudes of sentient beings in the three realms all look up with thirsty longing, so that they may establish the aspiration for the Way and all be granted deliverance.
The Buddhas, the universal Great Sages, are adorned with the Dharma of a hundred blessings;
having attained the state of the Infinite Immortals, their wisdom is most supreme and wondrous.
He preaches the Dharma for the devas and for the people of the world;
may he deliver beings such as ourselves and extend his grace to all living creatures.
May the meaning of the Tathāgata’s wisdom be revealed at this opportune moment.
Just as here and now, you manifest and guide us toward the supreme, honored Way;
causing all classes of beings, including ourselves,
to obtain this Dharma and fully understand the beginning and end of the wisdom of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
He explains them all through detailed analysis— the virtues practiced in previous lives,
the universal perceptions and cognitions of sentient beings, and the fundamental inclinations of their hearts.
Thus he turns the wheel of Dharma, the most supreme and peerless.
"Exert yourselves to deliver sentient beings from their distress, and cause them all to reach the Great Way.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"At that time, the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, manifested transformations throughout the worlds of the ten directions. Each of the fifty billion hundred thousand buddha-lands shook in six ways; his radiance shone everywhere without exception. Within the realms of all the Buddhas, the various kinds of brilliant light of the great deities of space, the far-reaching brilliance of the sun and moon, the peerless splendor of the celestial palaces and dwellings, and the natural majestic radiance of the Brahmā heavens—all were eclipsed by the auspicious light of the Buddha’s manifestations, such that they were entirely obscured and made to disappear."

In the heavens and the world, there was a brilliant and radiant splendor; when beings of various classes were born into that realm, they all saw one another and recognized each other, saying to themselves:
"Today, suddenly, someone has been born here, and the manifestations that have shaken the heavens have pervaded everywhere."
"At that time, in the boundless hundreds of thousands of millions of Brahma palaces at the edge of the Buddha-lands in the eastern direction, a natural radiance appeared, majestic and towering.
The various Brahmas thought to themselves:
'The countless Brahma palaces, temples, and mansions are brilliantly illuminated, reaching everywhere. What auspicious omen is there that has caused this transformation to appear?'"
At that time, hundreds of thousands of millions of great Brahmā deities from five hundred worlds gathered together, assembling like clouds from their respective palaces.
Among the assembly was a great Brahmā named Guardian of Living Beings, who, for the sake of the Brahmās, uttered this eulogy:
"Today, we, our palaces and dwellings— O worthy ones, you should know!"
This great radiance, supreme among all devas, is what their minds delight in.
By what causes and conditions does this auspicious omen appear?
"Excellent! You should go and seek the meaning of this.
At that time, the sons of the gods thought to themselves:
"By what holy intent has he arisen today? Why does he manifest such divine power? What is it that we now behold?"
This is truly unprecedented: that you have drawn near to the various devas and become a king among men.
Could it be that a Great Sage has arisen in the world?
His most wondrous radiance illuminates the ten directions; that his transformations and movements should be such as this!
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"At that time, five hundred worlds of hundreds of thousands of koṭis of Brahmā devas all came together from the east, harmonizing their voices. From afar they saw the Tathāgata, the Samyaksaṃbuddha Mahāsāgaraprabhāsa-vidyuddeśa, seated upon a lion throne at the site of enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree."

The devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans, together with their sixteen sons and retinues, having beheld this, all joined in exhorting him, desiring that he preach the sūtra.

He immediately went before the Tathāgata and prostrated himself on the ground, circumambulating the Buddha countless times. Holding his lotus flower, which was as large as Mount Sumeru, he scattered it over the Buddha’s tree, which stood forty *li* high; he also brought forth the palaces of the Brahmā heavens from his own land and presented them to the World-Honored One, praying: "I only wish that you would compassionately accept these offerings of palaces, flowers, and lands."
He praised him in verse, saying:
“Beholding the Buddha’s immeasurability, I have attained what I never had before;
Moved by great compassion, He has arisen in this world.”
What the World-Honored One has proclaimed is like the lion’s roar; thus he has already protected the common people of the ten directions.
We have traveled from where we came, five hundred billion worlds away from here.
Calculated across all worlds, beings of various kinds have all abandoned their palaces and halls to go together to the Holy Honored One; all of them, by virtue of the pure merit of their past lives,
possess various exquisite and wondrous palaces made of many jewels.
"May you deign to look upon us and dwell within this place; we pray that you will arouse great compassion and take pity on us by accepting it.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"At that time, the assembly of Great Brahmā deities praised the Buddha face-to-face, and five hundred of them together addressed the World-Honored One, saying:"
"May you turn the wheel of Dharma and expound the great sacred scriptures, diligently delivering all sentient beings so that they may attain nirvana.
At that time, five hundred Brahmās and a multitude of hundreds of thousands of billions joined their voices in a single sound, praising him with this verse:
"World-Honored One, we pray you preach the sutra, O Supreme among the Two-Legged Beings, distinguish it clearly."
"I shall now manifest the power of compassion, To deliver all beings from their diligent toil and suffering.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"At that time, the World-Honored One, seeing the palaces offered by the Brahmā devas, accepted them in silence."

At that time, in the southeast, five hundred billion hundreds of thousands of worlds away, the assemblies of Brahmā devas each saw from their respective palaces a brilliant radiance, shimmering and dazzling, pervading everywhere; they marveled at this unprecedented occurrence.
They all assembled together. Within that assembly was a Great Brahmā Heaven-ruler named Most Compassionate, who praised them in verse for the sake of all the Brahmās:
"O Great Devas, you should know: This is indeed a primordial auspicious omen;
The palaces are all shaken, And the most renowned fame spreads abroad."
The sons of heaven, endowed with virtue, have gathered here from every quarter like clouds;
it is by their majestic spiritual power that these palaces are made so lofty.
Now the Buddha has appeared in the world, the most honored among those who possess two feet.
This is why our dwellings manifest such radiance.
We must go to inquire about this; it cannot be false.
From antiquity until now, we have never beheld an auspicious omen like this.
"A radiance shines forth in the four directions, reaching across billions of lands;
now that there is fixed sincerity, a Buddha shall surely appear in the world.

The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "At that time, five hundred billion hundreds of thousands of Brahmā devas each emerged in succession from their palaces. Carrying celestial flowers as vast as Mount Sumeru, they proceeded to the northwest corner. From afar they beheld the Tathāgata, possessed of great pervasive holy wisdom, dwelling at the site of enlightenment, seated upon a lion throne beneath the Bodhi tree."
Surrounded by a retinue of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas, he preached the Dharma for them.
Having seen the Buddha, he immediately approached, prostrated himself upon the ground, and circumambulated him countless times, scattering great flowers from his hands over the Buddha.
At that time, Mahābrahmā and his retinue praised him in verse, saying:
“Homage to the Peerless One, The Great Sage, The God among Gods.”
His voice is like the mournful cry of the phoenix; as he leads and guides, he universally protects all devas and humans—may we prostrate ourselves before him in worship.

He takes pity on the mundane world, having attained what has never been known before; difficult to encounter anywhere, we have long yearned for his radiant countenance, and today at last we behold it.
Based on a hundred kalpas, he has accumulated merit and realized emptiness; under eighty billion Buddhas, his lifespan was as vast as atoms of kalpas.
Furthermore, as the Honored One among men, he discerns the wisdom of emptiness and constantly expounds upon skillful means.
The various devas, ministers, and people were able to behold him; they numbered in the full billions and eighty millions.
With eyes that see through all, he provides relief wherever it is needed and offers extensive protection within the Dharma of the Buddha-way.
"Therefore he has appeared in the world out of compassion for the multitude; this assembly of our merit is exceedingly difficult to encounter.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"Countless billions of Brahmā deities exhorted the World-Honored One, wishing that he turn the wheel of Dharma, proclaim the sacred teachings to inform all living beings, and rescue those in the three realms so that they may attain peace and security."
At that time, all the Brahmā deities, with minds entirely equal and in unison, praised him, saying:
“O Supreme Great Being, we pray that you turn the wheel of Dharma; please preach the sūtras for the sake of the people of the ten directions.”
Delivering all living beings from the afflictions of suffering and distress, causing all people to leap for joy with boundless rapture;
those who hear this shall attain the Buddha-way, and all devas and humans alike shall receive peace and security.
"The bodies of the asuras shall further diminish; bestow upon them the practice of patience and the matter of peace and security.
Thus the Buddha told the bhikṣus:
The Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū remained silent, thereby granting his approval.

Then, throughout the hundreds of thousands of koṭis of Buddha-worlds in the south and west, the palaces and mansions of all the Great Brahmās were suffused with universal radiance; they shone brilliantly and resplendently, reaching everywhere without exception.
At that time, the various Brahmā devas saw that the majesty of their own palaces had undergone a transformation, becoming brilliantly radiant; they marveled at this unprecedented occurrence.
They all assembled together and each thought to themselves:
"Why have our palaces become like this?"
Within that assembly, there was a Great Brahmā named Sudharma, who alone uttered this eulogy:
"The Great Sage has arisen; what he raises is not in vain. All palaces are re-illuminated by his majestic radiance."
This auspicious omen appears in the world; how excellent it is that you seek such profound meaning!
Throughout countless billions of kalpas in the past, such a manifestation has never been seen.
"I shall cause the Tathāgata to appear in the world, so that all the sons of the gods will naturally come to this assembly.
The Buddha then addressed the bhikṣus:

At that time, five hundred trillion Brahmā devas, from their respective abodes, saw from afar a great flower as vast as Mount Sumeru. Each grasped various articles of offering and proceeded toward the north to behold the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū at his place of enlightenment, seated beneath a tree upon a lion throne, surrounded by an immeasurable multitude of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas, as he preached the Dharma.

He immediately went to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself upon the ground, and circumambulated him countless times. Holding great flowers as vast as Mount Sumeru in his hands, he scattered them as an offering over the Buddha.
He then offered his palace to the World-Honored One, praying only that the Buddha would take pity on him and accept it for his dwelling.
Then the Brahmā deities and others, with one mind and in unison, uttered this eulogy:
“The appearance of the Buddhas in the world is extremely difficult to encounter; having not beheld them for a long time, we behold them today at last.”
Having arrived by fortunate chance, they have cast off craving and desire, becoming fully perfected throughout the three thousandfold world-systems.
These great guides have satisfied the hunger and emptiness of beings; from antiquity until now, such a thing has never been seen or heard.
Like the auspicious *nirmāṇa* flower, which is rarely encountered, the wisdom of the Way is difficult to meet; it appears only from time to time.
Our palaces are exquisitely beautiful and immeasurable; by receiving the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, we have obtained this.
"Please deign to show great compassion and accept what we offer; we pray that you will abide therein and manifest the causes of the Way.

At that time, the Brahmā devas exhorted the World-Honored One, saying: "We pray only that you turn the wheel of Dharma and expound the scriptures, so that all gods, śramaṇas, and brahmins may be moved by your great pity, and all beings throughout the heavens and the world may universally find peace and receive your grace."
Thereupon, Brahmā, together with his retinue, with one mind and in unison, uttered this eulogy:
"May the World-Honored One, out of compassion, widely expound the scriptures;
may he turn the Great Wheel of the Dharma of the Sage."
Expounding various dharmas with a voice like the roll of thunder, we pray that you will take pity on us and blow the great Dharma conch.
With the Great Sūtras, let it rain upon the world; distinguish the excellent teachings and provide subtle, wondrous instructions.
“We exhort and assist you; we pray that you will expound the wisdom of the Way and deliver hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of sentient beings.
In the southwest, the northwest, and the northeast, it was likewise in each case, with countless Brahmā heavens beyond measure.
In the same manner above and below, throughout the sovereign palaces, they beheld the radiance reaching everywhere; it was a marvel never seen before.
From each of these directions, the multitudes of Brahmā devas from five hundred billion hundreds of thousands of worlds each abandoned their palaces and came to where the Buddha was.
There was a Great Brahmā named Sublime Consciousness (*Suviññāṇa*), who then uttered this verse of praise:
“Excellent! May all Buddhas, The Roarers in the World, attain holy wisdom;
For the sake of sentient beings in the three realms, May they reveal and teach the vehicle of perfect enlightenment.”
Universally serving as the eye of the world, He perceives clearly throughout the ten directions;
Opening the gateway to the nectar of immortality, He delivers and liberates countless beings.
In ages long past, The Honored One among Men manifested his transformations.
Empty, without thought or reflection, they manifest throughout the ten directions.
They increase their suffering in the hells for a long time, take pleasure in the realm of animals,
and later fall among the hungry ghosts— numbers beyond the reach of thought.
Having lost their celestial bodies, their lives ended and they fell into evil realms;
yet if they hear the Buddha-dharma, they will advance to attain the Path of Equanimity.
With resolve and practice directed toward the Buddha’s wisdom, they shall protect and sustain all the common people.
All shall attain peaceful security, never losing the perception of happiness.
Yet those who do not constantly practice the Buddha-way, who do not abide in the True Dharma,
and who violate the immeasurable holy teachings, will immediately fall into the evil realms.
Beholding the Light of the World, they have come here for the sake of goodness;
they awaken all sentient beings and practice loving-kindness and compassion.
Having encountered the World-Honored One, they understand the wisdom of emptiness that is free from outflows.
The devas and the world alike offer their full encouragement here;
with palaces of infinite excellence, corresponding to his majestic spiritual power,
they universally bestow moon-bright pearls— O Great Guide, we pray that you will accept them.
"O Honored among Men, we pray that you accept our offerings;
out of compassion, deign to enter our palace, so that these multitudes of beings may attain the unsurpassed path.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

At that time, an assembly of five hundred billion Great Brahmā deities, having praised the Buddha, entreated him to turn the great wheel of Dharma, to deliver and transform those in the ten directions, and to bring peace and security to all people in the world.
He further praised in verse:
“I aspire and pray that you will preach and expound the unsurpassed Wheel of Dharma; may the drum of the Dharma resound like thunder, and the sublime sound of the True Dharma be heard.”
To deliver sentient beings from the afflictions of toil and suffering, you manifest compassionately the unconditioned Great Way.
We exhort and assist you; O Sage, please preach the Dharma to rescue and protect other species as well as the people of the world.
“His voice is soft and gentle, spreading forth beautiful resonance; for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, he has accumulated virtuous conduct.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“At that time, the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, seeing the innumerable hundreds of thousands of billions of sentient beings in the ten directions entreating him to preach the Dharma,
as well as his sixteen sons— the princes and crown princes— turned the great wheel of Dharma with its three revolutions and twelve aspects,
thereby instructing, transforming, and inspiring śramaṇas, brahmins, devas, nāgas, spirits, and the multitudes.”
For Māra, Brahmā, and the people of the world, he explained that the root of suffering is the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*);

that through the accumulation [of causes], the cessation, and the path, suffering is exhausted; and that from the exhaustion of suffering comes the Path. He fully analyzed the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*):

from ignorance (*avidyā*) arise volitional formations (*saṃskāra*); from volitional formations arises consciousness (*vijñāna*); from consciousness arise name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); from name-and-form arise...
The six sense bases; from the six sense bases comes the accumulation of karma, from the accumulation of karma comes sensation,
from sensation comes craving, from craving comes grasping, from grasping comes becoming, from becoming comes birth, and from birth come old age, sickness, death, sorrow,
lamentation, and great suffering.
He further addressed the bhikṣus:

“The Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū preached the Dharma three times; in a mere moment, he analyzed this meaning, causing sixteen billion koṭis of beings to exhaust their outflows and attain liberation of mind, to achieve the six supernormal powers and the wisdom of the three types of omniscience, and enabling innumerable people to all attain deliverance.”

Thus it continued for three times; at the fourth recitation of the sutra, hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of sentient beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, heard the sutra, and each and every one attained the exhaustion of outflows and liberation of mind, while the assembly of śrāvakas was beyond all calculation.

"At that time, the crown princes of sixteen kings, having left the household life out of faith to pursue the Way, were all śrāmaṇeras. They were intelligent and wise, possessing many skillful means; having made offerings to hundreds of thousands of millions of buddhas and established various practices, they sought the unsurpassed, right, and true path. Together, they addressed the Buddha, saying:
'In this great assembly of śrāvakas, there are countless hundreds of thousands of millions of people who have already fully accomplished great supernormal powers.'"

We pray that you will expound for our sake the meaning of the unsurpassed, true, and correct path; we beseech you to extend your wisdom and insight to point out its location, so that we may follow the Tathāgata’s great and holy teaching, and together encourage one another to observe its fundamental source.

At that time, the World-Honored One, fully perceiving the thoughts in the minds of the young prince, the King, and their retinue, preached the Dharma for them. Eighty billion hundred thousand nayutas of people all became śramaṇas. Then, that Buddha, observing the fundamental nature of the minds of those śramaṇas, preached the Vaipulya sūtra *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* for twenty thousand kalpas; the practices of the bodhisattvas, protected by all Buddhas, were entirely and completely fulfilled.

The fourfold assembly was gathered together in universal equality without distinction; the sixteen young śrāmaṇeras, brothers, having heard what the Buddha taught, all received and upheld it together, reciting, chanting, and praising it.
That Buddha bestowed upon them the prediction that they would attain the unsurpassed, true, and correct path.
When he had finished preaching this sutra, the śrāvakas rejoiced; the sixteen śrāmaṇeras and the assembly of countless billions of koṭis of bodhisattvas all attained their original aspirations.
That Buddha preached this for eighty thousand kalpas without ever ceasing or becoming weary.
Having finished preaching this sutra, he immediately entered a quiet chamber to engage in profound reflection and tranquil concentration, remaining in samādhi for four hundred thousand kalpas.

"At that time, the sixteen princes who were śrāmaṇeras, having originally been sons of the Buddha practicing the bodhisattva path, beheld the World-Honored One dwelling alone in seclusion; they each prepared Dharma seats in advance, desiring to expound and propagate the broad meaning of the Dharma."

At that time, for eighty-four thousand kalpas, he preached the sutras with detailed analysis; each and every bodhisattva brought sixty million *koṭis* of beings—numerous as the sands of hundreds of thousands of rivers—to spiritual transformation and deliverance, establishing them all in the unsurpassed, right, and true path and causing them to abide in the Mahāyāna.

After eighty-four hundred thousand kalpas, the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū arose from samādhi, ascended the Dharma-seat, and addressed the entire assembly of bhikṣus: "The merit established by these sixteen princes is immeasurable and difficult to equal; their wisdom is unprecedented and most sublime.

They have made offerings to countless hundreds of thousands of millions of Buddhas, perfected all practices, and universally received holy wisdom. Having entered the light of the Way and gathered the Buddha-knowledge, you bhikṣus should all bow your heads and reverently take refuge in these sixteen benevolent and worthy ones. Do not be indolent repeatedly. Whether your resolve lies in the vehicle of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha, or if you have already attained the path of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha, or if you practice as bodhisattvas and have achieved realization—even those who have newly resolved to attain awakening—all should be entrusted to them."
Sons of good family, those who listen to the sutras being preached without rejecting or opposing them shall all attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path, and achieve the holy wisdom of a Buddha.

These sons of noble family, following the teachings of the World-Honored One, have repeatedly analyzed and expounded this True Dharma for the sake of all beings. His sixteen sons are fully endowed with the Bodhisattva Vehicle; each one has converted and transformed as many people as there are grains of sand in sixty Ganges Rivers. Wherever they are born, they always assemble together, and they also universally preach and listen to the meaning of the True Dharma. Each of them has encountered and seen forty billion hundred thousand Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, or will yet encounter more Buddhas in the future. Now, I proclaim and disseminate [this teaching] to the fourfold assembly.
The Buddha said,
"Do you wish to know who those sixteen princes of the kingdoms were at that time?
They replied:
"It is not yet so," the Buddha said.

"Now they have all attained the Way of the Unsurpassed, Right, and True; they are all presently existing throughout the ten directions, preaching the Dharma and providing protection for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of kotis of śrāvakas, and for incalculable bodhisattvas. In the present world of Great Joy in the eastern direction, there are two Buddhas named Anigha and Śikhin, Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas."
In the southeastern direction, there are two currently living Buddhas, named Siṃhaghoṣa and Siṃhadhvaja Tathāgatas;
in the southern direction, there are two currently living Buddhas, named Ekastha and Nityaparinirvṛta Tathāgatas;
in the southwestern direction, there are two currently living Buddhas, named Indradhvaja and Brahmadhvaja Tathāgatas.
In the western direction, there are two currently living Buddhas, named Amitāyus and Tārakāraṇa;
in the northwestern direction, there are two currently living Buddhas, named Candana-Ṛddhigiri and Smṛtigarbha;
in the northern direction, there are two currently living Buddhas, named Vṛṣṭiruci and Vṛṣṭisvararāja.
In the northeast, there are currently two Buddhas named Remover of Worldly Fear.
Now I, the Able One (Nengren), have attained the state of Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha within this Sahā world; together with these, there are sixteen honored ones in total.
He further addressed the bhikṣus:

"When we were sixteen śrāmaṇeras, we expounded the Dharma in the presence of that Buddha. Sentient beings listened and received it, and each of us bodhisattvas converted and transformed as many beings as there are grains of sand in hundreds of thousands of myriads of kotis of Ganges Rivers, causing them to resolve upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path; they have now attained fulfillment in the bodhisattva path."
Those who abide on the stage of the śrāvaka shall gradually be led forward toward the unsurpassed Great Way and will eventually attain supreme perfect enlightenment. Why is this?
Because the wisdom of the Tathāgata is difficult to limit and difficult to calculate; it is such that no one can ever reach its bounds.
He further addressed the bhikṣus:

"What is this? When I was a bodhisattva, I converted and enlightened beings as numerous as the sands of hundreds of thousands of billions of *koṭis* of Ganges Rivers; they heard, consulted, and received the teachings of all-encompassing wisdom. Yet in the future final age, there may be those who resolve their minds to study the vehicle of the disciples (*śrāvaka-yāna*) and become *śrāvakas*, who thereafter refuse to listen to or receive the bodhisattva teachings, do not understand the Buddha's wisdom, and do not practice as bodhisattvas, setting their entire will upon the notion of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), claiming that they have attained extinction (*nirvāṇa*)."

When you have just set out for the worlds of other Buddhas, following extraordinary practices to be born in various Buddha-lands, you shall seek the wisdom of the Way with a resolute mind to hear and receive its instruction; only then will you understand and know the Dharma of the Tathāgata, wherein there is but one parinirvāṇa and no two vehicles.
All these are merely the Tathāgata’s skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) in preaching the three vehicles.

At the time when the Tathāgata, the Perfectly Awakened One, enters parinirvāṇa, if there are those who make offerings with pure conduct, who believe in and delight in the wondrous words, who enter the sūtras, and who with a single-minded, concentrated intent engage in great meditative reflection (*dhyāna*), you should know that at such a time they behold the Tathāgata. All the assemblies of bodhisattvas gather together, as do the assemblies of śrāvakas, to hear and receive this Dharma; only then do they perceive the Buddha-way of the world, which is non-dual parinirvāṇa.

The Tathāgata’s perfect awakening is merely a teaching of skillful means; those who delight in the inferior practice of the Small Vehicle lose themselves and distance themselves from the human seed. Not understanding that the human root is bound by desire, if there are those who hear this teaching at the time of the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa and receive it with joy and faith, they shall be protected by the Buddha’s grace.

"Suppose there were a wilderness road five hundred *li* in length, remote and desolate, with neither people nor a sovereign. There was a guide, wise, intelligent, and far-sighted, possessing secret knowledge of both near and distant terrain; he led a group of merchants wishing to cross this vast expanse, but they all became weary and exhausted, unable to proceed further, each thinking with longing:

'We dwell in a land of holy prosperity; our native country is peaceful and refined, with its ruler and teachers. Now that we have traveled so far, we can no longer endure the journey; it would be better for us to return together and escape these hardships.'"

The guide took pity on them; though they had set out seeking treasure, they regretted it midway. He employed skillful means in a vast wilderness extending four thousand or eight thousand *li*, using his supernormal powers to conjure a great city. He told the merchants, "Do not harbor thoughts of despondency; you have reached a great kingdom and may stay here to rest. You may eat and drink as you desire at will, and if you wish to obtain great treasures, seek them here."
He further addressed the bhikṣus:

"The merchants, seeing the city’s inhabitants flourishing and their happiness boundless, marveled at such an unprecedented sight. Having escaped suffering and attained peace, they comforted themselves with joy; no longer beset by the anxieties of fear or the afflictions of hunger and want, they considered themselves to have attained the unconditioned state, as if they had reached nirvāṇa."
When the day for stopping arrived, knowing that [the merchants] were weary and desirous of rest, he immediately caused the illusory city to vanish without a trace and addressed the merchants, saying:
"You must quickly press onward to reach the ground of great jewels. Seeing that you were exhausted by the journey and your hearts were filled with fear, I manifested this city for you."
Again, he addressed the bhikṣus:

"The Tathāgata is likewise; for the sake of all people, he proclaims the principles of the sūtras. Beholding the long-lasting hardships and the affliction of emptiness within birth and death, he manifests the Three Vehicles, so that through single-minded meditative concentration, beings may attain nirvāṇa."

Furthermore, from the beginning the Buddha has taught that there is but one vehicle; yet when they hear the Buddha preach the Dharma, they do not accept the wisdom of the Path. If they are weary and disenchanted, they say that the accumulation of practice is exceedingly arduous and painful.

The Tathāgata perceives all that is in their minds and their thoughts of weariness; for them, he manifests the ease of attaining the stages of Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha, just as a leaderless city is magically conjured so that the people may have abundance and the merchants may rest in peace.
Seeing it as something to be weary of and playing with, he causes it to vanish; for the sake of the many merchants, he speaks of an illusory city. The leader therein refers to the Tathāgata.
The great wilderness refers to the cycle of birth and death within the five realms of existence;
the many merchants refer to those who are still in training.
Setting out to seek jewels refers to the bodhisattva’s practice of the path of wisdom;

those who grow weary along the way and refuse to proceed refer to those who find the Buddha-dharma difficult to attain, believing that it cannot be accomplished suddenly despite the accumulation of merit over many kalpas, and are thus enticed by the easier-to-attain vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
the conjured city refers to the nirvāṇa of the arhats.

When the city disappears and is no longer visible, it signifies that the Buddha is about to enter parinirvāṇa; he stands before them to exhort them to resolve upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path.

As for the state of an arhat, it is limited and obstructed, not being the ultimate reality, and thus does not reach the Great Way. Only when one reaches another realm and meets the Buddha there, attaining the stage of non-retrogression and the unborn, does one achieve the ultimate matter of the Great Jewel.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
“When you hear the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata, you consider yourselves to be fully provided for, yet you do not realize that what must be done is as yet unaccomplished.”

Furthermore, with the wisdom of a Tathāgata, he universally perceives the minds of all people in the world and manifests nirvāṇa; yet the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, through skillful means, teaches that there are three vehicles.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to explain the meaning once more, spoke these verses: "In the past,
there was a Greatly Penetrating One, A Guide of Universal Wisdom, Who had just sat at the site of enlightenment Beneath the Bodhi tree."
While that Buddha remained in meditative concentration for ten intermediate kalpas, he had not yet attained the ultimate realization of the Way.
Then the devas, nāgas, spirits, asuras, and others all exerted themselves with vigor to make offerings to the Most Victorious One.
A rain of celestial flowers fell, scattering profusely like a descent, as they were strewn upon the Equally Awakened One,
the Guide among Men. From within the void of space,
the roar of thunder resounded, as an offering presented to the Most Honored Great Sage.
The Most Victorious One was there, practicing with extreme diligence and austerity; his practice endured for a long time until he accomplished the Unsurpassed Way.
Through focused and dedicated contemplation over ten intermediate kalpas, he finally attained Perfect Enlightenment as Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū.
The devas and human beings, numbering in the hundreds of thousands of myriads, and all sentient beings, were filled with joy and leaped for gladness.
That Buddha originally had sixteen sons, all of whom followed his teachings and received them, transforming others through the Way among men.
The multitudes of beings, numbering in the hundreds of thousands of myriads, surrounded by their retinues, approached the Honored One Among Two-Legged Beings.
Prostrating themselves before him, the Teacher, the Holy Honored One, they earnestly entreated him, saying: "We pray that you will expound the sutras."
The valiant lion preaches that which was never heard before, filling us to satiety as well as the people of the world.
For the sixteen wild regions and this world, which have been desolate for a vast eternity,
a Great Sage has now arisen.
The palaces of the Brahma heavens were vast and brilliantly illuminated; manifesting various auspicious omens, he explained them all in detail.
In the worlds of the eastern direction, numbering hundreds of thousands of myriads of kotis, five hundred lands spontaneously shook.
There was a Great Brahmā dwelling in his own palace, whose majestic power and merit were most sublime and towering.
At that time, beholding these original auspicious omens, he immediately set out, moved by compassion for those in the mundane world.
Then, with celestial flowers, they scattered offerings upon the Great Benevolent One; using all manner of palaces, they presented them to the World-Honored One.
With drums, music, lutes, and song, they praised the Buddha’s merits, exhorting and advising the Right Guide to turn the Wheel of Dharma.
At that time, the Honored One among Men accepted [the offerings] in silence; he then, according to what was appropriate, expounded the teachings of the sutras.

From the world of the north, from the zenith and the nadir, and from the realms of the four intermediate directions, multitudes numbering in the hundreds of millions and billions—including the Brahmā deities—all came forth, each presenting their own precious treasures.
They offered these as an act of worship.
Furthermore, in all the worlds below, the Brahmā deities likewise did so everywhere, all being equal and without distinction.

All offered their palaces to the Great Sage; they sighed in praise of the Tathāgata and all joined together in encouragement, praying that he would turn the Wheel of Dharma. May you illuminate the eye and mind;
for countless billions of kalpas it is difficult to encounter such an opportunity—please deign to manifest the roots and powers of the ancient past.
Bestowing compassion, he opens wide the gateway of the nectar-like Dharma;
with the universal eye of the Dharma, he discerns the meaning of wisdom and proclaims the various categories of the many scriptures.
At that time, the Buddha preached for him, fully demonstrating the Four Noble Truths and providing complete understanding of the twelve links of dependent origination.
To manifest the absence of wisdom and grant him the eye of insight, he expounded upon the cycle of birth and death, its sorrows, sufferings, emptiness, and calamities.
All in the world arise from birth; know that it is because of this that they reach their ultimate end.
Just as the Tathāgata has finished preaching this Dharma, there were many kinds of beings, incalculable people—eighty *koṭis* of *nayutas* of sentient beings.
At that time, those who heard [the teaching] were established in the vehicle of the śrāvakas; how much more so those in other regions who stood upon the first bhūmi?
As numerous as the sands of the Ganges, these multitudes were pure, all of them resolved in their intent.
The conduct of the śrāvakas,
the noble assembly of teachers— if one were to calculate them in such numbers and all together reckon them, one could not measure their limit.
The various classes of beings were all exactly like this; they were all thus, establishing the great, supreme wisdom.
At that time, the Sovereign One’s sixteen noble sons, together with their fellow students, were of one mind;
they all left the household life and became śrāmaṇeras.
They shall fully discern the Buddha’s Vaipulya sutras;
we shall become the enlightened fathers of the world. Your followers shall likewise all attain supreme wisdom.
May all these sentient beings be made exactly like this.
Furthermore, as the World-Honored One is the Eye of the Dharma, most supreme and sincere,
he perceives the fundamental nature of the human mind.
In his youth as a child, he constantly practiced equanimity and preached the supreme, honored Way for the sake of sentient beings.
Through hundreds of thousands of millions of koṭis of inexhaustible parables, he manifested causes and conditions, whereby they immediately attained their retributions.
Arising from discernment, with all-pervasive and swift wisdom, they perform the practices appropriate for Bodhisattvas.
At that time, the Great Sage manifested the True Truth, proclaiming and disseminating this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
He universally rained down the preaching of the Mahāvaipulya sūtras— many thousands of verses,
inconceivable and immeasurable, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges— expounding these very scriptures at that time.
He then entered a quiet chamber and, through samādhi, practiced equanimous contemplation; for eighty-four thousand kalpas, he remained serenely absorbed.
With his mind thus fixed in concentration, the śrāmaṇeras came to visit the Great Sage while he was in his quiet chamber.
Seeing that he did not go out to wander about and transform the people, they were filled with wonder.
Countless billions,
for the very first time, have gathered at this great Dharma throne to proclaim and expound this noble and virtuous sutra,
spreading the Buddha’s transformation within the established teaching.
In such a manner, the deeds performed are vast and extensive;
more numerous than the sands of the Ganges, beyond all measure, numbering in the hundreds of thousands of millions, they have all been heard and accepted.
To each and every one of those sons who dwell in peace, he provides guidance, calculating the number of all sentient beings.
Incapable of being measured,
at that time, after the Parinirvāṇa of the Most Victorious One, they all succeeded in beholding forty billion Buddhas.
When those scholars first heard this name, they immediately made offerings to the Honored One among Two-Legged Beings.
By practicing four things— valuing freedom from defilement— they have all attained the Way of the Buddha throughout the ten directions in the present.
These sixteen youths are all sons of the Buddha; they are everywhere throughout the eight directions, propagating and expounding the principles of the Way.
Regarding those who preach there and those who listen and receive [the teaching], these śrāvakas are all disciples of the Buddha.
At every single step, there were various forms and appearances; now I shall draw near and resolve upon the Great Way.
At that time, I awakened those who were not yet awake, causing all of them to hear and receive [the teaching].
"You worthy ones, known as the sons of the Śrāvakas, through skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), you show the path to all people.
In my previous lives, the retribution was such as this; that which I have preached according to the Dharma is the causal condition for it."
If one cannot endure this while cultivating the honored path of the Buddha, O bhikṣu, you should know that this is the cause of being harassed by Māra.
Following their own natures, they are fierce, depraved, and unrestrained; their wills do not follow the practice, nor do they delight in the wisdom of emptiness.
For countless hundreds of lifetimes, one suffers from thirst without finding water; moreover, being foolish and ignorant, one dwells constantly in fear.
Countless men, in multitudes of hundreds and thousands, set out on their way, desiring to cross the vast wilderness.
Furthermore, he beholds a vast wilderness, remote and arduous; its extent, measured by the *yojana*, is five hundred.
Therein is a great man, virtuous, holy, and wise—a guide who transforms others through teaching, his mind free from fear.
For the sake of those merchants, he guides them along the path; the wilderness is vast and remote, filled with many hardships and fears.
Countless billions of people, exhausted by their initial obstacles and weariness, each address the Guide and present their own grievances.
We are exhausted and unable to proceed further;
today we wish to turn back and return home.
You have repeatedly proclaimed the teaching and instructed us with exhaustive detail, out of compassion for our ignorance and obstruction.
Wishing to abandon his treasures and retreat, he ruined his original plan and intended to turn back midway.
"I should now, by employing my power of divine feet (*ṛddhi*), magically create and establish a vast city wall,
adorned with various splendors and populated by billions of people."
He established chambers and dwellings, making them exquisite and beautiful.
Great rivers and flowing streams, gardens and groves, and bathing pools abounded; flowers and fruits flourished in profusion.
There were terraces, pavilions, and palatial halls, with walls and enclosures adorned in intricate patterns. Within were many men and women.
Hundreds of thousands of millions were enticed, comforted, and encouraged, so that they were no longer afraid; each considered themselves fortunate and rejoiced with great delight.
Having arrived today at this great city, I enter the marketplace to enjoy the objects of my desire;
my heart is filled with joy, as if I have attained nirvana, and thus both you and I shall be freed from all hardships.
Today, everyone may act as they please; follow your own inclinations and examine everything thoroughly.
Since we are of one mind with you, I speak with great earnestness: all of you, gather here and listen to what is being said.
By means of my supernormal power, I have conjured this great city.
As I observe it, it is parched and overgrown with thorns; I fear that you, sirs, may suffer from the pain of your wounds and regret your return.
Thereupon, he established skillful means and manifested various transformations; he exhorted them to refine their resolve and proceed forward along the path.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "I am also like this; I see countless billions of sentient beings who are weary of and distressed by their toil and suffering, wandering about in confusion."
By means of skillful instruction, he guides and enlightens them. Therefore, the Buddha reflects upon this:
such is the benefit and purpose [of his teaching], yet they remain weary of the Buddha-way and do not attain extinction (*nirvāṇa*).
The Father of all paths has awakened to them; the noble ones have accomplished their tasks and now attained arhatship.
Therefore, through my encouragement and support, they abide in this reward of merit; having observed these noble ones, they have reached the state of arhatship.
"All of you, cast off all suffering; for this entire assembly, I shall now expound this Dharma.
The Great Sages, the Buddhas, through their skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), preach the Buddha’s teachings as the Great Seers who provide salvation and protection."
That vehicle is but one; it has never been two.
I have taught these distinctions in order to bring you to rest.
Through this instruction, these bhikṣus shall arouse diligence that is foremost and most sublime.
Virtuous ones, you should resolve: all that is swift and wise, the scriptural teachings of the Bodhisattvas, is subject to no extinction.
I have constantly sought to achieve all-encompassing wisdom, so as to attain the most supreme Dharma throughout the ten directions.
With countenances most wondrous and the thirty-two marks, they shall attain the Way of the Buddha and then enter parinirvāṇa.
These great leaders teach the Dharma in this way, causing others to rest for a time while they themselves claim to have entered parinirvāṇa.
Having just attained rest, one speaks of attaining non-action; for this reason, all supernormal powers and wisdoms are fully developed.
*Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, Scroll Four;
*Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, Scroll Five.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Yuezhi Nation during the Western Jin Dynasty. Chapter Eight: Bestowing Predictions upon Five Hundred Disciples.

At that time, the Venerable Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, having heard the Buddha, the World-Honored One, expound the skillful means (*upāya*) and manifest expedient devices to bestow predictions of future Buddhahood upon the śrāvakas; and having reflected upon the practices he had established in the past, and beholding the realm of the Tathāgatas and all Buddhas, attained a state of unprecedented joy and leaped for gladness. Free from thoughts of food or clothing, his body was filled with rapture such that he could not contain himself. Moved by both sorrow and joy toward the Great True Dharma, he immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and forthwith resolved his mind, saying: [...]* *Note: The original Chinese text provided here is incomplete, ending abruptly after "尋發心言" (forthwith resolved his mind, saying). The translation reflects the available portion.*
"It is most difficult to reach,
World-Honored One!
It is unprecedented!"
"Abide in peace!

The strategies devised by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, are profoundly deep; they cannot be proclaimed by words. These worlds consist of various categories, and through countless skillful means, he manifests the meaning of wisdom to transform sentient beings in accordance with their needs, discerning and clarifying the Dharma for them. For the sake of these multitudes, he explains their fundamental origins and employs expedient means to deliver them."

The World-Honored One’s noble wisdom fully knows the tracks of our conduct, our dispositions, and the destinations to which we incline; he has thus further employed analogies to speak of past events and the initial arousal of the aspiration for enlightenment.

Then Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra bowed his head at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to stand to one side, took refuge in the World-Honored One, and gazed upon His radiant countenance with eyes that never blinked.
The Buddha said:
“Excellent!”
It is exactly as you have said.

The Tathāgata perceives all fundamental origins through his supernormal vision; he discerns their depth and shallowness and bestows teachings according to their causal practices. For instance, he shows the Śrāvakas the inferior Lesser Vehicle, whereby they eliminate the defilements of lust and anger and attain rest, and then guides them toward the boundless wisdom of the Bodhisattvas.

It was as if, in the past, there was a guide who practiced loving-kindness and felt great compassion for those in poverty and distress; seeing that they lacked sufficient food and clothing and could find nothing through begging, being destitute of all resources, he beat a drum throughout the realm to proclaim: "Who wishes to enter the sea to gather precious treasures?"
The people all assembled and again followed his words, saying:
"Whoever does not cherish their own bodies, does not dote on their parents, and does not look back upon their wives and children, shall enter the sea together to seek and gather precious treasures."
Upon hearing this command, many of the people retreated and returned.

Furthermore, there were those who were poor and begging, wishing to seek out the treasures; yet, having no clothes to cover their bodies and no means to sustain themselves, they hesitated back and forth, unable to resolve their course.
The leader, knowing this, summoned them all and said,
"If you wish to enter the sea, I shall provide you with clothing and provisions so that you do not suffer from want.
The poor ones rejoiced and immediately followed his instructions, boarding the ship all at once.

Sailing upon the great ocean with the wind as his guide, he encountered no great fish and struck no mountain cliffs; even malevolent spirits and rākṣasas did not dare to harass him. Having reached the dragon palace, he requested from the Dragon King the wish-fulfilling jewel.
"Laypeople suffer from poverty and distress, unable to sustain themselves; I pray that you will grant us alms to rescue those both far and near.
The Dragon King immediately granted their wishes as requested, telling them, "If there is anything you wish to obtain, let all come and take it."
The Guide further commanded that those who went to fetch [the water] should be few, while those who did not go should be many.
Why was this? Because they harbored fear and timidity; having reached the abode of the Dragon King, they feared being submerged and not returning.
At that time, the leader addressed the merchants, allowing each to take whatever they desired.
The merchants gathered gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, amber, musaragalva, and agate, filling their ships to capacity with each; the leader issued strict orders for them to return to Jambudvīpa.

The multitude followed his instructions and returned to their native land. Their wives, children, kinsmen, and relatives, along with food, drink, music, and chariots with horses and attendants, all came out to welcome them. They enjoyed themselves together for seven days and seven nights, after which they returned to their homes. There, each person asked the others what kind of treasures they had obtained.
Those of little wisdom who were poor beggars obtained only the seven treasures, while the wise companions of the guide obtained the wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*).

The teacher ascended a high tower and, holding the precious jewel in his hand, turned it toward the four cardinal directions, the four intermediate points, above, and below. By the power of this jewel, it caused the rain of the seven treasures to fall; immediately, as he had spoken, the seven treasures rained down, filling the entire kingdom so that there was nowhere it did not reach.
The rest of his wise companions distributed themselves among various kingdoms, traveling in all four directions and likewise raining down the seven treasures.
A man of meager wisdom and poverty then sighed in lamentation:
"We entered the sea together, yet I regret that I did not encounter this."
The guide said:
"I commanded you, yet you did not go to fetch it.
Now, what do you hope for?"
The multitude abandoned their treasures and gathered together once more, returning jointly to gather jewels.

They went to the Dragon King of the Ocean and requested the wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*), obtaining them all; they then returned to Jambudvīpa, whereupon the seven treasures rained down as well.
The Buddha said:
"To resolve upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path with the desire to deliver all beings is like a guide setting out across the great ocean;
to have compassion for those who are impoverished and lead them into the sea, expounding the Way of the sutras for their sake, is what is meant by this."
Sailing upon the great ocean by observing the wind signifies learning expedient wisdom;
the three perils of the sea signify emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*); the sea signifies birth and death (*saṃsāra*);
and obtaining the wish-fulfilling jewel signifies attaining the Tathāgata’s infinite Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
