The multitude also followed him to obtain the wish-fulfilling jewel, which signifies that upon hearing the Bodhisattva path, they resolve their great intention and attain the state of non-arising;
the poor, the lowly, and the inferior gathered the seven treasures, each filling their own ship, which signifies that they have attained the seven factors of enlightenment;
and when they returned to their hometowns and were welcomed by their families, this signifies that people from the ten directions come to receive the teachings of the Way.
Ascending the tower and holding the jewel toward the eight directions, above, and below signifies attaining the Buddha-way;
delivering and liberating the ten directions signifies that the various wise ones (bodhisattvas) equally arrive at all lands;
and raining down the seven treasures signifies that each proceeds to other regions to achieve supreme perfect enlightenment.

The multitude of the poor, repenting their retreat, exhorted one another to enter the sea; they were like the śrāvakas who heard that there is but the One Vehicle and no second path, whereupon they subsequently gave rise to the aspiration for supreme, true, and correct enlightenment, destined later to become Buddhas, each with their own name and title.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:

"Bhikṣus, listen as I explain this through a parable: Suppose there were a guide who, out of compassion for the people of a land, saw that they were largely impoverished and destitute, constantly suffering in their frantic toil."
Beating the drum to proclaim the command: "Who wishes to enter the sea?
He further addressed them, saying: "If you do not spare your own lives, do not dote on your parents, and have no regard for your wives and children, you shall enter the sea together."
There are perils in the sea; do not harbor regrets that might lead you to change your course.
At that time, those who were poor and begging also wished to have their own purpose, yet fearing they would not reach it themselves, they hesitated and could not decide.
The guide forgave them and provided them with food and clothing; they then entered the great ocean, each seeking the seven treasures.
Thereupon, the guide went to the palace of the Dragon King and informed those under his command that they sought the wish-fulfilling jewel.
The companions received the teaching and obtained wish-fulfilling jewels; returning to their native land, they were welcomed by all, both great and small.
At that time, the Guide ascended a high tower and rained down precious treasures everywhere throughout the eight directions.
Their factions separated and traveled to different lands, where they likewise rained down the seven treasures, so that none failed to receive its grace.
Those who had gathered the seven treasures then felt regret and remorse; together they set out for the sea, lamenting that they had not encountered such things there.
Previously, when you were commanded by me, you yourselves refused to take [the treasure]; this was your own fault—what cause is there for resentment?
I have now returned to the sea and sought the wish-fulfilling jewel, and have already found it; even so, the bodhisattva who has resolved his mind attains the true and right path.
Fearing and weary of birth and death, they follow the śrāvakas;
practicing the matters of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, they attain deliverance from the triple world and reach the gate of nirvāṇa.
Beholding the Buddha, the World-Honored One, who has subdued the hosts of Māra and attained the unsurpassed,
true, and correct Way; he transforms and enlightens all beings,
emitting ten billion voices, so that among the multitudes of living beings in the ten directions, there are none who do not receive his teaching.
Heavenly beings, dragons, ghosts, and spirits all come to prostrate themselves, resolving their minds on Bodhisattvahood until they reach the state of non-arising.
Some become Śrāvakas, severing the three poisons of defilement,
perceiving the ten directions without any obstruction.
The various arhats then reproached themselves, saying: "We have all practiced the Way together; why have we attained this?

Distressed and self-reproaching, they were subsequently met by the Tathāgata, who manifested the three vehicles through skillful means and expedient devices to guide them accordingly. Yet the Way is not dual.
How much more so when it was three times!
The śrāvakas and others then leaped for joy, their minds suddenly clear like the sun emerging from behind the clouds.
The Buddha bestowed predictions upon them all that they shall attain the Great Way, each with their own respective buddha-fields and names.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“Do you see the śrāvaka Pūrṇa?”

Among the assembly of bhikṣus, he served as the chief expounder of the Dharma, gloriously extolling and praising the virtues of all Buddhas; he set forth the orthodox scriptures with diligent encouragement and assistance. Hearing the Buddha preach the Dharma, he recited, received, and propagated it; he disseminated what had not yet been heard without ever becoming weary or negligent. He elucidated the profound meanings and resolved entanglements, responding to the fourfold assembly without weariness, manifesting all pure conducts so that everyone was made to rejoice.
Setting aside the Tathāgata, among the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who possess eloquence for inquiry, there has never been anyone like Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra.
Regarding the assembly of bhikṣus, what do you think?
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, do not hold the view that he has received the Dharma scriptures solely for the sake of the Śrāvaka Vehicle.

You should know that he has already attended upon ninety billion Buddhas, receiving the essential teachings from those World-Honored Ones. In every assembly where he was present, he constantly preached the Dharma, expounding and disseminating the meaning of the sutras and discerning the wisdom of emptiness, his mind remaining free from attachment.

When preaching the sutras, he is without hesitation; there is nothing he does not thoroughly understand, and he is never obstructed. Constantly and universally exerting his heart toward the supernatural powers of all Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, and Bodhisattvas, he causes them to practice the pure life (*brahmacarya*) for the remainder of their lives. Among the assembly of śrāvakas, he inspires faith and confidence in them through such skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) to benefit and rescue them. Among the countless billions of trillions of classes of sentient beings, he transforms and enlightens immeasurable asaṃkhyeya people, causing them to resolve upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*). Wherever he travels, he acts for the sake of the common people, manifesting and expounding the Great Way so that they may attain the state of Buddhahood.

All that they cultivate is always for the sake of purifying their own buddha-fields; they act as is appropriate to transform and enlighten sentient beings, and they universally manifest to serve and attend all perfectly awakened ones.
Now, in my world, he shall serve as the chief lecturer on the Honored Dharma; whenever he receives the true scriptures, his discourse and debate shall be unsurpassed.

Among the thousand Buddhas who will appear during the Worthy Kalpa, and furthermore, when he makes offerings to the World-Honored Ones of future ages, he shall likewise serve as the chief lecturer on the Honored Dharma. He shall constantly act for the benefit of immeasurable and infinite classes of beings, illuminating and augmenting their teachings and meanings, and exhorting and transforming all limitless sentient beings, causing them to resolve upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path, to fulfill and perfect the practices of the bodhisattva way, and after incalculable kalpas, to attain Buddhahood. His title shall be Dharmaprabhāsa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyak-saṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-sampanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣa-damya-sārathi, Śāstā deva-manuṣyāṇām; he shall become a Great Sage in this very land.

At that time, the trichiliocosm, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, shall become a single buddha-field. Its ground shall consist of the seven treasures, level as the palm of a hand, without mountains, hills, mounds, valleys, thorns, or pebbles. Multi-storied pavilions and monasteries, constructed of the seven treasures, shall fill the area everywhere; they will be so exquisite and wondrous that they can be seen from afar, just as the palaces of the devas. As those in heaven look down upon the world, those in the world shall likewise see the heavens, and devas and humans shall come and go, interacting with one another.
In that land, there are no nets of pride consisting of the ninety-six types of heterodox paths or the sixty-two views.

All beings are born by transformation and not from women; they purely cultivate the holy life (*brahmacarya*), each possessing majestic virtue. With great supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*), they fly through the void; they are constantly intent on diligence, their accomplishments are complete, and their wisdom is universally penetrating. Their bodies are the color of purple-polished gold, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*).
At that time, the people always had two kinds of sustenance: first, the food of the Dharma; second, the joy and delight of meditative concentration (dhyāna-prīti). These were their two sustenances.

There were incalculable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of bodhisattvas, all of whom had attained supernatural powers (abhijñā) and could thoroughly investigate and discern the meanings and principles of the scriptures.

His śrāvakas and others all attained the noble practices; they traversed the eight gates of liberation through the power of their majestic skillful means, possessing marvelous names and virtues, and attained the perfection of deliverance.
The kalpa was named Jewel Radiance, the world was called Pure Excellence, and the Buddha’s lifespan lasted for immeasurable kalpas.

After his parinirvāṇa, the Dharma will remain for a very long time; stupas made of the seven precious jewels will arise throughout this world, and the Buddhas of the ten directions will all join in singing praises of the merits of this land.
When the Buddha had spoken thus, wishing to further clarify the meaning, he spoke in verse:
“Listen, O bhikṣus, to the purport of this teaching.
The devas and the people of the world, practicing through skillful means, have attained ultimate mastery in their training.”
If one should honor and revere [the path], practicing the conduct of the Buddha-way,
yet remains fragile, inferior, indolent, or negligent,
then for such a person one should expound the subtle and tranquil vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, establishing them therein as a permanent abiding.
The Great Path of the Bodhisattvas,
through hundreds of thousands of millions of skillful means, transforms and enlightens countless bodhisattvas as well as this assembly of śrāvakas.
Therefore, it is further said: The supreme path of the Buddha is extremely difficult to attain.
Yet, hundreds of millions of sentient beings have been graced by his profound transformation and have already been able to practice such conduct.
Those who are base and indolent, who indulge in arrogance and negligence, shall nevertheless gradually immerse themselves until they all attain the Buddha-way.
Constantly adhering to their practice, such śrāvakas—
though their power and influence be slight and they fear and weary of all the afflictions from beginning to end— shall further cultivate and refine themselves.
They purify their own buddha-fields;
or again, they manifest themselves as being within desire, anger, malice, hatred, and the darkness of ignorance.
Beholding all sentient beings who are deluded by false views, I shatter and eliminate their nets of doubt and their fetters of affliction.
My assembly of śrāvakas acts in this same way; according to the time and as is appropriate, they transform these multitudes, employing skillful means to inspire all.
For the sake of all people, they explain it extensively and in accordance with the truth.
My śrāvakas are complete; their practice is fully perfected, for they desire to rescue and protect [beings] under billions of buddhas.
This Buddha’s True Dharma awakens through meditative reflection; seeking liberation, one dwells wherever one may be.

With extensive learning and great wisdom, preaching the Dharma with courage, one should gladden sentient beings without weariness of heart, performing the work of a Buddha and establishing them on the Path.
Having attained great supernormal powers, dwelling securely in universal penetration, and being fully endowed with the guidance that benefits others,
such a one is a Lamp of Light.
Discerning all sentient beings and constantly perceiving their fundamental natures, he preaches the sutras for them, causing them to reach purity.
He guides millions of billions of sentient beings, clearly explaining and proclaiming the supreme,
sublime, and true Dharma. Abiding in this Mahāyāna, the unsurpassed, right, and true, he beholds his own land as magnificent,
wondrous, and pure.
In future ages, you shall serve and attend upon hundreds of thousands of millions of Buddhas, honoring them in this manner.
You shall always protect and uphold the sublime True Dharma, and furthermore, you shall adorn and purify your own Buddha-field.
He expounds the sutras, numbering in the hundreds of thousands of millions; with skillful means and expedients, he always adheres to valor.
He shall further transform and enlighten countless sentient beings, so that they all abide in the wisdom of the Way and are free from all outflows.
He shall always show reverence toward all the great sages and heroes, and constantly uphold this sublime Dharma of the Buddha.
He shall attain the Way of the Buddha, becoming a sovereign guide named Dharmaprabhāsa,
whose fame and light shall illuminate the ten directions.
That buddha-field shall be most honored and blissful, a land of the seven treasures, entirely pure.
At that time, the kalpa shall be named Radiance of Jewels, and the world shall be called Well-Purified and Adorned.
Countless billions of thousands of bodhisattvas, and others of such a kind, have attained great supernormal powers.
At that time, the Buddha-world was praised by all; its supernormal powers were vast and expansive, and it was excellent, wondrous, and pure.
Furthermore, there were śrāvakas numbering in the hundreds of millions, all of whom were great sages and a host of noble and valiant ones.
Their supernormal powers were supreme; they practiced the eight doors of liberation, analyzing and deconstructing all things with complete penetration and understanding.
All practice purity, constantly cultivating the holy life;
they are endowed with eloquence and wisdom, lacking in none of the manifold virtues. Among the common people, the worthy arise, flourishing and exceedingly numerous.
The various worthy ones and the populace will be numerous and flourishing; they shall delight only in the scriptures and have no other desires.
In that land there will be no assembly of women, nor will there be the afflictions of the evil realms or the suffering of toil.
The purple-golden hue will naturally appear upon their bodies, adorned by the thirty-two marks.
Furthermore, in that Buddha-land, there will be no thought of food or clothing; whatever one desires shall be obtained—this I shall now explain.
At that time, the twelve hundred practitioners each thought to themselves:
"How extraordinary and unprecedented! We are all filled with joy and exultation.
If the World-Honored One extends his compassion so that the rest have all received their predictions, he must surely pity us as well and grant us the same."
Thereupon, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the śrāvakas, addressed the Venerable Mahākāśyapa:

"In this assembly of one thousand two hundred arhats present before me—excluding Ānanda and Rāhula—and these other śrāvakas who know the ultimate limit [of existence], they shall make offerings to sixty-two billion buddhas. After that number has passed, all five hundred disciples shall become buddhas, titled Universal Radiance Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, and Blessed One."

Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa, Nadī-Kāśyapa, Gayā-Kāśyapa, Kālaka, Udayin, Ānanda, Revata, Kapphiṇa, Bakula, Subhūti, and others—these five hundred arhats shall all attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path and become most perfectly enlightened Buddhas, all sharing the same name.
Thereupon the World-Honored One uttered these verses in praise:
“The honored disciple of the Buddha, whose family name is Mūlapratiṣṭhāna, shall become a Tathāgata,
a guide for the world.”
He shall transform countless billions of sentient beings, Causing them to attain the state of supreme victory,
known as Universal Radiance.
The land of that Buddha shall be named Pure.
In future ages, throughout incalculable kalpas, you shall constantly behold immeasurable Buddhas.
With radiant voice and supernormal powers,
great strength, and brilliant wisdom, your renown shall spread far and wide throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
Surrounded on all sides by hundreds of millions of sentient beings, he speaks only of the supreme Buddha-way.
All the bodhisattvas constantly cultivate right practice, riding upon majestic vehicles and dwelling in sublime,
magnificent palaces.
In whatever places they travel, they remain free from conceptual thought; they receive and hear the Dharma from the Honored One among Two-Legged Beings.
They constantly go about and circulate through the Buddha-lands of other directions, where the Great Sages, the Buddhas, are like this.
Having further made offerings to the Most Honored One, whose majesty is vast and universal, their hearts were joyful and filled with great delight.
All those lands were of one and the same kind; the many Great Holy Heroes bore no different names.
The supreme among men were all named Samantaprabha; such as these, they were diligent and practiced with vigor.
Their lifespan was exceedingly long and beyond limit, lasting for a full sixty-two thousand kalpas.
After his parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma shall remain; the scriptures bequeathed by the Sage shall endure for three times the duration of a kalpa.
Furthermore, the Semblance Dharma shall likewise be established and endure for a period exceeding that of the True Dharma by another threefold.
Even if, after the True Dharma has utterly perished, many men and women encounter great suffering and affliction—
these most excellent ones, the peers of the Great Sages, whose names are Universal Radiance, are the supreme among Great Beings.
Fully endowed with what they ought to do, these five hundred guides shall each be equal and all attain the path of Buddhahood.
Their names shall be heard everywhere throughout the Buddha-lands of the ten directions;
their supernormal powers and great strength, as well as their spheres of influence and the merits of their True Dharma, shall be exactly like this.
One should fully practice and propagate this sublime classic;
all that is attained shall be like this, manifesting both in the heavens and within the world.
Just as in the past, I practiced pure giving, Radiating vast and universal light, supreme among men.
The conduct I established was entirely patient and self-reliant; Each has received their prophecy, out of great compassion for many.
Countless matters converge into a single equality; just as the Buddha now is the true and correct one in the world, he has arisen out of his venerability to speak for Kāśyapa:
"You should mindfully uphold the names of these five hundred Buddhas."
"All the śrāvakas, as well as all others—therefore these disciples have likewise attained mastery.

At that time, the five hundred who were free from attachment, having personally seen and heard the Tathāgata bestow this prophecy, leaped for joy and went to the Buddha’s presence. Casting themselves upon the ground, they prostrated with their heads at his feet, repenting and reproaching themselves:

"We of base character always recalled our former state, believing we had already attained nirvāṇa and parinirvāṇa. Lacking skillful means, we could not recognize, cultivate, or discern the true refuge; we turned our backs on wisdom and harbored thoughts of weariness. Now, finally, we have attained the wisdom of the Tathāgata and shall realize perfect enlightenment."

"Yes, indeed, World-Honored One. It is like a man who enters a chamber of loving-kindness and places a bright moon pearl within his knot; yet, having become intoxicated and fallen asleep, he does not take notice of it himself. Upon waking, he forgets the bright pearl and does not know where it is. He departs for another land without any provisions; hungry and destitute, he seeks food but finds no means to obtain it. Only after devising various schemes and traveling back and forth does he finally obtain a meal, and his heart is filled with joy."
At that time, he thought to himself, "I wonder if the bright pearl tied to my knot has fallen into the storehouse of my former chamber?
He hurried back to search for it and soon went to see the Elder Maitrāyaṇīputra.
The Elder Maitrāyaṇīputra said to him:
"For what reason do you trouble yourself so?
You wander about seeking food and drink with ceaseless thoughts."
Do you wish to know?

At that time, I dressed myself in solemn and orderly attire and went about collecting *ji* (sacrificial grain) to honor what was right. While traveling, I came upon this place and saw the bright moon pearl fastened to your knot; the pearl is now upon your person—do you not reflect upon this?
For what reason have you come to my plan? What skillful means shall I employ so that you may exert yourself to the utmost?

The reason it is difficult for you, my son, to obtain wealth and treasures now is that you do not examine whether a matter is feasible or not; instead, take this bright pearl gem and go quickly to trade it with the great dragon. By doing so, you will obtain all manner of treasure-troves and may bestow them as you please.

"In the past, when the World-Honored One first began his practice, while he was a bodhisattva, he developed various supernormal powers and wisdoms; we did not understand them nor were we awakened to them. Now that we all abide in the stage of arhatship, we believe we have attained final nirvana."

Having dwelt amidst perilous and difficult karmic conditions and always being as if impoverished, you are now able to set your will upon all-encompassing wisdom; you should employ this Dharma to transform and enlighten others, using the wisdom of the Tathāgata to discern the intent of the Path.
"O bhikṣus, you must not take this meaning to mean that it is nirvāṇa.
You, worthy ones, must further personally cultivate the roots of all virtues.
In the past, the Tathāgata used skillful means to guide you; now he likewise preaches the Dharma once more, so that those like you may attain extinction for yourselves."
"Now the World-Honored One has bestowed upon us the prediction of unsurpassed, right, and true enlightenment.
Thereupon, the five hundred śrāvakas, including Benjie and the others, sighed in praise and said in verse:
"Having heard this, we now realize our former errors; having already received this prediction,"
This is the supreme Buddha-way.
I prostrate to the World-Honored One, the immeasurable sun of wisdom; out of compassion, please preach this which you have expounded with such radiant brilliance.
Like those who are ignorant and deluded, unable to discern how each and every one attains extinction,
today they rejoice, dwelling in peace within that which has been transformed; their aspirations are vast and universal,
directed toward the matters of all-encompassing wisdom.
Like an only son who wanders about seeking [his father], he immediately enters the hall of loving-kindness.
There he beholds one of great wealth; at that time, the wealthy man has prepared a vast array of food and drink.
That person slept for a single night, abstaining from food and drink;
a bright moon-jewel was tied within his knot.
Because of this sleep, when he rose from his slumber, he sat in the Chamber of the Treasury of Compassion, filled with joy and gladness.
Disregarding his own benefit and righteousness, he departed immediately;
traveling far into the city, he sought clothing and food, yet could obtain nothing at all. Wandering about seeking provisions, he sustained himself by whatever means came his way;
receiving food from others, he considered this to be the attainment of the Unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
A bright pearl was fastened in a knot, and he thought to himself: "Is this precious jewel still here or not?
It remained upon his person as before, yet though he sought it, he could not find its place.
Thus, once again beholding the Elder Maitreya’s act of giving—the deeds of a true man—he immediately spoke these words of praise: "Excellent!
How delightful! He clearly manifested the wondrous jewels, teaching and transforming him so that he might cross over.
When that person first beholds it, they experience supreme peace and security; having received the grace of the jewels, they have attained this state.
Possessing inexhaustible wealth, their treasuries are full and overflowing, and they further delight themselves with the five desires.
Thus it is, World-Honored One; as this parable illustrates, in our previous lives we all together resolved upon our vows.
This was not something first initiated by the Tathāgata alone; rather, throughout the long night of the past, he applied himself with diligent effort.
“World-Honored One, we were of inferior and debased mind; we could not awaken to or understand the Tathāgata’s teaching.
Lacking aspiration in our hearts, we were unwilling to advance, yet we took joy and congratulated ourselves upon [attaining] nirvāṇa.”
According to the Buddha’s holy teaching, those who are awakened and delivered—when reckoned in this way—do not attain extinction.
The Supreme among Men, out of compassion, gives rise to the meaning of wisdom; this is what constitutes extinction, the foremost unconditioned state.
This bound bright pearl, a stainless and supreme treasure, that which we have heard today is limitless.
Through this transformative guidance, joy and serenity are universally manifested; each and every one has attained it, and has been granted a distinct and extraordinary prediction.

Chapter Nine: The Bestowal of Prophecy upon Ānanda and Rāhula In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, Chapter Nine: The Bestowal of Prophecy upon Ānanda and Rāhula, the venerable Ānanda thought to himself:
"Might I also receive a prophecy of my own?"
Having thought this in his mind, he made a solemn vow and immediately rose from his seat to prostrate at the Buddha’s feet.
The Venerable Rāhula also stepped forward and threw himself beneath the World-Honored One’s feet, and together they said:

“Please expound for us the flavor of the Ambrosia. Great Sage, you are our father; there is nothing you do not clearly perceive. To those without refuge, you provide refuge; to those without rescue, you provide rescue; to those without protection, you provide protection. For the sake of all devas, humans, and asuras, you manifest various kinds of majestic transformations.”

Ānanda and Rāhula are the sons of the Buddha and also his attendants; they uphold the treasury of the holy Dharma. We only pray that the World-Honored One will fulfill our aspirations and bestow upon us the unsurpassed, right, and true [enlightenment].

Furthermore, another two thousand śrāvakas, who were still possessed of worldly afflictions, all rose from their seats, bared their right shoulders, and with single-minded palms joined together, gazed up at the Honored One’s countenance, saying, "We have now attained the sight of him."
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"In a future age, you shall attain Buddhahood, and your name shall be Sāgaradhārī-bodhi-rati-ṛddhi Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavat. First, you shall make offerings to sixty-two billion Buddhas, serving them with reverence and obedience; you shall uphold the True Dharma and protect the scriptures, and only thereafter will you ultimately achieve supreme perfect enlightenment."

Thereupon, he converted and transformed as many devas and humans as there are grains of sand in twenty hundred thousand Ganges Rivers, causing them to resolve upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path.

That Buddha-land was pure and flawless; its ground was of lapis lazuli, with various banners and pennants erected throughout. The world was naturally adorned, level and even, devoid of grit, pebbles, stones, mountains, hills, valleys, or ravines. The ground was everywhere soft and supple like celestial silk. The eon was named "Gentle," and there were no thunderclaps.

At that time, the Buddha’s lifespan was incalculable—hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis, beyond all analogy and impossible to fathom; the assembly of his disciples who received the teachings of the Way was likewise incalculable—hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis, without limit or measure.

When Ānanda attains Buddhahood as a Great Sage, he shall be named Sāgaradhara-jñāna-vikrīḍita-abhijña; the people of that land will frequently manifest divine transformations and move with effortless mastery.
After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma shall remain for twice as long as that; the Semblance Dharma shall endure for twice as long as the True Dharma.
The Buddhas of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of Ganges Rivers, shall all extol and praise the merits of that Buddha.
Then the World-Honored One praised him with these verses:
"Now the Buddha proclaims to the assembly of bhikṣus: O virtuous Ānanda, you uphold my Dharma;
In a future age, you shall become most excellent."
He made offerings to sixty-two billion Buddhas, all named Sāgaradhara,
who were awakened through the power of the vehicle of spiritual penetrations.
Their lands were pure, manifesting in subtle and wondrous ways, standing forth spontaneously.
Countless banners and streamers;
the multitude of bodhisattvas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, were all established and inspired by the Tathāgata.
He is entirely like the Most Victorious One, possessing infinite supernormal powers; his virtue and fame spread throughout the ten directions.
His lifespan, if one were to calculate it, is immeasurable and beyond limit;
he transforms the world, feeling deep compassion for many.
Even after that Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma shall remain for twice that number of years;
the Semblance Dharma shall endure for even twice as long again—such is the teaching proclaimed by the Most Victorious One.
"Furthermore, these sentient beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, shall give rise to the mind of retribution and response,
establishing themselves in the Buddha-way.
At that time, eighty thousand bodhisattvas who had newly resolved their minds each thought to themselves:
"This is strange and unprecedented, never heard of since time immemorial; what use have we for the meaning of 'bodhisattva'?
Even those among the śrāvakas who are dull and ignorant are now granted the prediction that they shall attain the Great Way."
"What is the cause for this?
The World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in his mind, addressed him, saying:
"Listen, sons of noble family and bhikṣus: the Buddha-dharma is equal."

Son of good family, this one has generated the aspiration for unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment; previously, in the presence of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Vimalagaganaprabha, he extensively heard various sūtras and constantly practiced with diligence, coming now to me with a desire to establish himself with earnest resolve.
For this reason, you shall swiftly attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path and achieve supreme perfect enlightenment.

Ānanda, you are worthy and virtuous; as a recipient of the Dharma-treasury for the Buddha, the World-Honored One, you have cultivated the bodhisattva practices. Out of your intention to fulfill noble vows through the conditions of leaving the household life, I entrust the sons of good family to you.

At that time, Ānanda, having personally heard from the Buddha these immeasurable meanings of emptiness and non-existence, was destined to receive the prediction of his future attainment of Buddhahood and the granting of a buddha-field; hearing of his original vows and practices, he rejoiced with great delight and immediately recalled countless billions of hundreds of thousands of koṭis of sūtras of the Perfectly Enlightened Ones.
Furthermore, observing the traces of his past conduct throughout the preceding and succeeding kalpas,
he immediately uttered this eulogy:
"I have previously heard that there were immeasurable Buddhas, all of whom took thought for me."
When I preach the sutras,
all those who have attained parinirvāṇa— the most supreme and great sages— I remember them all exactly as I have heard them described.
Having established the Buddha-way, their minds harbor no doubt; those such as these dwell securely through skillful means and expedient devices.
Established in the station of an attendant, they uphold the True Dharma for the sake of the Great Way.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Rāhula: "Rāhula, reflect upon this:

in a future age you shall become a Buddha, named Duqībǎoliánhuá (Saptaratnapadmaprabha) Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavat. You shall serve as many Tathāgatas as there are atoms in ten worlds; you shall appear as the honored son of all those Buddhas, just as you are now my son."

The land, lifespan, teaching of sentient beings, and all adornments of that Tathāgata Saptaratnapadma will be just like the purity of the world Samudradhara-bodhinandita-ṛddhi; Rāhula shall become the honored son of that Buddha, and after this period has passed, he shall attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path and achieve supreme perfect enlightenment.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"Rāhula is my son, My most honored and eldest child; A youth of refined character, Gentle, mild, and sublime."
This son of the Buddha shall attain the Great Way; constantly bestowing the Dharma as a gift, he brings joy to many.
He is looked upon with compassion by countless billions of Buddhas; were one to wish to calculate this, it would be beyond all measure.
Universally supreme, these sons of the Buddhas shall all attain the Great Way;
they are like a multitude of bhikṣus.
Furthermore, this Rāhula conducts himself with gentleness and elegance, having established extraordinary vows and upholding my true precepts.
Praising and proclaiming the World-Hero, the Great Teacher: "I am now this very one, the son of the Tathāgata.
My virtues are immeasurable, numbering in the billions; even if one were to contemplate them, they could not be measured."
"As for Rāhula, he is the eldest son of the Buddha; that which he now traverses is because he abides in the Buddha-way.
At that time, Ānanda and Rāhula together addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Now we see these two thousand śrāvakas, who study the precepts of the disciples with hearts full of joy. Beholding the Honored Countenance, the Dharma and the orthodox scriptures are inconceivable; we pray that we may attain this state at this very moment."
The Buddha addressed Ānanda and Rāhula:
“Do you see these two thousand śrāvaka disciples who train in the Dharma and precepts?
Ānanda replied to the Buddha:
“Yes, I have seen them,” [Ānanda replied]. The Buddha told Ānanda:

“This group of fellow practitioners who study the Mahāyāna together shall make offerings to as many Tathāgatas as there are atoms in five hundred worlds and uphold the true scriptures. Then, in a future age, they will gather together at one time and disperse throughout the ten directions, each in a different land. There they will attain unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment as Most Perfect Buddhas, known by the name Ratnaketu Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavat.”

Their lifespan shall be one kalpa, and their awakened wisdom shall be equal; the number of śrāvakas shall be the same for all without distinction, and it shall be the same for the assembly of bodhisattvas as well.
After their parinirvāṇa, the duration that the True Dharma remains shall likewise be no different.
Then the Buddha spoke in verse:
"These śrāvakas, this assembly of two thousand followers, now all stand before the World-Honored One."
These sages of holy wisdom have all been granted predictions by the Buddha that in a future age they shall become Buddhas.
He has manifested this through immeasurable parables, showing them that they shall behold all Buddhas and offer worship to them all.
They shall immediately attain and realize the unsurpassed, most honored Way; abiding in the practice of the Way, they will likewise achieve mastery.
Though their names and practices differ, as they travel through the ten directions, they shall all practice patience, remaining unchanging for even a moment.
When I again dwell alone, sitting beneath the grove of trees, I shall attain the Way of the Buddha and fulfill the meaning of wisdom.
All shall achieve enlightenment; our titles shall be identical and equal, named "Jewel Excellence," as this renown spreads throughout the world.
That Buddha’s land is equal and extraordinary; the assembly of śrāvakas is likewise so.
Their supernormal powers and radiance pervade the entire world, circulating throughout all lands in the ten directions.
"Distinguishing the teachings of the sūtras, they have something upon which to rely;
the True Dharma stands firm, equal and without distinction.
Thereupon, having heard the Buddha bestow this prediction, all the trainees were filled with joy and exultation beyond measure, and they praised the Buddha in verse:
"Having heard the Buddha grant me this prediction, I am fully satiated by the sight of the Light of the World;
as if drenched with nectar, I have already attained infinite peace.
— *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, Scroll Five.
The Lotus Sutra, Scroll Six, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Yuezhi Kingdom during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Chapter Ten: The Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyarāja. The Lotus Sutra, Chapter Ten: The Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyarāja.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The Dharma of the Path is uniform and of one kind; there are no two vehicles, namely, only the unsurpassed, right, and true path.

From antiquity to the present, there have never been two truths. It is just as the many streams and four great rivers flow back to the sea and merge into a single flavor; or like the light of the sun, which shines everywhere without exception, never increasing or decreasing."

If a son of noble family wishes to attain perfect enlightenment and understand that the three miserable realms are non-existent throughout the past, future, and present, he should study and uphold the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, discerning the wisdom of emptiness without the notion of the six perfections; he should not regard offerings of flowers, incense, or music as true worship.
Only by realizing the three liberations and attaining the infinite wisdom of the three types of omniscience does one truly perform worship.

Why is this so? Because in the distant past, through kalpas beyond measure, there was a Buddha named Bhaiṣajyarāja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, and Blessed One. His world was named Mahāviśuddhā, and the kalpa was called Viśodhana.

The Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyarāja lived for twenty intermediate kalpas; his assembly of śrāvakas numbered three billion six hundred million, and his bodhisattva-mahāsattvas numbered one billion two hundred million.

At that time, there was a universal monarch named Ratnacchattra who ruled over the four quarters. The king had a thousand sons, handsome and valiant, and he possessed seven precious jewels and noble ministers who subdued all enemies.
That king made offerings to the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyarāja for the duration of five intermediate kalpas; together with his retinue, he bestowed all things upon him, serving and honoring Bhaiṣajyarāja.
After those five kalpas had passed, he addressed his thousand sons:
"I have already served and attended upon the Tathāgata; you all should likewise follow and honor this precedent."

At that time, the thousand sons, having heard the instruction of their father the king, again made offerings to the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyarāja for five kalpas, presenting him with the most excellent and sublime things in accordance with his needs.
"One of those princes, named Śubhacchattra, dwelt in seclusion and reflected quietly:
'As we now make offerings to the Tathāgata, is there perhaps someone else who has made an offering even more distinguished and surpassing ours?'"
Empowered by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual authority, a deity in the void spoke to him, saying:
"Noble son, do you wish to know?
There is a Dharma-offering that is most supreme and peerless."
He asked again:
"What is meant by the 'Dharma-offering'?
The deva replied:
"You should go and ask the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyarāja; he will surely explain it to you in detail.
Thereupon, Supraticchatara rose and went to the place where the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyarāja was. Prostrating himself on the ground, he addressed the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyarāja, saying:
"What is meant by 'the offering of the Dharma' for one who reverently follows the scriptures?"
The World-Honored One replied:
"As for the offering of the Dharma, it is to accord with the profound, subtle, and sublime sūtras spoken by the Tathāgata;

to transform and enlighten all the people of the world; and to seek with resolve that which is difficult to receive and difficult to see—the renunciation of worldly gain upon leaving the household life."
The Bodhisattva’s treasury of various caskets dwells in vast seclusion, sealed with the seal of *dhāraṇī*.
With diligent and forceful practice, he turns the wheel of non-retrogression and manifests the wisdom of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*).

Earnestly grasping and gathering the factors of the Buddha-way (*buddha-dharma*), he enters the true scriptures through the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), for the sake of all living beings.
Establishing great compassion, he subdues the armies of Māra and leaves behind all views of dharmas;

he awakens to and expounds the twelve links of dependent origination—teaching that there is no self, no person, no life-span, and no vital principle—and resolves his mind upon the dharmas of emptiness, wishlessness, and signlessness.
Without relying on the various [conditioned] practices, he dwells at the site of enlightenment and turns the wheel of Dharma, exhorting all...

The devas, nāgas, gandharvas, and others all look up to him with joy; he opens and reveals the treasury of the Dharma, protects the worthy and holy ones, and proclaims and spreads the practices of the bodhisattvas.
He brings to an end all suffering through the realization of non-self and the absence of a personal body;

for sentient beings who violate prohibitions, he establishes them in what is most beneficial. Against the various māras and heterodox paths that fall into inverted views and cling to craving, [he acts as their antidote].
Those in the conditioned realm constantly harbor fear and sigh with lamentation.

The virtues of the Buddhas cause them to extinguish birth and death, console and eliminate their afflictions, and enable them to see the secure state of the unconditioned; this is how the Buddhas of the past, future, and present have praised it.

To discern and distinguish subtle forms and images, to maintain the dharma-patience regarding all dharmas at their fundamental limit, to open the path and proclaim it by elucidating the various capacities of beings, and to nurture the True Dharma through the meaning of skillful means—this is the offering of the Dharma.

If one sets one's will upon the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*) regarding all sūtras, expounding the scriptures in their forward and reverse order, elucidating their essentials so that there are no false views,
attaining the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*), being without self or person and entering into all causes and conditions,
being without anger, without contention, and without litigation, and following the practice of being without self or life-span— this is called the perfection of wisdom.
Regarding the meaning of phrases, one should be without attachment through wisdom and remain free from negligence;

guiding the mind and consciousness so they abide in non-abiding, one discerns the principles and directions of consciousness to lead away from what is not the true meaning. One purifies and flows through all phenomena upon which one relies, refraining from creating views that depend on a person, and instead relying on the True Truth (*satya*).
Following the destination of the Dharma, one is without attachment and without entry, severing all dependencies.
To extinguish all ignorance, to eliminate birth, old age, sickness, and death, to contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination as inexhaustible,
and to perceive all established views without following delusion— this, noble son, is the Dharma-offering.

“Prince Supraticchatishnu, having heard the teaching on the ‘Dharma-offering’ from the Buddha Bhaiṣajyarāja, immediately attained the patient acceptance of the compliant Dharma (*anulomikī-dharma-kṣānti*). He then removed his own robe to cover the Buddha and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:

‘May you graciously establish my resolve; after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, I vow to protect the True Dharma, perform Dharma-offerings, subdue the hosts of Māra and enemies, and welcome the future Dharma.’”
At that time, the Buddha knew the prince’s mind and [perceived] that in the final age he would protect the city of the Dharma.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

“Prince Śubhacchada, because the Buddha was present in the world, left the household life for the sake of the Way out of faith in his family. He constantly applied himself with diligence to learning and cultivated the roots of all virtues. Before long, he achieved and established the five supernormal powers (pañcābhijñā), possessing dhāraṇīs and eloquence that none could interrupt.”
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, they will be fully endowed with supernormal powers, dhāraṇīs, the [ten] powers, and the fearlessnesses.
For ten intermediate kalpas, they shall turn the wheel of Dharma by means of the sūtras and teachings spoken by the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyarāja.

Because the bhikṣu Śubhacchada protected the True Dharma, during a single lifetime he transformed a thousand billion people, causing them all to resolve upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path without ever regressing; for fourteen years he established people in the stages of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and incalculable numbers of people attained rebirth in the heavens.
"Monks! Do you wish to know who that King Ratnacchattra was?
It was none other than the present Buddha, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Ratnārcis."
The king’s thousand sons are those who will appear as the thousand Buddhas of this Bhadrakalpa; they begin with Tathāgata Krakucchanda and end with the one named Priyaṃkara.
The Crown Prince Supraticchatra was none other than my own self in this life.
Therefore, you should know that among all forms of sustenance, there is none superior to the nourishment of the Dharma; it is from this that all Buddhas of the past, future, and present emerge.

If sons or daughters of good family wish to make offerings to the Buddhas of the ten directions, they should immediately receive, uphold, recite, chant, and read the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, proclaiming it to all, and discerning that there is but the One Vehicle and no three vehicles of the path.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"Suppose there were one person who, desiring to understand the Great Dharma, would transform and enlighten all beings so that they all attain perfect awakening."
You should faithfully receive and uphold this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, proclaiming it far and near to all who have not yet heard it.
Just as flowing springs all return to the sea, merging into a single flavor without any diversity.
The paths of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, as well as those of the bodhisattvas—all these ultimately return to the unsurpassed, true, and correct [enlightenment].
It is like the sun and moon, which illuminate all under heaven: the hundred grains, medicinal herbs, trees, and even the thorns and brambles alike.
This scripture is thus: with boundless wisdom, it illuminates the three realms, causing all to enter into the single meaning.
In the past, there was a Tathāgata named Bhaiṣajyarāja; at that time, there was a noble king named Ratnacchattra.
For five kalpas he made offerings to that Medicine King Buddha, providing all things for his peace and comfort, leaving him in no want.
He commanded his thousand sons to likewise make offerings to the Buddha.
The thousand sons received the teaching and, with hearts leaping with equal joy,
made offerings to the Tathāgata for five kalpas each, providing food, drink, bedding,
canopies, banners, and music.
Prince Śuddhodana, dwelling in seclusion, reflected to himself: "Is there perhaps any offering that surpasses this?
A deity in the sky spoke: "The offering of the Dharma is supreme."
He then asked himself: "What is meant by 'nourishment through the Dharma'?
The deva then told him: "You should go and ask the Buddha.
The Buddha explained it for him in detail—those difficult-to-understand phrases, the profound and wondrous treasury of the Dharma.
Through emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, one enters into right wisdom.
With great kindness and great compassion, one subdues all demons; the sixty-two views are naturally eliminated.
Impermanence, suffering, and emptiness are not matters of the self; there is no self, no person, no life-span, and no vital principle.
Proceeding in accordance with this, one upholds the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas, turns the wheel of non-retrogression, and allows each dharma to illuminate every other dharma.
The twelve links of dependent origination arise from one another in succession; having understood that they are fundamentally non-existent, they have neither beginning nor end.
Thereupon, Śobhita attained the patience of compliance (*anulomikī kṣānti*) and, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, guarded the city of the Dharma.
With unremitting diligence, he attained the five supernormal powers, dhāraṇīs, and eloquence, transforming and enlightening all beings.
He established fourteen thousand people in the Great Way;
countless śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas were reborn in the heavens, for which reason they offered praise.
The Dharma-offering is supreme.
Should anyone wish to make an offering, they should receive and uphold this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
"The Tathāgata’s skillful means are discerned; there are no two vehicles, for all return to the One Way.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed eighty thousand bodhisattvas:

“Bhaiṣajyarāja, because of these bodhisattvas and others, you should carefully observe this assembly of the fourfold community—countless billions of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans; bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās; śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas—who are now present before my eyes, desiring to hear the Tathāgata preach this sūtra. When this entire assembly hears even a single verse or a single stanza, they shall, in the space of a single thought-moment, rejoice and offer their support. The Buddha shall bestow upon all these members of the fourfold community the prediction of their future attainment of the mind set on supreme, perfect, and true enlightenment.”
The Buddha told Bhaiṣajyarāja:

"If, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, one should hear even a single four-line verse of this sutra and, for the duration of a single thought-moment, offer encouragement and assistance, the Buddha shall grant them all the prediction that they shall attain the unsurpassed, true, and correct path."

Having previously served hundreds of thousands of millions of Buddhas and having resolved their minds and established their vows under those hundreds of thousands of millions of Buddhas, these beings of such a kind have come to be born here out of compassion for all people.

If one receives and upholds even a single verse from this sutra, reciting it, copying it onto bamboo or silk, engraving it upon the heart so as not to forget it, or listening to its verses with reverent examination as if they were the supreme words of the Tathāgata, and if one intends to make offerings to this scroll with flowers, incense, silken banners, and streamers, joining one's palms toward it and prostrating in homage, then one should be called a true refuge in the world.
He further addressed Bhaiṣajyarāja:

"If sons or daughters of good family can maintain even a single verse, or if they encourage others with joy upon hearing the name of this sutra, and if they hear that name, they shall realize this: in future ages, as the World-Honored One passes it on from one to another, those sons or daughters of good family will become Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas."

Why is this so? If those sons or daughters of good family receive, uphold, read, recite, copy, observe, listen to, and make offerings to this sutra—with banners, flowers, silks, and various fragrant incenses—they shall be said to have accomplished the unsurpassed, perfect, true path. Having attained parinirvāṇa, they will be as if beholding the Tathāgata; they will universally pity the devas and people of the world, and according to their aspirations, they will attain self-mastery. Always being born among humans with the desire to expound this sutra, such persons have already cultivated subtle and wondrous practices; by virtue of those performed deeds, they shall be born in a majestic and pure Buddha-field. Because they constantly contemplate conditions with the intent to preach the Dharma, one should know that these followers pity all living beings and have come to be born here because the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa; thus, they act in accordance with the Tathāgata’s mission.

That son of good family will say of that person: "He performs the work of the Tathāgata and has been dispatched by the World-Honored One; yet, regarding this Dharma instruction proclaimed by the Tathāgata which he expounds, if it is not fully elucidated, his own body shall continue to suffer."

Suppose there is a person whose disposition is wicked and treacherous, who constantly harbors malice; if, in a mere instant of thought, one speaks of unspeakable matters to such a person, the resulting calamity is unfathomable. If, for the duration of an eon, one slanders the Tathāgata while simultaneously defaming this person, the offenses are equal and no different; both are entirely of the same nature as that of the World-Honored One.
If a son of good family is preaching this sutra and a young child receives this scripture,

and if a layperson or a śramaṇa should direct harsh words or evil deeds toward him, treating him with displeasure and making him hear offensive speech— uttering falsehoods with sincere intent and proclaiming cries of resentment— then that person incurs calamity and sin as if they had harbored harmful intentions toward the Tathāgata.
Noble sons and noble daughters who receive this sutra, uphold it, recite it, and read it, yet do not travel abroad to preach it for others, shall incur transgression and fault.

If one receives and upholds this sutra, they should offer it worship and scatter offerings of robes, fine food and drink, incense, flowers, lamps, and rare, exquisite jewels; such noble sons and noble daughters are truly great treasures and should be paid homage.
Why is this? It is because even those who hear this sutra but once, or those who listen to it while making offerings, do so with the aspiration for supreme, perfect, and true enlightenment.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"If one wishes to abide in the Buddha-way, And aspire to one's own merit, One should make offerings to such a person: To those who uphold this sutra."
If one delights in the various supernormal knowledges and speaks freely as one wishes,
then one should receive this scripture and also provide offerings and service to the attendant.
One who preaches this Dharma of the sutra does so out of compassion for sentient beings.
Sent by the Lion of the World to transform the various classes of living beings,
if one upholds this scripture, they will always be diligent in every birth;
coming forth with strength and courage, they shall take pity upon the multitudes.
Born at will wherever one desires, in the final age of the end times,
one shall behold and encounter this sutra as the most supreme.
It is that which should be honored and sustained with the incense and flowers of all devas and humans.
One should constantly provide robes and all manner of coverings for the Dharma Master.
One should revere that person as one would always revere a Buddha; by immediately joining one's palms in salutation, the noble path will manifest of itself.
If, at the final time, one encounters this sutra and, after the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, upholds its scrolls;
if one honors it as the Most Victorious One with offerings of food and drink,
all manner of flavorful delicacies, chambers, beds, bedding, and billions of garments— yet hears it but once.
When one’s advancement is thus honored, the Tathāgata bestows upon that person the prediction [of enlightenment].
The Buddha dispatches those sons to come into the human world; if there are those who are most excellent, they shall encounter this scripture.
Should there be those who hear this, transcribe it, uphold it, or even see it before their eyes while the present Buddha still dwells;
yet if for a full kalpa they harbor resentment in their hearts and their countenances change from their natural state,
such persons shall immediately incur countless calamities and transgressions.
If there are those who uphold this sutra scroll, explain it in detail, and provide interpretations for others,
yet some should slander such individuals as these, their transgression would be incalculably greater than that of the former.
Suppose there were someone who, manifesting before [the Buddha], praised him with palms joined, doing so for the full duration of an eon;
with pure resolve seeking this sublime path of the Buddha, they offered hundreds of thousands of millions of hymns of praise and eulogy.
To praise and chant the praises of the Dharma Master with a joyful and delighted mind,
that person shall obtain merit beyond measure.
To proclaim his renown and the virtue of this wise one, that gentleman shall obtain merit even more transcendent than this.
If one were to provide offerings to a learner for eighteen billion *koṭis* of *kalpas*,
presenting them with exquisite delicacies of every flavor, celestial incense and flowers,
and the finest, most refined silks— counting for eighteen thousand billion *kalpas*— such a person would offer these gifts.
With harmonious voices and joyful countenances, they offer [this] through rugged terrain.
If there should be even one who, upon hearing this sutra, attains all manner of benefits and blessings, they shall be infinite and beyond compare.

The Buddha told Bhaiṣajyarāja Bodhisattva: "I have frequently proclaimed and taught immeasurable chapters of sutras in the past and present; those yet to be spoken shall be even more numerous. Compared to all phenomena in the world, this present scripture and its verses are named with such manifest and vast glory that they are most honored and supreme. Though none throughout the heavens or across the lands believe in or delight in them, the Tathāgata’s perfect enlightenment remains unimpaired. Those who dwell in seclusion within and secretly receive this scripture from a Dharma Master are protected by the majestic power of the Tathāgata; no one can destroy it, for they have already heard it in previous lives."

Even while the Tathāgata is currently present, there are many who hear this scripture and slander it; how much more so after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, when it will be difficult to encounter? Their aspirations will be obscured; observe, sons and daughters of good family, that such is the case for them.

The Tathāgatas currently residing in other worlds all behold them; wherever they abide, they hear their own voices. Such is the power of faith, the power of roots of goodness, and the power of aspiration. Abiding together in one place within the chamber of the Tathāgata, the virtues of such a company are as follows.
To seek the water of the Tathāgata with one’s resolve fixed upon the Buddha’s palm is brought about by the vows and practices of former lives.

After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, if there are those who believe in this canonical scripture of the True Dharma, and who receive, uphold, transcribe, make offerings to, follow it in accordance with, and explain it to others, their merit shall be as such.
The Buddha told Bhaisajyarāja Bodhisattva:

"If there are those who can preach this sutra’s instructions, or who copy it and behold it, one should erect a divine temple for the Buddha for such a person, established with great jewels, high, broad, and vast; it need not contain the relics of the Buddha."
Why is this? It is because one would be fully honoring the relics of the Tathāgata.

Wherever this Dharma of the sutra is spoken, recited, chanted, or transcribed—and once it has been transcribed—the bamboo slips, silk, and scrolls should be venerated and served; one should take refuge in them and pay homage as if to a Buddha’s stupa or monastery, offering all kinds of incense, flowers, blended perfumes, and fragrant fumigations, as well as lutes, harps, cymbals, banners, canopies, silken streamers, and pennants.
"If there are sentient beings who wish to visit Buddhist temples and prostrate in worship, they should draw near to this unsurpassed teaching of the Dharma.
He then addressed Bhaisajyarāja:

"There are many bodhisattvas who have left the household life for the sake of the Way, as well as ordinary laypeople practicing the bodhisattva path, yet they are unable to obtain such a sūtra as this, nor see it being read, recited, copied, or made offerings to."

If there are bodhisattvas who practice the bodhisattva path and understand skillful means, and should they hear this model of the Buddha—the Dharma practiced and shared by bodhisattvas—and if those who hear it believe and delight in entering therein, understanding it clearly and receiving offerings, they shall, upon a single seat, draw near to the unsurpassed, true, and correct Way. If anyone sees such a person as this who has entered into this principle, their merit is incalculable.
The Buddha told Bhaiṣajyarāja:

"Suppose there is a man who, being extremely thirsty, seeks water; yet instead of digging in level ground, he digs into high plateaus. Day after day he exerts his labor, but sees only dry earth. Although time passes, the spring remains deep and hidden, and he does not obtain water."
Again, at another time, he dug up a great deal of earth until he saw muddy water; it was so turbid that it could not be drunk, so what was to be done?

That man did not slacken his efforts and gradually advanced until he reached the water. At that moment, the man beheld the original auspicious sign; he cast off his doubts and was no longer hesitant, thinking: "I have exerted labor for many days and months, and now I am finally able to obtain this water."
In this way, Bhaiṣajyarāja!
If there should be a bodhisattva who hears this sutra but does not receive, uphold, recite, or study it, they will be very far removed from the unsurpassed, right, and true path.

Those who emulate this are the practitioners of the bodhisattvas' deeds; if they hear this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, recite it with diligent cultivation, cherish it in their hearts, and put it into practice, they shall then swiftly attain supreme perfect enlightenment.
The Buddha said to Bhaiṣajyarāja:
"Any bodhisattva who is unwilling to accept and recite [this teaching] shall not be able to attain unexcelled, perfect, true, and complete enlightenment."
Why is this? As I have previously declared and proclaimed these words: if there is anyone who does not delight in this sutra, they are far removed from all the Tathāgatas.
This sutra is the foremost of all dharmas of the Path and the source of all wisdom, by which bodhisattvas achieve perfection.
If there are bodhisattvas who, upon hearing this sutra, feel terror, dread, and anxiety, and do not find joy in it, one should know that they are beginners on the Vehicle.
If one is not terrified, it means they have long cultivated the bodhisattva practice.
If a śrāvaka encounters this sutra-dharma and becomes fearful, terrified, or harbors dread, it is because of their arrogance and self-indulgence.
The Buddha said to Bhaiṣajyarāja:

"After the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, if there are bodhisattvas and mahāsattvas who wish to expound this sūtra for the fourfold assembly, they should don the robe of the Tathāgata and sit upon the lion throne of the World-Honored One; only then shall they proclaim this sūtra to the fourfold assembly."
What is meant by wearing the robes of the Tathāgata?
It means that when a person is patient, gentle, and composed, this is called wearing the robes of the Tathāgata.
Noble son, you should cultivate this robe.
What is meant by the World-Honored One’s lion throne?
To understand that all dharmas are entirely empty and quiescent, and to abide in the state of no-thought and no-vow—this is the World-Honored One’s lion throne.

Furthermore, son of good family, you should dwell and sit in this manner, and for the sake of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, devas, nāgas, and spirits, you should extensively analyze and expound this Dharma of the sutra. With a heart leaping with joy and free from cowardice, you should set your mind upon the Great Way and open the path for the fourfold assembly.

If that son of good family should again dwell in another world-system, manifesting transformation-bodies along with their retinue of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās to proclaim this Dharma, should there be any who hear it but do not rejoice, I shall cause them to rejoice and ensure they attain love and delight.

If one dwells in seclusion amidst the wilderness and desolate lands, and there are devas, nāgas, spirits, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, or mahoragas, I shall dispatch transformed beings to preach the Dharma for them; even if they are far away in other directions or buddha-fields, I will cause them to manifest themselves everywhere so that all people may see them.

"If there are those who receive this scripture but do not understand its phrases and meanings, losing their sequence, I shall cause those who recite and study it to be blessed by its majestic spiritual power so that they may comprehend the meaning and the order.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"All who abandon one another out of fear and confusion, Should listen to this sutra."
This Dharma is difficult to encounter, and those who have faith in it are likewise rare to find.
It is like a person seeking water who digs into a high plateau;
though they repeatedly exert great effort, they see only dry and parched earth.
He observes and reflects to himself: "The water is still very far off;
though the pit I have dug is this deep, I continue to see only dry earth.
Only then does he gradually perceive that moist earth begins to appear little by little."
Thus, having resolved his doubts in his heart, he has now attained proximity to the water.
Those who do not hear this sutra and do not practice it repeatedly are far removed from the Way;
their distance from the Buddha’s wisdom is just like this.
This sutra is profound and sublime; it resolves all matters concerning the śrāvakas.
Upon hearing this king of sutras again and contemplating its meaning, one draws near to the Great Way, and the wise attain noble wisdom.
Just as one knows that water has been found upon seeing moist soil,
so too, when one enters the Buddha’s chamber, dons the Tathāgata’s robe,
and sits upon my noble seat, the wise one speaks thus.
Entering my chamber with a mind of loving-kindness, clad in the robes of patience and gentleness,
and seated upon the lion throne of the realization of emptiness, he speaks without fear.
Even if struck by knives, tiles, or stones, or reviled and cursed by others, he remains undaunted.
Therefore, I shall preach this Dharma, and I will endure all these sounds.
Wandering through billions of lands, my body shall remain steadfast throughout inconceivable hundreds of millions of kalpas,
as I distinguish the teachings for the sake of sentient beings.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, in order to eliminate the knots of enmity for the sake of the multitude,
he dispatched many emanated beings to preach this sūtra.
To the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, as well as the laymen and laywomen of pure faith—
One should make offerings to these people, as well as to all those gathered in the assembly.
Whether they strike with stones or beat with staves, revile, harbor resentment, or speak with malice—
if there are such violent ones, the transformed beings shall all admonish and instruct them.
Even if one wanders alone, reciting, chanting, and practicing [the teachings],
without being beset by an evil reputation, and dwelling in solitude with integrity—
such a person, while engaged in that practice, remains thus by themselves day and night.
I shall dispatch them to go together with you as companions to preach this scripture.
These people possess eloquence without hindrance; they are highly capable of clear understanding and act in accordance with the Dharma.
They shall bring joy to hundreds of thousands of myriads of beings, just as the holy Buddhas have established it.
If there should be anyone who does not rely on this Dharma, they shall be called a "contrary Bodhisattva."
"Whether the seekers are wandering or sitting, they shall behold Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Chapter Eleven:

The Seven-Jeweled Stupa From the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, Chapter Eleven: The Seven-Jeweled Stupa. At that time, before the Buddha, a stupa made of the seven precious jewels emerged from the earth. Extending twenty thousand *li*, it appeared and circled the Buddha, then leaped up into the void and stood there spontaneously.
That stupa was exquisitely beautiful, its colors shifting in a thousand ways; five kinds of flowers rained down upon it, falling in profusion like snow.

The stupa and temple, as well as the lecture hall, were magnificently adorned and constructed from countless jewels; with hundreds of thousands of railings, windows, and balconies, they were beyond all calculation.
Numerous banners and canopies were suspended, with precious necklaces hanging down; bright moon pearls were arrayed throughout the void like a multitude of stars.
Incense burners and jeweled vases were filled with famous incenses, their fragrance of sandalwood wafting everywhere to permeate the entire trichiliocosm Buddha-field.
With gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, coral, amber, musaragalva, and agate, they fashioned precious canopies; these canopies were so lofty and prominent that they reached the first heaven.
The gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and the Four Heavenly Kings all scattered *manojñā* flowers as an offering to the stupa made of the seven treasures.
Within that stupa temple, a voice spontaneously issued forth, exclaiming:
"Excellent! Wonderful!"
Excellent!
World-Honored One, you dwell in peace!
It is exactly as you have said: the Way and its Virtue are profound and subtle, transcending all and peerless; wisdom is equal and one, like empty space, truly without any difference.

At that time, the fourfold assembly beheld the stupa made of the seven treasures suspended in the void, lofty and sublime, towering and immeasurable, with a brilliance so radiant it illuminated everything without exception. Uttering cries of "Excellent!", they leaped for joy, stood with palms joined, gazing up at it without weariness.

At that time, there was a bodhisattva named Mahāpratibhāna. Seeing that the hearts of the devas and humans were filled with hesitation—alternately moved by sorrow and joy—and desiring to know what auspicious omen this portended, he [inquired].
Therefore, he previously asked the Buddha:

"Indeed, World-Honored One, for what reason has this stupa of the seven treasures now appeared before the Great Sage—so high and vast that there is none who does not see it—and why does this stupa spontaneously emit a voice, praising: 'Excellent!'"
"What has moved you such that this auspicious omen appears?
The World-Honored One then addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāprajñā:
"Within this jeweled stupa-temple resides the body of a Tathāgata, complete in every respect and without any deficiency."
To the east, beyond incalculable assemblies of Buddha-worlds from here, there is a Buddha named Prabhūtaratna Tathāgata, whose land is called Ratnaviśuddha.
When he was originally practicing the Way, he made this vow:

"I shall surely cultivate and perfect this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* myself, so that all bodhisattvas may hear it; only then shall I sit beneath the Bodhi tree and attain supreme, true, and correct enlightenment."
The Buddha’s thoughts were exactly as he had spoken; he preached the Dharma for the sake of those in the ten directions, transforming and enlightening all so that they might attain the Way.
At that time, when the Buddha was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he addressed the devas, the people of the world, and the bhikṣus:
"After my parinirvāṇa, you shall receive the Tathāgata’s body and take its entirety; having preserved it whole and complete, erect a great stūpa and temple."
"If those who see the stupa all find their proper place, its merit will be beyond limit.
At that time, that Buddha established such infinite and holy transformation:

"In the worlds of the ten directions, wherever this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is expounded, my stupa made of the seven treasures shall emerge at the places where the Buddhas preach the sutra; there, my śarīra within the stupa of the seven treasures shall praise them, saying, 'Excellent!'"

The Buddha told Mahāpratibhāna: "This stupa made of the seven treasures is located in the eastern direction, situated below, at a distance from here of as many buddha-fields as there are sands in immeasurable Ganges Rivers. It has remained in the void without ever appearing, until now it beholds the Tathāgata, the Samyaksaṃbuddha Śākyamuni. When he was practicing the path and training as a bodhisattva, for the sake of sentient beings, he did not begrudge his own body or life. With diligent and tireless effort, he practiced skillful means—generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, single-minded concentration, and wisdom. Seeking a head, he gave his head; seeking eyes, he gave his eyes; seeking a nose, he gave his nose; seeking ears, he gave his ears; he gave his hands, feet, limbs, wife, children, and attendants; he gave seven-jeweled carriages, elephants, horses, furs and garments, and cities, towns, villages, and hamlets, granting whatever others requested. Without any attachment or regret, he brought himself to the attainment of Buddhahood."

I have now come here specifically to pay my respects to the Able One (Śākyamuni), desiring that the Buddha Śākyamuni sit upon my lion-gold throne to preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, thereby transforming and enlightening all beings so that they may receive his grace.
The Tathāgata Śākyamuni, following the exhortation he had received, ascended the lion throne in the lecture hall and expounded the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, speaking in verse:
"If one hears of the Buddha Prabhūtaratna And knows his name,
One shall never fear the beginning or the end, Nor shall one again encounter suffering or affliction."
If one hears the name of the Medicine King and takes up his title,
all ailments will naturally be healed, and one will immediately know one's past lives.
Of all forms of making offerings, honoring the Dharma is supreme.
Discerning emptiness and devoid of [deluded] wisdom, one attains the Buddha-way by oneself.
Proclaiming the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* to reveal it to those who have not yet reached it,
one understands that fundamentally there are no three vehicles, thereby conforming to the singular, unsurpassed truth.
The Buddha told Mahāpratibhāna:

"At this time, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Prabhūtaratna is in that stupa temple; having heard from afar the preaching of this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* scripture, he has leaped forth and praised it, saying, 'Excellent!'"
The Bodhisattva Mahāprajñā again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Indeed, World-Honored One, we and all those gathered here now wish to behold the form of the Buddha Prabhūtaratna. We pray that you will bestow your compassionate grace and exercise your majestic spiritual power, so that all who have come may each attain the realization of the Great Way."
The Buddha told Mahāpratibhāna Bodhisattva:
“The Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna also made this vow in the past:

‘In whatever direction my stupa and temple may be, wherever this sutra is heard, if the Tathāgatas and the fourfold assembly wish to behold my body, they shall all be able to see it according to their respective aspirations throughout the ten directions, and they shall all together make offerings to this manifested image.’”
"O Mahāpratibhāna!
If you wish to know my own person, you should likewise cause all the Tathāgatas who have appeared in the worlds of the ten directions, those who transform beings and preach the Dharma, to come here."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāprajñā again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Indeed, World-Honored One, may you bestow your great grace and universally manifest the holy virtues of all Buddhas throughout the lands of the ten directions."

The Buddha silently gave his consent. Immediately, he emitted from the hair-tuft between his brows a subtle and wondrous light that universally illumined hundreds of thousands of millions of buddha-lands, each as numerous as the sands of five hundred *gaṅgā* rivers. All the World-Honored Ones appeared everywhere within those lands, sitting beneath trees upon marvelous and magnificently adorned lion-thrones.
