Accompanied by countless hundreds of thousands of bodhisattvas, they sat upon exquisite seats of interlaced jewels; rare and extraordinary silk banners and canopies hung from all four sides above the thrones of the Buddhas. For the sake of all sentient beings, they preached the Dharma with voices so gentle and harmonious that none failed to understand, while hundreds of thousands of bodhisattvas received and accepted what they heard.

In the four cardinal directions—east, west, south, and north—as well as the four intermediate corners and above and below, throughout countless hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddha-worlds, as numerous as the sands of immeasurable Ganges Rivers, all were likewise seen in this same manner.
At that time, each of the Buddhas of the ten directions addressed their respective bodhisattvas:

"Sons of noble family, you should go to the Sahā world to see the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Śākyamuni, and you should also behold and pay homage to the stupa and temple containing the physical image of the World-Honored One Prabhūtaratna."

At that time, all the meritorious virtues and sublime spiritual power of this Sahā world-system manifested spontaneously; trees made of the seven treasures grew all around, and the entire ground was transformed into deep blue lapis lazuli. With cords of purple-golden sandalwood, the eight-fold intersecting paths were continuously adorned. The ground became level and even, and all cities, states, counties, villages, towns, great oceans, rivers, streams, and springs vanished from sight. Only natural celestial incense burners were seen, burning various famous incenses, while heavenly flowers rained down everywhere.
In this buddha-field, at that opportune time, the devas and human beings were transported to other buddha-lands.

At that time, the entire assembly was present within pavilions made of the seven precious jewels; these pavilions were exquisitely adorned and their splendor was beyond measure, pervading this entire buddha-field.
At that time, all the Buddhas of the ten directions each had their own attendants, who likewise all came to this Sahā world and each arrived beneath the various jewel-trees.

These jewel trees are twenty-two thousand li in height; their branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits are each luxuriantly flourishing. Beneath these jewel trees are lion thrones twenty thousand li in height, all fashioned from various rare jewels and precious substances.

Upon the seats of the Tathāgatas, such as these, throughout this trichiliocosm, all Buddhas were seen without exception, pervading everywhere; it was not merely a manifestation produced by the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Śākyamuni, but rather [Buddhas] who had each come from the various Buddha-fields of the ten directions to this place to manifest the virtue of the infinite Great Way.

At that time, the World-Honored One Śākyamuni transformed himself into the manifested images of all Tathāgatas, residing in twenty-two billion lands in each of the eight directions; in all these places, there were no hells, hungry ghosts, or animals, and he had transferred all devas and asuras to other Buddha-worlds in other directions.

He caused the lands of twenty trillion Buddha-fields to become of dark-blue lapis lazuli; all were transformed into trees made of the seven treasures. These various jewel-trees were twenty-two thousand li in height, with branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits each flourishing profusely. The lion-thrones were twenty thousand li high, and these Buddha-lands were all level and even. They were devoid of rivers, seas, streams, or springs, nor were there any mountains—neither the Mucilinda, Mahāmucilinda, Sumeru King of Mountains, nor the Cakravāḍa and Mahācakravāḍa ranges. Each and every Buddha-field was level ground, composed of the seven treasures and individually adorned. The interlacing lattices of jewels provided immeasurable joy, with various flowers strewn everywhere and manifold famous incenses being burned.
Beneath each of the various jeweled trees, a Tathāgata sat upon a lion throne.

In this manner, there were further twenty thousand other worlds where the Tathāgata Śākyamuni individually adorned each direction, manifesting them as pure and serving as the dwelling places for all Buddhas. In these Buddha-lands, there were likewise no hells, hungry ghosts, or animals; nor were there dragons, spirits, or asuras. Furthermore, the devas and human inhabitants had all been transferred to other Buddha-lands.
The ground of these buddha-fields is of dark-blue lapis lazuli, with cords of purple-golden sandalwood (*cāmpeya*) connecting the various trees at eightfold intersections.
Furthermore, those trees are as tall, magnificent, and exquisite as previously described, and their lion thrones are likewise adorned and embellished.

The ground there is level and even, devoid of mountains, rivers, oceans, or seas; it is covered with fragrant flowers, various jewels, and rare treasures forming a lattice canopy, while bright moon pearls hang down as before. Whether walking or stopping, the paths and thoroughfares are uniform and without distinction.

At that time, the Tathāgatas manifested by Śākyamuni Buddha, who were proclaiming the teachings of the Way in lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the eastern direction, all returned. From each of the ten directions, three thousand billion Buddhas, the Perfectly Awakened Ones, all arrived there. These Tathāgatas all sat upon lion thrones made of precious jewels, and each took a precious flower and handed it to their attendants, saying:

"Sons of good family, go to Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa to the presence of the Buddha Śākyamuni. Convey our names and respectfully inquire after him: Is his holy body healthy and strong? Is his power as usual? Is he dwelling in peace?"
"With these many flowers, scatter them as an offering upon that Buddha, the assembly of bodhisattvas, and his disciples, and proclaim my words so that many may be inspired and transformed.

Thereupon, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Śākyamuni, seeing that all those who had been transformed were each seated upon lion thrones, and that the attendants had all gathered together bringing flowers as offerings, immediately rose from his seat and stood in mid-air; the fourfold assembly likewise all rose and stood with palms joined.

The Buddha opened the doors of the lecture hall of the Seven-Jewels Monastery with his finger; it became suddenly and completely transparent, radiant as the rising sun. It was like opening the city gates of a great kingdom and removing the bolts and pivots so that there is no obstruction between the inside and outside.

Śākyamuni Buddha opened the door of the lecture hall of the Seven-Jewels Monastery with two fingers of his hand; the manifestation of his majestic virtue was likewise beyond measure and limit, just as it had been before.

As soon as the Tathāgata opened the door of this temple of the seven treasures, the body of the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna—the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha—immediately appeared. Seated upon his lion throne, his complexion remained as it was, neither withered nor parched; his majestic radiance and upright features were as if depicted in a painting. He proclaimed once more:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
Excellent,
Śākyamuni Buddha!
How wonderful it is that you preach this sutra!
"It is because I wish to hear this Dharma of the sutra that I have appeared here.

At that time, the fourfold assembly saw the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Prabhūtaratna; hearing that he had entered parinirvāṇa and passed away incalculable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas ago, they cried out, "Excellent! and listened with rapt attention.
They were greatly astonished and marveled, thinking it had never occurred before.
They immediately took celestial flowers and scattered them as an offering over Śākyamuni Buddha and the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna.
At that time, the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna offered half of his seat to Śākyamuni, and from within the temple made of the seven treasures, a voice issued forth, saying:
“Śākyamuni Buddha!
I pray that you will sit upon this throne.

Śākyamuni Buddha immediately complied with these words; at that time, the two Tathāgatas were together in one place in the void, sitting upon lion thrones draped with canopies of the seven precious gems.
At that time, the fourfold assembly each thought to themselves:

"The Buddhas, the Truly Realized Ones, possess a Way and virtue so lofty and remote as to be unattainable; they are so majestic and immeasurable as to be beyond all praise or limit. We pray only that the Tathāgata will deign to look upon us with compassion and bestow his majestic spiritual power and grace, so that we may all dwell together in the void."
The Buddha, knowing their thoughts, manifested his power of supernatural transformation (*ṛddhi*), causing the fourfold assembly to spontaneously ascend into the air.
Then, Śākyamuni Buddha addressed the fourfold assembly, including the bhikṣus:
"In this Sahā world-system, who is capable of enduring and proclaiming this sutra?"
Now is the time, and this is a great occasion; whether the Tathāgata is currently present or has entered parinirvāṇa, you should receive this Dharma and uphold, recite, and chant it.

Now that the body of the Tathāgata is about to enter parinirvāṇa, bhikṣus should set aside the customary duties of making offerings and serving the Tathāgata, and instead honor, revere, and comply with this sutra.
At that time, he spoke in verse:
"The Great Sage of Infinite Excellence has arrived here; because the Guide has appeared, this wondrous and marvelous stupa temple is revealed."
Bhikṣus, you who wish to know: for the sake of hearing the Dharma, you have raised yourselves up; yet who among you has examined this and failed to arouse diligence?
Since my parinirvāṇa until now, throughout incalculable kalpas, it is only today that you are able to desire to hear the sūtras.
For this reason I have come forth, and through these causes and conditions I proclaim the teaching; may you attain the boundless liberation that is the sublime benefit of the Dharma.
In past lives, I myself made this vow; it is by this very path that the aspiration of the Guide is fulfilled.
Since his parinirvāṇa, such a vast eon has passed; yet now he is seen again throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
From here, he dwells at a distance so immense and remote that it exceeds hundreds of thousands of millions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Because of the sūtras, they have come forth to this place; the holy generals who have attained parinirvāṇa have manifested themselves.
Each abides in their respective lands, and all their aspirations and inclinations are toward the practice of the śrāvakas.
All desire to protect and preserve the True Dharma; for what reason should the scriptures be made to endure for a long time?
Throughout the countless worlds of the Buddhas, they shall gather and harmonize with all sentient beings.
Having come to this place, they cultivate and adorn it with purity through the power of their spiritual feet (*ṛddhipāda*).
Each speaks of such extensive meanings; by what cause can one speak thus regarding this Dharma-eye?
The Buddhas dwell here, beyond all measure or calculation; beneath the trees, they abide in the site of enlightenment.
Their bodies, the ultimate truth, are majestic and vast as billions of *koṭis*; these multitudes of Guides sit upon lion thrones.
Pure and eternally upright, as brilliant as the sun, like a blaze of fire that dispels the gloom;
with soft and exquisite fragrance wafting through the ten directions, he who brings offerings reaches out in compassion for the world.
Those who deliver and liberate all sentient beings, whose grace and virtue spread abroad, shall always have access to this.
After my parinirvāṇa, those who uphold this sutra will swiftly attain the prediction of enlightenment and behold the World’s Teacher with their own eyes.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, that benevolent and worthy Prabhūtaratna,
having heard and seen the lion throne, [will appear] at the location where the stupa-temple stands.
My body shall follow in his wake, and ten billion [bodhisattvas] will come here to this place.
The Son of the Most Victorious One is the one from whom this sutra may be preached.
If, upon hearing this Dharma, one is able to receive it to its ultimate conclusion,
that person shall be serving and taking refuge in my own body, as well as in the Honored Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna.
I reverently follow and obey the Buddhas of the ten directions in the present.
To the assembly of all Teachers, whose holy bodies are adorned with marvelous and immeasurable excellence,
I offer complete and boundless worship, receiving it with the utmost reverence.
By virtue of this sutra,
one shall further behold the World-Honored One within the monastery,
together with countless other assemblies of Teachers who have come here from hundreds of thousands of billions of lands.
O sons of noble family with wisdom as their life, you take pity on sentient beings;
this place is difficult to encounter, for it is what all the Teachers delight in.
The countless volumes of sutras are like the sands of the Ganges River.
Although the Buddha spoke that sūtra, it is not to be considered extraordinary.
As for lifting Mount Sumeru with one’s hand and leaping across billions of lands, that is not to be considered difficult.
Even if one were to engage in analytical exposition,
composing hundreds of thousands of marvelous verses and hearing of billions of Buddha-fields, it would not be considered difficult.
But if one dwells in the highest realms and preaches the Dharma for devas and humans— this is truly hard to do.
To eloquently expound immeasurable sutras is not to be considered extraordinary.
But that after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, one is able to endure and receive this scripture in the final age and proclaim it far and wide— only that is truly sublime.
If one were to roll up the entirety of empty space with a single hand,
reaching even to where there is nowhere to go, it would not be considered difficult.
After my parinirvāṇa, if one returns to such an image as this, [it will be no small matter].
In a future age, to transcribe this sutra would be truly extraordinary.
Suppose one were to take the lands of the ten directions, lift them up onto the tip of a fingernail,
carry them about as one wanders at will, and place them high in the Brahma Heaven.
This is not far off; diligence need not be extraordinary.
Rather than [practicing for] a future age, it is better to read this sutra for even a moment.
Even if one were to walk through fire during the time of the kalpa-conflagration, [this would be preferable].
To carry grass that does not burn is not enough to be considered extraordinary.
But after my parinirvāṇa, if one upholds this sūtra and explains it for even a single person, that indeed shall be most exceptional.
Suppose there were one who upholds the eighty thousand treasuries of Dharma,
proclaiming them exactly as they were taught, and revealing them to billions of people;
that bhikṣu, in that world, would transform and enlighten all the śrāvakas.
To abide in the supernormal powers is not to be considered extraordinary;
but to uphold this sutra, to believe in it with joy and delight,
and to inquire about and praise it again and again— that indeed is truly extraordinary.
If there were countless billions who erected towers for the Unattached One—
great sages endowed with the six supernormal powers, as numerous as the sands along the banks of the Ganges—
and yet, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, someone were to uphold this sutra;
The merit and reward obtained by that person shall exceed this limitlessness.
Throughout hundreds of thousands of worlds, they shall preach the Dharma beyond calculation;
now I, too, proclaim what has been distinguished by the Buddha’s wisdom.
As for this sutra, it is the most honored among all sutras;
whoever upholds this scripture serves the bodies of all Buddhas.
When a son of noble family expounds it before the Tathāgatas of the present,
Those who uphold this sutra in future ages are indeed worthy sages and saints.
To uphold this sutra for even a moment is to pay homage to the Buddhas and all the Teachers;
such a sutra is difficult to encounter.
All the Buddhas of the ten directions manifest themselves for him to praise;
he is courageous and possesses majestic spiritual power, having attained mastery in supernormal faculties.
His fame and virtue spread far and wide, and he is beloved by all the Buddhas.
By virtue of upholding this sutra, one attains the stage of tranquil concentration.
After the Guide has entered parinirvāṇa,
one shall serve as eyes for gods and humans by proclaiming this sutra.
"In a future age, should anyone preach this scripture for even a moment, all sentient beings shall prostrate and pay homage to that wise one.
In various editions, a "Brahmin Chapter" is added here, making twenty-eight chapters in total. At that time, the Buddha Śākyamuni addressed the assembled multitude:
"In the past, throughout incalculable, ineffable, and limitless kalpas, I sought the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* without ever growing weary.

At that time, I was a king who practiced the Great Dharma and the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*). I gave away gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, amber, coral, pearls, jade, giant clam shells, and agate; I gave my head, eyes, flesh, and muscles, as well as my hands, feet, limbs, wife, children, sons, daughters, elephants, horses, and carriages. I did not begrudge my own body or life, for at that time the human lifespan was immeasurable."

In accordance with my principles, I have renounced my royal rank and entrusted the governance of the state to the Crown Prince, departing to seek the Great Canon. I have beaten the drums and sounded the gongs to proclaim my command throughout the lands of the Hua and the Yi:
"Should there be anyone capable of expounding the Great Canon for me, I shall become their servant to provide them with all necessary attendance and service."
At that time, there was a brahmin who replied to him, saying:
"I possess a great canon, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*. If you can serve as my servant, I shall repay you with wisdom."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

“When I heard his words, I joyfully accepted his command and attended upon the brahmin. I provided him with whatever he required—water, broth, food, and drink; I swept and sprinkled, responded to his needs, ran errands, and gathered fruit. I stored up provisions and never grew weary or negligent, serving him for a thousand years so that he lacked nothing and suffered no thirst.”
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
"Beat the drums and ring the bells, Proclaiming the command far and near: Those who seek the Great Canon, The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*."
If you would grant me this, I shall become your servant, running and serving at your command, providing whatever is required.
I shall take pleasure in hearing [your teachings] with a willing heart and never grow weary; in all that I must provide for your support, I will not spare my own body or strength.
He aspired to hear and receive the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, wishing that its benefits extend to the ten directions rather than being for himself alone.
That king was diligent and never grew weary or indolent; he provided food and clothing to sustain his life, seeking neither delicacies nor rare luxuries.
"Out of compassion for sentient beings who have not yet been delivered, they shall immediately obtain the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The king at that time was none other than myself."
The brahmin was Devadatta.

Now that I am fully endowed with the six perfections, great kindness and great compassion, have accomplished the four immeasurable minds, the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics of purple-gold hue, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four ways in which nothing needs to be guarded, and the eighteen unique qualities—my majestic spirit being honored and my deliverance of beings throughout the ten directions—all this is due to the power of Devadatta’s kindness and virtue.

After an incalculable number of kalpas, Devadatta shall attain Buddhahood; he shall be named Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, and Blessed One. His world shall be named Devasaṃpāta.

At that time, as the Buddha, King of Heaven, extensively expounded the Dharma, sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges attained the realization of non-attachment; countless and incalculable people set their minds upon pratyekabuddhahood; and immeasurable multitudes of people, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, all gave rise to the aspiration for supreme, true, and correct enlightenment, reaching the stage of non-retrogression.

That Buddha’s lifespan shall be twenty intermediate kalpas. After his parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma shall remain for twenty intermediate kalpas. His body shall not be divided into bones, but his entire śarīra shall be enshrined in a stupa made of the seven precious gems, sixty li in height and eighty li in circumference. All people throughout the world shall go there to make offerings, using incense, flowers, music, and songs to praise his merit; they shall circumambulate the stupa and pay homage. Incalculable numbers of people shall attain the realization of non-attachment, countless people shall set their minds upon the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas, and inconceivable, immeasurable devas and humans shall resolve to attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path, vowing never to regress.

If sons or daughters of noble family hear this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* and attain a state of radiant clarity in their hearts free from doubt, they will block off the three miserable realms and shall not fall into hell, the realm of hungry ghosts, or the animal realm. They will immediately be born before the Buddhas of the ten directions to inquire about and receive the True Dharma; whether they are among the wealthy and noble of the heavens or the world, or before a Buddha, they will be spontaneously reborn within lotus flowers made of the seven treasures.
At that time, from below, the bodhisattva named Zhijī (Jñānakūṭa), who had come with the World-Honored One Prabhūtaratna, addressed his own Buddha, saying he was about to return to his native land.
Then the Buddha Śākyamuni said to Jñānakūṭa:

"I have a bodhisattva named Pǔshǒu Tóngzhēn (Mañjuśrīkumārabhūta); wait for a brief moment so that you may meet him. It would be fitting to discuss our long separation and consult upon the sūtras before returning to your native land."

Thereupon, Puṣya sat upon a seven-jeweled lotus flower with a thousand petals as large as a chariot wheel; together with the various bodhisattvas seated upon the lotuses, he leaped forth from the palace of the nāga king into the great ocean.
When the youth Samantabhadra and his retinue had all descended from their lotuses and paid homage to the two Buddhas, they exchanged greetings with the Bodhisattva Prajñākūṭa.
The Bodhisattva Prajñākūṭa asked Samantabhadra:
"In the ocean depths you visited, how many did you transform and deliver?"
He replied:
"Their number is immeasurable and beyond limit; it cannot be proclaimed by mouth nor calculated by mind. Before long, the response shall manifest of itself."

Before his speech had concluded, a lotus flower suddenly emerged from the sea and rose into the air; upon it sat countless bodhisattvas, all of whom had been transformed by Pūrṇa while at the sea and had all resolved their minds on the Great Vehicle.
Those whose resolve is set upon the unsurpassed, true, and perfect path universally discourse upon the matters of the Mahāyāna while in mid-air;
those who originally conceived the intention of a śrāvaka remain in the void expounding the practices of disciples, thereby coming to understand the Mahāyāna.
Samantabhadra then said to Jñānākara,
"The manifestations of my transformations upon the sea have been such as these.
Bodhisattva Jñānākara then questioned him with a verse:
“O you of boundless supreme benevolence and wisdom, who transforms the ocean-like multitude into a number of jewels—
pray reveal the Sage’s intent and explain its meaning.
Mañjuśrī replied:
"While in the midst of the ocean, he has been solely expounding the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
Zhijí asked again:
"That Dharma is exceedingly profound, supreme, and marvelous, difficult to equal; is there anyone who can attain Buddhahood within a short time?"
Puṣya replied: "The Dragon King has a daughter who is eight years of age;

she is intelligent and wise, surpassing all others. She has resolved her mind upon the Great Way with vast aspirations, and her nature and conduct are harmonious and refined rather than impulsive; she is capable of attaining Buddhahood."
Jñānakoṭi asked again:

"I observe that the Benevolent One, our Great Teacher, when he originally sought the Buddha-way as a bodhisattva, accumulated merit and practiced with unflagging diligence over incalculable kalpas before attaining the Buddha-way; I cannot believe that this woman has so suddenly attained perfect enlightenment."
Before his speech was finished, the woman suddenly appeared; she prostrated in salutation, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and then stood back to offer praise:
“Your meritorious virtues are most wondrous and sublime; You manifest the thirty-two marks of excellence.
All the devas pay you reverent service, And all the divine nāgas look up to you with devotion.”
"Among all classes of sentient beings, there are none who do not revere her.
Now I wish to attain Buddhahood and preach the Dharma to save all living beings.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the girl, saying:
"Although you have resolved to attain the boundless wisdom, a Buddha cannot be found.
Furthermore, even as a woman, though your diligent efforts over many kalpas have accumulated to such a degree that they are manifest, you still cannot become a Buddha."
Why is this so? Because a woman's body has not yet attained five ranks:
first, the Lord of Devas; second, Brahmā; third, the Māra-king; fourth, the Wheel-Turning Sage King; and fifth, the Great Being (Mahāsattva).
The girl then took a cintāmaṇi jewel worth as much as this world and offered it to the Buddha; the Buddha immediately accepted it.
The girl said to Śāriputra and Zhiji (Jñānakośa):
"I have offered this jewel to the World-Honored One; did the Buddha receive it quickly?"
He replied,
"Both are ill.
The woman said:
"Now, my attainment of the unsurpassed, right, and true path and my realization of supreme perfect enlightenment shall be swifter than this.

At that moment, he transformed into a male bodhisattva and immediately attained Buddhahood; his thirty-two marks and his complete array of minor characteristics were visible to all in the lands, names, and assemblies, which they marveled at as something unprecedented. Countless humans, devas, nāgas, and spirits all resolved to attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path. The three-thousandfold world system shook in six ways, and thirty thousand who had entered the stages of the Path attained the stage of non-retrogression, all destined to realize the unsurpassed, right, and true path.
Śāriputra and the Bodhisattva Jñānakośa remained silent and said nothing. Chapter Twelve:

Encouragement and Instruction *The Lotus Sutra of the True Dharma*, Chapter Twelve: Encouragement and Instruction At that time, there was a bodhisattva named Bhaiṣajyarāja, and another bodhisattva named Mahāpratibhāna, together with twenty thousand bodhisattvas, addressed the World-Honored One from before him, saying:
"We pray only that the Great Sage will remain at ease in teaching the Dharma and not harbor any anxiety."
After the Tathāgata, the Arhat, has entered parinirvāṇa, we shall together distribute this sutra and expound it to others.

Suppose there are those who are obstinate and self-willed, whose natures are not disciplined, who lack virtue and merit while harboring arrogance, who are attached to the benefits of offerings and fail to prepare the roots of goodness; they are far removed from liberation and will find it difficult to achieve it.

"O World-Honored One, we shall exert the power of patience in that world, receive this sutra, copy it, uphold it, recite it, explain it, make offerings to it, serve it, and wear it upon our bodies; we shall proclaim this sutra to eliminate our own afflictions and repay the kindness of the One Who Abides in Peace."
At that time, five hundred bhikṣus in the assembly—both those who were still training and those who were no longer training—came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Indeed, World-Honored One!
We are capable of proclaiming this sutra.”

Furthermore, Great Sage, the Tathāgatas of other worlds have all bestowed predictions upon their śrāvakas—both those still in training and those beyond training—that they shall attain the unsurpassed, true, and perfect path; they all join their palms and pay homage to the World-Honored One.
The eight thousand bhikṣus again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Great Sage, may you rest in peace; do not harbor such concerns.
After your parinirvāṇa, we shall extensively explain and transmit the path of this sutra, and we shall also proclaim it throughout other worlds.”

Why is this so? Because in this Sahā world, people are mostly arrogant and their fundamental virtue is meager; their minds are constantly filled with turmoil like fire or poison, deluded within the three realms and unable to find peace for themselves.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī, together with six thousand bhikṣuṇīs, gazed upon the Honored Countenance without ever growing weary, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Your virtue and wisdom are most supreme and majestic, immeasurable; they transcend empty space, and none can equal them."
The Buddha then addressed them, saying:

"You, Gopikā and the others, do not harbor such distress or look upon the Buddha with a sorrowful countenance, lamenting that the Tathāgata has not proclaimed [the teaching] nor granted you the prediction of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

When the entire assembly is in perfect harmony and agreement, he shall then expound and bestow upon all people the prediction [of their future enlightenment], so that they shall all attain the unsurpassed, true, and correct path, wherein all are of one and the same flavor, with no difference in that flavor.

From this point forward, you shall encounter and serve thirty-eight thousand billion assemblies of Buddhas, making offerings and attending upon them; you shall always act as a Dharma-preacher for bodhisattvas, and these six thousand bhikṣuṇīs—both those who have studied and those who have not—shall do so for the sake of all sentient beings.

Once the Bodhisattva Dharma Master has fully perfected the bodhisattva practices in successive stages, he shall become a Buddha, named Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Venerated by All Sentient Beings.

After attaining Buddhahood, he will transform and enlighten the people, each of whom shall successively transmit the prediction of enlightenment to one another, so that they shall all become Buddhas and deliver countless, incalculable beings.
Thereupon, the bhikṣuṇī Rāhulamātā and Yaśodharā each thought to themselves:
"Now the Buddha, the World-Honored One, does not take pity on us; we alone have been cast aside."
Then the Great Sage addressed the bhikṣuṇī Yaśodharā: "I now proclaim and announce to you far and near:

you shall cultivate the Way under a hundred trillion buddhas; you shall always serve as a Dharma-preacher and uphold the bodhisattva practices. When you have fully fulfilled that which you follow, you shall attain buddhahood, with the name Śatasa-hasra-raśmi-dhvaja-patāka-saṃpūrṇa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-carana-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavat. Your world shall be named Bhadra."
At that time, that Buddha’s radiance and majestic spiritual power were countless hundreds of thousands, and his lifespan was beyond measure.

Then, Mahāprajāpatī, the bhikṣuṇī Rāhulamātā, and the others, having attained what they had never experienced before, were filled with wonder, joy, and delight. They immediately spoke these verses to praise the Buddha:
“The World-Honored One who has revealed this teaching, The guide for the sake of the multitudes.”
He has brought transformation to the world, extending even to devas and humans.
Honored and served by devas and humans, he now offers us consolation;
as our guide, he fills my heart with joy.
When the bhikṣuṇīs had spoken this verse, they addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"Indeed, O Great Sage!
We believe in and delight in these teachings of the Buddha-dharma; we are capable of reciting them, as well as transmitting them to others in other worlds."
At that time, the World-Honored One looked upon eighty quadrillion bodhisattvas who had attained the various *dhāraṇīs* as they preached the irreversible wheel of Dharma.
When those bodhisattvas saw the Buddha’s radiant presence, they immediately joined their palms and addressed him, saying:
“We pray only that the Great Sage will entrust this sutra to us, so that we may preach and proclaim it.”
"Having obtained this sutra scroll, we shall single-mindedly contemplate the virtues of the Buddha.

The sons of noble family, looking up with joy and reverence toward the World-Honored One and looking down upon their own past lives and the vows they had made for equality, then uttered a lion’s roar before the Buddha:

"After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, if this Dharma of the sutra exists throughout the ten directions, we shall transcribe, uphold, recite, and contemplate its meaning, explaining and disseminating it. We shall manifest and transform others so that they may likewise do so. Receiving the holy decree of the Buddha, our associates in various different lands shall be graced by the Great Sage’s benevolence, who will receive us and cause us to achieve fulfillment."
At that time, all the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, with one mind and equal intent, spoke these verses before the Buddha:
“Indeed, World-Honored One, you remain silent and serene, O Sage; after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, may you illuminate and propagate the shadow-like teachings.”
Thereafter, in the final age, fearing there may be calamities and hardships, one should widely proclaim and explain this in detail.
If one is beaten, struck, reviled, or pelted with stones,
the Great Sage who comes and goes through the world would consider such a base person’s folly as something to be endured.
Their speech is difficult to comprehend; they are flatterers, deluded, and arrogant.
Only then do they dwell among mountain crags, claiming to have attained what they have not attained.
Lacking skill in wisdom, how can they ever offer a true response?
Walking alone in accordance with one's own will, harboring malice and lacking forbearance;
dwelling amidst greed and evil reputation— one should preach the Dharma for such a person,
and through the discourse delivered, resolve and eliminate [their afflictions], just as these six supernormal powers do.
Evil and violent, harboring a poisonous mind, they dwell in stillness yet harbor such thoughts;
entering seclusion to dwell alone, they do not avoid the prospect of being reviled.
This is our lack of forbearance, for we are attached to gain and offerings.
Thus these followers of external paths claim that what they have taught has already been given as a gift;
yet they exert themselves in their own scriptures, seeking only the benefit of offerings,
and preach within the assemblies, proclaiming the reputations of those such as us.
If one goes to the palace of a king, to ministers and their subordinates,
to brahmins and householders, or to the quarters of other bhikṣus,
and slanders me by speaking of my evils, saying that my conduct is like that of a false path—
"I shall endure all of this and serve the Great Sage.
At that time, free from sorrow and grief, if one is able to practice patience,
one should, according to what the Buddha has taught, reprove and instruct them all.
In an age of turmoil, when bhikṣus quarrel and there is great fear from wicked violence,
they will all revile us, saying, "These bhikṣus are like ghosts.
Yet those who practice reverence while in the world shall cause them all to endure such suffering and affliction.
Because we possess a compliant and gentle nature, we shall preach this sutra.
We do not crave our bodies, nor do we begrudge our lives;
we shall be able to uphold this [sutra] with our resolve set upon the Buddha-way.
The World-Honored One fully knows them; like wicked bhikṣus who will appear later in the final age, they shall be analyzed and explained [as follows]:
their countenances are constantly displeased, and they repeatedly commit what is improper.
Wandering at improper times, their robes often ill-arranged;
yet even in this final age after the Hero of the World has entered parinirvāṇa,
they shall be courageous amidst the assembly and expound this sutra with discernment.
If one goes about seeking entry into a city and happens to desire or seek anything, one should practice giving wherever it is appropriate;
the Buddha knows this and will not let such a person fall.
By using love and joy as the foundation for the world, one gives rise to and cultivates a heart of benevolence and goodness.
Practicing few desires and observing moderation, one attains the sublime and tranquil nirvana.
All the luminaries of the world gather from the ten directions;
I shall speak with utmost sincerity, so that all may see that my heart is not false.
The Lotus Sutra, Scroll Six;
The Lotus Sutra, Scroll Seven.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Yuezhi Nation during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Chapter Thirteen: On Peaceful Practice At that time, the Great Being Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha:

“O Great Sage, these bodhisattvas pay homage to the World-Honored One; the manner in which they should be encouraged and gladdened is truly beyond compare, even more so than the most difficult to reach.”
"At what time should one preach this sutra for the sake of all sentient beings?
The Buddha said to Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra:
"A bodhisattva must first abide in two dharmas before they may expound the sutra: the first is dignified deportment (īryāpatha), and the second is ritual propriety (vidhi)."
What is meant by a bodhisattva’s understanding of dignified demeanor (*īryāpatha*)?

It is when one maintains the mind with patience and gentleness, guarding the intention and fearing self-centeredness; when one’s resolve is like the earth and perceives no person; when one practices the Dharma without perceiving a person, observing the natural mark that all phenomena are fundamentally non-existent; and when these phenomena—the models for all practices—are likewise free from conceptualization. This is called dignified demeanor.
What is meant by "ritual propriety"?
It means that a bodhisattva does not engage in affairs with kings, crown princes, ministers, officials, or commoners;
does not initiate interactions with those of external paths or heterodox studies; and does not esteem worldly classics, praise refined music, or conform to vulgar customs.
They do not covet, they do not study, and they do not associate with those who slaughter fish or hunt, or those who engage in the killing of poultry and ducks by means of nets and traps;
they do not dwell together with those engaged in song, music, or worldly assemblies;
nor do they associate with śrāvaka bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās, nor do they draw near to their conduct.

Regarding the etiquette of inquiry and greeting: one does not share the same lodging, nor does one engage in walking meditation, burning incense, scattering flowers, or lighting lamps with those who are not of like mind—except when attending assemblies for the preaching of the sutras.
One associates only with those at such preaching assemblies to participate in their activities;
even if one speaks, one remains free from attachment. This is the proper code of conduct.
He further addressed Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra: "A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva does not remain attached to his home, clan, or relatives;

he does not eagerly long to see his women or those of tender years to preach the Dharma alone; nor does he frequently visit his kinsmen, young boys or girls, or other outsiders to speak gentle words. He does not preach the sūtras for his own self-reliance when it is inappropriate to do so, nor does he stand with others or share their aspirations. Furthermore, he does not enter a private chamber alone with a single bhikṣuṇī, except when he is mindful of the Tathāgata and practicing with diligence."

Even if one has the occasion to preach the sutras to women, one must not defile the flavor of the Dharma therein, nor cause them to grasp it superficially while failing to broaden their understanding of its principles.

One should not dwell in the same place as śrāmaṇeras, bhikṣuṇīs, boys, or girls; rather, one should always delight in quiet sitting, diligently cultivating practice in secluded and solitary retreats—this is what constitutes proper decorum.
He further addressed Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra: "Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas contemplate all dharmas as entirely empty and non-existent.

Having fallen into perversion regarding what they abide in and establish, they instead take the established True Dharma as their constant abiding according to reality. They single-mindedly maintain body and mind, remaining unmoving and unshakable; they do not regress or turn back, but relinquish, extinguish, and bring to cessation. They are neither born nor existent, being naturally non-existent; they are unconditioned, innumerable, and have nothing that can be grasped. Reaching the state of non-possession, they eliminate all verbal expressions; they do not dwell in the unconditioned, nor in thought or non-thought, thereby attaining mastery over all conceptualizations."

If a bodhisattva closely and minutely observes all these dharmas and sincerely practices what ought to be practiced, they shall always abide in the two matters of majestic deportment and ritual propriety.
The World-Honored One, wishing to further clarify this meaning, uttered these verses of praise:
“If a bodhisattva who delights in it preaches this sutra,
In future ages to come, they shall be courageous and free from timidity.”
He accords with dignified deportment and ritual propriety, and his conduct is virtuous, pure, and upright. Whether it be kings and crown princes,
ministers and their subordinates and officials,
followers of external paths or heterodox schools, or those of evil and harmful character such as butchers and hunters— [he treats them all with equanimity].
Restraining the arousal of habitual tendencies, he does not engage in mutual exchange with them.
The bhikṣu who has attained arhatship stands firm in the Dharma and Vinaya;
he does not associate with those who are arrogant, nor does he keep company with those who violate the prohibitions.
Bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, having abandoned idle chatter and jesting with those of pure faith, should not engage in useless speech.
Those who wish to attain the Dharma in the present should always cease from what is improper.
Abiding well in the stage of extinction— this is called majestic deportment.
Even if one is unwilling to go and inquire about the Dharma,
for the sake of upholding and expounding this Dharma, one remains undaunted and unattached.
If sentient beings suffer from leprosy, whether they be kinsmen, members of one's clan, women,
or those of lowly appearance— one should abandon them all and depart;
not dwelling together with such as these, one should instead cultivate the roots of virtue.
One should abandon the trade of selling [living beings], as well as all forms of pride and lack of reverence;
one should cast away all attachments and standings that bring harm to oneself,
such as various kinds of insects and fleas, and one should not practice the eating of meat.
Having abandoned all that is unrighteous, those who delight in anger and resentment act in such a manner.
One should not associate with those of forced countenances, nor with others of a self-willed nature.
Those who practice in such a manner should all eliminate these faults.
Even if a wise person has a reason to preach the sutras to women,
they should not travel alone, nor should they dwell in frivolous play.
Whether entering or leaving a village, or repeatedly wandering for alms,
one should take a fellow bhikṣu as a companion and always keep the Buddha in mind.
It was the Buddha himself who first manifested these modes of conduct and etiquette.
Those who uphold this scripture should practice it with diligence.

Whether they be superior, middling, or inferior persons, if they do not practice the Dharma, there shall be no offerings made with the awareness of impermanence; all must be performed with the utmost sincerity.
The Great Being is free from conceptual thought;
firm and courageous in his practice, he does not perceive any phenomena, nor does he see their cessation.
All such Bodhisattvas are said to possess this majestic deportment.
As one would normally observe the rites of courtesy, you should now listen and examine this.
This is what shall be expounded: the Dharma of non-action, wherein nothing arises and nothing is produced.
Establishing one’s will with constancy, one contemplates and gathers the meaning of emptiness; this is what the wise practice as their ritual decorum.
Whatever one perceives is entirely a perverted conception: taking the non-existent to be existent, and using the void to create the real.
Although there is arising, all phenomena are unborn; it is through the confusion of conceptualization that the various realms of existence arise.
With a mind always single-pointed, skillfully cultivating samādhi and establishing one's practice, one shall be like the summit of Mount Sumeru.
Abiding thus, one universally contemplates all phenomena; these all phenomena are like empty space.
They are like nothingness, equally lacking solidity; one does not conceive thoughts of superiority, nor is there anything to be discarded.
The abiding place of all dharmas has no permanent name; this is the ritual conduct practiced by the wise.
After my parinirvāṇa, if there should be a bhikṣu who dares to guard such dharma rules as these, [he shall be protected].
Without any timidity or weakness, and with no thoughts arising in the mind,
one shall preach this sutra for the sake of countless people.
Whether entering a house or acting in such a manner, one should contemplate all dharmas.
All-pervading and universally pure, he expounds the meaning with serene composure, remaining unshakable.
When the sovereign kings and emperors, as well as their crown princes, desire to hear the Dharma,
they all provide him with offerings.
"Along with other elders and various brahmins, they will establish their kinsmen, all of whom shall be free from desire. He then spoke further to Puṣya:

"If, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, one wishes to preach this sutra, one should abide in peace and have already established oneself in peace; being free from flattery and without a deluded mind, one may then preach the treasury of the Dharma. Whether out of weariness with the body or out of compassion, one may record it on bamboo or silk and preach it for others. One should not use excessive words nor harbor any [selfish] intent; one should not treat other bhikṣus with contempt, nor should one praise or disparage those who act as Dharma-preachers."

Regarding those bhikṣus of different minds who are śrāvakas, he never mentions their names to speak of their faults or impurities; nor does he slander them, nor does he treat them with thoughts of enmity.

They have never disparaged those who practice while living at home; they harbor no ambitions, do not establish such practices, nor do they form any conceptualizations, yet they dwell securely in their conduct and maintain their essential commitments.
Whether coming or going, moving about, or attending dharma assemblies, he protects himself so that his conduct is without fault as he expounds the sutras and teachings.
If there are those who inquire, his mind remains unattached; having departed from the Śrāvaka vehicle, he dispatches them toward the awakening of Buddha-wisdom.
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
"The wise are ever at peace, abiding in the path of the Buddha; first they settle themselves in meditative concentration, and only then do they preach the sutras."
If one is to spread out a seat, one must ensure it is soft;
with various kinds of implements arranged in a brilliant display, one should always wear clean and pure garments, and for seven periods of seven days, practice walking meditation.
Like a dark cloud suspended in the void, he has gathered and accumulated vast and sublime merit.
His seat is fully equipped with a chest, its legs firm and solid, level and resplendent.
Countless seats, cotton rugs, and fine coverlets were prepared; he sat upright with his head facing forward, his gaze dignified and majestic.
With serene composure, he ascended and took his place upon the lofty and broad Dharma throne, regarding all people with a mind of universal equanimity.
As well as the bhikṣus, the assembly of bhikṣuṇīs, the laymen of pure faith,
and the laywomen of pure faith— whosoever should wish to hear it— I shall preach this immeasurable [Dharma] for them.
With infinite wisdom, he analyzes and discerns in due order, expounding for them various subtle and profound meanings.
Following and attending him, they request explanations on these meanings; then this sagely and wise one further provides the elucidation.
Entering into the supernormal powers and the patience of gentleness, all who hear this shall attain the Buddha-way.
These wise ones, for the sake of all beings, advance toward and eliminate all indolence,
weariness, and aversion.
Always with a compassionate heart, he preached the Dharma for the sake of the multitude, never giving rise to thoughts of weariness or indolence.
Day and night he chanted and recited, singing the sublime teachings of the Dharma, analyzing and expounding them through billions of parables.
He is universally able to exhort and gladden the hearts of all those in the assembly, such that none dare to give rise to thoughts of causing harm.
His bedding and seating are comfortable, as are his clothing, coverlets, pillows, and the medicines for his ailments.
Without harboring vain hopes, he does not follow the crowd nor make any requests.
Dispelling their weariness, he dwells in temples and monasteries, desiring that the multitudes may all understand the Buddha-way.
If all people come to listen to the Dharma of the sutras, I shall rejoice as if having attained great peace.
If there are bhikṣus who proclaim the Dharma of the sutras without expectation and without hindrance,
and who do not encounter suffering or affliction, but always observe themselves with diligence—
Free from illness, they do not suffer the pain of being struck with a staff; they harbor no thoughts of slander, their bodies are free from weariness, and they have no cause for affliction.
Such a person abides in patience and attains power such as this.
The wise person dwells in peace and security; wherever they establish themselves, they act according to the Buddha’s instructions.
Even if one were to praise them for hundreds of millions of virtues and extol all their merits, one could never reach the end.
He further addressed Pūrṇa:

“After the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, if there be a bodhisattva who harbors doubts regarding this sūtra and fails to understand it; if, when preaching or teaching, his hearing is not firm and his nature is not harmonious; if, seeing other bodhisattvas seeking the Mahāyāna, he fabricates falsehoods and slanders them; or if, seeing śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, or encountering bodhisattvas, his mind wavers and he does not immediately go to visit them—such a son of good family will remain far from the unsurpassed, right, and true path, and shall not draw near to the dwelling place of the Buddha, the God among Gods.”

Even if one were ultimately not to receive the power of merit and fail to attain supreme perfect enlightenment, the Bodhisattva practicing the Three Vehicles is like a lion in the forest; if there is any hesitation, it naturally departs, for he neither delights in what is pleasurable nor does he not delight in it.

If one cultivates the power of loving-kindness toward sentient beings, conceiving of the Tathāgata as a great father; regarding all Bodhisattvas as the World-Honored One; and even toward those householders who have not yet abandoned worldly defilements, maintaining broad and impartial respect with solemn decorum; purifying the meaning of all dharmas so that there is no doubt or fetter; adorning all dharmas with careful and settled mindfulness; reverently conforming to equality without clinging to the teachings of the sutras; and finding ultimate joy therein while reaching nowhere at all—then wherever one may be, day or night, one shall reverently protect this scripture.
"Samantabhadra!
These are the practices of the three dharmas.
When a bodhisattva observes the proper time before speaking, he performs acts of peace and security; he is neither afflicted by defilements nor harmed by them."

Those who preach this Dharma-sūtra, as well as those fellow students who are their equal-minded dharma-friends—whether they lecture upon it or hear it, believe and delight in this scripture, recite and uphold it, copy it onto bamboo or silk, or honor and serve it with offerings—their merit shall be immeasurable; speak thus so that they may dwell in peace.
Then he spoke in verse:
"If there is jealousy, harboring countless difficulties, the Dharma Master, out of compassion,
should distance himself from such hatred."
If one wishes to read this model of the orthodox canon,
one must never slander others or speak of their faults, nor fall into error, doubt, or false views.
The mind is always radiant, free from hesitation; through compassion, one attains this samādhi.
A son who dwells in peace is also able to practice patience; such a person always remains secluded, avoiding arrogance and self-importance.
Repeatedly reciting and chanting the Buddha’s scriptures, they never grew weary or indolent because of this.
There are Bodhisattvas in the ten directions who, out of compassion for sentient beings,
carry out their practices in the world.
Those who follow in the creation of reverence and study the noble wisdom should all keep this in mind: "This is my World-Honored One.
Contemplate all Buddhas, the supreme among two-legged beings; regard all Bodhisattvas as you would contemplate your own parents.
If there are those who seek the Way, let them be free from sensual desires and abandon the conceit of self and ego.
If they listen to and examine such a Dharma as this, these wise ones should guard themselves with vigilance.
"His conduct shall be secure and peaceful, and he will always attain harmony and concentration; he will lead others toward the Buddha-way and rescue billions of sentient beings.
He then spoke again to Pṛthuśāsana:

"After the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, if there is a bodhisattva mahāsattva who upholds and practices this scripture at the proper times, that bhikṣu should practice compassion toward laypeople, renunciants, śramaṇas, and all sentient beings who practice the bodhisattva path. He should constantly remember those of the past who practiced the Mahāyāna and skillfully employ expedient means to expound the meaning of the True Dharma. Yet, if there are those who hear it and do not understand or comprehend it, who find no joy in it and do not believe it, who fail to reflect upon it or master it, and instead merely sigh and say:"
"I shall attain the unsurpassed, true, and correct path and realize supreme perfect enlightenment, and by the power of my majestic spiritual authority, I wish to fly.
Mañjuśrī, you should know that when I see such as these after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there are four matters in which a bodhisattva preaches the Dharma without contention or anger.
What are these four? They are:

being seen with reverence and honored by bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās; being provided for and supported by kings, crown princes, ministers, officials, and the people of the provinces and kingdoms; being collectively received and followed by elders and brahmins; and having their recitation of the sūtras heard by the deities of space and countless sons of heaven, while devas, nāgas, and spirits attend to their rear and provide protection.
These are the four.

If he enters a county or town and returns to his dwelling, people come from all quarters day and night to inquire about the teachings of the sutras; whether he explains them for them or analyzes their ultimate destination, there are none who do not rejoice.

Why is this so? Universal Chief, you should know that it is all due to the Buddha’s establishment and the grace bestowed upon this sutra; all Buddhas of the past, future, and present are born from this, and they likewise protect this scripture.
If one hears this chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* in this Sahā world, those who receive its name and listen to its sound are extremely rare to encounter.

"Mañjuśrī! It is like a powerful Wheel-turning Sage King whose majestic virtue is vast and flourishing; over whom he rules through transformation, all other hostile nations that have not yet submitted dare not even look upon him with suspicion."

If a Wheel-Turning King mobilizes his military forces for a campaign of conquest, and rebellious ministers seek to resist the great state, his valiant and fierce generals and soldiers will exert their martial prowess to achieve victory; there shall be none who do not prostrate themselves with bowed heads in submission.

The king, filled with joy, terminated his labors and bestowed a fixed reward: he enfeoffed him with a city and a fief, granted him lands and fields, the seven treasures and rare curiosities, elephants, horses, and carriages, as well as male and female slaves.
When a minister’s achievements and meritorious services were exceptionally distinguished, the King would untie the bright pearl from within his topknot and bestow it upon him.
Why was this so? Because it was the ministers who ensured the state remained powerful and the various ethnic groups lived in peace.

The Tathāgata’s perfect enlightenment is likewise so: he is the Great Dharma King of the infinite truths of the Path. Having himself subdued his own mind, he transforms others through the Dharma; he dispels harm through virtue and battles with wisdom. He has conquered the countless hosts of various Dharma Kings and bestowed upon all living beings the immeasurable sūtras and hundreds of thousands of essential meanings without any concealment. He proclaims the City of Equanimity, wherein one perceives the Māras within oneself and is able to battle them with the dharmas of the noble ones (ārya). Attacking lust, anger, and delusion, he subdues the retinues of Māra; exhausting the afflictions of the three realms, he reaches extinction (nirvāṇa). His achievements are victorious and thus he is greatly courageous; yet in the end, there is neither destruction nor substantial reality. Because of various emptinesses, this world comes into being, just as forms and images arise from all causes and conditions.
Throughout all worlds, from antiquity to the present, there has been none who has believed in this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, nor has it ever been fully expounded.

The reason it is spoken now is due to the great compassion of universal wisdom; it is like the bright pearl within the topknot of a Great Sage-King, serving as the foremost essential teaching of the World-Honored One. By means of such practice, the Tathāgata causes them to hear this profound and wondrous scripture. From the past until the present, among all teachings proclaimed, this sūtra is the most supreme.

To eliminate all afflictions arising from dependent origination is like a holy sovereign who cherishes and protects the precious pearl within his topknot, only releasing it after a long time to bestow it upon those of original merit.

The Tathāgata has likewise guarded this most wondrous and flawless treasure day and night; having long since established it at the pinnacle of all dharmas, he now extends his compassion and reveals it to the world.
The World-Honored One, wishing to further manifest the essential meaning, uttered these verses in praise:
"Now the Tathāgata appears, by the power of his compassionate mind, ever pitying sentient beings within the realm of all living creatures."
Abiding in praise of this most honored scripture, I therefore explain it through such teachings as these.
Whether those who have set their will upon the Bodhisattva path and left the household life,
or those who remain at home, should they hear this sutra, their hearts shall tremble with compassion, and [the truth] shall manifest everywhere.
Do not slander.
When I first attained the Way of the Buddha, it was just as it is now for the Tathāgata in the present time.
If one is able to hear this honored sutra, one will then establish hundreds of millions of skillful means.
Just as a powerful Wheel-Turning Sage King, through combat,
subdues the kings of foreign lands.
He was granted elephants and horses, chariots and chests for storage, as well as the addition of fiefdoms, walled cities, and territories.
There were precious bracelets for his hands and feet, objects of exquisite beauty, and treasures of purple-polished gold,
pearls, and moonstones, along with musaragalva, green jade, and various other distinct varieties.
With rare treasures, wondrous and extraordinary, and various kinds of objects, he bestowed them each upon them,
causing all the multitudes to leap for joy and be struck with wonder.
Beholding the deeds he has accomplished, one marvels at what has never before occurred: at the very end, he untied his topknot and bestowed the bright moon-jewel as a gift.
The Buddha is likewise so; now he is the Dharma King, possessing the power of forbearance and the voice of infinite wisdom.
Constantly practicing loving-kindness and compassion, he gives rise to pity and protection; transforming all the world through the Dharma and its principles.
Beholding the afflictions of sorrow and distress among the multitudes, he expounds the sutras and teachings in numbers reaching hundreds of millions.
He clearly knows the sentient beings and the skillful means appropriate for them; today he regards all sentient beings as having reached their ultimate source.
He distinguishes hundreds of thousands of millions of koṭis of sūtra scrolls, thereby knowing the multitudes.
With resolute power and fierce wisdom, one shall preach this sutra as the bright jewel in the topknot.
In the final age, wherever this authentic scripture resides, no other teaching among all dharmas can equal it.
Reverently admiring this sutra, never speak lightly of it; those who understand and master its subtle mysteries and possess clear wisdom shall hear it.
I have expounded and manifested such a semblance-dharma (śaddharma); after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, you should rely upon it as your refuge.
Those who have the aspiration to seek and honor this sublime Way shall all receive the prediction of enlightenment,
just as the Buddha has spoken.
Free from illness and the hardships of manifold afflictions, they shall, at the end of time, [attain their goal].
In a future age, one shall immediately attain and perfect the unsurpassed true wisdom.
This most excellent and extraordinary state shall be fully possessed by all, and the fourfold assembly shall likewise encounter it in accordance with the Dharma.
Marveling at his state of non-action, they all joined their palms in reverent submission;
their own bodies shone with brilliance, emitting radiant light. Such is the attainment of those who practice this way.
Having attained perfect enlightenment and turned the wheel of Dharma, one beholds the vast model and perceives the Most Victorious One.
Within dreams, one hears and sees the hundred marks of merit, the color of purple-polished gold.
If one has heard the sūtras spoken by the Buddha and explains them for the sake of the assembly and all their kinsmen, they shall all be fully perfected.
Furthermore, whatever is protected, all is cast away; whether lying down or awake, what one perceives is thus.
Abandoning and distancing oneself from it all, one goes forth into homelessness and reaches the Buddha’s site of enlightenment.
He immediately took his place upon the lion throne; this is the benefit and merit gained by seeking the Way.
That which is called the seven treasures all converge here; by practicing this, one serves the most supreme Tathāgata.
Having already attained the Way of the Buddha, he established himself in the practice of giving; he then turned the wheel of Dharma, free from all outflows.
For the sake of the fourfold assembly, he preached the sutras and the Dharma for inconceivable billions of kalpas.
He expounded and analyzed the untainted Dharma, teaching and transforming countless billions of sentient beings.
The forms and images seen within his dreams, as well as the causes and conditions of their parinirvāṇa, were all entirely free from birth and death.
"Samantabhadra, you should know that those who constantly set their minds on the Way will bring about much instruction and transformation beyond measure.
In the final age of the Dharma's end, those who seek this sublime Dharma shall analyze and expound it extensively,
abiding securely in what they proclaim."

Chapter 14: The Emergence of Bodhisattvas from the Earth From the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, Chapter Fourteen: The Emergence of Bodhisattvas from the Earth. At that time, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as the sands of eight Ganges Rivers from other world-systems, each wearing different forms and garments, came to where the Buddha was. They prostrated themselves upon the ground, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:

"We, your humble followers, have come to this Sahā world desiring to hear this scripture, to receive, uphold, recite, and transcribe it; we shall practice with diligence, make offerings, and carry it out according to the Dharma. We pray only that the Great Sage will turn his mind toward us and, after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, graciously entrust us with the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*."
The World-Honored One said: "Stop,
son of good family!"
"Virtuous ones, you need not conceive such a plan.

In this Sahā world-system, there are already as many great beings (mahāsattvas) as the sands of eight Ganges Rivers; each of these great beings has their own retinue, numbering as many bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as the sands of sixty billion Ganges Rivers. In the future, during the final age, they shall all receive, uphold, distribute, and proclaim [this teaching]."

At that time, in this buddha-field, countless hundreds of thousands of myriads of kotis of bodhisattvas gathered spontaneously like clouds from all directions. Their countenances were exquisite, with the color of purple-polished gold, and their bodies were adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man. While they had been dwelling beneath the earth protecting this realm, and while the people’s practice of the Way relied upon this Sahā world, they heard the sound of the Buddha proclaiming the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and leaped forth from the earth. Each bodhisattva was accompanied by as many bodhisattvas as there are grains of sand in sixty billion Ganges Rivers; they followed one another in attendance, with a single mind and a single practice, without any distinction.

Some came as bodhisattvas numbering half a hundred thousand *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* (Ganges-sand) particles; some as forty parts of a *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka*; some as fifty parts; some as one hundred parts; some as five hundred parts; some as one thousand parts; some as one hundred thousand parts; and some as a hundred thousand times ten million parts of *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka*—bodhisattvas such as these, each coming accompanied by their respective retinues.

Furthermore, there were those who arrived with retinues of countless hundreds of thousands of millions of bodhisattvas; some traveled together in groups of two hundred practicing the bodhisattva path, while others came in groups of hundreds or thousands.

Each had their own retinue—some with a thousand followers, some with five hundred, some with four hundred, some with three hundred, some with two hundred, some with one hundred, some with fifty, some with forty, some with thirty, some with twenty, some with ten, some with five, some with four, some with three, some with two, or some with a single follower; others arrived alone. Their number was beyond measure, difficult to compare, as they sprang forth from the earth.

Some came from above or below, and some from the four directions; arriving at the Sahā world, they all remained suspended in mid-air. They beheld the Parinirvāṇa of the World-Honored One Prabhūtaratna and the Great Sage Śākyamuni, each seated upon a lion throne beneath a tree made of the seven precious gems. They then prostrated themselves in homage to these two Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, circumambulated them three times to the right, and withdrew to stand to one side.

There were some bodhisattvas who, with various kinds of wondrous meanings, extolled the two Honored Ones and praised all the Buddhas; even if they had continued from the very beginning for a full fifty intermediate kalpas, they could not have fully exhausted their expressions. The World-Honored One Śākyamuni’s diligent and arduous practices, as well as his separation from the Buddha, were likewise so vast that the fourfold assembly remained silent, without distinction or variation.
At that time, the World-Honored One manifested his supernormal powers in accordance with their physical forms, enabling the fourfold assembly to see them all universally.

He further caused them to perceive and know that in this Sahā world, throughout the void of space, there were assemblies of bodhisattvas, each individually protecting and upholding hundreds of thousands of buddha-fields; these assemblies of bodhisattvas completely filled and pervaded hundreds of thousands of buddha-fields.
Furthermore, this great assembly has four bodhisattvas as its leaders, whose names are:
Bodhisattva Various Practices, Bodhisattva Immeasurable Practices, Bodhisattva Pure Practices, and Bodhisattva Established Practices;
these are the four.
Among the vast assembly of Bodhisattvas, gathered like clouds in numbers as infinite and immeasurable as atoms, these were the most eminent.

Then, four great Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, each accompanied by an inconceivable multitude of followers, stood in their respective groups before the World-Honored One. With palms joined, they addressed him, saying:
"Great Sage, your venerable body is healthy and strong; have you cast off all ailments, and is your conduct at peace?"
"Are all living beings each well-accordant with the practice of the precepts, dwelling in cool serenity free from all afflictions?
Will these classes of beings not fall into the precipitous valleys?
Then the four Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas praised him in verse, saying:
“The Hero of the World has manifested radiant light; is his conduct secure and strong?
He who rescues and delivers those in the present has no afflictions in his manifold practices.
For sentient beings, he is a chamber of virtuous causes; he resolutely receives the truth of purity.”
"May I never grow weary or fatigued; I would rather accept the command of the World-Honored Lion.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the great assembly of bodhisattvas, saying:

"O sons of noble family, the conduct of the Buddha is peaceful, free from ailment, and free from affliction. All the multitudes have received the precepts and practices; they have well studied the teachings of the Way and do not dare to give rise to weariness, desiring to reach the state of sublime purity."

Why is this so? These classes of beings have each performed their respective practices under various Perfectly Enlightened Ones of the past; these śrāvakas, having faith in and delighting in my teaching, enter the Buddha’s wisdom. Furthermore, those who were students of the three vehicles, each abiding in the vehicle of the śrāvaka, I have caused them all to resolve their minds on entering the great wisdom of the Buddha.
Then the bodhisattvas uttered this eulogy in verse:

“Excellent and marvelous, O World-Honored One! We all offer our encouragement and support, so as to bring all sentient beings into unity, and skillfully transform them through the subtle and wondrous discipline.”
"Desiring to hear the Great Sage’s instructions on the profound essentials,
one listens with joy and faith, thereby entering the offering of the Dharma.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One praised the assembly of bodhisattvas, saying:
“Excellent! Excellent, noble sons! It is truly as you have said.”
"The teachings of the Tathāgata each accord with what is appropriate to the occasion, yet do not deviate from the fundamental intent.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva Mahāsattva and the other eight hundred million bodhisattvas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, raised their voices in unison and praised him, saying:
"From antiquity until now, we have never before seen or heard of such a thing!"
The assembly of bodhisattvas, having leaped forth from the earth, stood before the World-Honored One,
making offerings and taking refuge.
From where have these companions come?
Maitreya immediately discerned the thoughts in the minds of eight hundred million bodhisattvas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and at once joined his palms and asked in verse:
"For hundreds of thousands of incalculable eons, Throughout billions of vast ages, It has been impossible to measure or limit;
Never before have we seen such a bodhisattva."
Coming to visit the Honored One Among Two-Legged Beings, for what cause and of what nature?
From where has this Great Penetrator come? His form is vast and immeasurable;
all his resolves are firm and courageous, and he is a fierce hero, a Great Sage.
Elegant and worthy of reverence, from where have you come now?
The World-Honored One beholds each one:
the wise and noble Bodhisattvas, with their retinues numbering as many as the sands of the Ganges.
Their number surpasses the rivers; fully possessing the Buddha-dharma, the assembly of all Bodhisattvas has all established the path of perfect enlightenment.
Such a host of eminent beings gathers to pay homage to the Great Sage.
Fully complete for sixty times, The number exceeds that of hundreds of thousands of Ganges sands;
Their retinues are beyond conception.
[There are those with] five hundred Ganges sands, Or four, or three hundred.
Or two hundred rivers—such were their various retinues;
their limits again differed from this, being either five or ten.
Each and every one of these attendants was a son of the World-Honored One, the Great Sage.
Whence have these multitudes come, arriving at the place of the Teacher?
Whether four, three, or two, or as many as the sands of one or many Ganges Rivers—each group comes from the number of sands in the Ganges; their companions are all well-trained.
So vast they are beyond measure; except for those dwelling in the sky, they could not be gathered together all at once even in hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas.
Whether it be half a river, or a third, or ten, or twenty parts—
Fully endowed with manifold established practices,
the wise and sagacious bodhisattvas all dwell in the midst of space; their limits are immeasurable,
yet they appear without distinction between self and other, having practiced purity for billions of eons.
Furthermore, there are immeasurable other schools, their retinues beyond reckoning—
billions upon billions, even exceeding that; some have half a billion,
or ten, or twenty, or five, four, three, or two.
Among all the heroic ones and their retinues, none are able to fathom them.
Each practices the path individually, joyfully adhering to the sublime stillness;
as tranquil as space, those who have parted from them are beyond measure.
Like the rivers and streams throughout kalpas, none can calculate their number;
dwelling in monasteries and silent chambers, they have each come from their respective directions.
All the celestial deities and sages have arrived because of the Venerable One’s majesty.
These heroic and valiant bodhisattvas—whence have they suddenly appeared?
Who has preached this sutra for them?
And who has established them in the Buddha-way?
To manifest which Buddha’s teaching?
To establish which Buddha’s practice?
Subtle and each worthy of reverence, they come from all four directions.
By means of the divine power of clear vision, great wisdom suddenly manifests.
Within this frail and desolate world, the Capable One (Muni) causes it to become fully endowed;
the benevolent and worthy Bodhisattvas arrive spontaneously in their multitudes.
Since birth until now, I have never seen such a transformation;
I pray that you will describe that land, O Great Sage who has exhausted all names.
From which of the ten directions have they come, each harboring the eighteen dharmas?
I have never before seen such bodhisattvas as these.
As the most excellent son, I have never heard or seen this;
now that this great assembly is here, O Able One (Śākyamuni), I pray you speak of their practice.
Bodhisattvas numbering in the thousands, In the hundreds of koṭis beyond limit, Countless billions—where did they originally dwell?
These bodhisattvas are courageous and valiant; Their resolve and nature are immeasurable.
"O Great Hero, please explain such categories as these.

At that time, incalculable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas from other worlds came from all ten directions to the presence of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni to exhort him to preach the Dharma; they each sat upon lion thrones beneath trees made of the seven precious jewels.
The attendants of these Tathāgatas each saw great assemblies of bodhisattvas, appearing in countless manifestations, suddenly emerge from the earth; they each stood before their own Buddha and asked:
"From where have these great bodhisattva-mahāsattvas come? They are incalculable and boundless."
At that time, each of those Buddhas addressed their respective attendants, saying: "Noble sons, wait but a moment.

There is a bodhisattva named Maitreya who has received the prediction of enlightenment from the Tathāgata Śākyamuni; he shall attain the unsurpassed, true, and correct path and realize supreme perfect awakening. He will inquire of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni regarding that which you find strange.
