The Buddha will explain the essential meaning of these matters in detail for each point; all of you should quiet your minds and listen together."
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Great Being Maitreya:
"Excellent, Ajita!
"What you have asked, O Benevolent One, is exceedingly subtle, profound, and immeasurable.
Listen, listen! Now I shall speak of it."

May all Bodhisattvas and those gathered in this assembly universally become firm and steadfast, possessing powerful and fierce resolve toward the unsurpassed mind. You should know that the Tathāgata’s wisdom-vision is bottomless; the realms established by the great sages are immeasurable. In the blissful mastery of meditative concentration and wisdom, nothing can be fully proclaimed or analyzed and explained; the skillful means employed to transform and edify beings are beyond measure.
Then the Buddha spoke in verse:
"O sons of noble family, all listen to the Buddha-way; that which I now proclaim is wisdom, gentle, harmonious, and joyful."
If one is clear-sighted and discerning, one regards it as a sublime fragrance; the wisdom of the Tathāgata is inconceivable.
All should exert their resolve and maintain universal steadfastness; each should establish their aspiration with a single-minded equanimity.
The Great Sage is difficult to encounter; out of compassion for the world, he shall now cause you to hear and receive this unprecedented Dharma.
The Buddha will establish you, O virtuous ones; let none among you give rise to a mind of doubt.
The instructions of the Guide are without variation; his wisdom is impartial, peaceful, and without distinction.
The treatment he provides rests in tranquility; the Dharma is profoundly deep and subtle, beyond the reach of thought and immeasurable.
"Now I shall expound the causes and conditions of the infinite; let all listen together as to where the meaning leads.
Having thus praised them, the World-Honored One addressed Maitreya, saying:
"Proclaim it to all, Ajita!"
If you wish to know these bodhisattva mahāsattvas who have emerged from the earth in an immeasurable and inconceivable assembly—those never seen before—all now gathered in this Sahā world-system.

When I first attained the unsurpassed, true, and correct path and realized supreme perfect enlightenment, I exhorted and gladdened these beings, establishing them in non-retrogression and causing them to achieve the Great Way through instruction and transformation. This assembly of noble sons, bodhisattvas, and mahāsattvas dwells in the lower regions; therein they provide protection and rescue, praise and recite the sutras, contemplate in meditative concentration, single-mindedly examine their ultimate destination, and joyfully delight in the practice of non-action.

Sons of good family, you who are intent upon tranquility and indifference, neither dwelling on the distant nor the near, should always practice with single-minded devotion among gods and humans. You should turn the wheel of Dharma, which is unconditioned and without assembly; you should delight in the joy of the Dharma through profound supernormal powers, and with diligent aspiration, seek the wisdom of the Buddha.
Then the World-Honored One uttered this eulogy in verse:
"These countless multitudes of bodhisattvas, Inconceivable and beyond measure,
Have practiced for billions of aeons, For kalpas that cannot be limited."

Having cultivated the bases of supernormal power and attained vast learning and wisdom, I have exhorted them all toward the Great Path of the Sages; now the Buddha has bestowed upon them all the prediction of their future enlightenment.
These bodhisattvas are all the sons of the Buddhas;
they all dwell within my land.
Having completely abandoned all stages of habitual practice, they all abide in seclusion and attain liberation.
These sons of the Buddhas practice the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); with diligent cultivation and study, they revere and follow the supreme path.
These wise and sagacious ones, who reside in the lower regions, have come today for this very purpose:
to protect and sustain this land.
Accumulating virtuous conduct, distinguishing the path of the Buddha, always practicing with diligent cultivation,

Today, having heard the sūtras, I have beheld them face-to-face in their abiding state and now explain them through detailed analysis.
Establishing sentient beings, numbering in the hundreds of thousands of millions, the Great Sage and Guide is preeminent in the world;
with the wheel of non-retrogression, he abides in the Buddha-way.
Some may attain establishment, grasping the subtle and profound;
some may attain the station of boundless meaning, the essential dhāraṇīs numbering in the hundreds of millions.
Those who have limited desires, as well as those who engage in contemplation, who establish themselves in practice and transcend birth—
whether they abide in the two stages or the eight stages— they shall attain the Buddha-way, and those delivered by them shall be immeasurable.
There may be practitioners who transcend fourteen [thousand kalpas], or some who reach three, or those who abide in two.
Having followed the Teacher and heard this sutra, they shall attain the Buddha-way and manifest the supreme meaning.
Having accomplished all supernormal wisdoms, they roam through the various realms of existence;
having heard and examined what has been taught by the Great Sage, they achieve the fruit of realization and are free from all outflows.
Just as the lands of the eight Buddhas contain a certain number of atoms, such is the limit of those who would wish to count them.
If there were multitudes numbering in the hundreds of millions who heard this sutra, upon hearing it, they would all give rise to the supreme mind of enlightenment.
The Great Immortal of the Infinite has cultivated such virtue that he can analyze and expound upon it, establishing the ground of the ultimate truth.
His immeasurable bodies cannot be measured or limited; they are like space, having no boundaries.
The various devas have rained down countless billions of flowers, beyond all measure.
Billions of sons of gods, including Śakra and Brahmā, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, have come here.
With various fragrances and exquisite incenses, they made offerings to the One Abiding in Peace;
with honeyed scents and supreme perfumes, they scattered them before the Buddha, single-mindedly performing their practice.
Like soaring birds, they come from all directions to scatter offerings before the Tathāgata, who dwells in peace.
Above in the void, thunder spontaneously resounds; with soft and gentle voices, the profound and wondrous Dharma is proclaimed.
Hundreds of thousands of millions of devas all join in song and praise; moon-bright jewel gems descend spontaneously.
Hundreds of thousands of millions of *nayutas* of seven-jeweled precious vases are arrayed throughout the void.
Like geese flying in formation, they made offerings to the Great Sage, the Honored One of majestic spiritual power.
Countless billions of parasols, beyond measure, were vast and all-encompassing,
adorned with the seven treasures.
His body was tall and long, reaching up to the Brahma Heaven; subtle, exquisite, and beautiful, his majestic radiance was towering and sublime.
With magnificent banners and streamers, he made offerings to the Supreme Buddha.
They extol all the sages, chanting praises by the hundreds of millions; their hearts leap with joy as they respectfully abide in the names [of the Buddhas].
They see various kinds of diverse guides, who manifest themselves everywhere.
Regarding the limit of their lifespan, all these sentient beings now behold it with joy.
Its significance is vast and universal, reaching throughout the ten directions; there is nowhere the voice of the Guide does not arrive.
"Satisfying sentient beings, numbering in the hundreds of thousands of millions, they shall awaken to the intent of the Way and be fully adorned.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Maitreya, saying:

"If those who hear the lifespan manifested by the Tathāgata and the sūtra-dharma he has preached should, for even a moment, give rise to a joyful mind and profound faith, the merit they obtain will be immeasurable."

Suppose, noble son or noble daughter, you wish to attain the unsurpassed, perfect, and true path, and for eight hundred million times ten thousand kalpas practice the five perfections—giving, morality, patience, diligence, and single-minded concentration—this would not equal the merit of a noble son or noble daughter who, upon hearing of the lifespan limit of this Tathāgata, conceives a thought of joy, faith, and delight at that very moment, and without harboring doubt, dedicates various kinds of practices toward the one path.

If one wishes to know the measure of this merit, it surpasses the practice of the five perfections for eight hundred million times ten thousand kalpas by a factor of a hundredfold, a thousandfold, ten-thousandfold, a hundred-millionfold, and even a hundred-billionfold; its blessings are beyond comparison and cannot be illustrated by any analogy.
The Buddha said:

"Ajita! If sons of good family or daughters of good family, upon hearing this Dharma of the sutra, experience joy and faith for even a single moment of thought, they shall be firmly established in the unsurpassed, right, and true path and attain supreme perfect enlightenment."
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
"If one practices all things in accordance with them, practicing the five perfections (pāramitās) to the utmost,
aspiring for this wisdom, and keeping the mind fixed upon the supreme path of the Buddha."
Even if, throughout billions of kalpas, one were to fully practice for eight preceding kalpas,
making offerings to the Buddhas repeatedly, as well as to the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and to billions of koṭis of bodhisattvas;
I offer various foods and drinks, clothing, beds, and bedding,
as well as mats and dwellings, all perfumed with sandalwood;
with gardens and pavilions provided in abundance, I give them as places for walking meditation.
Having thus practiced such various and innumerable kinds of giving throughout hundreds of millions of kalpas,
he sought the noble path of the Buddha.
Furthermore, he guarded the prohibitive precepts and, with faith and joy, prostrated before the Buddha.
Clearly establishing that there is nothing to transgress, one still attains the Buddha’s wisdom.
Furthermore, by conforming to patience and abiding in the stage of disciplined concentration,
with a noble resolve that is limitless, one endures countless insults.
Even if one encounters those who are violent, arrogant, and conceited,
one should be able to endure them with resolve for the sake of seeking the Buddha-way.
Always diligent and persevering, with a vast and firm mind, one remains steadfast.
With mental attention focused on other thoughts, he travels to billions of Buddha-lands.
If he dwells in seclusion and desires to cast off sleep,
that person practices walking meditation for billions of kalpas, constantly training therein.
Desiring to compare it with that which is peerless, one practices meditative concentration for billions of kalpas,
further adding eight thousand billion more, while maintaining a single-minded focus.
With the aspiration to attain the supreme Buddha-way, one seeks to obtain all supernormal powers and wisdom.
Perfectly endowed with the supreme concentration, all meditations are tranquil.
All the merits and virtues they have cultivated gather and accumulate;
throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of eons, they remain as previously extolled.
If any man or woman, upon hearing the limit of the Buddha’s lifespan,
should for a moment rejoice with faith, this merit shall be supreme.
They should cast away all hesitation and every thought of attachment.
The merit of one who has faith and delight in the profound meaning of the Great Dharma is such as this:
if a bodhisattva seeks the Way and reverently honors it for billions of kalpas,
yet does not consider even this hearing as "hearing," having heard that the Buddha’s lifespan is immeasurable.
Having prostrated with the highest reverence to such persons as these,
one shall, in a future age, deliver and liberate billions of people,
just like the World-Honored One, the Sage of the Śākyas, the Great Man, the Lion of the Śākyas.
Seated beneath the Bodhi tree, he utters the lion’s roar.
This is why I have come now— to receive the offerings and reverence of sentient beings—
and while abiding in the Buddha’s place of enlightenment, it is likewise appropriate that I speak of his lifespan.
"His will and nature are fully perfected; that person is widely learned and retains what he has heard.
His teachings are truthful and transform others, so that no doubt remains.
The Buddha again addressed Ajita:
"Whoever hears this *Tathāgatāyuṣpramāṇa-sūtra*, enters into it, upholds it, analyzes it, and understands it thoroughly, will obtain merit that is beyond measure and limit.

This shall exceed the merit of those who, for many hundreds of millions of kalpas, practice the five perfections (*pāramitās*) up to the Buddha-wisdom, including all that should be manifested and all that should be practiced."

Furthermore, if one hears this sutra, copies it, and having transcribed it upon bamboo slips or silk, honors and serves it by scattering flowers, burning incense, offering powdered incense and blended perfumes, silken banners and streamers, lamps of sesame oil, and lamps of oil or clarified butter (ghṛta), their merit shall exceed that of the former by an immeasurably vast amount; they shall attain the state of the Tathāgata’s wisdom and vision, just like Ajita.

If that son of noble family should hear this *Tathāgata-āyus-pramāṇa-sūtra* and, with a sincere and upright mind, feel joy and faith, he should contemplate this sign according to his disposition and immediately come to know it: when the Tathāgata was teaching this sūtra on Vulture Peak Mountain, surrounded by a retinue of bodhisattvas and a multitude of śrāvakas, within this buddha-field of a trichiliocosm, there was universal patience; the ground was of deep-blue lapis lazuli and purple-gold, with crossroads of eight paths and rows of trees made of the seven treasures, and various billions of dwellings and residences where the assembly of bodhisattvas resided.

"Ajita! If you wish to know those people whose minds are constant, upright, peaceful, joyful, and faithful, you may discern their characteristics and conduct by these physical appearances; they have previously seen the assemblies of Buddhas."
Furthermore, the Tathāgata perceives all that is believed and cherished in the minds of those people.

After the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, if sons or daughters of noble family hear this sutra and do not slander it, but instead joyfully accept and uphold it, they shall be seen and protected by the Tathāgata.

That son of good family surpasses those who merely build stūpas and temples for the Buddha, or erect monasteries and lecture halls; he surpasses those who merely look after the illnesses of bhikṣus by providing them with medicine and articles of sustenance.

Why is this? Because these sons of noble family have fully established stūpas and temples, and constructed monasteries of the seven precious substances reaching as high as the Brahma-heaven, all for the purpose of making offerings to every relic.

The stupas and temples surrounding it were infinite, extending as far as the horizon, hung with clusters of precious bells. These shrines for the relics—the supreme treasury—were honored with offerings of flowers, incense, blended perfumes, and pounded aromatics; with jeweled canopies, banners, streamers, music, and hymns; and with various kinds of fragrances, including all the rare and exquisite treasures found in both heaven and the world. There were celestial flowers, celestial incense, and celestial music; thunder rolled through the air, emitting a profound resonance. With bells, chimes, great drums, lutes, flutes, harps, zithers, gongs, mirrors, and various other instruments, their soft and plaintive sounds, songs, and dances were perfectly harmonized and attuned. For countless billions of hundreds of thousands of kalpas, they made offerings and served [the Buddhas], fully perfecting all the *pāramitās*.
"After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, those who hear this sutra and uphold, read, copy, or explain it in detail will attain immeasurable merit.

If they cultivate loving-kindness and compassion, widely upholding and practicing it, and provide monasteries, lecture halls, beds, and silken furnishings for the community of bhikṣus to dwell within; if they provide gardens, groves, flowers, fruits, bright moon-jewels, walking paths, seats, food, and drink as offerings; if they provide medical treatment for the sick and bestow all manner of peace and security, making everything complete; and if the legs of their beds and couches are adorned with various kinds of jewels, exquisitely beautiful and reaching as high as the Brahma-heaven, decorated with banners and canopies—then because of the merit thus encouraged and supported, they will gradually become more fully endowed and eliminate their transgressions, until nothing is not radiant and magnificent."

With wholehearted diligence, he dwelt in seclusion and accumulated merit; throughout countless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas, his name was extolled, and all his majestic adornments and spiritual powers were most sublime and universally pervasive.
Thereupon the World-Honored One uttered this verse in praise:
“If one were to build a temple of the seven treasures reaching as high as the Brahma Heaven,
and offer flowers, incense, music, banners, and canopies— all as acts of worship;”
Various couches and bedding, fine food and delicacies,
medicine for those who are ill or emaciated, and many kinds of precious beds,
all exquisitely adorned, reaching as high as the Brahma Heaven.
Universally adorning the Buddha-fields, they provide both encouragement and assistance in full measure.
Encouraging the five practices for dwelling in seclusion, they cause billions to arise in transformation;
that which all people delight in is the most supreme, subtle, and wondrous giving.
All offerings were fully prepared—fresh, pure flowers, canopies, and banners;
these served as their garments. Repeatedly sounding like the roll of thunder, with various musical performances soft and plaintive, they made offerings to the śarīra.
Using fragrant oil to light lamps, arranged in a circle all around;
whoever upholds this sutra and preaches the Dharma amidst confusion,
thereby possessing perfect eloquence— these are various forms of offering.
Countless billions of chambers, all fashioned from sandalwood;
thirty-two lecture halls, exceedingly high and beyond measure;
all furnished with various seats and bedding, providing whatever food and drink one desires.
In this way, hundreds of thousands of millions [of offerings], including precious and exquisite delicacies,
gardens, pavilions, and walking paths, with flowers spread everywhere upon the ground,
canopies in infinite variety, and various painted images—
By making offerings to the assembly of monks, those who uphold this sutra and its Dharma have already accomplished this in the present.
If they read, recite, or copy the sutra with joy and faith, [they shall attain the same].
The merit they obtain shall be immeasurable, surpassing all other blessings.
Should there be those who transcribe it, making it pure, clean, and well-settled,
they should honor the scripture with flowers and incense that waft their fragrance everywhere.
One should always light lamps, using fragrant oil for the wicks;
wherever one is born, one shall always be joyful, frequently offering *sītī* flowers.
Such is the manner in which one who honors this scripture should make offerings.
The merit obtained is exceedingly vast; its limit cannot be measured.
Just as the realm of empty space has no limit that can be found, so too is this merit immeasurable throughout the ten directions.
How much more so could one further bestow upon them constant peace and security?
By upholding the precepts, practicing meditative reflection, and engaging in quiet sitting,
one remains free from anger and harsh speech, establishing oneself in reverent contemplation.
A bhikṣuṇī should always be humble and reverent, never conceited;
with wisdom like the bright moon, she asks the wise without fear.
Distinguishing things in their proper order, her mind harbors compassion, and she shall attain Buddhahood.
Even if one were to behold such a person as this,
a Dharma teacher who upholds this supreme sūtra, the measure of that individual’s qualities of merit could not be grasped.
One should uphold this sutra scroll, honoring it with increased offerings.
Should there be someone who uses celestial flowers and incense, or celestial jeweled canopies,
to provide shelter and shade over it.
One should bow one's head to the feet of that person and constantly keep them in mind, for the Tathāgata is most supreme.
Those who see him at that time should reflect thus and seek him beneath the King of Trees.
When he attains enlightenment as a Buddha, wherever he may be venerated, he brings abundant benefit to the devas and the world.
Whether standing, sitting in peace, or walking in meditation, his virtue is thus.
Whether reclining on a couch or dressed in robes, he constantly expounds this sūtra of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the man, regarding this scroll of the sūtra, gives rise to various kinds of sublime and subtle insights into the Truths.
The World-Honored One, the Guide, whose words are most sincere— those who make offerings with countless treasures to him,
just as I have praised, shall find that all the lands they possess become the Buddha’s body, and there they shall walk.
The Buddha is holy within it, as if sitting upon his throne; he is fully awakened to his location and the place where he dwells.
Chapter 17: Encouragement and Assistance. From the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, Chapter Seventeen: Encouragement and Assistance. At that time, the Great Being Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What merit and blessings shall those obtain who hear this spoken sutra?
He spoke in verse:
"When the Great Hero has entered parinirvāṇa, those who hear this sutra..."
"If one reflects upon this and offers encouragement and assistance, what blessings and protection will one obtain?
Thereupon, the World-Honored One addressed Maitreya, saying:
"After the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa, should there be any bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs who hear this spoken sūtra..."
When bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās— men and women, great and small members of their retinues— have heard it,
they shall encourage and assist in its propagation; they shall proclaim and expound it for others within assemblies,
whether in houses or in open spaces, or while dwelling in seclusion in provinces, kingdoms, districts, or towns, acting exactly as prescribed.
Having heard the sutra, one should abide by its power and potential as received and explain it for others;

if one praises and recites it for the sake of parents or kinsmen, or hears the words of a Mahāsattva and reads them with sympathetic joy, whatever has been heard and known should be transmitted from one to another.
Even if one does not behold the majestic presence or physical appearance of the Dharma Master, those who transmit the teachings should assist one another in encouragement.
By these causes and conditions, I employ skillful means so that those in the five realms of existence who possess the five hindrances may all see one another;

each shall, according to what they have heard, exhort and transform one another, listening to the merit of the encouragement I provide and the merit of the Dharma teachings and scriptures heard from the Dharma Master.

Noble sons and daughters, throughout the thousand-year kalpa and across the four quarters of the world, as long as the six realms of sentient beings have not yet been entirely freed from the net—whether they possess form or are formless, whether they possess perception, lack perception, or possess neither perception nor non-perception;
whether they have feet, lack feet, have two feet, four feet, or many feet; including all devas and humans—there may be some among them who...
If a person desires to seek merit, they should provide for each and every sentient being— according to their individual inclinations, pleasures, and joys—
an abundance of the most cherished, supreme, and exquisite articles of offering throughout Jambudvīpa,
making vast gifts to each one according to their wishes: houses, gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, coral, and amber.
Adorned with carnelian and agate, and composed of various treasures such as elephants, horses, chariots, and oxen, for countless years they provided whatever was sought after,
fulfilling all desires to their hearts' content, and supplied food and drink without any lack.
He thought to himself:

"My years are advanced and my strength is failing; my mind is weary and exhausted. How could I possibly enter the Tathāgata’s Dharma and Vinaya to instruct sentient beings with the teachings commanded by the Buddha?"

Then, acting according to his thoughts, he examined what was non-accordant with the disciplinary codes and the guiding scriptures; the common people all at once trod upon the tracks of the Path, attaining the fruits of the Once-returner, the Non-returner, and Arhatship. Their outflows were exhausted, their meditative concentrations were perfected, and they attained the eight gates of liberation with towering spiritual power and single-minded composure.
"What do you think, Ajita?
Is it possible for anyone to conceive of or measure the merit and generosity established by that man at that time?
Maitreya replied:

"It is exceedingly vast and beyond calculation that you are able to comfort immeasurable sentient beings, providing for their deficiencies and further establishing them in the realization of non-attachment."
The Buddha told Ajita:
"I now speak to you for this very reason, to proclaim it far and wide.
Just as that man initiated great acts of giving, providing for the countless beings of the four quarters, and established them in the realization of non-attachment."
The Buddha said:
"If one hears even a single phrase or a single verse of this sutra and encourages others with sympathetic joy, their merit shall surpass that of the person who has made the aforementioned offering.

The merit of encouraging others through a single phrase or a single verse is beyond measure; it is a hundredfold, a thousandfold, ten-thousandfold, a hundred-millionfold, and a hundred-billionfold greater than before. Even across hundreds of thousands of kalpas, it cannot be calculated and is beyond all analogy."
How much more so for one who sees this sutra with their own eyes or hears it with their ears and rejoices on their behalf—their merit would be beyond calculation.

Suppose there were someone who, desiring to hear this sutra, enters a monastery or goes wherever they may be; whether entering a district or city, or whether standing or sitting, they hear the Dharma of this sutra even for a single moment; or if they return again and again to the place where it is heard and apply themselves with focused diligence, the blessings and merits obtained in their present life will be such that they shall always naturally possess countless precious jewels, palaces, monasteries, couches, seats, and furnishings, as well as elephants, horses, and carriages, all elegant and immeasurable. Whether they preach the sutra, move about, stand, or sit, the Heavenly King Śikhin will come to protect them, ensuring they do not encounter calamities or afflictions. Śakra, Brahmā, and the Four Heavenly Kings will assist and guard them, and they shall draw near to the lion throne of a Wheel-Turning Sage King.
Suppose a son of good family were to proclaim:
"There is a sutra titled *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*; it is truly worthy of veneration and should be heard and received together.
If, after inviting one another, they decline due to mud and rain or become indolent and do not go, [they would incur a fault].
If one should hear this for even a brief moment, one will understand the retributions of sin and merit, as well as good and evil;
one shall immediately attain the root of virtue and obtain *dhāraṇī*, accompany all bodhisattvas from lifetime to lifetime, possess intelligence and wisdom in every place of birth,
and for hundreds of thousands of millions of lifetimes, one’s body shall always be fragrant and pure, never falling into the evil realms.
One encounters no harm from thieves or weapons; one possesses no deviant intent; one’s facial complexion is radiant and smooth;

one is born into a noble and virtuous family; those who see one rejoice, with none feeling hatred or aversion; one is neither blind nor deaf, nor is the nose crooked, nor is it congested or foul-smelling;
one is neither mute nor dumb; one is neither bald, nor lame, nor hunchbacked, nor afflicted by chronic ailments; and one is not foolish.
He was neither dull-witted nor foolish; he was neither short nor tall, neither soft nor rigid, and neither white nor black.

His face was not sallow, his body was complete and well-proportioned, and his countenance was upright and handsome. His complexion was like that of a peach blossom, such that all people loved and revered him.

His mind was benevolent and virtuous, and his speech was eloquent and wise. He swiftly attained meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) through the teachings of the Tathāgata, desiring to behold the various Buddhas.
"If you wish to see the World-Honored One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, you should study this sutra.
The Buddha said to Ajita:
"Behold its merit: if there were a person who, upon hearing the name even once, offers encouragement and rejoices in another's merit, they shall obtain such blessings as these."
"How much more so for those who single-mindedly listen to, receive, make offerings to, and contemplate it, and furthermore fully explain it to others!
At that time, the World-Honored One uttered these verses of praise:
"If, at the very end, there should be one who encounters this sutra scroll, and should happen to obtain it..."
To hear and grasp the meaning of even a single verse, and with a joyful heart to offer encouragement and support—
the merit of such a person is immeasurable.
He alone is able to bestow gifts, constantly providing for sentient beings in numbers reaching billions;
as in the parables manifested by the Buddha just now, he causes them all to be fully satisfied throughout countless kalpas.
At that time, the man beheld his own face transformed, with white hair and fallen teeth, aged and decrepit.
Seeing that these classes of living beings were destined for ultimate extinction, he thought: "I wish to teach and transform them, leading them into the Way and its Dharma."
At the very end, by means of the teachings and parables of the Dharma, he shall analyze and expound for them the ground of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
All five destinies are like the plantain tree; he shall cause them all to swiftly attain the matter of *nirvāṇa*.
They all listened to and received the sutras, followed the gentleman, drew near to him to inquire and seek instruction,
and subdued their minds; they were all rendered free from outflows, and in a single moment,
they attained the realization of non-attachment.
If one hears a single verse and provides encouragement and assistance for it, the merit obtained will exceed that [of the former] immeasurably.
If one were to distinguish each and every gift individually, the virtue of a single stanza would be difficult to calculate and beyond limit.
To hear even a single verse expounded in a moment of haste is beyond measure;
its impact is boundless.
The merit such a person gains is likewise incalculable—how much more so for one who, in the present, receives it face-to-face through direct instruction!
Having come to this assembly, upon hearing the sutra but once, they leap for joy;
for hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas, this Dharma has been difficult to encounter and difficult to comprehend.
Should one hear this sutra scroll for even a brief moment, one should listen to it;
as for the fruit and retribution obtained thereby, wherever one may go, there shall be no great illness.
In every life one is born into, the tongue shall be free from ailment;
the teeth will be firm and strong, never falling out.
One shall never commit harm or violence, eliminating all perils and perverse rebelliousness, and one’s parents shall be virtuous and noble.
Establishing skillful means, one’s lifespan shall always be long; one shall never be born blind, nor shall one’s vision be obscured.
One’s nose and ears will be beautiful, without any deficiency; one’s lips and mouth will be elegant and refined, and one’s face shall always be fresh and pure.
He is always loved and respected by the multitude; his breath is fragrant, free from any foul odor.
His body is perpetually perfumed like a blue lotus, its fragrance spreading abroad, reaching everywhere.
Whether dwelling in a hall or chamber, or traveling to a vihāra, wherever one may go,
there are those who hear this sutra.
In a mere moment, the listener shall again come to know that those who have heard it are joyful and leaping with delight, receiving the teaching at their side.
That person’s physical form attains peace and security; with extraordinary and wondrous carriages and horses, they personally go out to welcome them.
Furthermore, riding upon noble and excellent elephant-chariots, wherever they travel, they obtain various kinds of jewels.
He constantly attains the most sublime necklaces; hundreds of thousands of people all together resolve their minds.
Abiding at that place where he creates [merit], he then expounds this fruit of the Dharma—this pure instruction.
Because of the purity of the Dharma, what is established is brilliant; one attains the status of a Lord of Devas and a seat upon the Brahma-heaven.
One swiftly reaches the state of a Wheel-Turning Sage King, long remaining amidst the assemblies to expound the meaning of the sutras.

Chapter 18: Praising the Dharma Master *The Lotus Sutra of the True Dharma*, Chapter Eighteen: Praising the Dharma Master At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Nityodyukta:

"If sons of good family or daughters of good family receive this sutra, uphold it, read it, and transcribe it, they shall obtain the root of merit for the ten eyes known as the eight hundred names; they shall obtain twelve hundred faculties of the ear, twelve hundred faculties of the nose, twelve hundred faculties of the tongue, twelve hundred bodily actions, and twelve hundred purities of the mind. These constitute hundreds of thousands of countless virtues, by which they will be able to adorn and purify the meritorious functions of the six sense organs."

If that person purifies the eye-faculty and perceives all things with the fleshly eye—whether it be clusters of trees of honey-flavored stones filling a trichiliocosm, reaching down as far as the Avīci Great Hell and up as high as the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven—they see everything universally and are able to grasp it all; therefore, it is called the "fleshly eye."
"If there are common folk born therein, they shall all behold it and fully understand where transgressions and blessings lead.
At that time, the World-Honored One uttered this verse in praise:
"Those who uphold this sutra scroll, Brave and courageous amidst the assembly,"
What is spoken is without timidity; listen now to these names and virtues.
These eight hundred names are pure and the eyes are bright and clear;
as if already free from all defilements, that which the eyes perceive is universal.
With their physical eyes, born of father and mother,
they behold the worlds of the Buddhas and see all that transcends the immortals.
They view the various mountains and Mount Sumeru, and likewise behold the Iron Ring Mountains.
Together with all the tombs, mounds, and hills, he further examines the great ocean.
Remaining silently and upright in one place, he gazes universally upon everything without fail;
reaching down as far as the Avīci Hell, such is the power of his physical eye.
"Having not yet attained the divine eye, nor being fully aware of the domain of the fleshly eye, the faculties are still light and agile.
The Buddha again addressed the Bodhisattva Nityakāla:

"If a son of noble family or a daughter of noble family speaks this sutra, or explains it for the sake of others belonging to the Śrāvaka vehicle, they shall immediately attain the renown of 'one with twelve hundred ears,' such that their fame will be heard throughout the trichiliocosm, reaching down to the Avīci Great Hell and up to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, surpassing even external seers and immortals."
What is meant by "hearing" refers to the sounds of elephants, horses, and oxen; the sounds of music, chariots, weeping, and lamentation;
the sounds of drums and bells; the sounds of singing, dancing, and laughter; the voices of men and women; the voices of young boys and girls;
the sound of the wind and wondrous sounds; and the sound of the True Dharma, as well as that which is not [the True Dharma].
The sound of the Dharma; the sounds of pleasure and suffering; the sounds of power and of mental disposition; the sounds of gentleness and coarseness;
the sounds of devas and nāgas; the sounds of ghosts, spirits, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas;
the sounds of fire, water, and from within the earth—[these are heard by] the bhikṣu.
The sounds of śrāvakas, the sounds of bodhisattvas, the sounds of Tathāgatas, and all the sounds existing within the trichiliocosm—penetrating both internally and externally, all are pure.
With his physical faculty of hearing, he hears all the voices spoken by sentient beings; even before attaining the divine ear, he hears them all universally and understands their origins.
Regarding all sounds, they do not engage in discursive thought or observation concerning the origins and ends of sentient beings.
Furthermore, although their ears hear everything, they do not seek out or pursue any sounds; rather, they listen in accordance with the sublime and majestic reality as it is.
“Constantly and at the proper time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, even before attaining the divine ear, hears with his ears in such a manner as this.
Having spoken these words, the Buddha, wishing to further explain their meaning, spoke in verse:
“Pure and comprehensive, Of various kinds and categories— With the ear of purity...”
One thousand two hundred [yojanas].
Within this world, by means of this hearing and discernment, one hears their sounds without exception.
Thus they listen and hear: the sounds of various vehicles such as carts and ox-carts, the cries of elephants and horses,
the clapping of hands and the beating of drums, as well as both mournful and pleasant melodies, and likewise the ringing of gongs and cymbals, and the whirring of fans.
The music is gentle and harmonious, its tones exceptionally beautiful; though he is amidst them, he remains free from attachment.
Hearing the countless people discourse upon all manner of things, he distinguishes with delight the various categories of those teachings.
All hear the various devas, heard by the divine ear, who are ever-subdued,
sweet, and gentle.
The deeds performed by the boys and girls have the sound of the mournful phoenix.
As well as red-faced crows, gallinules, mandarin ducks, and parrots—
those that dwell within the mountain forests— all are able to hear these various sounds.
The sounds of wailing and lamentation, the cries of intense suffering, the thoughts of food and drink,
the pursuits and searches undertaken, the activities initiated, and the voices that are uttered.
The various asuras, dwelling within the ocean, each emit their own distinct and resonant cries.
At that time, the Dharma Master remains stationed here; whatever words he speaks are immediately heard everywhere.
The sounds of animals and hungry ghosts, weary with hunger and thirst, each proclaiming their own cries—
whether chirping or roaring— at that time, the Dharma master remains silent as if standing still,
yet he is able to hear all these various sounds.
In the Ābhāsvara Heaven and the Sudṛśa Heaven, as well as other extraordinary realms,
each with its distinct sounds— the Dharma Master universally attains them, hearing every such resonance.
While dwelling in the world, he has gone forth from the home; among the assembly of bhikṣus,
he recites their conduct, analyzes and explains it, and the Dharma Master hears all this as they preach the sūtras according to the dispositions of others.
Abiding in this state, whatever one recites or explains to others may be compiled as a meaningful collection to form a scripture,
so that all may universally hear it in various kinds of sounds.
For the sake of sentient beings, he preaches countless sutras; standing alone beneath a tree, they all hear them.
All throughout the three thousandfold world system, this is the Buddha’s land, where innumerable sentient beings [gather].
Their voices flow with ease, whether they are within a room or outside;
whatever they say, coarse or subtle, is heard everywhere and grasped in its entirety.
They hear all the sounds of every living being; yet amidst all these voices, they remain entirely unattached.
They fully know the inner and outer states of others everywhere; their ears are thus pure and their hearing is profoundly penetrating.
This person, though not yet having attained the light of the divine ear, will immediately be able to hear as soon as they encounter the necessary conditions.
At that time, the Dharma Master’s merit shall be such as this; by studying this scripture, their renown shall be like this.
The Buddha again addressed the Bodhisattva Nityakāla:

"If sons or daughters of good family who uphold this sutra scroll and explain it in detail, or who recite it and commit it to bamboo slips or silk, shall attain eight hundred merits, their faculties will be firm and solid, and their olfactory faculty will be pure. By means of this olfactory faculty, they will be able to universally perceive all the various fragrances within the trichiliocosm."
There were various fragrances: soft scents, *sumana* flower scents, and birth-scents; scents for anointing the beard, *atimuktaka* flower scents;
blue lotuses, red lotuses, yellow lotuses, and white lotuses; the scents of various trees and fruits, *kunduruka* resin, *sugandha* resin, and flower scents;
*candana* sandalwood, *tagara*, and various kinds of diverse perfumes—hundreds [of them].
Regarding "thousands of distinct varieties arising everywhere": these are the fragrances of various simple substances that people smell;
the fragrances of men, women, boys, and girls, which they each perceive themselves; the fragrance of one's own body;
the fragrance of elephants, horses, the six domestic animals, birds, and wild beasts; the fragrances of various trees and plants; and the fragrant species containing blood that dwell among the trees.
There were fragrances of various *yakṣas* and *rākṣasas*, fragrances of utmost sincerity, celestial fragrances, *pārijātaka* fragrances,
*cūta* tree fragrances, mental fragrances, great mental fragrances, soft fragrances, fragrances of the various devas, and fragrances of the celestial palaces;
there was the fragrance from the body of Śakra, by which one knows the place of birth, as music and song resounded upon the lecture hall.
Regarding the various great Dharma rules that should be practiced and established, he preached the Dharma for the devas of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Those who had leaped forth from the earth and were born spontaneously offered the fragrances of the *Geyi-liyi* devas’ jade maidens, as well as the fragrances of the boys and girls;
by these causes and conditions, they provisionally took birth as sons of the Brahmā devas and other great celestial beings.
Regarding the body-fragrance of Mahābrahmā, from each of his bodies flow forth countless hundreds of thousands of various celestial incenses, each with a distinct name.

These include the fragrances associated with the dwellings and spheres of influence of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, and Tathāgatas, as well as the fragrances used for their conversion of beings. Although the Dharma Master dwells in this very place, he is at a great distance from them; he does not draw near to their edges, nor does he go toward them to smell them. Yet he perceives all those fragrances without attachment or seeking, without dwelling on them, and without being startled by them. Remaining in a state of single-minded concentration, while amidst the assembly, he discerns and explains all such fragrances, yet his mind remains unattached and free from any longing or pursuit.
Thereupon the World-Honored One uttered this verse in praise:
"The person's faculty of the nose is thus purified, and the many varieties of fragrances they perceive are exceedingly numerous."
In this world, all that exists and all that can be born possesses most excellent fragrances.
Furthermore, there are various forms, the scents of blooming flowers, and the diverse varieties of sandalwood and other perfumes.
Those various fragrant fruits are each of a different kind;
they are subtle and exquisitely perfumed, along with the scents of many woods and incense.
Whether it be men, women, boys, or girls, wherever their minds dwell, each belongs to a distinct category.
The various fragrances produced by humans differ one from another; they grow everywhere, lush and verdant in their profusion.
Furthermore, we know that the Great Kingdom is ruled by a Wheel-Turning Sage King, who abides in gentleness and benevolence, possessing sovereign power and great strength.
Regarding all that exists therein—difficult-to-thread words and names, and various manifold fragrances—he discerns them all.
Having stored away many such things, he then considers: "In what place is the precious jewel of a jade maiden, as well as other rare and extraordinary treasures? At that time, the Bodhisattva...
He fully understands all fragrances:
those that adorn him with pearl rings, those on his well-arranged robes, whether he is seated or reclining upon a bed,
and those used as perfumes for his body— the Bodhisattva knows them all.
The sounds of song, dance, and entertainment, as well as all supernormal powers— the wise and sagacious perceive them all with the power of their sense of smell.
Whether it be exquisite and wondrous fragrances or the scent of sesame oil, they discern these various kinds in their entirety.
As well as the fragrance of flowers and fruits, wherever they abide, he smells them and knows them all.
In whatever place these various fragrances exist, he is able to distinguish each of their many kinds.
Furthermore, regarding all the countless varieties of sandalwood flower fragrances found within the mountain crags,
as well as every fragrance possessed by the people dwelling there— he knows them all completely.
Whatever is beloved and pleasing to a Wheel-Turning King,
or that which may dwell in secret within the great ocean;
whatever insects and moths are produced within the earth— all these various fragrances are mastered by the wise.
He knows the asuras—their queens, consorts, sons, and daughters—along with their ministers and subjects, discerning them all individually.
He smells the fragrance of the asura kings' singing, dancing, and merriment;
such is the fruit of their retribution.
There are many lions, tigers, wolves, dragons, and elephants;
he fully knows all their various species, including water buffaloes, bulls, and cows.
If there is a woman who, according to her desire, [seeks to know] whether she is with a boy or a girl—
even among groups of boys and girls— if she is pregnant and her body is utterly exhausted,
she may distinguish male or female within her womb by means of incense.
Furthermore, he personally recognizes the origin of his own body; he also clearly understands the meaning of the Dharma and the Vinaya.
Observing such persons, he perceives their peace and security, their suffering and joy, the strength of young men, and the blessings they receive as a result of their karma.
Whatever the man desires, he knows them all in their multiplicity; he perceives and distinguishes every fragrance he wishes for.
Having already found satisfaction within himself, such [fragrances] are inexhaustible; furthermore, he perceives and distinguishes the tranquil fragrance of his own body.
Wherever he dwells, among the various treasuries in the earth— be they wealth, precious gems, gold, silver,
or various colors, or soft coral shaped like purple-gold—
he can smell and know them all from wherever he stays.
The moon-bright jewel exists in this world; though it is beyond human reach,
one may smell it entirely with the nose, discerning its beauty or ugliness, and distinguishing its goodness or evil through its movements and stillness.
The various devas above, within the midst of space, with flowers of the mind and all manner of blossoms, and flowers of supple sound—
whatever flowers exist within this assembly, he perceives them all by the power of his nose while remaining here.
All the celestial palaces of those devas— whether supreme, inferior,
or intermediate, and of every variety— along with their forms and appearances,
stand there as he perceives them by the power of his nose.
The gardens for strolling and viewing, the dharmas of the various devas,
the manifold luminosities that are tranquil and likewise fully understood, the sublime and wondrous palaces,
and the places where the sons of the devas sport and play.
By means of the discernment of fragrances, they shall smell the scents of all the hosts of devaputras—
wherein they dwell, what practices they undertake, and wherever they roam and reside.
The celestial jade maidens possessed flowers and fruits, as well as various precious necklaces;
as they moved about in enjoyment, the Bodhisattva at that time recognized the fragrance of them all.
From the Heaven of the Thirty-two Devas down to the First Heaven,
including the palaces where the Great Brahmās roam— their scents he perceives with his nose and knows them all completely.
Abiding yet not abiding, he understands them all; whether far or near, there is nothing he does not penetrate.
Whether at death or birth, regarding his past lives and destinies, he smells them with his nose and knows their beginning and end.
If there be a bhikṣu who upholds this sūtra scroll, who dwells peacefully in accordance with the teaching,
constantly cultivates diligence, and remains in quietude practicing walking meditation;
if he has already attained sincerity and recites or explains it— those Bodhisattvas shall all know him.
Furthermore, he distinguishes the śrāvakas, the most excellent sons;
always beneath trees, dwelling alone in solitude, those who are wise perceive through their sense of smell and see all:
that such-and-such a bhikṣu is staying in such-and-such a place, and he can discern them all.
Wherever they may be, they constantly find joy in themselves, reciting and expounding [the teachings], and furthermore,
they lecture upon and explain the Dharma for others.
The Great Being dwells in peace, traveling through every direction; out of compassion he practices loving-kindness and discerns the teaching of the Dharma.
Seated upon his throne, surrounded by his disciples, he is recognized by his fragrance—the presence of the King of Dharma.
If sentient beings should hear this sutra-dharma and receive its transmission, their hearts will leap with joy.
At that time, the Bodhisattva abides here and perceives them all: those gathered in the assembly and those in every location;
the power and majesty of the Bodhisattva, and such forms as these.
Not yet having attained the nose of devas and humans, one naturally obtains this through the original auspicious response;
it is the nose of the various devas, free from all outflows.
The Buddha again addressed the son of good family:
"Whoever upholds this sutra, recites it, or transcribes it, shall obtain the extraordinary faculty of the tongue with twelve hundred merits;
their tongue-faculty will be fully perfected in discerning all flavors, such that even if they encounter something sweet and delicious, it shall be transformed into..."
The food and drink of the heavens are spontaneous; even if pungent, astringent, salty, or bitter flavors are presented, they transform into celestial delicacies of immeasurable taste.
When entering an assembly to expound the essentials of the Dharma, the common people rejoice and hold his regulations in profound reverence.
When entering into conflict or anger, his virtuous voice remains supple; his discourse on principles is eloquent and wise, pure and knowing moderation.

His compassion penetrates all, and the multitude joyfully harmonizes as they are moved by the lingering resonance of his teachings. Those who follow him hear that his discourses on the sutras are exquisite;
gods and humans approach him, including Śakra, Brahmā, the Four Heavenly Kings, those with pure celestial bodies, and the jade maidens of the devas.
They long to go and see him, as do the sons of heaven, the nāgas, their queens, and the asuras.
The consorts of the Cāturmahārājika devas, the consorts of the Garuḍas, the Kinnaras and their consorts,
the Mahoragas and their consorts, the Gandharvas and their consorts,
as well as the women of the yakṣas and the women of the piśācas, all desired to go and behold him, prostrating themselves in homage.
Having paid homage, they listen to and receive the sutras and precepts, inquire after their welfare, and take leave.

Whether they be bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās; kings, crown princes, ministers, and officials; those of great power and influence, or universal monarchs (cakravartin) endowed with the majestic seven treasures, along with their crown princes, retinues, jade women, and handmaidens; or likewise brahmins, gentlemen, and lay devotees, together with their entourages from provinces, cities, commanderies, kingdoms, districts, and villages—all wish to go and behold him, desiring to prostrate themselves and take refuge for as long as life lasts, making offerings, serving him, and listening to the Dharma.

Their speech and instruction were harmonious and gentle, just as the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata, has praised; they perceived and examined things directly, attaining the profound and subtle essentials of the Buddha’s enlightened wisdom, understanding suchness spontaneously as they heard it.
Furthermore, he knows the direction toward which the World-Honored One is facing as He sits and preaches the Dharma.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One uttered this verse of praise:
"The tongue-faculty of that person Is entirely supple and soft; He discerns all flavors."
Discriminating between the beautiful and the ugly, it is naturally sweet and delicious;
like the food and drink of the heavens, with their manifold flavors, they arise in succession.
Their speech is harmonious and elegant; those who hear it find it extraordinary.
Their minds are filled with joy and delight, and among those gathered in the assembly, there is none who does not hold them in reverence.
Furthermore, they shall produce sounds of profound depth.
Observing the retribution of cause and effect, which is pure and vast as billions, one immediately gives rise to joy;
understanding the supreme [truth], one makes offerings to the sutra scrolls in incalculable measure.
The devas, nāgas, and spirits, as well as the kumbhāṇḍas and asuras, always harbor feelings of reverence and desire to see them;
with humility, solemnity, and deference, they inquire about the scriptures.
Such is the name, virtue, and merit attained by that person.
In this world, in the mere instant of forming that thought, he causes all to hear by means of his voice and is able to announce it everywhere.
That resonance is gentle and supple, subtle, exquisite, and extraordinary;
it is profound and refined, yet possesses measured restraint.
Desiring to make offerings, they went everywhere to where [the Buddha] was;
the queen and the jade maidens all joined their palms together, and with constant sincerity, they listened to and received the scriptures.
All the ghosts and spirits honor him together with reverence; the devas, gandharvas,
and their retinues, as well as the foot-reversing female spirits and all male and female beings,
universally pay him homage and all attend upon him with service.
The King of the Brahma Heaven, the Great and Wondrous Devas, and all the sons of heaven—
the Lord Śakra, the Honored Brahmā, the retinue of the sons of heaven,
and countless jade maidens— all came to his abode.
In this world there is a Buddha, a holy and enlightened guide; his śrāvaka disciples all listen to his wondrous voice.
Wherever he is seen, they all protect him with one mind; observing the Dharma he preaches, they all rejoice.

The Buddha again addressed the son of good family: "If a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva hears this sutra and maintains, recites, reads, or copies it, they shall attain eight hundred merits of bodily conduct. Their complexion will be lustrous, radiant, fierce, and majestic; they will be like lapis lazuli—pure, wondrous, and stainless. Whatever they do will be emulated by the people; their deportment will be worthy of veneration, and their every advance and retreat will bring benefit. Being unchangeable, all sentient beings throughout the trichiliocosm will bow their heads in prostration before them. Whether they be among the multitudes of all Buddha-lands—be they beautiful or ugly, of fair or foul color, born in happy or miserable destinies—from the Cakravāḍa and Mahācakravāḍa mountains, the small and great mountains, and the dwellings of men, down to the Avīci Great Hell, and up to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven—they shall see them all through their own majestic virtue."
Within this world-system, he beheld with his own majestic radiance all that the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and tathāgatas dwell in, travel through, and where they preach the Dharma.
"Why is this so? It is because it is brought about by the purity of bodily conduct.
At that time, the World-Honored One uttered these verses in praise:
That person’s own body is pure in its conduct;
like lapis lazuli, it is without flaw, and is thus loved and respected by all people.
Whoever holds this subtle and wondrous scripture, just as one sees the reflection of one's own face in a clear mirror,
so too shall they see the forms and types of beings in the world.
Beholding its own beginning and end, and seeing others as well,
his body is pure like Mount Sumeru; throughout this world, among all sentient beings—
gods and humans, *nāgas* and *asuras*, those in the hells and hungry ghosts— [he is thus].
And all the various animals— everyone beholds their bodies and their facial features.
All the palaces and chambers of the devas, the earthen mountains and rocky mountains,
as well as the Cakravāḍa ranges, the Snowy Mountains and Mount Sumeru, and all the great mountains.
They are all able to behold it.
In whatever place they may be, by means of great majestic power and sanctity, they gaze upon all Buddhas, as well as all śrāvakas and the disciples of the Buddha.
If there is a bodhisattva who is alone in a secluded place, [the Buddha] can fully know the sutras and teachings they expound.
Their body is likewise pure, and in this same way, they clearly perceive all worlds.
If one with an ordinary body can awaken to this realization, such a person has not yet attained the Way of the Sages.
The Buddha further addressed the son of good family:

"After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva upholds, recites, and explains this sutra, they shall obtain the merit of the twelve hundred purities of the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*). By means of that purified mental faculty, there shall be nothing they do not penetrate and master."
Upon hearing a single verse, what he investigates becomes increasingly vast and what he penetrates and understands is manifold.
Through this expansive awakening and comprehension, he is able to lecture upon the Dharma for an entire month.
Having integrated and refined his experience over four months or a year, he retains it in memory without forgetting.

Regarding all the activities of worldly people—buying, selling, commerce, and speech—he perceives them all through the Dharma, distinguishing them in their proper sequence without losing their continuity.

He knows the thoughts in the minds of all beings within the six realms of existence across the trichiliocosm, whether they are wholesome or unwholesome, appropriate or inappropriate; among them, he universally perceives those who are śramaṇas, whether noble or non-noble, and those who are inappropriate.

With a pure will, he no longer requires further reflection; he naturally discerns the meaning and intent of the Dharma teachings, and his words are always sincere. Wherever there are those who preach with excellence, they all receive his instruction. He analyzes everything as commanded by the Tathāgata, including the most sublime sūtras of antiquity.
At that time, the World-Honored One uttered this verse in praise:
"The faculties of that person’s mind are pure and pristine; their radiance is penetrating and brilliant, perceiving the thoughts within the heart."
For this reason, one who understands various categories— the defiled and the base, as well as that which lies between the good and the evil—
and who, upon hearing a single verse, is able to uphold it, will comprehend countless meanings and the principles of wisdom.
Whether for one month, four months, or even up to a year, what is spoken regarding good and evil does not deviate from ultimate sincerity.
Should there be any among the multitudes of living beings— of all various kinds, including the gods and the people of the world—
As well as the asuras, the various classes of spirits and anomalies,
and all those among the six realms of existence— among these common folk, whatever their thoughts and various kinds of mental inclinations may be,
for each of them with their differing intentions, the one who upholds this sutra [will be able to perceive them].
In a single moment, they behold and know them all.
The Great Sages, the Buddhas, endowed with the marks of a hundred merits, all of them preach the Dharma for the sake of the world.
At that moment, what was preached was heard universally and equally; what was spoken was pure, and they were immediately able to receive and recite it.
Having passed through previous lives, the sutras they had studied and the teachings they had expounded throughout the long night, they shall now comprehend and understand them all.
There is that which is constantly expounded, the essence of the sūtras; having attained it amidst the great assembly, one is free from fear or dread.
Those who uphold this sūtra and propagate its various sections shall never encounter the afflictions of manifold conceptualizations.
Their branches, followers, and kinsmen are all virtuous and wise; their mental faculties are clear and penetrating, and it is likewise so for them.
The ground upon which the Bodhisattva dwells is one never before attained; for the sake of all sentient beings, he expounds the sutras with detailed analysis.
"Those who are able to receive and uphold [this teaching], dwelling securely in the True Dharma with skillful means and mental fitness,
shall know what is appropriate. —
*Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, Scroll Eight.
The Lotus Sutra of the True Dharma, Scroll Nine, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Yuezhi Kingdom during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Chapter Nineteen: On Being Constantly Despised. Chapter Nineteen: On Being Constantly Despised.
Thereupon the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta:

"Therefore, you should know that if there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās who uphold this sūtra, even if the fourfold assembly should revile and slander them, uttering coarse and violent words to scold and obstruct them, their transgressions would be beyond measure."

Furthermore, if there should be a person who hears this sutra scroll, receives and upholds it, recites it, explains it to others, and extensively elucidates its meaning, they shall obtain supreme and wondrous merit.
Such a person as this is one whom the Buddha praises; their eyes, ears, nose, mouth, body, and mind will be pure, free from all obscuration and hindrance.
Again, he addressed Mahāsthāmaprāpta:

"In the past, in a time long ago, incalculable, vast, immeasurable, and inconceivable eons [ago], there was a Buddha named Śāntigatirāja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttarapuruṣa, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. The eon was named Mahādhanavipramukta, and the world was called Mahāstambha."
The Buddha said to Mahāsthāmaprāpta:

“The Tathāgata Śāntigatirāja universally preaches the sutras for the sake of the devas and those within his own realm, transforming and guiding them. For those of the Śrāvaka vehicle, he expounds the Four Noble Truths to deliver them from old age, sickness, and death, bringing them close to Nirvāṇa, and explaining the origins and conditions from which the twelve links of dependent origination arise. For the Bodhisattvas, he expounds the six perfections (pāramitās) to lead them to the unsurpassed, right, and true path, manifesting the constant continuity of the practices of Tathāgata wisdom.”
The lifespan of the Buddha shall be as many hundreds of thousands of koṭis of kalpas as there are grains of sand in four Ganges Rivers;
after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma shall remain for as many hundreds of thousands of koṭis of kalpas as there are dust motes in one Jambudvīpa;
and the Semblance Dharma shall remain for as many hundreds of thousands of koṭis of kalpas as there are dust motes in the four continents.
He further addressed Mahāsthāmaprāpta:

"After that Buddha has passed into parinirvāṇa and the period of the Semblance Dharma has completely ended, there shall successively appear other Buddhas, continuing under the name Śāntigatirāja (King of the Sound of Peaceful Access). In succession, twenty billion koṭis of Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, Perfectly Enlightened Ones, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, Sugatas, knowers of the world, unsurpassed leaders, trainers of men, and teachers of gods and humans shall appear."

At that time, these Buddhas will successively pass into parinirvāṇa; once the True Dharma has vanished and the Semblance Dharma has likewise come to an end, the bhikṣus of that world will be arrogant and conceited, transgressing and disregarding the commands of the Dharma.
There was a bhikṣu named Constantly Subjected to Contempt who trained as a bodhisattva.
Why was he called Constantly Subjected to Contempt?
Whenever that bodhisattva saw bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās, he would always say to them:
"Virtuous ones, do not become arrogant or self-exalting. Why is this?
You virtuous ones should aspire to the Bodhisattvas, the Tathāgatas, the Arhats, the Samyaksaṃbuddhas; by this means, be careful regarding the objects of your focus."
He preached the bodhisattva practices for the bhikṣus, yet he did not accept their instructions nor was he willing to recite them. Seeing the fourfold assembly from afar, he said to them:
"I shall never treat these worthy men with contempt; I shall universally study the sublime conduct of bodhisattvas so as to attain the state of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha."
The Buddha said to Mahāsthāmaprāpta:
"At that time, when the fourfold assembly heard these words, they all rose in indignation and reviled him with insults, saying:

'This one bhikṣu, without asking us or discerning our minds, has instead become arrogant and claimed to see into our hearts. He bestows upon us the prediction that we shall attain supreme, perfect enlightenment—speaking to others of such extraordinary matters as no one desires.'"
He further addressed Mahāsthāmaprāpta: "Suppose a bhikṣu encounters heavy rain while traveling;

protected by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power as if covered by a canopy, his body remains unsoaked. Even if he is seen and reviled, his mind feels no resentment and his facial expression does not change. If he hears words that provoke hatred or displeasure, and someone throws tiles or stones at him, he continues to raise his voice from afar to instruct them, saying:
'Do not act with contempt; cultivate a heart of forbearance and resolve upon the Bodhisattva path.'"
Why is this so? At that time, the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās were arrogant and conceited, having heard and seen [this teaching] repeatedly.
The Great Being taught them, saying:
"My mind is always humble; I do not slight these worthy ones, and though I am seen to be reviled and insulted, my mind neither increases nor diminishes.
Because of this, those four classes of followers collectively named him "He Who Is Constantly Slighted."

When this Great Being was about to reach the end of his life, he heard the Tathāgata King of the Sound of the Path to Quiescence preach twenty verses of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, containing hundreds of thousands of profound and wondrous meanings.
When the Great Being was near death, he leaped into the air and raised a great voice, extolling this sutra and addressing them, saying:

"Virtuous ones, you should receive this sutra; you shall also attain the pure vision as before, and your ears, nose, mouth, body, and mind shall likewise be purified. Having attained this purity, your lifespan shall further increase by twenty *koṭīs* of *nayutas*, and having attained a concentrated mind, you shall again preach this sutra for the sake of all people."

Previously, when the fourfold assembly heard what he said, they reviled him, calling this Great Being one who was "constantly subjected to contempt yet harbors great pride. But now, having witnessed this Great Being’s subtle spiritual powers, his eloquence and power of wisdom, and his skillful means and power of the Path, they all come to submit, revere him as their leader, and take him as their friend, listening to the teachings of the sutras.
These and other countless, incalculable billions of people likewise established the aspiration for unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment.
After that Great Being passed away, they encountered twenty hundred thousand billion Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, all of whom preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* for them.

Advancing forward little by little, by virtue of these roots of merit, he further encountered two hundred billion nayutas of Tathāgatas, all bearing the same name, Vajrasvararāja, from whom he likewise heard this very sūtra.

Furthermore, he encountered twenty billion hundred thousand Tathāgatas, all of whom shared the same name, Rāvaṇarāja (King of Thunder Sound). From them as well, he heard the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, received and upheld it, recited it, and expounded it for the fourfold assembly. In every place where he was born, he naturally attained purity of eye, purity of ear, purity of nose, purity of mouth, purity of body, and purity of mind. His vision and hearing were penetrating; his olfactory faculty was unimpeded and his eloquence was boundless; his body could rise with ease, and his mind perceived the thoughts of sentient beings. He universally expounded this sūtra for the fourfold assembly, analyzing its meanings.
The Buddha said to Mahāsthāmaprāpta:

"This Bodhisattva, who was frequently treated with contempt, has already made offerings to and served several hundred thousand million Tathāgatas; furthermore, he has encountered countless hundreds of thousands of millions more Tathāgatas and likewise received the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* from them. By virtue of these roots of merit, he shall personally attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path and achieve supreme perfect enlightenment."
Mahāsthāmaprāpta!
Does the Bodhisattva wish to know the Great Being who was constantly slighted during the era of the Tathāgata Śāntigatirāja, while he was preaching the Dharma to the fourfold assembly?
That was I myself.

Had I not at that time received this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, nor upheld, recited, or explained it to others, I would not have been able so swiftly to attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path and achieve supreme, perfect enlightenment.
I have heard this sutra from the past Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones; having received, upheld, recited, and widely expounded it for others, I attained supreme perfect enlightenment.

At that time, the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—whenever a Mahāsattva preached this sutra, saying, "I practice reverence and do not slight these worthy ones; you shall all attain the wisdom of the Tathāgata’s true enlightenment and the Way"—[they were thereby inspired].

Furthermore, those among the fourfold assembly who treat that Great Being with contempt, revile him, mock his appearance, or laugh at him without reforming themselves, shall for twenty billion kalpas never encounter a Buddha nor hear the sound of the Dharma in their places of birth; moreover, for ten thousand kalpas they shall fall into the Avīci Great Hell, where they will be tortured, flogged, scorched, and roasted with unspeakable agony.

Having reached the ultimate end of their offenses, they emerged from hell; because that Great Being taught and transformed them, he caused them to resolve upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path, so that they all attained supernatural powers and wisdom free from obstruction, and they are all present here now.
The Buddha said to Mahāsthāmaprāpta:
"Do you wish to know those members of the fourfold assembly who at that time reviled, mocked with derisive gestures, and angrily abused the Mahāsattva?

They are these five hundred bodhisattvas in this assembly, such as Bhadrapāla and others; these five hundred bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, such as Siṃhacandra and others; and these five hundred upāsakas and five hundred upāsikās now before the Buddha. All of them are non-retrogressive and shall attain the unsurpassed, true, and correct path."
The Buddha told Mahāsthāmaprāpta:
"The meaning of this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is vast, its majestic power is immeasurable, and it is unsurpassed by all; it is that which all bodhisattva mahāsattvas should revere and honor."
"After the Tathāgata has passed into extinction, those who receive this sutra, uphold, recite, and read it, shall obtain blessings such as these and attain the unsurpassed, true, and correct path.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One uttered this verse of praise:
"In my recollection of the past, of events long ago, there was a Buddha named Śāntigati."
King of sounds, with immeasurable majestic power,
revered by gods and humans, he expounds the Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings and the people.
After my parinirvāṇa, when the True Dharma is burning out, during the final age,
there will be a bhikṣu who practices the bodhisattva path; at that time, he shall be known by a name and will frequently be treated with contempt.
He immediately went there, among the assembly of bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs; seeing their inverted views, he did nothing but exhort and transform them.
As I practice the path of the Buddha, I shall proclaim my own mind; I harbor no arrogance or self-indulgence, nor do I revile or disparage others.
Whenever I see those who mock me with their appearance, at such times I shall always cause them to hear these words.
If, at the time of hearing this Dharma of the sutra, one should stand or remain firm, or even engage in some activity,
then as one approaches the end of one's life, through the analytical exposition of this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*,
an immediate response will occur: one’s lifespan will be increased and one’s body will be transformed.
Attaining mastery,
they dwell in the void, expounding the sutras and transforming all beings, so that everyone awakens to the wisdom of the Way.
When that Great Being has passed away at the end of his life, he shall behold hundreds of thousands of millions of Buddhas.
Gradually and step by step, he shall be transformed and led into the Dharma, as [the Buddhas] explain this sutra for him in detail.
All those most excellent sons who have attained Buddhahood are none other than my own self, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni.
Those who were fond of slandering the bhikṣuṇīs,
as well as the upāsakas and all the upāsikās existing at that time, have all been brought to transformation and enlightenment.
Those who hear this sutra and attain wisdom shall always behold countless billions of Buddhas;
these are Bhaṭṭika and his five hundred followers.
The assembly of bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, as well as the upāsakas and upāsikās, now stand before the Buddha.
At that time, I shall cause them all to hear the honored Dharma and transform them all,
so that they may attain clear understanding.
Now, after the parinirvāṇa of the Buddha’s body, you shall repeatedly receive and honor this sutra scroll.
For countless billions of eons, you shall contemplate this Dharma such as you have never before heard.
Even if there were Buddhas numbering in the hundreds of thousands of millions, it would be rare to hear the preaching of such sūtras as these.
Therefore, having heard such scriptures as these, the Sovereign Holy Honored One praises this sūtra.
"After my parinirvāṇa, if there should be those who preach this, you must repeatedly endure [difficulties] and receive the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

Chapter 20: The Tathāgata’s Practice of Divine Power. At that time, the bodhisattvas—as numerous as the atoms of three thousandfold world-systems, numbering in the hundreds of thousands of koṭis—who had leaped forth from the earth, all stood before the World-Honored One. With palms joined, they addressed the Great Sage, saying:

"After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, we shall propagate this sūtra throughout all Buddha-lands and wherever the World-Honored One attains parinirvāṇa. We shall preach this sūtra in those places for the great benefit of many."
"If there be anyone who receives, upholds, recites, copies, or explains this essential and sublime scripture for others, their merit shall be immeasurable.

At that time, Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra was present in the Sahā world-system, surrounded by countless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of bodhisattvas, as well as bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans; the Tathāgata manifested supernatural transformations for them all.

The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha manifested auspicious signs and responses, whereby all attained the patient acceptance of the compliant Dharma (anulomikī-dharmanidhyānā-kṣānti). He caused them all to transcribe the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* and transformed hundreds of thousands of millions of bodhisattvas from other worlds, each of whom sat beneath various jeweled trees upon lion thrones.
