At that time, the World-Honored One Śākyamuni, together with all these Tathāgatas and Perfectly Awakened Ones, manifested their supernatural powers (ṛddhi) in full abundance. For a hundred thousand years, they established whatever was to be done; during those hundred thousand years, their merits spontaneously manifested, and a great radiance dispelled the dark clouds. In the mere snap of a finger, a natural sound arose that reached everywhere, and the lands of the Buddhas in the ten directions—the entire world-systems—trembled in six ways. The devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas, sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, each remained in their respective abodes throughout incalculable thousands of Buddha-worlds, and all beheld this Sahā Buddha-land.

Furthermore, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, numbering in the hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis, each sat upon a lion throne beneath various jeweled trees. The Tathāgata Śākyamuni and the World-Honored One Prabhūtaratna likewise occupied naturally adorned and pure lion thrones within the lecture hall of that temple of seven treasures, their majestic radiance brilliantly manifest.

Countless, limitless, and incalculable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, along with the fourfold assembly, beheld this transformation; their hearts were struck with amazement and they experienced immeasurable joy at having attained what they had never known before.
Then, a voice was heard from the sky, singing in praise:
"O Benevolent One!

If you wish to know, beyond these infinite, inconceivable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of Buddha-worlds, there is a Buddha-world named Sahā. Therein dwells a Buddha titled Śākyamuni Tathāgata, who for the sake of all Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas preaches the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, a Vaipulya scripture. All Buddhas universally protect this sūtra in order to rescue the Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas."
"Therefore, worthy ones, you should make your minds upright, honest, and pure; you should prostrate, take refuge, praise, serve, and make offerings to that Able Sage, the Perfectly Awakened One.

At that time, the sentient beings heard a spontaneous voice from the air saying, "There is a Buddha, a World-Honored One, named Able Sage (Śākyamuni). Upon hearing this name, they immediately joined their palms and scattered various kinds of flowers, incense, robes, banners, flags, and mixed perfumes toward the Sahā world. They also made offerings with necklaces, jewels, strings of pearls, and wish-fulfilling gems.

Flowers, incense, banners, canopies, necklaces, pearls, and bright moon jewels spontaneously arrived in the Sahā world; they immediately joined together to form precious flower-canopies, which remained in the void and completely covered all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas above them.
Then that Blessed One addressed the practitioners of various paths and the assembly of bodhisattvas standing before the Buddha:
"The merit and majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata’s perfect enlightenment are inconceivable."

Noble sons, even if one were to expound the meaning of this sutra for incalculable billions of nayutas of hundreds of thousands of koṭis of kalpas, it could never be exhausted; though there be countless varieties of other sutras, none can equal or limit it, for its further shore is difficult to reach and its boundaries hard to find.

Sons of good family, to state the essentials: suppose there were someone who wished to fully comprehend the core of this sutra—the universal majesty and spiritual power of all Buddhas, the realms of all World-Honored Ones, the diligence of all Buddhas, the solitary seclusion of all Buddhas, and the wondrous powers of all Buddhas—it is these that this sutra reveals.

Therefore, son of good family, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, you should zealously seek this sūtra, receive and uphold it, copy it, practice it with diligence, make offerings to it, serve it, and explain it to others.

Suppose there is a person who carries this sutra along, reciting, praising, copying, contemplating, and propagating it by inscribing it upon bamboo slips or silk; whether they are in a monastery, a hall for observances, a private residence, beneath the trees of a great forest, or by the side of water, one should erect a stupa and temple for them.

Why is this so? Because it is the ground where the Tathāgatas dwell; one should observe this site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) and the tree under which the Buddha sits, for it is the place where all Tathāgatas, the Perfectly Awakened Ones, have wandered, and where the Sages, the Heroes of the World, have turned the wheel of Dharma. It is within this that the Buddhas of the ten directions attain parinirvāṇa, all being equal and without distinction.
At this, the World-Honored One uttered this verse of praise:
“The Dharma for which the World feels compassion is inconceivable;
He constantly establishes the wisdom of supernormal powers, And likewise manifests them, Universally and equally with clear vision.”
All sentient beings without exception attained great joy.
His divine faculty of the tongue produced sounds as resonant as those of Brahmā, while he radiated hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of beams of light.
All classes of sentient beings, beholding his supernormal powers, marveled at this unprecedented wonder and all entered the Great Way.
In the space of a finger-snap, he proclaimed a vast sound, instantly announcing it everywhere.
Throughout all Buddha-lands, pervading the ten directions across all Buddha-worlds—
such transformations and other manifestations as these are the auspicious responses revealed by the Great Sage.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, those who uphold this sutra scroll and dwell securely in its teaching of merit and dharma will,
for incalculable and inconceivable kalpas, [attain such rewards].
The limit of the merit and blessings of one who holds this sutra scroll is such that the Teacher praises it as being manifold and immeasurable.
To exhaust its limit is impossible, for it is like empty space, which cannot be reached to its furthest bounds.
His fame and supreme virtue are beyond the reach of thought; those who uphold this sutra possess ever-pure virtues.
This is to behold the Buddha, the Great Sage and Guide, as well as myself in this world, having attained great enlightenment through parinirvāṇa.
Furthermore, behold this assembly of the four classes;
whoever encounters this sutra shall have witnessed the assembly of today.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, those who are able to uphold this sutra scroll shall likewise be here, as well as in all the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions;
they will behold all the Buddhas of the past and those throughout the ten directions.
Now, seeing the Buddhas of the present with one's own eyes, one shall worship and uphold them all with a joyful mind, turning toward those who are supreme among men.
Whatever one contemplates, one should swiftly receive and uphold;
regarding this sutra, one will naturally possess eloquence, free from all hindrance.
Those who are unable to recite it at length should discern and understand its meaning;
they should then receive and uphold it, for herein lies the World-Honored One’s clear comprehension of all sutras and their sequential ultimate destination.
After the Great Sage, the World-Honored One, has entered parinirvāṇa, if there should be someone who speaks with utmost sincerity,
analyzing this sutra and deliberating upon its underlying principles, then they shall expound and examine the profound meanings of all the scriptural volumes.
That person’s radiance distinguishes all that is awakened; like the sun and moon, it shines universally upon the far and the near.
Wandering throughout the world, wherever they arrive, they exhort and inspire countless bodhisattvas.
Therefore, those wise bodhisattvas who hear such a sūtra as this, peerless and without equal,
shall, after my parinirvāṇa, uphold this scripture; such persons will have no doubt regarding the Great Way of the Buddha.

Chapter 21: The Chapter on the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, Chapter Twenty-one: The Chapter on the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja. At that time, the Bodhisattva Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña addressed the Buddha, saying:
“For what reason does the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja travel through this Sahā world and endure such countless hardships and difficulties?”

Excellent, World-Honored One! We pray that you will, for the sake of the bodhisattvas and śrāvakas gathered here from the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, proclaim the merits of the original practices and the initial aspiration for the Way of the Medicine King. May those present in this assembly and those of future generations everywhere hear, uphold, and pursue this study to its ultimate end. May devas, humans, nāgas, ghosts, and all the honored divine kings be filled with joy and resolve their minds upon the Great Way, thereby attaining perfect enlightenment themselves and delivering all beings.
At that time, the World-Honored One, seeing that the King of the Constellations had given rise to a sincere resolve, praised him on behalf of all Buddhas, saying:
"Excellent! You have bestowed a gift upon the bodhisattvas of the future, exhorting and encouraging those who come after to enter the wisdom of the Way."
"Listen attentively, listen attentively!
Reflect upon this well.
"So be it, World-Honored One; we wish to hear it with joy."
The Buddha said:

"In the past, incalculable kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there was a Buddha named Vimalasūryacandraprabhaśiri Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who appeared in the world. The lifespan in that land was forty-two thousand years; he taught and transformed sentient beings, delivering them from peril and distress. At that time, there were eight billion bodhisattvas in the great assembly from the ten directions, and the multitude of śrāvakas numbered as many as the sands of seventy-two Ganges Rivers."
Furthermore, in that buddha-field there are no women and no realms of the three evil destinies; it is free from the afflictions of the asuras and the eight difficult conditions.

Its ground is level and upright, the color of deep blue lapis lazuli, adorned with various jewels, magnificent and pure. It is surrounded by rows of jewel trees, covered on all sides by precious necklaces and pendants, and features erected banners and streamers. Precious vases and incense burners emit various famous fragrances. Beneath every tree are set up jeweled couches and seats, their furnishings so exquisitely decorated as to be beyond description. Upon these seats are five thousand *koṭis* of thrones for the devas, where they play various musical instruments and sing of the Buddha’s virtues as an offering.
At that time, that Buddha was expounding and analyzing the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* for the assembly of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas.

There was then a bodhisattva named Satatābhirati (Always Delighted to See), who, upon hearing the Buddha’s exposition and detailed explanation of the essential meanings, reverently upheld the Buddha-dharma and practiced asceticism. For twelve thousand years he exerted himself with diligence day and night; for twelve thousand years he practiced walking meditation without sitting down, and thereupon attained the Samādhi of Universal Manifestation.
Having attained this concentration, he immediately reflected:
"Since I have attained this Samādhi of Universal Manifestation, I am now able to bring forth this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*."
Thereupon, having attained concentration, he leaped for joy and thought to himself:
"I shall make offerings to the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Vimalasūryacandraprabhāśrī, and receive the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*."

Thereupon, entering into meditative absorption (*samādhi*) just as he had visualized it, he remained in mid-air and rained down celestial flowers, various incenses, and sandalwood to make offerings to the Buddha.

At that moment, the multitude of flowers and various incenses that were rained down pervasively perfumed the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions; all who smelled the fragrance attained the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*), and all classes of sentient beings turned toward one another with harmonious hearts.
The Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana arose from his meditative concentration and reflected:
"Although one may offer various material things to the Buddha, they cannot fully express the virtue of the Ultimate Truth; only by offering one's own body is the offering unsurpassed."

Then, acting upon this thought, he ceased the consumption of the five grains and ate exclusively various fragrances, drinking the juices of various fragrant flowers so that his body became perfumed both internally and externally; in this manner, he consumed these fragrances for a full twelve years.
Furthermore, he blended various fragrances to anoint his body and moistened his robes with scented oil, then made this vow:
"I shall take my own body as a lamp for the sake of all beings."
He immediately set his own body ablaze as an offering to the Buddhas.

Because of his utmost sincerity, its light shone everywhere throughout Buddha-worlds as numerous as the sands of eighty Ganges Rivers. At that moment, all the Buddhas praised him with one voice, saying:
"Excellent!"
Excellent, son of noble family! Such diligence is truly rare in this world.

This is the true offering of the Tathāgata’s sūtras; for the sake of sentient beings, you endure suffering without weariness, surpassing all the practices of devas and humans. It exceeds the giving of kingdoms, wealth, wives, and children; among all forms of offering, it is the most honored, the highest, the foremost, the longest-lasting, and peerless. To give one's own body is to accomplish the gift of the Dharma.
After the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, had praised these virtues, they remained silent.

At that time, the Bodhisattva set his body ablaze; although the fire continued for twelve hundred years, it did not extinguish, and because he maintained a single-minded concentration, he experienced no suffering or affliction.

Thereafter, the flames were extinguished. Because he had diligently practiced and made offerings to the Dharma, at the end of his life he returned to that world and again encountered the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Vimalasūryacandraprabhāśirṣa. He was born by spontaneous transformation within the royal palace of King Vimaladatta, sitting cross-legged, and spoke these verses to his parents:
"O Honored King, remember my former conduct: With firm and steadfast great diligence, I gave away even my cherished body; Thus established and abiding, I attained this samādhi."
Having spoken these verses, he addressed his parents:

"The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vimalasūryacandraprabhāśirī, is currently present in the world. In the past, I made offerings to him with a sincere heart, and by virtue of this, I attained the essential dharma-door of the dhāraṇī of All-Sounding Voices."

This *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the unsurpassed sūtra and the essential core of all study, originally consists of eighty *koṭī-nayuta-śata-sahasra* verses; one should contemplate it with a single-minded focus. What need is there to create images or cast molds of the Buddha, when one can always maintain a mind free from anger and resentment?

This *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the practice of bodhisattvas, is that which I myself studied in previous lives—some hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of verses—which I heard and received from that Tathāgata.
King Vimaladatta praised his son, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"Let us go together in person to visit and make offerings to the Holy Honored One.

Having spoken these words, he and his father king leapt up into the air; seven fathoms above the ground, they walked through the void without their feet touching the earth. Their bodies sat upright within a precious canopy adorned with necklaces of the seven jewels, as they proceeded to the Buddha’s dwelling, joined their palms in salutation, and praised him with a verse:
"The Honored One among Men, Your countenance and form are free from defilement; Your radiance is most majestic."
Illuminating the ten directions, you whom I have originally worshipped as the infinite, holy Honored One, now come again in person; therefore, I have come to pay homage before your face.
At that time, after the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Delight-to-See had spoken these verses, he stepped forward and addressed the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Moon-and-Sun-Peak-Free-from-Stain:

“World-Honored One, you bestow grace and compassion upon the ten directions; therefore, you remain present now to instruct all beings, delivering and liberating sentient beings so that none fail to receive your benefit.”
At that time, the Tathāgata Vimalasūryacandraprabhāśrī addressed the Bodhisattva Satvābhipramodanadarśana:

"The time has now arrived and I wish to enter parinirvāṇa. I entrust this Dharma teaching to you; for the Buddha, having reached the proper time and completed his instruction, is about to depart as the age of disorder approaches. For the sake of the Buddha, prepare a seat, for I shall now attain parinirvāṇa."
He further addressed them, saying:
"I entrust this sutra to you with great earnestness, so that it may be widely disseminated to equally moisten the ten directions, causing all beings everywhere to receive its blessings and joy."
The sentient being Priyadarśana replied,
"I shall receive the instruction.
That Buddha then entered parinirvāṇa at midnight.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Priyadarśana, seeing that the Buddha had entered parinirvāṇa, cremated the Buddha’s body with sandalwood and other rare, wondrous incenses. He collected the relics and washed them with fragrant liquid; moved by deep longing and grief, his tears fell like rain. He constructed eighty-four thousand precious vases and erected stupas made of the seven treasures, reaching as high as the Brahma Heaven, adorned with banners, canopies, and suspended clusters of precious bells.
He thought to himself:
"I have already made offerings to the relics of the World-Honored One; I ought now to perform an act even more extraordinary than before.
He then addressed the bodhisattvas, the great śrāvakas, the devas, nāgas, spirits, and all the people:
"May all you sons of noble family together reflect upon this: let us collectively make offerings to the relics of the World-Honored One.
Thereupon, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva宿王華 (Śrīkūṭarāja):

"At that time, the Bodhisattva 眾生憙見 (Sarvasattvapriyadarśana) exhorted and led the multitude to offer worship to eighty-four thousand stūpas containing the relics. Before these stūpas and temples, they erected images endowed with the marks of a hundred merits, lit countless lamps, burned incense, and scattered flowers, thereby illuminating the Way and the Dharma, making offerings and serving them for seventy-two thousand years."

Having completed the offerings, within that assembly he transformed countless thousands of śrāvakas and opened the way for all bodhisattvas, causing them all to attain the Samādhi of Universal Manifestation.
Seeing that the assembly of bodhisattvas had established themselves in meditative concentration, [the Buddha] manifested his own body with its sense faculties impaired and deficient.
The assembly of bodhisattvas, as well as the disciples, devas, nāgas, ghosts, and spirits, raised their voices in lamentation, their tears falling like rain, saying:

"This son of noble family, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana, was our teacher who enlightened and transformed us; now he manifests with impaired and incomplete sense faculties. For this reason, we are so overcome with grief and sorrow that we cannot control ourselves."
At that time, the sentient beings Delighted-to-See addressed the bodhisattvas, the great disciples, and the devas, nāgas, and spirits, saying:

"I have established a solemn vow and a sincere aspiration. If my words are true and unfailing, may these arms of mine become a body of purple-gold; let my arms be restored as they were before, the earth shall shake greatly, and a rain of various flowers and incense shall fall from the void."
No sooner had he finished speaking than the earth shook violently and the heavens rained down various flowers; immediately, his arms were restored to their former state.

The beings Delighted-to-See (Sudarśana), desiring to deliver all beings, manifested this through the practice of the power of wisdom, brought about by the influence of his merit, virtue, and majestic power.
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña:
"If you wish to know who that Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sattvālokanandī was at that time, he is none other than the present-day Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja."

Furthermore, son of good family, the diligent austerities of a bodhisattva are beyond measure; they sacrifice their bodies and abandon their lives without limit, constantly establishing the Great Vehicle and the will for the Unsurpassed Way, and giving rise to great meritorious virtues that are infinite. To burn even a single toe before a Tathāgata produces merit that is difficult to compare; how much more so to burn one's own body as an offering, which surpasses the gift of kingdoms, wives, children, or one's own flesh and blood.

Even if one were to fill a Buddha-world with rare jewels and offer them as alms to the assembly of Buddhas and noble ones, although the merit would be vast, it would not equal that [merit]. Why is this so?
The retribution of such merit is finite and does not benefit sentient beings.

If a son or daughter of noble family receives even a single four-line verse of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, analyzes and practices it, and explains it to others, the merit of that gift of dharma exceeds by ten thousandfold the merit of material giving.
Just as the great ocean is the destination to which all rivers flow, so too is this sutra the foremost of all dharmas.

Just as Mount Sumeru is the highest among all mountains, and as the full moon is the most luminous among the stars, its great wisdom-light shines throughout the three realms; it is the head of all dharmas, the unsurpassed King of the Path, just as the rising sun illuminates the world at large and dispels all darkness.
This sutra is likewise: it eliminates all the darkness and obscurations of ignorance, leading all to enter the light of the Way.
It is like Śakra, the Lord of Devas among the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven;
this sutra is likewise the sovereign of all dharmas and all other scriptures, encompassing the ten directions to deliver and liberate all beings.
Just as the Brahma King dwells in the seventh palace, exercising control over all the devas so that none fail to obey his commands;
so too is this sutra, universally saving sentient beings—whether they have studied or not—and instructing those of the three vehicles to perform the duties of a sovereign and a father.
Just as those on the four paths up to the pratyekabuddhas all transcend all ordinary persons and learners;
so too is the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, for it transcends all the upper, middle, and lower vehicles, abiding at the source of sentient beings to transform all who have not yet attained.
Just as the conduct of a bodhisattva is lofty and far-reaching, surpassing the deeds of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas and providing protection throughout the three periods of time;
so too is this sutra, which governs all dharmas and causes them all to achieve unsurpassed, perfect, and true awakening.
Just as the World-Honored One, the Dharma King of the three realms, dons the robes of the Way and, with the thirty-two marks, guides the masses of the ignorant and obscured;

so too is this sutra: from the training of bodhisattvas up to the stage of Tathāgata, it instructs the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, causing them all to achieve unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment.

"O son of noble family, this sutra serves as a protector for the three realms; it delivers sentient beings from the perils and hardships of calamity, satisfies the suffering of hunger and emptiness in all hearts, provides warmth to the cold and coolness to the hot, and ensures that those who are naked all obtain clothing. It guides and instructs all sentient beings, causing them all to enter the Way."
Just as a guide protects and guards a multitude of merchants;
so too does a bodhisattva nurture sentient beings like a compassionate mother.
For example, it is like a boatman ferrying people back and forth across the water.

In this way, the bodhisattva circulates throughout the three realms to deliver all beings and extinguish the darkness of the multitudes, just as a torch extinguishes the darkness; he transforms birth, old age, and death, just as a wheel-turning monarch controls the four quarters;
and so too is this sutra, for with the light of the noble path it illuminates the three realms.
"Just as the great light dispels the darkness of the world, so too is this sutra:
it brings about non-retrogression, the patience of non-arising, and leads to the path of Buddhahood.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña:

"This sutra delivers all beings from the afflictions of every suffering; it eradicates the maladies of the various defilements and the three poisons, and rescues those bound within the prisons of birth and death."

If one hears this sutra and immediately understands it, or is able to transcribe it, the merit and blessings thereof are beyond calculation; how much more so for those who hear, uphold, cherish, recite, and explain it, and offer worship with flowers, incense, blended fragrances, scented oils, lamps, banners, and streamers.

If there are those who hear and uphold this "Chapter on the Ancient Training of Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja," and receive, maintain, and contemplate it, their merit shall surpass that of offering all those various material goods; it cannot be fully described.
If there is a woman who, upon hearing this Dharma of the sutra, immediately receives and upholds it, she shall at the end of her life as a woman in this world attain manhood.

If there is a woman who, during the final dregs of the five turbidities in the last age, hears this Dharma of the sutra and is able to practice it, then when her life ends, she will be reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nourishment (Sukhāvatī). There she will behold the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, surrounded by a retinue of bodhisattvas; she will be born within a precious lotus flower and sit upon a lion throne. Free from lust, anger, and delusion, she will cast off all fetters; she will be without greed or envy, and never harbor resentment.
Upon being born in that land, he attained the five supernormal powers and reached the stage of non-retrogression and the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Having attained this patience, he immediately beheld as many Tathāgatas as there are grains of sand in seventy-two *koṭī-nayuta* of *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka*.
Upon seeing the various Buddhas, their faculty of the eye became pure.
With the faculty of the eye purified, they saw all the Buddhas of the ten directions from afar, who praised them, saying: "Excellent!
Excellent, son of good family!

That you have encountered this world of the Buddha Śākyamuni, and that you receive, uphold, recite, and explain to others the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* spoken by the Buddha—this merit and virtue cannot be burned by fire nor swept away by water; thieves, enemies, and government officials cannot invade it. Even a thousand Buddhas could not exhaustively praise it; the merit you have obtained is immeasurable and its majesty is thus sublime.
By virtue of this merit, you shall subdue all Māras, cast off all enemies, cross over the perils of birth and death, and transcend all worldly afflictions.

Furthermore, son of good family, through this Dharma of the sutra, you shall subdue all evils and rebellious forces, and be established by the thousands of Buddhas who will protect your person. In both the heavens and the world, there is no peer to you; except for the Tathāgata himself, among all śrāvakas and bodhisattvas, there is none equal to you in merit, blessings, wisdom, and meditative concentration.
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña:
"If there are practitioners who receive this sutra, the power, majesty, and virtue of the holy wisdom they attain shall transcend [all others] to such an extent."

Therefore, O virtuous one, if there are those who preach this "Chapter on the Medicine King" and offer praise for it, when they are reborn as humans in a future life, their mouths will naturally have the fragrance of the *utpala* lotus, and their bodies will have the fragrance of sandalwood.

"If anyone hears this sutra and praises its excellence, their merit in the present life will be heard far and wide; the Buddha has already pre-emptively praised that person's achievements. The Buddha told Śuddharaśmiprabha: "I entrust this sutra to you all.

When the world of the five turbidities reaches its final decadence, this 'Chapter on the Ancient Dharma of the Beings Who Delight in Seeing' shall be circulated throughout Jambudvīpa. None shall be able to destroy it midway; Māra Pāpīyān shall find no opportunity, nor shall the hosts of Māra, nor heterodox deities, spirits, or demons, be able to cause harm. Neither devas, nāgas, rākṣasas, kumbhāṇḍas, nor yakṣas shall dare to oppose it."
Furthermore, Rājapadmavṛṣabhitābhijña!

This is established by the majestic power of the "Chapter on the Medicine King. Wherever it is circulated, if there is illness, the disease shall be eliminated upon hearing this Dharma of the sutra, and no further afflictions shall remain. By virtue of this merit, one shall later attain true correctness, free from old age, sickness, and death.
If there is a bhikṣu in the final age who takes a blue lotus in his hand, fills it with various incenses, and scatters them as an offering to a Dharma Master, thinking to himself:

"Should anyone seeking the Bodhisattva vehicle arrive at this site of enlightenment, I shall offer this flower as a seat of grass, so that they may sit beneath the Bodhi tree and subdue all Māras; by means of this, they shall fully sound the Dharma drum and blow the great Dharma conch, thereby delivering beings from the sea of birth and death"—if a student of the Mahāyāna sees such a bhikṣu holding this scripture, they should regard that person's merit as being thus.

When the Buddha had spoken this "Chapter on the Ancient Deeds of the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja," eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas immediately attained the dhāraṇī of skillful means for understanding all sounds.
At that time, the Tathāgata Sarvaratna praised him, saying:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
“Suvikrāntavikramin Bodhisattva!
It is truly a joy that you are able to inquire about the inconceivable practices and deeds of the sūtras, which the Tathāgata shall now expound! Chapter 22:

The Chapter on the Bodhisattva Wonderful Roar (*Suvarṇaghoṣa*). Thereupon, the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, immediately emitted hundreds of thousands of rays of light from the mark of the Great Man between his eyebrows and the crown of his head. These lights illuminated eighteen hundred million *koṭis* of Buddha-lands, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River in the eastern direction, pervading them all without exception.

Beyond these Buddha-lands, there is a world named Adorned Illumination. In that land dwells a Buddha, titled Vimala-suvarṇa-pūrvapadma-rāja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who, surrounded by a retinue of countless bodhisattvas, proclaims and transforms beings.
The radiance emanated by the Tathāgata Śākyamuni shone everywhere throughout that land.

Furthermore, in that buddha-field, there was a bodhisattva named Gadgadasvara, who had planted the roots of manifold virtues under past buddhas and had made offerings to hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of tathāgatas; whenever he beheld those buddhas...
Having consulted and received the sūtras, they attained holy wisdom; they achieved the Samādhi of Venerable Respect, the Samādhi of the Fixed Lotus Sūtra,
the Samādhi of Bestowing Freedom from Defilement, the Samādhi of Delighting in the King of Constellations,
the Samādhi of Unattached Radiance, the Samādhi of the Seal of Wisdom, the Samādhi of Universally Illuminating All Sounds, and the Samādhi of Equally Gathering All Virtues.
The Samādhi of Joyful Faith and Purity, the Samādhi of Divine Power and Playful Delight,
the Samādhi of Wisdom Light, the Samādhi of the Adorned Pure King, the Samādhi of Stainless Light, the Samādhi of the Stainless Treasury, the Samādhi of the Objectless,
and the Samādhi of the Turning Sun— to speak briefly, he has universally attained hundreds of thousands of millions of nayutas of such rivers of samādhis.

With samādhis as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, the Buddha’s radiance pervaded everywhere, illuminating the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara. Having received the Buddha’s holy light, the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara went to the Buddha’s abode and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:

“I wish to travel to the Sahā world to see the Buddha Śākyamuni, to prostrate and pay homage, and to inquire about and receive the sūtras. Furthermore, I wish to pay my respects to Mañjuśrī, Bhaiṣajyarāja Bodhisattva, Suvikrāntavikrāmin Bodhisattva, Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña Bodhisattva, Ghoṣadatta Bodhisattva, Viśuddharāja Bodhisattva, and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata Bodhisattva; to consult them on the meaning of the sūtras, to receive what I have not yet attained, and to cause all who hear it to resolve upon the path of enlightenment.”
That Buddha said to him:
"Go, son of good family!
Although you arrive in that land, do not give rise to divergent thoughts or conceive of that land as weary, inferior, or lowly."

Why is this so? Furthermore, noble son, in that world of Endurance (*sahā-lokadhātu*), the great lands are interspersed with Black Mountains (*kṛṣṇaparvata*); it is filled with various impurities, stones, sand, and foulness, and its streams, ravines, and valleys are not like those of ordinary worlds. In that land, the Buddha’s body is short and small, measuring one *zhang* and six *chi*, while the bodies of the bodhisattvas are seven or eight *chi* tall.

Furthermore, while your original body is forty-two thousand yojanas in height, my manifested body is eighty-four thousand yojanas in height; it is upright and exceptionally beautiful, with the foremost of forms and features. Its majestic radiance and wondrous marks and signs are beyond comparison, and having accumulated hundreds of thousands of virtues, all who behold it are filled with joy.

Furthermore, when you go there and see the people of that land, be careful not to give rise in your mind to the thought that the Buddha-lands of the Tathāgatas and Bodhisattvas are inferior. Why is this?
“The Buddha-lands are fundamentally empty; it is only due to the transgressions and blessings of sentient beings that they currently appear to be different.
The Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“Relying upon the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha and the holy might of the Tathāgata, I shall take delight in the lofty virtue and morality as I proceed to the Sahā world. Regarding the pure karma of the Tathāgata’s wisdom and path, I shall immediately act in accordance with the Dharma without any error or omission, and I dare not give rise to conceptual thoughts.”

At that time, the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara thought to himself; without rising from his seat, he immediately entered the samādhi of "Just as it is" (yathāvad-ākāra). He traveled to the Sahā world and arrived at Vulture Peak Mountain, where he stood amidst the Dharma-seat of the Tathāgata. There, he manifested eighty-four thousand *koṭis* of lotus flowers made of various jewels, with stems of purple gold and leaves of white silver. They were exquisitely adorned, pure and beautiful, with a towering radiance that illuminated all those in the assembly. Whatever he had intended, it was instantly and perfectly accomplished.
Mañjuśrī asked the Buddha Śākyamuni:

"Indeed, World-Honored One, you have now manifested these eighty-four thousand lotus flowers made of various jewels, with stems of purple gold and leaves of white silver, pure, magnificent, and beautiful."
“Whose auspicious omen is this that such a transformation has appeared?
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:

“There is a bodhisattva named Gadgadasvara who has come from the buddha-field of the Tathāgata Padmavṛṣabhavikrāmin, the King of Pure Lodges of Gold and Purple Radiance. Accompanied by eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas, he has arrived here in this Sahā world-system desiring to see my body, prostrate, and inquire; he also desires to hear the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, and therefore these omens have first appeared.”
Mañjuśrī again asked the Buddha:
"What roots of merit did this person accumulate in his past lives, and what sublime practices did he perform, that he has now attained such extraordinary and magnificent merit?"
In which samādhi do you abide to originally establish these practices?

We wish to hear about the samādhis and the transformations of the supernormal powers (ṛddhi) that you employ; having heard them, we shall receive and practice them. Furthermore, what are the features and physical appearances of the various bodhisattvas that we see?
What benefit is served by your movements and comings and goings?
How profound it is, World-Honored One!
You have manifested this auspicious omen solely to cause the bodhisattvas to come here, for the assembled multitude desires to see them.
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī,

“You should address the Tathāgata Sarvaratna, requesting him to manifest auspicious signs so that all the bodhisattvas may come here, each manifesting their own physical form, for the entire assembly desires to see them.”
Mañjuśrī immediately accepted his instructions and promptly petitioned the Tathāgata Samantaratna for entry into parinirvāṇa; thereupon, an auspicious omen appeared.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara suddenly vanished from his own land and, together with eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas, caused all Buddha-lands to tremble and rained down precious lotus flowers. Simultaneously, hundreds of thousands of billions of musical instruments were played. Each of the arriving bodhisattvas manifested their own form; their eyes were clear and beautiful like deep blue sapphire, their countenances full and radiant like the moon at its peak, and their bodies possessed the luster of purple-gold light. Their bodies were adorned with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of merits, their majestic spiritual power was towering, and the light of their wisdom was brilliant. With marvelous marks and various fine features adorning their radiant faces, their physical strength was infinite. Their bodies remained suspended in mid-air, four *zhang* and nine *chi* above the ground, surrounded by their assembly of bodhisattvas, as they arrived at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa in this Sahā world.

Descending from the jeweled intersecting paths, holding in his hand precious gems worth hundreds of thousands, he approached the Buddha Śākyamuni, prostrated at his feet, and presented them as an offering to the Tathāgata Śākyamuni.
He addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"The Tathāgata King of Pure Gold and Flower of Freedom from Defilement sends his boundless greetings, inquiring whether your daily life is light and easy and your movements are robust and healthy.
He further asks: "
"Does the World-Honored One teach the Dharma as usual?
Do all sentient beings who receive it progress?
Have they cast off their doubts and accorded with the Dharma and Vinaya?"
Are you not harboring much lust, anger, and delusion, nor practicing hatred, envy, or greed?
Are you able to be respectful and filial toward your parents, and to listen to and receive the Dharma, practicing it in accordance with the Dharma?
Do you follow false views and cherish wealth and treasures so that your faculties are unsettled, merely to subdue the hosts and retainers of Māra?
Furthermore, do all sentient beings listen to and receive the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata Destroyer of All Treasures?

Now these bodhisattvas have come here specifically, dispatched by the Tathāgatas of their own lands, desiring to pay homage to the stupa-temple of the seven treasures and to see the Tathāgata Samantaratna who has entered parinirvāṇa; they wish to inquire after his well-being and receive his instructions on how he taught the Dharma.
"Do all sentient beings universally receive and practice according to the Dharma?

For how long has the Tathāgata Sarvaratna been currently residing? We have come for this reason, desiring to behold the likeness of the form of the Tathāgata Sarvaratna; we pray that the Buddha will manifest it."
At that time, the Buddha Śākyamuni said to the Tathāgata Sarvaratna:
"Now the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara and his retinue wish to behold the physical form and image of the World-Honored One."
The Tathāgata Sarvaratna immediately praised him, saying:
“Excellent! Excellent!”

Noble son, it is because you have come here to see the Buddha Śākyamuni, to prostrate and inquire about and receive the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, and furthermore, because you wish to behold Mañjuśrī and resolve your various deficiencies.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Padmaśrī asked the Buddha,
“When the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara was in his past lives, what roots of virtue did he accumulate to achieve such infinite, divine, and sacred transformations?”
At that time, the Buddha Śākyamuni addressed the Bodhisattva Padmaśrī, saying:

"In the distant past, long ago, there was a Buddha named Cloud-Thunder-Voice King Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. He expounded the path of the sūtras, the six perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā), and the Dharma-treasury of the bodhisattvas; throughout the heavens above and the earth below, there were none who did not receive peace and security."

At that time, the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara, having heard what was said, joyfully understood its meaning. He played hundreds of thousands of musical instruments to entertain his Buddha and presented eighty-four thousand exquisite vessels made of various jewels as offerings to the Supreme Honored One. In this manner, he diligently made offerings to the Tathāgata for twelve thousand years.

Furthermore, noble son, when the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara was in a former life, during the era of the Tathāgata Meghadundubhisvararāja, he cultivated the seeds of the unsurpassed Dharma and planted these roots of merit without ever becoming weary or negligent. Transmitting the intent of the Tathāgata, he transformed those who were ignorant and deluded, causing all who did not recognize the Ultimate Truth to come to believe in and delight in it.
If you wish to know who that Bodhisattva Wonderful Sound was at that time, it is this very Bodhisattva Wonderful Sound here.

By means of those offerings of precious vessels and the sounds of various musical instruments during that world-age, and furthermore by making offerings to countless Buddhas, he planted the roots of all virtues and cultivated various practices in the presence of billions of Buddhas. In his previous lives, he encountered as many Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, as there are grains of sand in hundreds of thousands of millions of Ganges Rivers.

"Now, Padmaśrī, manifesting the conduct of the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara, has assumed immeasurable and countless transformations to proclaim, expound, and transform sentient beings through the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*."
Sometimes they manifest the form and appearance of Brahmā to lead and establish beings;
sometimes they manifest the form of Śakra, or the form of a noble lord, or the form of a general to transform and guide the various troops;

or they appear in the forms of the Heavenly King Śikhin, a Wheel-Turning Sage King, various minor kings, honored elders, village headmen, or the physical appearances and features of śramaṇas and brahmins.

They preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, sometimes manifesting in the forms of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās; or in the forms of palace attendants, court ladies, the wives of elders, or women of humble station; and they thus entice and establish [beings] as men, women, the young, or the old.

They preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, assuming the forms of asuras, or the appearances and features of garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans, thereby enticing and establishing them [in the Dharma].

While preaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, he enters the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, animals, and the eight difficult conditions; wherever they may be, he protects and delivers them. Whether they be superior, middling, or inferior persons, advancing or retreating, he transforms and enlightens them according to their physical forms and whether they appear as male or female.
He preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, or entered the inner palace to manifest in the form of the Queen, thereby delivering all the nobility.
"Lotus-Head, you should know that the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara protects and sustains all sentient beings in this Sahā world."

Furthermore, noble son, the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara, through various transformations and countless skillful means, has been preaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* in the Buddha-land of Sahe; his supernormal powers and majestic virtue have never diminished but have instead increased, and it is the same with his noble wisdom and the knowledge of the Path.

Furthermore, noble son, the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara possesses a majesty of light, merit, and wisdom so sublime that he travels throughout the ten directions, transforming beings according to the time. He revolves without end, causing all to enter the discipline of the Dharma; he ensures that those with superior, middling, and inferior aspirations each attain their proper place. Having reached this Sahā world, he further proceeds to Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in other directions, manifesting the body of a bodhisattva to preach the Dharma.

Furthermore, he manifests in the forms of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas to transform and guide others, demonstrating the practices they originally studied; upon hearing this, they attain a state of vast clarity, each fulfilling their own aspirations without contradicting their original vows.

If there are sentient beings who uphold the discipline of the Tathāgata, [the Buddha] manifests his physical form according to their respective paths and disciplines, clearly bestowing the Great Way, the unsurpassed, true, and correct [enlightenment]. Desiring to guide those who long for Nirvāṇa, he manifests his own parinirvāṇa, thereby displaying his demeanor to open and transform them through the wisdom of the Way.
“The power and noble wisdom of the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara are unfathomable; his transcendent and towering merits are such that they can have no comparison.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Padmaśrī came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying, “The Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara has accumulated merit and cultivated virtue until he is so magnificent and eminent.”
“Yes, World-Honored One; in what samādhi do you abide to transform and guide immeasurable sentient beings?
The Tathāgata Śākyamuni told Padmaśrī Bodhisattva:
“Listen, son of good family!

There is a samādhi named Manifesting Entry into All Images; when the Bodhisattva Wondrous Sound dwells in this state of meditative concentration, he benefits and transforms limitless sentient beings, causing them to enter the discourse of the Way.

When the Buddha spoke this chapter on the Verses of the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara, all those bodhisattvas who had come together with the bodhisattva-mahāsattva Gadgadasvara immediately attained the samādhi of "Manifest Entry into All Forms" (sarvarūpasaṃdarśana).
His practice is preeminent; thus, he surpasses all the limited meditative concentrations cultivated by the bodhisattvas in this Sahā world.
If one attains the Samādhi of Manifest Entry into All Forms, one immediately acquires dhāraṇī, grasping and upholding the three periods of time so that none fail to receive salvation.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara made offerings to the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, the Arhat, and fully served the stūpas, temples, and śarīras of the Tathāgatas of All Jewels. Desiring to return to his own land, he first prostrated before the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, took his leave, and departed from the assembly. As he shook the various lands and rained down myriad lotus flowers, hundreds of thousands of billions of koṭis of elegant songs and musical instruments played in harmony. Together with an assembly of eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas, he returned to his own land, where he prostrated and paid homage to the Tathāgata Wondrous Purple-Gold Dust-Free Constellation Flower King, before proceeding to the Sahā world to guide and benefit sentient beings.

Furthermore, beholding the relics of the Tathāgata Ratnakūṭa’s Jewel Temple, as well as the power of the boundless path of diligence attained by Mañjuśrī and Bhaiṣajyarāja Bodhisattvas, and seeing the Bodhisattva Subhaparākrama, he caused these eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas to all attain right practice and enter the Samādhi of Manifesting All Forms, so that they might travel together to that realm and proceed in unison.
Forty-two thousand devaputras, upon hearing the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, all attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*);
the Bodhisattva Padmaśrī attained the concentration of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
The Lotus Sutra of the True Dharma, Scroll Nine;
The Lotus Sutra of the True Dharma, Scroll Ten.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Yuezhi Kingdom during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Chapter Twenty-Three: The Universal Gate of Avalokiteśvara.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Indeed, World-Honored One!"
"For what reason is he named 'Light of the World' (Avalokiteśvara), and what is the meaning of this title?
The Buddha told Akṣayamati:

"Noble son, if there are sentient beings who encounter hundreds of thousands of millions of calamities, misfortunes, and immeasurable bitter sufferings, as soon as they hear the name of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, they immediately attain liberation and are freed from all afflictions; therefore, he is named 'Light of the World.'"

If there are those who hold his name and keep it in their hearts, even if they encounter a great fire burning through mountains and wilds, consuming hundreds of grasses, trees, thickets, forests, and dwellings, and their bodies fall into the midst of the flames, as soon as they hear the name of Avalokiteśvara, the fire will immediately be extinguished.

If one enters a great body of water or a swift-flowing river and feels fear in one's heart, by invoking the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara and taking refuge with single-minded devotion, his majestic spiritual power will protect them so that they do not drown, leading them out to safety and peace.

If one enters the great ocean, where hundreds of thousands of billions of beings—both noble and base—dwell in the bottomless depths of the abyss, gathering and bringing forth gold, silver, various pearls, moon-bright gems, wish-fulfilling jewels (*cintāmaṇi*), crystal, lapis lazuli, musaragalva, agate, coral, and amber, their ships filled to the brim with treasures;

and even if a wind should blow their ship so that it drifts toward the Black Mountains or turbulent waves, or if they pass through the realm of ghosts and encounter the *makara* fish, if among the multitude there is even a single person who secretly and privately calls to mind the merit and majestic spiritual power of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara and utters his name, all shall be liberated from every affliction. Thus, the entire company of companions shall attain safe passage and not meet with the calamities of demons or malevolent spirits; for this reason, he is named Avalokiteśvara.
The Buddha said,

“Noble son! If you see an enemy or bandit coming to harm you, and you immediately invoke the name of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara and take refuge in him, the sword or staff held by that thief will instantly break into pieces so that his hands cannot lift them, and he will naturally develop a heart of compassion.”

Suppose, noble son, that this great trichiliocosm were filled with various ghosts and spirits, and a multitude of malevolent and perverse demons wishing to come and harass people; if one single-mindedly invokes the name of Avalokiteśvara, they will naturally submit and be unable to commit offenses at will, their evil intentions will not arise, and they will not engage in perverse views.

If a person has committed a crime or is innocent, or if they are seized by wicked men or government officials, their bodies bound with shackles and fetters upon them, or if they are placed in stocks and manacles and confined in a prison, undergoing the bitter torment of interrogation and punishment—if they single-mindedly take refuge and invoke the name of Avalokiteśvara, they will quickly attain liberation; the prison doors shall open and they will emerge, unable to be restrained. Therefore, he is named Avalokiteśvara.
The Buddha said, “It is so, son of good family. The realm of Avalokiteśvara and his majestic spiritual merit are difficult to measure; because his radiance is thus, he is named Avalokiteśvara.”
The Buddha addressed Akṣayamati:

"Suppose, son of good family, this trichiliocosm were filled with rebels, bandits, and enemies intent on harm, who brandished weapons such as spears, swords, blades, and halberds, wishing to kill the myriad people. A single caravan of merchants, traveling alone along that road, carried heavy treasures; their leader was terrified and thought to himself:
'There are many thieves here; they might endanger me and plunder my wealth. I must devise a skillful stratagem to escape these manifold perils and avoid being harmed.'"
He said to the merchants: "You should not be afraid.

With one mind and in unison, all of you together raise your voices and invoke the majestic spiritual power of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva; he will immediately come to protect you so that you shall have no fear. By universally taking refuge with a sincere heart, you shall be delivered from these many perils and shall not encounter harm from bandits."

Upon hearing this, all the merchants together accepted the instruction; with one voice they invoked Avalokiteśvara, surrendering their very lives and vowing to be delivered from this peril. As soon as they uttered his name, the bandits retreated and did not dare to attack, and the merchants were liberated, forever free from fear.
“Because the majestic power and the sphere of activity of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara are as lofty and sublime as this, he is called ‘Avalokiteśvara.
The Buddha further addressed the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati:

“If there are practitioners whose lust, anger, and delusion are rampant, and they prostrate and take refuge in the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, their lust, anger, and delusion will cease; they will contemplate impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self, and with a single mind, they will attain concentration.”

If there are women who have no offspring and seek either a son or a daughter, and they take refuge in Avalokiteśvara, they will immediately obtain them. Those who single-mindedly apply themselves with diligence and take refuge in him will, in every lifetime, possess upright features and incomparable countenances that bring joy to all who see them; the children they bear will possess majestic marks, be beloved by the multitude, and be desired by all to behold, as they plant many roots of virtue and do not engage in sinful karma.

The majestic spiritual power and meritorious virtues of Avalokiteśvara, as well as the loftiness of his realm of wisdom, are such that for those who hear his name, wherever they go, it shall never be in vain; they shall not encounter evil harm and shall attain the fruit of the unsurpassed Way and virtue. They will constantly meet with various Buddhas, True Persons, and Bodhisattvas of high virtue and integrity, never associating with perverse people nor meeting with those who act with duplicity. If one hears his name and holds it fast within one’s heart, the resulting merit shall be immeasurable and beyond all calculation.

If one were to make offerings to as many bodhisattvas as there are grains of sand in sixty-two billion Ganges Rivers, and cause all these bodhisattvas to practice universal loving-kindness in the present;
If a son or daughter of noble family were to provide clothing, food and drink, bedding and seating, and medicines for the sick and frail— everything necessary for comfort—
for as long as their life lasts, would their merit not be great?
Akṣayamati said: “It is much,
World-Honored One!”
They are immeasurable. Why is this?
These bodhisattvas are incalculable billions in number, beyond all analogy.
The Buddha said:

"Though one were to make offerings to these infinite bodhisattvas, it would not equal the merit of taking refuge in Avalokiteśvara, prostrating with reverence, and upholding his name; the latter's blessing exceeds the former, let alone the merit of making offerings."

Even if one were to make offerings to as many bodhisattvas as there are grains of sand in sixty-two billion Ganges Rivers, and were to maintain their names, if one were to calculate these two merits, they would not reach exhaustion even in hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas; they could never be compared. For this reason, he is named Avalokiteśvara.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"For what causes and conditions does Avalokiteśvara travel through this Sahā world?
How does he preach the Dharma?"
"What is meant by 'aspiration' (praṇidhāna)?
What is the realm of the skillful means (upāyakauśalya) regarding the dharmas practiced?
The Buddha said:
“O son of noble family!
In the worlds where the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara wanders, he may manifest in the body of a Buddha to proclaim the Dharma;
or he may manifest in the form and appearance of a bodhisattva, preaching the sūtras to transform and enlighten beings.”
Sometimes he manifests as a Pratyekabuddha, or as a Śrāvaka; sometimes he manifests in the form of Brahmā or Śakra to preach the Way of the Sūtras;

or in the form of a Gandharva. To deliver ghosts and spirits, he manifests in the form of a ghost or spirit; to deliver the noble and honored, he manifests in the form of the noble and honored; or again, he manifests in the form of a great and wondrous Deva, or in the form of a Cakravartin King who transforms the four realms, or in a particularly extraordinary form. Or again, he manifests in the form of an inverted-footed Rākṣasa, or in the form of a general, or manifests in the form of a śramaṇa or a brahmacārin, or in the form of a Vajra deity, a hermit dwelling in solitude, a rishi, or a young scholar.
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara wanders through the lands of all Buddhas, universally manifesting in various forms; wherever he transforms his appearance, he brings liberation to all.
Therefore, son of good family, all sentient beings should offer worship to Avalokiteśvara.

Whichever sons of good family may encounter fear in their travels, he causes them to be without dread; having brought them to fearlessness, he makes them all universally secure and at peace, so that each rejoices within themselves as they roam the realm of endurance.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati untied from his own body a hundred thousand jeweled necklaces and offered them to Avalokiteśvara, saying:
"I pray that the Righteous One will accept this Dharma-offering."
He was unwilling to accept the extraordinary jewel necklaces he himself possessed.
Then, the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati again addressed Avalokiteśvara:
"I pray that you will look upon me with compassion and accept them at this time; I beseech you not to refuse or reject them."
At that time, Avalokiteśvara thought to himself,
"I have no need for these jewels.
Akṣayamati said:

"Furthermore, out of compassion for the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans, please accept this precious necklace and divide it into two parts: one part to offer to the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, and one part to offer to the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Ratnagarbha, presenting it to his precious temple."

Because that son of noble family acts for the sake of all beings, he employs his supernormal powers and transformations to travel throughout the world-system of Endurance, providing salvation to all without exception.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Dharanimdhara rose from his seat, came forward, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If there should be anyone who hears of the roots of virtue practiced by Avalokiteśvara, they shall never be in vain; through successive lives they will abide in peace and security until they reach ultimate wisdom. This Avalokiteśvara possesses supernatural powers and transformations that reach everywhere to the gates of the Way, and the majestic spiritual power he manifests is inexhaustible."

When the Buddha had preached this "Universal Gate Chapter," eighty-four thousand people within that assembly attained the peerless state and immediately resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path.

Chapter Twenty-Four: The Chapter on Dharanis In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, the Chapter on Dharanis, the twenty-fourth: At that time, the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja rose from his seat, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If sons of good family or daughters of good family hear this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* sūtra, receive and uphold it, cherish it in their hearts, and transcribe its scrolls—what kind of merit will they obtain?"
The Buddha said:
"Noble sons and daughters, those who receive and uphold this sutra, recite it from memory, or transcribe its scrolls, their merit shall be immeasurable and beyond all analogy."

If a son of noble family were to make offerings to as many Tathāgatas as there are grains of sand in eighty billion hundreds of thousands of koṭis of Ganges Rivers, yet another were to receive, uphold, cherish, write out, expound, and make offerings to this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*—[the latter would generate far greater merit].
Which brings greater merit?
What do you think:
would it be more meritorious to single-mindedly uphold the sutras, or to provide offerings of food and clothing to the Buddhas?
The Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If sons of noble family or daughters of noble family receive the essentials of this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* sūtra, and uphold, transcribe, explain, recite, or even practice a single four-line verse, they will fully achieve the greatest merit, surpassing that of making offerings to as many Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, as there are grains of sand in various rivers."
The Buddha said:
"How profound!
The offering of the Dharma is the most supreme."
The Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“I shall protect such individuals as these—sons and daughters of good family, those who receive this sutra, and these Dharma masters—and by means of its meaning, I shall guard them constantly so that they remain free from affliction and recite the dhāraṇī verses.”
He then recited the mantra:
"The wondrous and extraordinary that is contemplated; the thought that is free from thought; the eternal practice, reverently cultivating stillness.
Serene and silent in aspiration, liberated and crossing over; impartial and without deviance, peaceful, harmonious, and universally equanimous."
Extinguishing the exhaustible until nothing remains, there is nothing that surpasses profound silence; it is a state of tranquil total retention.
Observing its radiant brilliance, there is that upon which one relies; relying inwardly, one attains ultimate purity.
There are no pits or chasms, nor any high or low places, nor any winding paths where one might wander.
His eyes are pure; they are equal and have nothing with which to be compared. Having awakened and transcended, he examines all phenomena.
The entire assembly remained silent; what was taught was clear and lucid, yet they maintained contentment.

All limitations were completely eliminated as the resonance of the voice was proclaimed; they understood all sounds and mastered written characters, which were inexhaustible, forever devoid of power or force, and beyond all conceptual thought.
The Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja addressed [the Buddha], saying:
"Indeed, World-Honored One, these dhāraṇī phrases have been spoken by Buddhas as numerous as the sands of sixty-two Ganges Rivers."
"If there should be anyone who violates the words of this mantra, or who further opposes or disparages such Dharma-preachers, they shall have lost the teaching of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.
The Buddha then praised the Great Being, Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja: "Excellent!"
"Excellent!
If a son of noble family were to proclaim these dhāraṇī phrases for the sake of sentient beings, out of compassion he would protect them and bring great peace and security.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Subhavyūha came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Indeed, World-Honored One, for the sake of sentient beings, I also desire that they be brought to eternal peace.

If there are those who uphold this sutra, I shall bestow upon them the phrases of *dhāraṇī* and protect such Dharma masters, ensuring that no one seeking to harm them can find an opportunity. Even if ghosts, spirits, various *mārīcīs*, the hosts of latrine ghosts, *tūnaka* ghosts, *yātudhāna* ghosts, hungry ghosts, and foot-inverted ghosts should come to harass them, none shall be able to gain the advantage.”
The Bodhisattva Wondrous Courage concentrated his mind in contemplation and spoke this dhāraṇī:

“Resplendent and great brilliance, blazing light radiating its glow; arriving in accordance with the auspicious chapter of wealth, dwelling here with joy and delight; establishing regulations for eternal practice, neither conjoined nor accumulated.”
"These dhāraṇī phrases have been spoken by Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, all of whom collectively offer their encouragement and support.
If one violates the teachings of the Tathāgata and such Dharma masters, one will bring about one's own ruin and destruction."
Then King Vaiśravaṇa came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I, too, shall expound these dhāraṇī phrases; with a heart of loving-kindness and for the sake of sentient beings, I shall protect and defend the Dharma-preacher."
"Abundant playfulness and non-playfulness, immeasurable and non-abundance—what abundance is there?
For this reason, one shall protect these Dharma-preachers so that within a hundred yojanas no one dares to offend them, guarding and attending them."

"Sons of good family, it is through such analogies that those who study as Dharma-preachers are able to receive and uphold [this teaching]; by this protection, they shall always obtain auspicious fortune.

At that time, the Heavenly King Anuvaiṣṇava was seated in that assembly, surrounded by hundreds of thousands of millions of *yakṣas* and *gandharvas*. He approached the Buddha and addressed him, saying:
"Indeed, World-Honored One, I too shall proclaim these dhāraṇī phrases."
"Innumerable yet numbered, illuminating the dark while upholding fragrance; the great essence of malevolent mantras, recorded in accordance with the vessel, reaching even to violent speech.
"So it is, World-Honored One! These dhāraṇī phrases have been spoken by four thousand two hundred billion Buddhas."
"By means of this dhāraṇī, may those who study the sūtras be protected and honored, so that no one seeking to harm them may find an opportunity.

At that time, there was a malevolent spirit named Saṃyojana (Bound), also named Vigata-saṃyojana (Free from Bonds), also named Datta-rāśi (Accumulated Gifts), also named Datta-puṣpa (Gifted Flowers), also named Datta-kṛṣṇa (Gifted Black), also named Mukta-keśa (Long Hair), also named Asakta (Unattached), also named Puṣpadhara (Holding Flowers), also named Kva-stha (Where Staying), and also named Sarva-tejo-hara (Taking All Vitality). He went to where the Buddha was, accompanied by Hārītī and her sons; with one voice they all came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We, World-Honored One!"
"You should always protect such Dharma-preachers as these, bestowing upon them auspiciousness and ensuring that no one seeking an opportunity can find fault in them.
At that time, the various malevolent spirits raised their voices together and proclaimed this dhāraṇī to support the Dharma-preacher: "Yu-she, yu-si, yu-er, yu-shi;

most profoundly without self, without 'I', without body, and without anything with which to be joined or equal; already arisen, already born, already accomplished, abiding and standing, likewise abiding in praise, and not subject to destruction—may no great calamity befall you or cause you harm."
"These beings are my retinue; they shall ensure that no offense is committed and protect the Dharma Master.

They will eliminate ghosts and spirits, various malevolent demons, hungry ghosts, latrine deities, *tuo* ghosts, sorcery, talismans, and incantations, as well as those who are deluded, insane, or possessed by demons. They will manifest in these forms, whether in the shape of ghosts and spirits or non-human figures, appearing on the second, third, or even the fourth day, or causing chronic fevers."

Furthermore, if while lying down at night one encounters a bad dream, or if various forms of men, women, large or small beings appear, we shall provide protection so that no one seeking an opportunity may find an opening.
Then the various malevolent spirits together recited these verses before the Buddha:
"Your head shall be split into seven pieces, Just like a flower or a leaf being torn asunder;
You shall incur the crime of killing your mother, And likewise suffer the calamity of harming your father."
Those who offend the Dharma Master shall all incur this transgression;
throughout successive lifetimes they shall find no peace and shall not meet with the Buddhas.
Such is the sin of destroying Buddhist temples and the calamity of inciting strife among the holy assembly.
Just as when a mass of sesame oil is gathered in one place and set on fire,
it all burns away until it is completely consumed with nothing remaining;
so too shall those who offend the Dharma Master incur such calamity.
"Just as a scale carries a heavy burden, so too is one who offends a Dharma Master a vessel for the accumulation of sinful defilements;
such a person shall incur this grave transgression.
Having spoken these verses, the generals of the various ghost-spirit armies addressed the Buddha, saying:

“We shall all protect such Dharma-preachers as these, ensuring they are always at peace and removing their enemies; we shall station ourselves around them as sentinels so that no harm may come to them, and if anyone attempts to administer poison, the poison shall not take effect.”
At that time, the Buddha praised those who had been cursed by the malevolent spirits, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"You all wish to protect these Dharma masters.

If they hear this sutra, the merit of proclaiming and upholding its name is immeasurable; how much more so for those who fully possess it, reciting and explaining it at all times, or transcribing it into volumes; or those who offer flowers, incense, banners, canopies, blended perfumes, powdered incense, burn lamps, hang silken streamers, and offer *sītā*, *saṃharṣaṇī*, blue lotuses, red lotuses, yellow lotuses, and white lotuses—using even a small amount of oil or ghee to light lamps—and thus reverently worship this sutra with diligent and tireless practice, their merit shall be hundreds of thousands of billions of times beyond limit."
"You all should protect such practitioners who train with such diligence.
When the Buddha spoke this Chapter on the Dhāraṇī, sixty-eight thousand people attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Chapter Twenty-Five: The King Śuddhābhirati The Buddha addressed the sons of good family:

"In the distant past, incalculable kalpas ago—beyond thought, vast, and immeasurable—there was a Buddha named Samudrareṇu-garjita-śubha-guṇa-rāja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. His world was called Prabhāsa-vyūha, and his kalpa was called Priyadarśana."
Furthermore, noble son, in the time of that Buddha, there was a king named Viśuddhaviśuddha.
At that time, that king had a principal queen named Vimaladattā.
Thereafter, he had two sons: the first was named Vimalagarbha (Li-gou-zang) and the second was named Vimalanetra (Li-gou-mu).

Furthermore, these two sons both attained supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), being able to fly with effortless levity; they were fully endowed with wisdom and possessed every merit. Their noble realization was sublime, and they practiced the deeds of a bodhisattva with diligence day and night, never becoming weary or negligent. With a diligent and focused mind, they applied themselves to the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*); through the four immeasurables (*catvāry apramāṇāni*) and skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), those they saved were limitless. They all followed and mastered the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipākṣika-dharmāḥ*), universally expounding the meaning of the Way and circulating its practice, until they advanced to attain the *Vimala-samādhi*.

He attained thorough mastery of the *Dūṣya-āloka-samādhi*, the *Vimala-prabhāsa-samādhi*, the *Vyūha-viśuddhi-samādhi*, and the *Mahā-teja-garbha-samādhi*; these samādhis and concentrations constitute his perfection of *samādhi*.

At that time, the Buddha’s assembly—consisting of the fourfold congregation, Śakra, Brahmā, the Four Heavenly Kings, the various devas, and the people—was gathered as he proclaimed and analyzed the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
Then the Buddha, out of compassion for all sentient beings and grieving for their lands, desired to transform them all and lead them into the Great Way.
"Furthermore, noble son, those two crown princes went to their mother’s place, joined their palms, and said:

'We pray that you will deign to consider us with compassion and focus your mind and body upon this; we wish to go to the Buddha to pay homage to the Tathāgata’s person, and we also wish to bow our heads in self-refuge.'"

Why is this? Today the Tathāgata, for the sake of all sentient beings in the heavens and on earth, is extensively proclaiming the essential scripture, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*; therefore, you should come to pay him homage and listen to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
The Queen Vimaladattā said to the two princes:

"Your father the King sets his will upon external heterodoxies and places his faith and joy in the Brahmins; he constantly harbors anger and resentment. For these reasons, it is not possible for you to go."
Then the two princes, with one mind and palms joined, spoke again to their mother:
"We are of meager fortune, born into a family of perverse views and no righteousness."

Furthermore, our bodies were originally those of Dharma-princes; we ought to transform the turbid world through the Way of the sutras, turning back from falsehood toward truth—only then are we true sons of the Buddha.
Thereupon, Queen Vimaladattā addressed her two princes:
"Excellent, go forth! You are truly filial sons;

for the sake of your parents, you have cultivated great compassion. Each of you has manifested your supernormal powers so that they may behold you with joy and their minds be opened to understanding. I now grant you permission to go together to the presence of the Buddha to prostrate yourselves and receive his teachings."

Then the two crown princes, having immediately received their mother’s instruction, leaped into the air and remained suspended seven fathoms above the ground; out of compassion for their kin, they each manifested miraculous transformations.

Remaining in the void, the two men simultaneously sat, lay down, and walked; fire issued from their upper bodies while water issued from their lower bodies, and water issued from their upper bodies while fire issued from their lower bodies. They emitted a great radiance that illuminated both the distant and the near; they manifested their bodies as vast and large, then again made them small; they descended from the void and entered into the earth, or if a person were in the water, they would leap forth from the earth, remaining in the void as if treading upon solid ground.
The two princes manifested various transformations to display their supernormal powers (*ṛddhipāda*), thereby instructing and transforming their parents.

At that time, the father king, beholding his two sons’ supernormal transformations and majestic virtue (*vibhūti*) such as this, was filled with joy and leaped for gladness; a wholesome mind arose within him, and he personally joined his palms toward the two sons, saying:
"Whom do you serve as your masters?"
At that time, the two crown princes addressed their father, the king, saying:

"Great King, if you wish to know who our teacher is, it is the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Sarvarūpasaṃdarśana-ghoṣeśvararāja, who is our teacher. He is currently traveling and staying beneath a jewel tree, seated upon the Dharma throne, extensively expounding and proclaiming the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* for the fourfold assembly, the devas, and the people."
"That Buddha, the World-Honored One, is my teacher and master.
The King said to his two sons:
"I wish to go to your teacher and master to pay my respects and personally receive the sublime, true, and unsurpassed teachings of the Great Sage."
Then the two sons descended from the void to their mother’s side and, with palms joined, addressed her:

"Mother, through your majestic virtue, you have transformed our father the king, causing him to establish a mind set upon the unsurpassed, true, and correct [enlightenment], thereby accomplishing the karma of a Holy Honored One of the Way. We pray that you will look upon us with compassion and grant us permission to go to the Buddha, leave the household life to practice the Way, and become śramaṇas."
Then the two crown princes spoke this verse to their mother:
“Mother, please listen to us: we shall leave the home life to become śramaṇas.
A Tathāgata is extremely difficult to encounter; while there is still time, we must study with diligence.”
"What is called 'difficult to encounter' is like the auspicious *ariṣṭa* flower;
even more difficult than that to meet is the attainment of tranquil seclusion.
At that time, the Queen Mother Vimaladattā addressed her with these verses:
“I grant you my permission; well done, sons, depart!
A Most Holy One is extremely difficult to encounter; I too shall go forth together with you.”
At that time, the two princes, having praised these Dharma verses in response to their parents, again addressed their father, the king, and their biological mother:

"We pray that you two parents, with one mind and at the same time, shall go together to the abode of the Buddha Universal Water Thunder-Sound Constellation Flower Wisdom King; may you deign to visit him simultaneously, pay homage, and take refuge in that World-Honored One."

Why is this? Your two parents should know that the appearance of a Buddha is difficult to encounter, like the auspicious *utpala* flower, or like the supreme wish-fulfilling jewel; so too is it with a Buddha—he cannot be encountered again. Therefore, we have been born in this land, and our hearts resolve that the merit of renouncing the household life is foremost.
"For this reason, there should be no objection; you may grant your consent.
He replied, "Excellent!"
They leave the household life to study, casting aside craving and abandoning their worldly occupations.

Why is this? Because when one beholds the immeasurable blessings and auspiciousness of the Tathāgata, human life is difficult to obtain and the appearance of a Buddha in the world is rare to encounter; having escaped the eight difficulties and attained leisure and tranquility is as hard as being born again after death.
The father king and queen replied to the prince, saying:
"Yes! You should know that now is the time."
The Buddha said:
"Son of good family!

At that time, within the palace of King Viśuddha-viśuddha, there were eighty-four thousand court ladies and handmaidens who, by virtue of the roots of merit from their past lives, were destined to receive and uphold this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* Sūtra; they were originally vessels for the Way."
Prince Vimalanetra had, in his past lives, fundamentally practiced and accumulated merit and virtue for an infinite duration.
